```html
<p style="padding:0 5vw"><label for="help-used">Assistance used (change this when using hints or supplied work): </label><input id="help-used" value="none"></p><div class="layout"><nav aria-label="Course units"><a href="#unit-01">01 — Decide which version exists for a reader</a><a href="#unit-02">02 — Publish concurrent transactions atomically</a><a href="#unit-03">03 — Distinguish isolation from an application invariant</a><a href="#unit-04">04 — Validate what a transaction depended on</a><a href="#unit-05">05 — Keep index candidates correct across time</a><a href="#unit-06">06 — Reclaim history without changing a live view</a><a href="#unit-07">07 — Explain a plan in the presence of old snapshots</a><a href="#unit-08">08 — Break and repair the concurrent database</a><a href="#unit-09">09 — Transfer to a protected export under churn</a><a href="#policy">Bounded policy checker</a><a href="#history">Your saved attempts</a></nav><main><section id="unit-01" class="lesson"><h1>01 — Decide which version exists for a reader</h1>
<p>A booking reader pauses while another client updates the equipment table. Implement the policy that keeps the paused reader&#x27;s view stable when it resumes.</p>
<p>Your project increment is <code>visibleVersion</code>. The supplied engine already stores immutable committed histories and each transaction&#x27;s private writes. You decide which committed version exists for one snapshot. Read the <a href="CONTRACTS.md">method contract</a> before editing.</p>
<h2>01.1 Read time and commit time</h2>
<p>A commit sequence number, or CSN, names a published write transaction. A snapshot is the largest published CSN included in a reader&#x27;s view. These are logical counters; elapsed time is irrelevant. A row can physically have a version at CSN 7 while a reader whose snapshot is 6 must still use its earlier version.</p>
<p>Commit a prediction before running the example: <code>node lab.mjs question 01a</code>. Record it using <code>node lab.mjs answer work 01a &#x27;YOUR_JSON&#x27; --help-used none</code>.</p>
<p>Consider a different row with versions <code>(CSN 3, value 14)</code> and <code>(CSN 8, value 22)</code>. A reader at snapshot 5 sees 14: 3 belongs to its view and 8 does not. At snapshot 8, the second version becomes visible. The equality boundary matters. A check using strictly less than the snapshot would hide a commit that was already included when the reader began.</p>
<p>Completion case: for versions at 1, 6 and 9, identify the qualifying prefix for snapshot 6 before choosing its final member. Then implement this decision for arbitrary ascending histories. An empty qualifying set returns <code>null</code>. The returned object is the version, not only its row payload.</p>
<h2>01.2 Visibility, deletion and own writes</h2>
<p>A tombstone is a version whose row is <code>null</code>. It records absence from that commit onward. Once it is the newest version in the reader&#x27;s view, searching backward for a non-null row is wrong: that would resurrect an earlier value. A later reinsertion is another version with a new CSN; it does not erase the interval of absence.</p>
<p>Use <code>question 01b</code> and record your response before looking at its feedback. Explain to yourself whether the newest qualifying version or the newest qualifying <em>non-deleted</em> version is the rule you are implementing.</p>
<p>The shell handles a transaction&#x27;s own private writes before it calls your method. If a client stages a new booking value, that client can read it immediately, while another client still sees committed history. A private deletion similarly means absence for its owner. This overlay is supplied so the exercise stays about historical visibility. Do not scan or mutate another transaction&#x27;s private write map.</p>
<h2>01.3 One query, one pinned view</h2>
<p>A scan can pause between rows. Its next call must use the same snapshot, even if new commits now exist. The supplied query handle retains the transaction&#x27;s view until exhaustion, close, abort or error. The later reclamation unit will make that lifetime important.</p>
<p>The query conditions are also fixed when the scan opens. The shell owns a deep copy of the predicate; changing the original object, even a nested range bound, does not change a paused scan. A different predicate requires a new scan.</p>
<p>Commit <code>01c</code>. Then implement <code>visibleVersion(history, snapshot, examine)</code> in <strong><code>work/engine.mjs</code></strong>, inside the class returned by <code>buildEngine(BaseEngine)</code>. <code>starter/engine.mjs</code> is the unchanged reset template. The caller is <code>BaseEngine.view</code> in <code>runtime/base.mjs</code>: it checks private writes first, calls your method, then detaches the returned row. <code>checks.mjs</code> contains the public unit-01 requirements; <code>check-runner.mjs</code> loads your saved attempt.</p>
<p>If a blank method is too large a step, replace only <code>visibleVersion</code> with this bounded scaffold. It executes but deliberately throws until you finish it. Type it or copy it, and declare that assistance. Keep every other method and the <code>buildEngine</code> wrapper for later units.</p>
<pre><code>visibleVersion(history, snapshot, examine = () =&gt; {}) {
  let chosen = null;
  for (const version of history) {
    examine(version);
    // TODO: decide whether this version replaces chosen.
  }
  // TODO: return the chosen version, or null if none qualifies.
  throw new Error(&#x27;Unfinished: choose a version for this snapshot.&#x27;);
}</code></pre>
<p><code>history</code> is ascending, so a forward traversal can keep one candidate. Decide the comparison, including equality, and whether <code>row: null</code> changes that decision. This scaffold scans the whole history; you may choose another correct traversal and compare its examination count later. Call the supplied <code>examine(version)</code> callback whenever you inspect a version; this produces a trace for later cost comparisons. You may traverse backward, scan forward, or use another correct strategy. Do not reorder or mutate the history.</p>
<p>Run <code>node lab.mjs check work 01 --help-used none</code>. Read each failed requirement and its observed value. The public checker tests exact boundaries, tombstones, absence, detached results and the supplied private overlay. It is normal for one scaffold-only case to pass before your visibility method exists; that does not complete the unit.</p>
<h2>01.4 Run a snapshot experiment</h2>
<p>Before running, write your prediction for each observation below. The probe uses your actual <code>visibleVersion</code> method, with an insertion at CSN 3 (value 14), deletion at 8, and reinsertion at 9 (value 22). An old reader keeps snapshot 3 as those later versions appear. Fresh readers choose snapshots 8 and 9. Predict the returned <strong>version CSN and row value</strong> for <code>before-insert</code>, <code>old-before-delete</code>, <code>old-after-delete</code>, <code>fresh-after-delete</code>, <code>old-after-reinsert</code>, and <code>fresh-after-reinsert</code>. Distinguish no qualifying version from a qualifying tombstone.</p>
<pre><code>node lab.mjs probe work --help-used &quot;unit 01 scaffold&quot; --prediction &quot;REPLACE with your six predictions and why the old reader should stay stable&quot;</code></pre>
<p>Use your actual assistance declaration, including other people or tools. The command saves your prediction and exact source before execution in a new <code>work/attempts/probe-*</code> directory, then writes <code>report.json</code> there. It prints version CSNs, row values and examined CSNs, without grading your prediction. A thrown unfinished-method error is saved there too; finish the method and rerun into a new attempt.</p>
<p>The executable probe lives in <code>snapshot-probe.mjs</code>. Its observation helper is shown exactly below: it preserves a tombstone as <code>{csn: 8, value: null}</code>, while no qualifying version becomes <code>null</code>.</p>
<pre><code>function observe(policy, label, history, snapshot) {
  const examined = [];
  const version = policy.visibleVersion(history, snapshot, v =&gt; examined.push(v.csn));
  return {
    label, snapshot,
    version: version === null ? null : { csn: version.csn, value: version.row?.value ?? null },
    examined
  };
}</code></pre>
<p>Compare the six observations with your saved prediction. If the old reader changes after deletion or reinsertion, identify the comparison that let a future version through. If a fresh reader at 8 sees 14, check whether your search wrongly skipped a tombstone. If a boundary disappears, revisit equality. Examination lists depend on your traversal; do not copy a particular count as the answer.</p>
<p>This is a <strong>pure-policy experiment</strong>: immutable history prefixes simulate publication, and a number represents the pinned reader. It does not execute a writer, a paused query handle, persistence or your unfinished <code>commitTransaction</code>. Unit 02 supplies that next step; passing the probe is not a full engine pass.</p>
<p>For transfer, change the CSNs, values and snapshots in a copy of <code>snapshot-probe.mjs</code> saved in your <code>work</code> directory, predict at least one snapshot between commits, and run that copy against your engine. You can append this entry point to your copy and run <code>node work/my-probe.mjs</code>:</p>
<pre><code>import { buildEngine } from &#x27;./engine.mjs&#x27;;
console.log(JSON.stringify(probeSnapshots(buildEngine), null, 2));</code></pre>
<p>Record the changed probe, prediction, assistance and output with your notes. Keep your implementation and continue to <a href="#unit-02">02</a>; checks there include unit 01 again. Navigation is not gated.</p>
<div class="questions" data-unit="01"></div></section><section id="unit-02" class="lesson"><h1>02 — Publish concurrent transactions atomically</h1>
<p>A transaction changes two equipment records, but a reader must never see only half the change. Implement the commit ordering that turns one private write set into one acknowledged database state.</p>
<p>Keep your visibility method. You now own <code>commitTransaction</code>; the shell supplies the accepted durable batch store and the narrow helpers in <a href="CONTRACTS.md">the contract</a>. This unit&#x27;s tests use a declared validation-free stage with independent writes. Same-key concurrency is the next unit, so do not call this stage Snapshot Isolation yet.</p>
<h2>02.1 Private writes and transaction states</h2>
<p>An active transaction holds proposed writes in its own map. Staging a write is not a commit: other clients cannot read it. A successful transaction becomes committed; a rejected one becomes aborted. Once terminal, its handle cannot read or write again. Repeating a commit must not apply its operations twice.</p>
<p>Work through <code>02c</code>: a read-only completion changes state without creating a row version. In your method, account for that case separately from a write batch. The supplied <code>finish</code> helper closes handles and clears private data only when you have chosen the outcome.</p>
<p>A query in the same transaction freezes the private overlay while it is open. The shell therefore refuses commit or new private writes until that query closes. This is a bounded API rule, not a universal property of databases.</p>
<h2>02.2 Validate, persist and publish</h2>
<p>There are three distinct boundaries. Preparation constructs a proposed complete update and can reject resource limits without writing. Persistence submits that update as one batch to the supplied engine. Publication makes the new logical history and CSN available to subsequent transactions. Client acknowledgement follows those effects.</p>
<p>Commit <code>02a</code> before implementing the order. As a sibling example, imagine publishing a replacement directory listing: calculating a new list does not make it visible, writing its bytes does not mean the application has switched to it, and sending success too early can claim a state that never became durable. The database has the same need to distinguish phases, although its supplied batch operation handles the bytes.</p>
<p>Use <code>this.conflicts(tx)</code> before effects. This helper is empty in the unit-02 stage and will call your conflict policies in later stages. Obtain a prepared update once, persist that exact update, then publish that exact update. The synchronous publication section does not yield to another client. A new reader starts with either the old CSN or the fully published new CSN.</p>
<h2>02.3 Acknowledgement and uncertain outcomes</h2>
<p>Commit <code>02b</code>. A process can stop after a batch became durable but before its client hears success. Neither “definitely committed” nor “definitely absent” follows from the lost acknowledgement alone. Reopening the supplied store can recover the whole batch. Retrying an arbitrary write as if it failed could duplicate an effect.</p>
<p>The shell&#x27;s <code>indeterminate</code> helper poisons the coordinator after a persistence/publication failure. Existing state is no longer safe to serve until reopen. This preserves uncertainty rather than inventing an abort. The course inherits a process-interruption model; it does not establish power-loss safety or a distributed exactly-once protocol.</p>
<p>Implement the method and run <code>node lab.mjs check work 02 --help-used none</code>. Inspect the recorded phase trace when the ordering check fails. The tests also stop after durable acknowledgement, reopen a fresh engine, and check both rows. They do not ask you to rewrite the WAL or interpret its byte frames.</p>
<p>Fresh application: identify which outcomes are possible if a stop happens immediately before persistence, after durability, and after publication. State what the client knows separately from what recovery might find. Continue to <a href="#unit-03">03</a> to decide when overlapping writes may commit.</p><div class="questions" data-unit="02"></div></section><section id="unit-03" class="lesson"><h1>03 — Distinguish isolation from an application invariant</h1>
<p>Two clients reserve the same equipment slot from the same old view. Implement write-conflict validation, then identify the kind of anomaly that it still permits.</p>
<p>Your increment is <code>writeConflicts</code>. The commit method from unit 02 calls it through the supplied validation dispatcher. Unit 03 and later turn that policy on.</p>
<h2>03.1 Statement snapshots and transaction snapshots</h2>
<p>A statement-snapshot reader can observe one committed state in its first query and a newer committed state in its second. A transaction-snapshot reader keeps the same committed view across its reads. Neither should read another transaction&#x27;s uncommitted private values.</p>
<p>Our learner engine uses one transaction snapshot. The current slice does not implement a full Read Committed write mode. Treat that comparison as a distinction in allowed observations, not a promise of compatibility with another database&#x27;s locking rules.</p>
<p>Before coding, commit <code>03a</code>. Let A and B begin at snapshot 12. If both stage key 6 and A publishes at 13, B&#x27;s starting view no longer includes the latest write to key 6. Publishing B unconditionally would hide A&#x27;s change. A conflict is about that timeline, not whether the final row happens to equal an earlier value.</p>
<h2>03.2 Same-key conflicts and first committer</h2>
<p>Snapshot Isolation keeps a stable view and refuses a writer whose target key changed after its snapshot. The comparison is strict here: a latest write at the snapshot is already included; a latest write after it is a conflict. Check every distinct key in the private write map. Missing history means no previous committed write, not a special exemption from future insert races.</p>
<p>Deletes matter. A tombstone carries a CSN and can conflict with a stale insertion or update. A change followed by a restoration also matters. Commit <code>03c</code>, then verify that your decision uses write occurrence rather than comparing endpoint row values.</p>
<p>The checker includes independent writers. If A writes key 1 and B writes key 2 without a dependency that this mode validates, both must be able to finish. Aborting every overlap avoids one race by destroying the intended behavior. Holding a global lock for each entire transaction would similarly evade the exercise.</p>
<h2>03.3 Write skew without a dirty read</h2>
<p>Now consider two equipment records whose combined availability must remain above a threshold. Each client reads both from the same valid old snapshot, then changes a different record. No same-key conflict is necessary, yet the combined result may violate the condition. This is write skew.</p>
<p>Commit <code>03b</code>. Stable snapshots answer “what did each transaction read?” They do not by themselves answer “could all successful transactions have run one at a time with those observations?” That second question is the motivation for the next unit&#x27;s dependency validation.</p>
<p>Implement <code>writeConflicts</code> and run <code>node lab.mjs check work 03 --help-used none</code>. Do not change the supplied private-map or disk code to make one fixture pass. Return a description for every conflicting key. Descriptions may use any clear shape and appear in any order; the checker does not require a particular witness format.</p>
<p>Fresh application: create an initially absent key. Let two clients both stage it, commit one, then attempt the other. Explain why an insert needs the same conflict rule as an update. Preserve both successful and rejected outcomes when you later write a schedule file.</p><div class="questions" data-unit="03"></div></section><section id="unit-04" class="lesson"><h1>04 — Validate what a transaction depended on</h1>
<p>A client checks that no booking exists, then another client creates one before it commits. Implement validation that includes the information in an empty result.</p>
<p>Your increment is <code>readConflicts</code>. The shell records point and predicate reads independently from how they are executed. You compare those logical dependencies with committed changes after the transaction&#x27;s snapshot.</p>
<h2>04.1 Point reads include absence</h2>
<p>A read does not stop being information because it returns no row. An absent key can determine which branch of a transaction runs. If another transaction inserts that key, the earlier branch may no longer be compatible with placing the reader after that write.</p>
<p>Commit <code>04a</code>. In this course&#x27;s conservative Serializable mode, every point dependency includes the key identity, regardless of whether it returned a row. A later change to that key intersects the dependency. The relevant question is whether the change committed after the reader&#x27;s snapshot, not whether a row happened to be returned earlier.</p>
<p>As a completion case, draw a timeline with a reader at 4, an insertion at 5, and the reader&#x27;s validation afterward. Mark where the reader would need to be placed if its absence observation were still true. Our mode chooses commit-order validation, so it rejects the reader rather than silently choosing another serialization order.</p>
<h2>04.2 Predicate reads include gaps</h2>
<p>A query such as <code>20 &lt;= value &lt; 30</code> reads a set defined by a predicate. Recording only the returned keys misses a new matching key. It also misses the dependency of an empty result. Record the predicate domain, then test relevant changes against it.</p>
<p>A change contains a before-image and an after-image. An insertion can enter the set. A deletion can leave it. An update can do either, both, or neither. Commit <code>04b</code> before choosing which images to test. <code>BaseEngine.matches</code> is the supplied typed evaluator; a null image does not match.</p>
<p>The recorded predicate must be the one the query actually executes. At scan creation the supplied shell captures one deep copy and uses it for both iteration and dependency recording. If a caller opens a query for A and later changes its original predicate object to B, the open query still asks for A. Recording A while executing B would make correct conflict validation miss a real dependency. That would be a shell defect, not an error you could repair by changing <code>readConflicts</code>.</p>
<p>The upper bound is exclusive. A change entirely outside the predicate should not create a conflict in the precise single-table case. This positive control matters: an implementation that always reports a conflict is safe only in the trivial sense that it prevents useful work.</p>
<h2>04.3 Serializable validation and whole-transaction retry</h2>
<p>At commit, first apply your same-key write policy, then the read-dependency policy when the database mode is Serializable. The current commit section is synchronous, so another client cannot slip a new published change between validation and publication. The earlier private work remains concurrent.</p>
<p>Ordinary Serializable transactions validate even when they happen to perform no writes. A read result used inside such a transaction is not a successful committed outcome until validation succeeds. A separate <code>begin({readOnly:true})</code> declaration prohibits every staged write and can serialize at its pinned snapshot instead. That narrow route supports a long export while writers proceed; it must not be applied to a transaction that might write later. This is an explicit teaching contract, not PostgreSQL&#x27;s implementation.</p>
<p>Commit <code>04c</code>. A conflict retry needs a new transaction and snapshot, followed by repeated reads and decisions. Calling commit again on the terminal old handle cannot repair an old branch decision. This slice exposes aborts but does not yet supply an automatic retry scheduler; a client can explicitly start and recompute its transaction.</p>
<p>Implement <code>readConflicts</code> and run <code>node lab.mjs check work 04 --help-used none</code>. The suite compares the same disjoint-write pattern under SI and Serializable, then checks absence, an empty range, a leaving update, the upper endpoint and a value-change-then-revert. Keep the SI anomaly: eliminating it by silently making both modes identical would hide the distinction being taught.</p>
<p>For a fresh case, use a predicate that is initially nonempty, then consider one outside-to-inside and one inside-to-outside update. Explain why both matter even though their final row counts may cancel. Continue to <a href="#unit-05">05</a> for the same logical query through an index.</p><div class="questions" data-unit="04"></div></section><section id="unit-05" class="lesson"><h1>05 — Keep index candidates correct across time</h1>
<p>An equipment record moves from group A to B while an older reader still needs to find it in A. Implement historical index membership without changing the query&#x27;s snapshot meaning.</p>
<p>Your increment is <code>indexMemberships(history, field)</code>. In this slice the shell materializes candidate maps and rebuilds enabled maps before publishing changes; an incremental ordered index is not implemented. The policy you build establishes the historical coverage that such an index must preserve.</p>
<h2>05.1 Candidate membership and visible truth</h2>
<p>An index candidate means “this key may match,” not “return this row without checking.” The shell first finds candidate identities, then asks your visibility method for the version in the reader&#x27;s view, and finally evaluates the predicate. This separates an index&#x27;s search role from the database&#x27;s visibility rule.</p>
<p>Candidate selection and the final filter use the same predicate captured when the scan opened. Otherwise a caller could change the filter after candidates were chosen and silently lose rows. The supplied shell preserves this boundary for both index and full-scan access.</p>
<p>Commit <code>05a</code>. In a sibling example, a row has historical locations East and West. Both memberships can be necessary while two snapshots remain active. The current row alone cannot answer every old reader. A candidate that proves invisible can be discarded; a needed row omitted from the candidate set cannot be recovered by a later filter.</p>
<p>Use typed value keys if you deduplicate membership. JavaScript object-property coercion can conflate values, and null must remain a deliberate value for <code>isNull</code>. The shell supplies <code>BaseEngine.valueKey</code> for this bookkeeping.</p>
<h2>05.2 Updates that move between index keys</h2>
<p>Commit <code>05b</code>. Several historical versions of one key do not become several logical rows in a single-table result. Conversely, two different keys sharing one indexed value must remain two rows. Candidate de-duplication and relational duplicate removal are different operations.</p>
<p>A tombstone has no indexed row fields. A reinserted row can add a new historical value without erasing an earlier one still needed by a snapshot. Uncommitted private writes are not added to shared committed history; the shell merges the owning transaction&#x27;s private candidates separately. Abort must not expose them to another client.</p>
<p>The future retention policy will decide which committed versions can disappear. Your index membership should be based on the retained history it receives, so cleanup and index coverage remain connected.</p>
<h2>05.3 Logical dependencies survive a faster access path</h2>
<p>Commit <code>05c</code>. Serializable validation is about what the query depended on, not which candidates a particular physical path happened to inspect. A query returning nothing can still depend on a gap. The shell records the predicate before selecting scan or index access; your membership method must not alter that record.</p>
<p>Implement the method and run <code>node lab.mjs check work 05 --help-used none</code>. The checks compare full scans and indexed scans under old and new snapshots, repeated membership, private aborts and reopen. They also insert into a predicate that an earlier index read found empty.</p>
<p>For a fresh test, make one key move A → B → A and give another key the same group. Keep a reader alive between the first two moves. Predict both readers&#x27; results before running either access path. A correct result must preserve the distinct keys while returning each key once.</p>
<p>There is no speed claim from passing this unit. Recomputing memberships scans history and can be expensive. The later planning work must measure that overhead honestly before comparing this prototype with a maintained index.</p><div class="questions" data-unit="05"></div></section><section id="unit-06" class="lesson"><h1>06 — Reclaim history without changing a live view</h1>
<p>A long reader keeps an old equipment view alive while writers accumulate versions. Implement the retention boundary that permits cleanup without invalidating that reader.</p>
<p>Your increment is <code>retainedVersions(history, watermark)</code>. The shell supplies the active transaction registry, persists version deletions, and records logical removals. You decide which versions must remain.</p>
<h2>06.1 Reader lifetimes and the low-water mark</h2>
<p>The watermark is the smallest snapshot still needed by an active transaction. Every active handle counts, including one that has not read yet. A future first read from that handle is entitled to its original view. A paused query also keeps its transaction&#x27;s snapshot alive.</p>
<p>Commit <code>06b</code>. Releasing a query handle is different from ending its transaction: the transaction can still issue another query. Exhaustion, close, cancellation and an exception release the query reference. Commit or abort ends the transaction&#x27;s pin. A cleanup policy must use these explicit lifetimes rather than guessing from inactivity.</p>
<p>The current shell does not silently time out old readers. Under pressure it can refuse a new write. This is preferable to changing an existing reader&#x27;s contract behind its back.</p>
<h2>06.2 Retain the boundary version</h2>
<p>Commit <code>06a</code>. The watermark can lie between versions. An old reader needs the newest version at or before its snapshot, which may have been written long before the watermark. Retaining only newer versions loses that predecessor.</p>
<p>For a different example, use versions at 1, 5, 13 and a watermark of 9. The version at 5 is still needed; 13 is needed by newer readers or the current view. The version at 1 can disappear under this simple global-watermark policy. If the boundary at 5 is a tombstone, retain it: absence can be the correct old view.</p>
<p>When no transactions remain, the shell uses the current CSN as the watermark. The policy should then make progress toward one latest version per key. This slice retains even a latest tombstone rather than trying to remove its key metadata. A precise per-snapshot policy could retain fewer intermediate versions, but it must preserve all live observations.</p>
<h2>06.3 Bounded cleanup and honest measurements</h2>
<p>Commit <code>06c</code>. Removing a version from the logical database does not prove the append-log file shrank. The accepted store records deletion as another operation; its own compaction is the separate mechanism that replaces the physical log. Process memory and physical disk size are separate measurements too.</p>
<p>The shell keeps a committed-change journal for Serializable validation. A row version becoming reclaimable does not automatically make every change record irrelevant. Changes after the oldest active snapshot remain available until the dependent transactions finish.</p>
<p>Implement retention and run <code>node lab.mjs check work 06 --help-used none</code>. The cumulative suite tests an idle pin, a paused iterator, a tombstone boundary, validation evidence, safe refusal at a small version limit and fresh reopen after cleanup. Keeping every version forever fails the progress control.</p>
<p>For a fresh investigation, hold one old transaction while repeatedly updating one key. Record retained-version count before cleanup, after cleanup with the pin, and after closing the pin and cleaning again. Explain the change using the actual boundary version. Carry this recorded investigation into the next unit: its retained history will become measured physical work in a query-plan comparison.</p><div class="questions" data-unit="06"></div></section><section id="unit-07" class="lesson"><h1>07 — Explain a plan in the presence of old snapshots</h1>
<p>A query returns one matching group, but finding that group may require examining many retained versions. Implement statistics and cost estimates that separate visible rows from physical work.</p>
<p>Your two increments are <code>summarizeSnapshot</code> and <code>planEqualityJoin</code>. The shell supplies three physical operators and an equality-join query interface. You do not build a SQL parser, optimizer search, hash table library or distributed worker system.</p>
<h2>07.1 Visible cardinality and stale statistics</h2>
<p><code>analyze</code> measures one declared read-only view. Its rows belong to a specific snapshot. Its metadata also identifies the current physical CSN, number of physical keys, measured version examinations, and the number of historical candidate keys under each indexed value. Your summary adds visible row count and value frequencies without changing that metadata.</p>
<p>Commit <code>07a</code>. Two snapshots can have the same number of visible rows but require different work to find them. An old reader may pass over several newer versions before reaching its own. A frequency table describes which visible values exist; it does not by itself describe that search cost.</p>
<p>The current prototype collects exact bounded frequencies rather than sampling or a compact histogram. Statistics can still become stale when new versions accumulate or cleanup removes old versions. The persisted physical revision distinguishes those changes from the logical snapshot: vacuum can change physical work without publishing a new logical value. <code>explain</code> reports that staleness; it does not secretly change the query&#x27;s snapshot. A stale estimate may choose poorly while execution remains correct.</p>
<h2>07.2 Index probes, version checks and join alternatives</h2>
<p>The supported query filters the left table on one value and equijoins that field to a second table. <code>scan-loop</code> scans the left input, then scans the right for each matching left row. <code>scan-hash</code> scans each input once and builds/probes a supplied hash table. <code>index-loop</code> uses historical candidate indexes on both sides.</p>
<p>The contract names every work component. Candidate visits and predicate checks are charged once per visited candidate. Estimate version examinations from each side&#x27;s measured mean per physical key, rounding each side upward. Hash build/probe and emitted pairs have their own charges. Left and right visible value frequencies estimate joined-pair multiplicity. For an equality value of null, there are no matching rows.</p>
<p>Commit <code>07b</code>. A narrow match can favor index loops; many matches can make repeated right-side probes more expensive than one hash build. The point is not that one operator is always better. It is that a declared cost assumption makes a testable prediction.</p>
<p>Indexes are built before a controlled comparison and maintained by rebuilding their candidate maps at publication. Setup and maintenance appear as separate <code>index-build</code> events. Do not describe a warm query comparison as total end-to-end savings without accounting for those events.</p>
<h2>07.3 Predicted cost versus observed work</h2>
<p>Commit <code>07c</code>, then implement both methods using <a href="CONTRACTS.md">the detailed interface</a>. <code>planEqualityJoin</code> returns all three estimates plus the selected candidate ID. Every candidate includes its work vector, estimated output rows and weighted cost. Any tied minimum is accepted. No candidate execution is allowed while planning.</p>
<p>Run <code>node lab.mjs check work 07 --help-used none</code>. The checks compare all plans&#x27; actual row bags, exercise selective and many-match cases, validate snapshot identities, test null and detect planning that changes measured work. They also retain logical read dependencies independently from the chosen physical operator.</p>
<p>For a fresh experiment, keep one read-only snapshot open while adding versions of indexed rows. Collect new statistics for that old snapshot, compare its estimates with actual counters, then close it and vacuum. Explain separately what changed in the logical view and in the physical work. Work units are not milliseconds, disk-page reads or a production-performance promise.</p><div class="questions" data-unit="07"></div></section><section id="unit-08" class="lesson"><h1>08 — Break and repair the concurrent database</h1>
<p>A result is wrong only when it contradicts a specific contract under a recorded execution. Build an investigation that reproduces a snapshot defect, repairs it and survives a changed schedule.</p>
<p>This unit supplies the run recorder and evidence checker. You author the scenario, preserve a faulty version of your policy code, repair it, and explain the causal difference. The instructor&#x27;s reference and calibration scenarios are not in this packet.</p>
<h2>08.1 Record a discriminating schedule</h2>
<p>Commit <code>08a</code>. Begin with a scenario that contains an old reader, a concurrent writer and a later read from the old transaction. Add an indexed read, cleanup while a pin remains, cleanup after all pins close, and a within-snapshot plan comparison. Use the operations and schema format in <a href="PROJECTS.md">the project contract</a>.</p>
<p>Record your prediction before execution with <code>--prediction</code>. Run directories contain exact engine source, scenario, result, runtime identity and hashes. Put scenarios, runs and your investigation JSON inside your project directory so export carries them together. Treat one successful run as an observation rather than a general guarantee.</p>
<p>Your broken source must complete the scenario but violate a snapshot result. You can preserve a naturally occurring bug or deliberately evaluate a labeled wrong implementation. A syntax error, hang or missing method is not the semantic failure this project asks you to diagnose.</p>
<p>The supplied <code>minimize</code> command can shrink a recorded failing run before you explain it. It preserves the first snapshot mismatch, exact saved policy and input order while trying to remove whole transactions, actions and initial versions. Read its <code>show-witness</code> trace: which removals left the same observation wrong, and which changes were rejected? A smaller reproducer is useful evidence, but neither a budget-limited result nor local irreducibility proves a globally minimal cause. The project contract links the exact command and limits.</p>
<h2>08.2 Connect wrong results to one violated invariant</h2>
<p>Commit <code>08b</code>. The evidence checker builds a simple copied-map snapshot model, separate from your version selection and index code. It compares logical point reads, scans, query pulls and joined row bags against that model. It requires an actual mismatch in the broken run and none in the repaired run.</p>
<p>Use exactly the same scenario bytes for the broken and repaired runs. Otherwise a changed workload could explain the changed outcome. Keep the failed source and result. Describe the relevant transaction, snapshot, version and operation ordering; avoid an explanation that only says a test became green.</p>
<p>The repaired source must also pass all seven component milestones. A repair that avoids one scenario by aborting every writer or retaining every version is insufficient. The component controls deliberately preserve useful independent work and reclamation progress.</p>
<h2>08.3 Replay the repair and its costs</h2>
<p>Commit <code>08c</code>. Create a second scenario with a changed transaction/read/write/cleanup structure, not only different names or numbers. Run it with the exact repaired source. The checker rejects a mere added <code>inspect</code> action as structural variation.</p>
<p>Write your investigation descriptor and run <code>node lab.mjs assess work work/investigation.json --help-used none</code>. It reruns the saved programs and scenarios, verifies byte identities, checks the independent snapshot observations and recomputes the costs cited in your report. Include at least one predicted cost and one observed cost; the checker rejects invented numeric observations.</p>
<p>The resulting <code>engineeringPassed</code> value covers those explicit checks. Your diagnosis still needs to satisfy the published causal rubric: identify the violated rule, explain why the schedule exposed it, describe why the repair preserves other valid histories, and distinguish estimate error from result error. Neither a nonempty explanation nor the automated flag establishes independent course acceptance.</p><div class="questions" data-unit="08"></div></section><section id="unit-09" class="lesson"><h1>09 — Transfer to a protected export under churn</h1>
<p>An archive export needs a stable old catalog while another client places a hold and a purge is being considered. Design the transactions and schedule that preserve both the export view and the hold dependency.</p>
<p>You receive a schema, an invariant and observable acceptance criteria in <a href="PROJECTS.md">the project contract</a>. There is no completed scenario or client for this unit. Use the same engine you built, not a second special-purpose database.</p>
<h2>09.1 Translate the new invariant and workload</h2>
<p>The archive has <code>items</code>, <code>collections</code> and <code>holds</code>. A purge reads the relevant holds predicate before staging item deletions. A concurrent hold changes the premise on which that purge depends. The invariant concerns that dependency, not whether a particular primary key had two writers.</p>
<p>Commit <code>09a</code>. Build one scenario and run it under Snapshot Isolation and Serializable mode with identical source and actions. The SI run must expose the unsafe purge outcome; the Serializable run must reject the purge because of a holds read dependency. Do not create an incidental same-key write conflict that would mask the missing predicate validation.</p>
<p>An explicit <code>readOnly:true</code> exporter is separate from an ordinary transaction that merely happens not to write. The declaration prohibits writes and allows the exporter to serialize at its original snapshot. It must not refresh its view to make cleanup easier.</p>
<h2>09.2 Preserve a long export while membership changes</h2>
<p>Commit <code>09b</code>. While the exporter is pinned, change an item&#x27;s collection or location through another committed transaction. Read the old view through its historical index, and keep a current observer to see the newer catalog. Both can be correct while returning different rows.</p>
<p>Vacuum before the exporter finishes and again after all pins close. Identify the history needed by the first cleanup and why more can disappear during the second. Finish the exporter successfully through the declared read-only route. An aborted or silently refreshed export does not meet this task.</p>
<p>Use plan comparisons within both the old and new views. Their results need not match across views. Each comparison must itself hold one snapshot fixed while changing only the physical plan.</p>
<h2>09.3 Defend correctness, retention and plan choice</h2>
<p>Commit <code>09c</code>. Create the transfer descriptor with your transaction-role aliases and run <code>node lab.mjs transfer work work/transfer.json --help-used none</code>. The checker verifies the same-source/mode-only comparison, the empty holds read, a committed hold, the disjoint item deletion, the different purge outcomes, the protected exporter and the snapshot observations.</p>
<p>The explanation must distinguish three claims: the old export is internally consistent; the current catalog reflects committed changes; and the purge&#x27;s dependency is validated under the stronger mode. Then explain the estimated versus measured work within each view. A changed result caused by a different snapshot is not evidence that one physical plan became faster for the same question.</p>
<p>Export your project and rerun the component checks and both project descriptors from the fresh directory. Preserve first attempts, failures, assistance and revision history. The local engineering result is a course milestone. Live Free to Learn delivery, independent review, a verified learner flow and appropriate learning evidence remain separate requirements.</p><div class="questions" data-unit="09"></div></section>

// Bounded pure-policy checks only. Full engine/persistence checks require Node.
function runPolicyChecks(module, unit) {
  class Shell { static valueKey(v) { return JSON.stringify([typeof v,v]); } }
  const Engine=module.buildEngine(Shell), engine=new Engine(), results=[];
  const equal=(a,b)=>{if(JSON.stringify(a)!==JSON.stringify(b))throw Error(`Expected ${JSON.stringify(b)}, observed ${JSON.stringify(a)}`);};
  const check=(id,fn)=>{try{fn();results.push({id,passed:true});}catch(e){results.push({id,passed:false,message:e.message});}};
  const h=[{csn:2,row:{group:'A',value:4}},{csn:5,row:null},{csn:9,row:{group:'B',value:7}}];
  if(unit==='01') {
    check('R03 boundary',()=>equal(engine.visibleVersion(h,2)?.row.value,4));
    check('R03 future exclusion',()=>equal(engine.visibleVersion(h,4)?.row.value,4));
    check('R03 deletion',()=>equal(engine.visibleVersion(h,8)?.row,null));
    check('R03 absence',()=>equal(engine.visibleVersion(h,1),null));
    check('R03 examine',()=>{const one=[h[0]], seen=[];equal(engine.visibleVersion(one,2,v=>seen.push(v))?.row.value,4);equal(seen.length>0&&seen.every(v=>one.includes(v)),true);});
  } else if(unit==='05') {
    check('R10 historical membership',()=>equal(engine.indexMemberships(h,'group').slice().sort(),['A','B']));
    check('R10 unique membership',()=>equal(engine.indexMemberships([...h,{csn:10,row:{group:'B'}}],'group').slice().sort(),['A','B']));
  } else if(unit==='06') {
    check('R11 boundary retention',()=>{const kept=engine.retainedVersions(h,8).map(v=>v.csn);equal(kept.includes(5)&&kept.includes(9),true);});
    check('R11 no-reader progress',()=>equal(engine.retainedVersions(h,9).map(v=>v.csn),[9]));
  } else if(unit==='07') {
    const weights={candidateVisits:1,versionExaminations:2,predicateEvaluations:1,hashBuild:2,hashProbe:1,outputRows:1};
    const stats=n=>({rowCount:n,physicalKeys:n,versionProbes:n,frequencies:[{value:'A',count:n}],indexCandidates:[{value:'A',count:n}]});
    check('R16 many-match crossover',()=>equal(engine.planEqualityJoin(stats(8),stats(12),'A',weights).selected,'scan-hash'));
    check('R15 visible frequencies',()=>equal(engine.summarizeSnapshot([{key:1,row:{group:'A'}}],'group',{snapshot:4}).frequencies,[{value:'A',count:1}]));
  } else throw Error('Choose a supported pure-policy unit.');
  return results;
}
```

```mjs
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { dirname, resolve, join } from 'node:path';
import { pathToFileURL } from 'node:url';
import { BaseEngine, matches, identity, copy } from './runtime/base.mjs';
import { executeScenario } from './runtime/scenario.mjs';
import { executionIdentity, sha256 } from './runtime/identity.mjs';
import { runChecks } from './checks.mjs';

const json = path => JSON.parse(readFileSync(path, 'utf8'));
const stable = value => JSON.stringify(canonical(value));
function canonical(value) {
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return value.map(canonical);
  if (value && typeof value === 'object') return Object.fromEntries(Object.keys(value).sort().map(k => [k, canonical(value[k])]));
  return value;
}

// Deliberately uses complete copied maps, not learner version selection/indexes.
export function snapshotOracle(scenario, execution) {
  const latest = new Map();
  for (const version of [...(scenario.initial ?? [])].sort((a,b) => a.csn-b.csn)) latest.set(identity(version.table, version.key), copy(version.row));
  const transactions = new Map(), queries = new Map(), mismatches = [];
  const facts = { starts: [], reads: [], deletions: [], changes: [], vacuums: [] };
  const features = { overlappingCommit: false, readAfterConcurrentCommit: false, indexedRead: false, vacuumWhilePinned: false, vacuumWithoutPins: false, planComparison: false };
  let commits = 0;
  const activeCount = () => [...transactions.values()].filter(t => t.active).length;
  const view = tx => new Map([...tx.snapshot, ...tx.writes]);
  const scan = (tx, table, p) => [...view(tx)].filter(([id,row]) => JSON.parse(id)[0] === table && matches(row,p)).map(([id,row]) => ({ key: JSON.parse(id)[1], row })).sort((a,b) => a.key-b.key);
  function expect(index, kind, expected, actual) { if (stable(expected) !== stable(actual)) mismatches.push({ index, kind, expected, actual }); }
  for (let i=0;i<execution.results.length;i++) {
    const { action:a, result:r } = execution.results[i]; const tx = transactions.get(a.tx);
    if (a.op === 'begin') { transactions.set(a.tx, { snapshot: copy(latest), writes: new Map(), active: true, start: commits }); facts.starts.push({index:i,tx:a.tx,snapshot:copy(latest)}); }
    else if (a.op === 'put' || a.op === 'delete') {
      if(a.op==='delete')facts.deletions.push({index:i,tx:a.tx,table:a.table,key:a.key,before:copy(view(tx).get(identity(a.table,a.key))??null)});
      tx.writes.set(identity(a.table,a.key), a.op==='delete'?null:copy(a.row));
    }
    else if (a.op === 'get') { expect(i,'point',view(tx).get(identity(a.table,a.key))??null,r); features.readAfterConcurrentCommit ||= commits>tx.start; }
    else if (a.op === 'scan') { const expected=scan(tx,a.table,a.predicate??{op:'true'}); expect(i,'scan',expected,r); facts.reads.push({index:i,tx:a.tx,table:a.table,predicate:a.predicate??{op:'true'},access:a.access??'scan',rows:expected,complete:true}); features.indexedRead ||= a.access==='index'; features.readAfterConcurrentCommit ||= commits>tx.start; }
    else if (a.op === 'open-scan') { const fact={index:i,tx:a.tx,table:a.table,predicate:a.predicate??{op:'true'},access:a.access??'scan',rows:[],complete:false}; facts.reads.push(fact); queries.set(a.as,{ rows:scan(tx,a.table,a.predicate??{op:'true'}), next:0, closed:false, tx:a.tx, fact }); features.indexedRead ||= a.access==='index'; }
    else if (a.op === 'pull') { const q=queries.get(a.query), expected=q.closed||q.next>=q.rows.length?{done:true}:{done:false,value:q.rows[q.next++]}; expect(i,'pull',expected,r); if(!expected.done)q.fact.rows.push(expected.value); else if(!q.closed)q.fact.complete=true; }
    else if (a.op === 'close-query') queries.get(a.query).closed=true;
    else if (a.op === 'commit') {
      features.overlappingCommit ||= activeCount()>1;
      if (r.status==='committed') { for (const [id,row] of tx.writes) { const [table,key]=JSON.parse(id); facts.changes.push({index:i,tx:a.tx,table,key,before:copy(latest.get(id)??null),row:copy(row)}); latest.set(id,copy(row)); } if(tx.writes.size)commits++; }
      tx.active=false;
    } else if (a.op === 'abort') { tx.active=false; for(const q of queries.values())if(q.tx===a.tx)q.closed=true; }
    else if (a.op === 'vacuum') { const active=[...transactions].filter(([,t])=>t.active).map(([name])=>name); facts.vacuums.push({index:i,active,removed:r.removed}); features.vacuumWhilePinned ||= activeCount()>0; features.vacuumWithoutPins ||= activeCount()===0; }
    else if (a.op === 'compare-plans') {
      features.planComparison=true; const q=a.query, left=scan(tx,q.left,{op:'eq',field:q.field,value:q.value}), right=scan(tx,q.right,{op:'true'}), expected=[];
      for(const l of left)for(const rr of right)if(l.row[q.field]!==null&&l.row[q.field]===rr.row[q.field])expected.push({leftKey:l.key,rightKey:rr.key,left:l.row,right:rr.row});
      for(const run of r.runs)expect(i,`plan:${run.id}`,expected,run.rows);
    }
  }
  return { mismatches, features, facts };
}

async function verifiedRun(directory) {
  const manifest=json(join(directory,'manifest.json')), source=readFileSync(join(directory,'engine.mjs')), scenarioBytes=readFileSync(join(directory,'scenario.json')), resultBytes=readFileSync(join(directory,'results.json'));
  for (const [key, bytes] of [['sourceSha256',source],['scenarioSha256',scenarioBytes],['resultSha256',resultBytes]]) if(manifest[key]!==sha256(bytes))throw Error(`${directory}: ${key} does not match actual bytes.`);
  if(manifest.executionIdentity!==executionIdentity())throw Error('Run used different or unrecorded runtime/checker bytes. Re-run explicitly; historical results stay historical.');
  if(typeof manifest.prediction!=='string'||!manifest.prediction.trim())throw Error('Run lacks a prediction committed before execution.');
  const module=await import(pathToFileURL(join(directory,'engine.mjs')).href+`?sha=${manifest.sourceSha256}`), Engine=module.buildEngine(BaseEngine), scenario=JSON.parse(scenarioBytes), recorded=JSON.parse(resultBytes), replay=executeScenario(Engine,scenario);
  if(stable(recorded)!==stable(replay))throw Error('Fresh replay differs from the recorded run.');
  return {manifest,scenario,replay,Engine,oracle:snapshotOracle(scenario,replay)};
}

export async function verifyInvestigation(path, expectedSourceSha256, runRoot) {
  const spec=json(path), root=runRoot??dirname(resolve(path)), checks=[];
  const check=(id,passed,details)=>checks.push({id,passed,details});
  if(spec.format!=='advanced-storage-investigation-v1')throw Error('Unknown investigation format.');
  const runs={};
  for(const name of ['broken','repaired','variant'])runs[name]=await verifiedRun(resolve(root,spec.runs[name]));
  const {broken,repaired,variant}=runs;
  check('I01-same-experiment',broken.manifest.scenarioSha256===repaired.manifest.scenarioSha256,'Broken and repaired runs must use identical scenario bytes.');
  check('I02-actual-repair',broken.manifest.sourceSha256!==repaired.manifest.sourceSha256&&repaired.manifest.sourceSha256===variant.manifest.sourceSha256&&(!expectedSourceSha256||expectedSourceSha256===repaired.manifest.sourceSha256),'Different broken source; one exact repaired source for both repaired cases and current project.');
  check('I03-observed-failure',broken.oracle.mismatches.length>0,broken.oracle.mismatches);
  check('I04-repaired-views',repaired.oracle.mismatches.length===0,repaired.oracle.mismatches);
  const structure=s=>s.actions.filter(a=>!['inspect','analyze','compare-plans'].includes(a.op)).map(a=>a.op);
  check('I05-transfer-variation',variant.oracle.mismatches.length===0&&stable(structure(variant.scenario))!==stable(structure(repaired.scenario)),'Variant must change transaction/read/write/cleanup structure, not just labels, numbers or bookkeeping.');
  check('I06-composed-mechanisms',Object.values(repaired.oracle.features).every(Boolean),repaired.oracle.features);
  const regression=runChecks(repaired.Engine,7); check('I07-regression',regression.passed,{total:regression.total,failures:regression.results.filter(r=>!r.passed)});
  let claimsValid=Array.isArray(spec.claims)&&spec.claims.length>=2, observed=false, estimated=false;
  for(const claim of spec.claims??[]) {
    const run=runs[claim.run], result=run?.replay.results[claim.action]?.result; let actual;
    if(claim.measure==='observedCost'){actual=result?.runs?.find(r=>r.id===claim.plan)?.cost;observed=true;}
    if(claim.measure==='estimatedCost'){actual=result?.explanation?.candidates?.find(r=>r.id===claim.plan)?.cost;estimated=true;}
    if(typeof actual!=='number'||typeof claim.value!=='number'||Math.abs(actual-claim.value)>1e-9)claimsValid=false;
  }
  check('I08-measured-claims',claimsValid&&observed&&estimated,'At least one actual and one estimated plan cost must equal their replayed observations; absolute tolerance 1e-9.');
  check('I09-diagnosis-present',typeof spec.diagnosis==='string'&&spec.diagnosis.trim().length>0,'Presence only. Judge the causal explanation with the published rubric; this is not an automatic writing-quality verdict.');
  return {format:'advanced-storage-investigation-report-v1',engineeringPassed:checks.every(c=>c.passed),checks,explanationQuality:'not automatically assessed',independentAcceptance:false,runSources:Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(runs).map(([k,v])=>[k,v.manifest.sourceSha256]))};
}

export async function verifyTransfer(path, expectedSourceSha256, runRoot) {
  const spec=json(path), root=runRoot??dirname(resolve(path));
  if(spec.format!=='advanced-storage-transfer-v1')throw Error('Unknown transfer format.');
  const si=await verifiedRun(resolve(root,spec.runs.snapshot)), serial=await verifiedRun(resolve(root,spec.runs.serializable)), checks=[];
  const check=(id,passed,details)=>checks.push({id,passed,details});
  const withoutMode=s=>({...s,mode:undefined});
  check('T01-controlled-isolation-comparison',si.scenario.mode==='snapshot'&&serial.scenario.mode==='serializable'&&stable(withoutMode(si.scenario))===stable(withoutMode(serial.scenario)),'Only the database-wide isolation mode changes.');
  check('T02-same-source',si.manifest.sourceSha256===serial.manifest.sourceSha256&&(!expectedSourceSha256||expectedSourceSha256===serial.manifest.sourceSha256),'Both modes use the current repaired source.');
  const roles=spec.roles??{}, collect=(run,op,who)=>run.replay.results.map((x,index)=>({...x,index})).filter(x=>x.action.op===op&&x.action.tx===who);
  const roleNames=['exporter','purger','holder'].map(k=>roles[k]);
  const validRoles=roleNames.every(x=>typeof x==='string'&&x.length>0)&&new Set(roleNames).size===3&&roleNames.every(x=>collect(serial,'begin',x).length===1);
  const initial=new Map(); for(const v of [...(serial.scenario.initial??[])].sort((a,b)=>a.csn-b.csn))initial.set(identity(v.table,v.key),v.row);
  const countTable=table=>[...initial].filter(([id,row])=>JSON.parse(id)[0]===table&&row!==null).length;
  check('T00-transfer-domain',validRoles&&countTable('items')>=2&&countTable('collections')>=2,'Use distinct role aliases, one transaction per role, at least two initial items and two collections.');
  const siPurge=collect(si,'commit',roles.purger).at(-1), serPurge=collect(serial,'commit',roles.purger).at(-1);
  // The contract leaves the description format of a conflict to the learner, so this check reads behaviour it can
  // verify itself: the purge commits under SI, aborts with at least one conflict under Serializable, and no other
  // transaction committed a write to a key the purge wrote (that would be a write conflict masking the read one).
  // T04 separately requires the matching holds change that the purge's empty read depended on.
  const purgeStart=collect(serial,'begin',roles.purger)[0]?.index, purgeKeys=new Set(serial.replay.results.filter(x=>x.action.tx===roles.purger&&['put','delete'].includes(x.action.op)).map(x=>identity(x.action.table,x.action.key)));
  const maskingWrite=serial.oracle.facts.changes.some(c=>c.tx!==roles.purger&&c.index>purgeStart&&c.index<serPurge?.index&&purgeKeys.has(identity(c.table,c.key)));
  check('T03-predicate-race',siPurge?.result.status==='committed'&&serPurge?.result.status==='aborted'&&Array.isArray(serPurge?.result.conflicts)&&serPurge.result.conflicts.length>0&&purgeKeys.size>0&&!maskingWrite,'The purge succeeds under SI but is rejected under Serializable with at least one reported conflict, and no other transaction committed a write to a key the purge wrote. Any clear conflict description format is accepted.');
  const facts=serial.oracle.facts;
  const causalHold=facts.changes.some(c=>c.tx===roles.holder&&c.table==='holds'&&c.row!==null&&c.index<serPurge?.index&&
    facts.reads.some(r=>r.tx===roles.purger&&r.table==='holds'&&r.complete&&r.rows.length===0&&r.index<c.index&&matches(c.row,r.predicate)&&
      facts.deletions.some(d=>d.tx===roles.purger&&d.table==='items'&&d.before!==null&&d.before.collection===c.row.collection&&d.index>r.index&&d.index<serPurge.index)));
  check('T04-negative-predicate-and-disjoint-write',causalHold,'An empty holds read governs a real item deletion for the same collection; the holder commits a matching hold before purge validation.');
  const reader=collect(serial,'begin',roles.exporter)[0], exportCommit=collect(serial,'commit',roles.exporter).at(-1);
  check('T05-protected-export',reader?.action.readOnly===true&&exportCommit?.result.status==='committed'&&serial.oracle.mismatches.length===0&&si.oracle.mismatches.length===0,'Explicit read-only export commits from its old snapshot; all independently checked views remain correct in both modes.');
  const comparisons=serial.replay.results.filter(x=>x.action.op==='compare-plans');
  const oldComparisons=comparisons.filter(x=>x.action.tx===roles.exporter);
  check('T06-separate-view-comparisons',oldComparisons.length>0&&comparisons.some(x=>x.action.tx!==roles.exporter&&x.result.explanation.snapshot>oldComparisons[0].result.explanation.snapshot),'Compare plans within the export view and a separately identified later snapshot.');
  const moved=facts.changes.filter(c=>c.table==='items'&&c.tx!==roles.exporter&&c.before!==null&&c.row!==null&&c.index>reader?.index&&c.index<exportCommit?.index&&['collection','location'].some(f=>c.before[f]!==c.row[f]));
  const exportView=facts.starts.find(s=>s.tx===roles.exporter)?.snapshot;
  const indexedMove=moved.some(c=>{const old=exportView?.get(identity('items',c.key));return old&&facts.reads.some(r=>r.tx===roles.exporter&&r.table==='items'&&r.access==='index'&&r.index>c.index&&matches(old,r.predicate)&&!matches(c.row,r.predicate)&&r.rows.some(x=>x.key===c.key&&stable(x.row)===stable(old)));});
  const pinnedVacuum=moved.some(c=>facts.vacuums.some(v=>v.index>c.index&&v.active.includes(roles.exporter)));
  const releasedVacuum=facts.vacuums.some(v=>v.index>exportCommit?.index&&v.active.length===0&&v.removed>0);
  check('T07-lifetime-and-index',indexedMove&&pinnedVacuum&&releasedVacuum,'The export retrieves a moved item through its old index membership, cleanup runs while it is pinned, and later cleanup removes versions after all pins close.');
  const regression=runChecks(serial.Engine,7);check('T08-regressions',regression.passed,{total:regression.total,failures:regression.failures});
  check('T09-explanation-present',typeof spec.explanation==='string'&&spec.explanation.trim().length>0,'Presence only; use the transfer rubric to assess the argument.');
  return {format:'advanced-storage-transfer-report-v1',engineeringPassed:checks.every(c=>c.passed),checks,explanationQuality:'not automatically assessed',independentAcceptance:false};
}
```

```mjs
function usage() {

    catch (error) { report = { runtimeError: error.signal ? `Stopped after runtime limit: ${error.signal}` : (error.stdout?.toString() || error.message) }; }

    const response = JSON.parse(args[3]); const out = attempt(dir, 'answer', { question: { id: q.id, version: q.version, objective: q.objective, stem: q.stem }, response });

    const out = attempt(dir, 'probe', { prediction, probeSha256: hash(readFileSync(join(root, 'snapshot-probe.mjs'))) });
    // Preserve the supplied probe alongside the exact learner source for replay.
```

# 01 — Decide which version exists for a reader

A booking reader pauses while another client updates the equipment table. Implement the policy that keeps the paused reader's view stable when it resumes.

Your project increment is `visibleVersion`. The supplied engine already stores immutable committed histories and each transaction's private writes. You decide which committed version exists for one snapshot. Read the [method contract](../CONTRACTS.md) before editing.

## 01.1 Read time and commit time

A commit sequence number, or CSN, names a published write transaction. A snapshot is the largest published CSN included in a reader's view. These are logical counters; elapsed time is irrelevant. A row can physically have a version at CSN 7 while a reader whose snapshot is 6 must still use its earlier version.

Commit a prediction before running the example: `node lab.mjs question 01a`. Record it using `node lab.mjs answer work 01a 'YOUR_JSON' --help-used none`.

Consider a different row with versions `(CSN 3, value 14)` and `(CSN 8, value 22)`. A reader at snapshot 5 sees 14: 3 belongs to its view and 8 does not. At snapshot 8, the second version becomes visible. The equality boundary matters. A check using strictly less than the snapshot would hide a commit that was already included when the reader began.

Completion case: for versions at 1, 6 and 9, identify the qualifying prefix for snapshot 6 before choosing its final member. Then implement this decision for arbitrary ascending histories. An empty qualifying set returns `null`. The returned object is the version, not only its row payload.

## 01.2 Visibility, deletion and own writes

A tombstone is a version whose row is `null`. It records absence from that commit onward. Once it is the newest version in the reader's view, searching backward for a non-null row is wrong: that would resurrect an earlier value. A later reinsertion is another version with a new CSN; it does not erase the interval of absence.

Use `question 01b` and record your response before looking at its feedback. Explain to yourself whether the newest qualifying version or the newest qualifying *non-deleted* version is the rule you are implementing.

The shell handles a transaction's own private writes before it calls your method. If a client stages a new booking value, that client can read it immediately, while another client still sees committed history. A private deletion similarly means absence for its owner. This overlay is supplied so the exercise stays about historical visibility. Do not scan or mutate another transaction's private write map.

## 01.3 One query, one pinned view

A scan can pause between rows. Its next call must use the same snapshot, even if new commits now exist. The supplied query handle retains the transaction's view until exhaustion, close, abort or error. The later reclamation unit will make that lifetime important.

The query conditions are also fixed when the scan opens. The shell owns a deep copy of the predicate; changing the original object, even a nested range bound, does not change a paused scan. A different predicate requires a new scan.

Commit `01c`. Then implement `visibleVersion(history, snapshot, examine)` in **`work/engine.mjs`**, inside the class returned by `buildEngine(BaseEngine)`. `starter/engine.mjs` is the unchanged reset template. The caller is `BaseEngine.view` in `runtime/base.mjs`: it checks private writes first, calls your method, then detaches the returned row. `checks.mjs` contains the public unit-01 requirements; `check-runner.mjs` loads your saved attempt.

If a blank method is too large a step, replace only `visibleVersion` with this bounded scaffold. It executes but deliberately throws until you finish it. Type it or copy it, and declare that assistance. Keep every other method and the `buildEngine` wrapper for later units.

<!-- opening-code: visibility-scaffold -->
```js
visibleVersion(history, snapshot, examine = () => {}) {
  let chosen = null;
  for (const version of history) {
    examine(version);
    // TODO: decide whether this version replaces chosen.
  }
  // TODO: return the chosen version, or null if none qualifies.
  throw new Error('Unfinished: choose a version for this snapshot.');
}
```

`history` is ascending, so a forward traversal can keep one candidate. Decide the comparison, including equality, and whether `row: null` changes that decision. This scaffold scans the whole history; you may choose another correct traversal and compare its examination count later. Call the supplied `examine(version)` callback whenever you inspect a version; this produces a trace for later cost comparisons. You may traverse backward, scan forward, or use another correct strategy. Do not reorder or mutate the history.

Run `node lab.mjs check work 01 --help-used none`. Read each failed requirement and its observed value. The public checker tests exact boundaries, tombstones, absence, detached results and the supplied private overlay. It is normal for one scaffold-only case to pass before your visibility method exists; that does not complete the unit.

## 01.4 Run a snapshot experiment

Before running, write your prediction for each observation below. The probe uses your actual `visibleVersion` method, with an insertion at CSN 3 (value 14), deletion at 8, and reinsertion at 9 (value 22). An old reader keeps snapshot 3 as those later versions appear. Fresh readers choose snapshots 8 and 9. Predict the returned **version CSN and row value** for `before-insert`, `old-before-delete`, `old-after-delete`, `fresh-after-delete`, `old-after-reinsert`, and `fresh-after-reinsert`. Distinguish no qualifying version from a qualifying tombstone.

```sh

```

Use your actual assistance declaration, including other people or tools. The command saves your prediction and exact source before execution in a new `work/attempts/probe-*` directory, then writes `report.json` there. It prints version CSNs, row values and examined CSNs, without grading your prediction. A thrown unfinished-method error is saved there too; finish the method and rerun into a new attempt.

The executable probe lives in `snapshot-probe.mjs`. Its observation helper is shown exactly below: it preserves a tombstone as `{csn: 8, value: null}`, while no qualifying version becomes `null`.

<!-- opening-code: observe-snapshot -->
```js
function observe(policy, label, history, snapshot) {
  const examined = [];
  const version = policy.visibleVersion(history, snapshot, v => examined.push(v.csn));
  return {
    label, snapshot,
    version: version === null ? null : { csn: version.csn, value: version.row?.value ?? null },
    examined
  };
}
```

Compare the six observations with your saved prediction. If the old reader changes after deletion or reinsertion, identify the comparison that let a future version through. If a fresh reader at 8 sees 14, check whether your search wrongly skipped a tombstone. If a boundary disappears, revisit equality. Examination lists depend on your traversal; do not copy a particular count as the answer.

This is a **pure-policy experiment**: immutable history prefixes simulate publication, and a number represents the pinned reader. It does not execute a writer, a paused query handle, persistence or your unfinished `commitTransaction`. Unit 02 supplies that next step; passing the probe is not a full engine pass.

```md
# 02 — Publish concurrent transactions atomically

A transaction changes two equipment records, but a reader must never see only half the change. Implement the commit ordering that turns one private write set into one acknowledged database state.

Keep your visibility method. You now own `commitTransaction`; the shell supplies the accepted durable batch store and the narrow helpers in [the contract](../CONTRACTS.md). This unit's tests use a declared validation-free stage with independent writes. Same-key concurrency is the next unit, so do not call this stage Snapshot Isolation yet.

## 02.1 Private writes and transaction states

An active transaction holds proposed writes in its own map. Staging a write is not a commit: other clients cannot read it. A successful transaction becomes committed; a rejected one becomes aborted. Once terminal, its handle cannot read or write again. Repeating a commit must not apply its operations twice.

Work through `02c`: a read-only completion changes state without creating a row version. In your method, account for that case separately from a write batch. The supplied `finish` helper closes handles and clears private data only when you have chosen the outcome.

A query in the same transaction freezes the private overlay while it is open. The shell therefore refuses commit or new private writes until that query closes. This is a bounded API rule, not a universal property of databases.

## 02.2 Validate, persist and publish

There are three distinct boundaries. Preparation constructs a proposed complete update and can reject resource limits without writing. Persistence submits that update as one batch to the supplied engine. Publication makes the new logical history and CSN available to subsequent transactions. Client acknowledgement follows those effects.

Commit `02a` before implementing the order. As a sibling example, imagine publishing a replacement directory listing: calculating a new list does not make it visible, writing its bytes does not mean the application has switched to it, and sending success too early can claim a state that never became durable. The database has the same need to distinguish phases, although its supplied batch operation handles the bytes.

Use `this.conflicts(tx)` before effects. This helper is empty in the unit-02 stage and will call your conflict policies in later stages. Obtain a prepared update once, persist that exact update, then publish that exact update. The synchronous publication section does not yield to another client. A new reader starts with either the old CSN or the fully published new CSN.

## 02.3 Acknowledgement and uncertain outcomes

Commit `02b`. A process can stop after a batch became durable but before its client hears success. Neither “definitely committed” nor “definitely absent” follows from the lost acknowledgement alone. Reopening the supplied store can recover the whole batch. Retrying an arbitrary write as if it failed could duplicate an effect.

The shell's `indeterminate` helper poisons the coordinator after a persistence/publication failure. Existing state is no longer safe to serve until reopen. This preserves uncertainty rather than inventing an abort. The course inherits a process-interruption model; it does not establish power-loss safety or a distributed exactly-once protocol.

Implement the method and run `node lab.mjs check work 02 --help-used none`. Inspect the recorded phase trace when the ordering check fails. The tests also stop after durable acknowledgement, reopen a fresh engine, and check both rows. They do not ask you to rewrite the WAL or interpret its byte frames.

Fresh application: identify which outcomes are possible if a stop happens immediately before persistence, after durability, and after publication. State what the client knows separately from what recovery might find. Continue to [03](03.md) to decide when overlapping writes may commit.
```

```md
# 03 — Distinguish isolation from an application invariant

Two clients reserve the same equipment slot from the same old view. Implement write-conflict validation, then identify the kind of anomaly that it still permits.

Your increment is `writeConflicts`. The commit method from unit 02 calls it through the supplied validation dispatcher. Unit 03 and later turn that policy on.

## 03.1 Statement snapshots and transaction snapshots

A statement-snapshot reader can observe one committed state in its first query and a newer committed state in its second. A transaction-snapshot reader keeps the same committed view across its reads. Neither should read another transaction's uncommitted private values.

Our learner engine uses one transaction snapshot. The current slice does not implement a full Read Committed write mode. Treat that comparison as a distinction in allowed observations, not a promise of compatibility with another database's locking rules.

Before coding, commit `03a`. Let A and B begin at snapshot 12. If both stage key 6 and A publishes at 13, B's starting view no longer includes the latest write to key 6. Publishing B unconditionally would hide A's change. A conflict is about that timeline, not whether the final row happens to equal an earlier value.

## 03.2 Same-key conflicts and first committer

Snapshot Isolation keeps a stable view and refuses a writer whose target key changed after its snapshot. The comparison is strict here: a latest write at the snapshot is already included; a latest write after it is a conflict. Check every distinct key in the private write map. Missing history means no previous committed write, not a special exemption from future insert races.

Deletes matter. A tombstone carries a CSN and can conflict with a stale insertion or update. A change followed by a restoration also matters. Commit `03c`, then verify that your decision uses write occurrence rather than comparing endpoint row values.

The checker includes independent writers. If A writes key 1 and B writes key 2 without a dependency that this mode validates, both must be able to finish. Aborting every overlap avoids one race by destroying the intended behavior. Holding a global lock for each entire transaction would similarly evade the exercise.

## 03.3 Write skew without a dirty read

Now consider two equipment records whose combined availability must remain above a threshold. Each client reads both from the same valid old snapshot, then changes a different record. No same-key conflict is necessary, yet the combined result may violate the condition. This is write skew.

Commit `03b`. Stable snapshots answer “what did each transaction read?” They do not by themselves answer “could all successful transactions have run one at a time with those observations?” That second question is the motivation for the next unit's dependency validation.

Implement `writeConflicts` and run `node lab.mjs check work 03 --help-used none`. Do not change the supplied private-map or disk code to make one fixture pass. Return a description for every conflicting key. Descriptions may use any clear shape and appear in any order; the checker does not require a particular witness format.

Fresh application: create an initially absent key. Let two clients both stage it, commit one, then attempt the other. Explain why an insert needs the same conflict rule as an update. Preserve both successful and rejected outcomes when you later write a schedule file.
```
