Each message holds what the screen draws at that moment and nothing else, and it is a fraction of the full view's size. A smaller message isn't the goal, though; the goal is that nothing hidden reaches it, and the next section tests that.

## Test by changing what is hidden

How would you know a view leaks? Searching its messages for the exact wind finds the obvious leak, `"wind": 2.4375`. It doesn't find the wind multiplied by 1,000, or written as the bytes of a float in base64, or used to choose the order of the fields.

Change the hidden thing instead, and see whether the message changes. `game.clone()` makes an independent copy of the game. `copy.setHidden(name, k)` changes one hidden thing on the copy without changing anything drawn: the wind to another value inside the same arrows' band, the flag to another position inside the same whole pace, the random state to another state. If the view of the copy differs from the view of the original by even one byte, that hidden thing reaches the client, whatever the encoding. This is called a non-interference test, because nothing hidden may interfere with what the client receives.

Write `findLeaks(viewFn, game, info)`, which returns the sorted list of hidden names that reach the message. The names come from `game.hidden`, and API.md's "Hidden things" table says what each one is. The game also has getters for the hidden values, such as `game.serverWind()` for the exact wind and `game.flagSpeed()` for the flag's speed. Compare the bytes of `JSON.stringify`, not parsed objects, because a view that puts its fields in a different order depending on the wind leaks the wind, and two parsed objects with the same fields in a different order compare equal. Try all three variants `k` of each hidden thing. A leak can show for some values and not others.

Check `13.leaks-finds` runs your `findLeaks` on views with leaks planted in them, one hidden thing at a time and two at once, and on a correct view, which must give an empty list.

Question 13b: a view adds a field `drift: Math.sign(game.flagSpeed())`. The flag's speed is now −50. `setHidden('flagSpeed', k)` sets −120.5 for k = 1, 33.25 for k = 2 and 97.75 for k = 3. For which values of k does the view's message change? Answer with the numbers, separated by commas:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 13b YOUR_ANSWER
```

### Find leaks by changing one thing at a time

Tour `public/lob.mjs` before you write this: find `HIDDEN`, the list `game.hidden` returns, then `clone`, which makes an independent copy of the game in the same state, and `setHidden`, which changes one hidden thing on that copy. Notice that `setHidden` returns false, changing nothing, when the thing is absent, such as the shell's position when no shell is in the air. In `server/leaks.mjs`, replace the `find-leaks` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/leaks-checkpoint.mjs","region":"find-leaks","language":"js","title":"Change one hidden thing on a copy, compare the bytes","change":"Replace the complete find-leaks region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/leaks-checkpoint.mjs","region":"find-leaks","title":"Change one hidden thing on a copy, compare the bytes","change":"Replace the complete find-leaks region."}
export function findLeaks(viewFn, game, info) {
  const before = JSON.stringify(viewFn(game, info));
  const leaking = [];
  for (const name of game.hidden) {
    for (let k = 1; k <= 3; k++) {
      const copy = game.clone();
      const changed = copy.setHidden(name, k);
      if (changed && JSON.stringify(viewFn(copy, info)) !== before) {
        leaking.push(name);
        break;
      }
    }
  }
  return leaking.sort();
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The message for the real game is turned into its bytes once, before anything changes. Each change happens on a fresh copy, so one change can't carry into the next and the real game is never touched. A copy where `setHidden` changed nothing can't show a leak, so it isn't compared. The comparison is of `JSON.stringify` text, so a different order of fields counts as a difference. The inner loop stops at the first variant that shows a leak, because one is enough to name it, and every name is tried, so the list holds each leaking name once. Sorting makes the answer the same whatever order the names are tried in.

Run the probe on the full view and on your view, at the same three moments:

```sh

```

It runs the non-interference test at many moments of a few sessions, and also searches every message for the hidden values under a list of encodings: decimals at many precisions, scaled integers, the bytes of each float as hex and base64. A search names the encoding it found, which makes a failure easy to act on, but it can never be complete, because encodings have no end. The non-interference test doesn't depend on guessing an encoding, and that's its strength, but it isn't complete either. It tries three changes of each hidden thing at the moments it looks at, so a leak that shows only for other values, or at other moments, passes it. Lesson 17 has an example. ## What hiding costs

A message is always old when it arrives, so a client has to work out where the flag is now from messages about the past. How well it can do that depends on what the messages hold, so hiding can cost an honest player something, and more as latency grows.

```
node lab.mjs cost project
```

It plays an expert (the strongest of the course's legal player models) and the searching client at five latencies, each with the full view and with your view, 200 sessions of 12 rounds per cell, the same seeds along a row. It takes from 30 to 180 seconds, depending on the machine:

```
   one-way  expert full  expert yours  searcher full  searcher yours
      0 ms        23.8%         25.0%         100.0%               ?
     50 ms        22.5%         23.1%         100.0%               ?
    100 ms        22.5%         22.0%         100.0%               ?
    200 ms        20.1%         19.0%         100.0%               ?
    400 ms        17.8%         14.6%         100.0%               ?
```

The last column, the searching client with your view, is left out here because question 13a asks about it. Your run fills it in.

Latency costs the expert with either view, because their aim is never better than the screen. Your run's last two columns show what hiding costs the searching client at each latency. With the full view it hits every shot at every latency.

Question 13d: why does the searching client hit every shot with the full view, even at 400 ms each way? (a) the full view tells it the flag's speed, its timer and the game's random state, so it can run the flag forward past any delay (b) it fires the moment a round starts, before latency matters (c) the full view sends where the shell will land (d) the server waits for its messages

```
node lab.mjs predict project 13d YOUR_ANSWER
```

With the drawn view a client can only extrapolate from the positions it has seen, and the flag picks a new speed every two to five seconds. That costs the expert little until the delay is long. At 400 ms each way the drawn screen's guess about the flag is often wrong, and the expert hits 14.6% instead of 17.8%.

Every rate in the table has noise. A rate p measured over n shots has a standard error of about the square root of p(1 − p)/n, which for a rate near 24% over 2,400 shots is about 0.9 points. The difference between two such rates, measured on different shots, has a standard error about 1.4 times as large, here about 1.2 points. A gap of one standard error is what chance gives all the time, while a gap of three is rare. This treats every shot as independent, and they aren't quite. A player's bias (each model player aims off by its own amount for the whole session) carries from one shot to the next, so 200 sessions vary more than 2,400 independent shots would, and the true noise is somewhat larger.

Question 13c: at 0 ms the expert hits 23.8% of 2,400 shots with the full view and 25.0% with the drawn view. Does the drawn view help experts? Answer `yes` or `no`:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 13c YOUR_ANSWER
```

# 14 · Meet the limit, then detect

The searching client sends legal inputs: one fire a round, an angle and a power in range, in order. Your admission admits every one of them, as it should, because an honest player could send each of them too. With the drawn view it still hits about 65% of its shots. No rule about a single message can stop it, because no single message is wrong.

The session, though, is unusual. Over twelve rounds the searching client fires at nearly the same moment every round, sends one message per round where people send several, and lands closer than people do. By the end of this lesson your `detect/` files will turn a session into a handful of numbers, score it, set a threshold on development sessions (the ones you design on) for a stated budget of false flags, freeze that threshold, measure it once on held-out sessions (kept back until the end), and work out what its flags would mean in a game where one session in 100 is a cheat. A flag here is the detector's mark on a session, not the flag a shell aims at, and it's a request for a person to look. Nothing in this course bans anyone.

Part one's unit M7 built the same discipline for the courier arena: case-level counts, frozen settings, and rates with their denominators.

The supplied route passes `14.features`, `14.threshold` and `14.counting`, and fails the other three with `not written yet`, because `detect/settings.json` is still the starter's on every route. Either is a starting point, not evidence of understanding. On the type-in route, keep the `// region: NAME` and `// endregion: NAME` lines: a listing replaces everything between its pair of marker lines. The regions, in the order the lesson shows them, are `features`, `cadence-cv` and `miss-lag1` in `detect/features.mjs`, then `robust-z`, `score`, `choose-threshold`, `count`, `evaluate` and `precision-at` in `detect/detector.mjs`.

## The corpus

`public/corpus.mjs` plays sessions on the defended server: lesson 12's rules, the drawn view of lesson 13, six kinds of legal player and the searching client. It plays them with the course's own server code, not yours, so every learner's corpus is the same.

| Kind | Who |
| --- | --- |
| `novice`, `skilled`, `expert` | three skill levels on an ordinary connection (30 ms each way) |
| `highLatency` | skilled players 250 ms away |
| `jitter` | skilled players whose delay varies by up to 60 ms, so messages overtake each other |
| `reconnects` | skilled players who lose the connection two or three times a session, for 2 to 6 s |
| `searcher` | the searching client, labelled `cheat` |

`makeCorpus({ split: 'dev' })` gives 1,100 sessions: 1,000 legal and 100 searcher. `makeCorpus({ split: 'heldout' })` gives 2,200 more, 2,000 legal and 200 searcher, played from seeds the dev split never uses. Each session comes as a case, `{ id, label, kind, record, rounds }` (API.md, "A case"). You fit everything on dev, choosing your settings and threshold from its sessions alone. Held-out is read once, at the end.

The legal players are models written for this course. They have reaction times, aim with noise and a personal bias, learn from where their last shell landed, and press keys at a human pace. They aren't people, and the lesson comes back to what that means.

## Features

A **session** is the unit. A detector that judged single shots would see thousands of them, and a few hundred lucky ones among honest players would look like a crowd of cheats. Counting sessions gives each session one decision, so the denominator counts sessions, not shots.

Write `features(c)`, with the definitions in API.md: hit rate, median miss, median time to fire and its spread, median inputs per round, how regular the gaps between inputs are (`cadenceCV`, their coefficient of variation, the standard deviation over the mean), and how a miss relates to the next one. Use only `c.record.inputs` and `c.rounds`. The checks give your function nothing else, so a detector can't read a session's label or name. Check `14.features` compares your features with the definitions on sessions of every kind. Run it alone with `node lab.mjs check project 14 --case 14.features`, because the whole unit includes `14.heldout`, which measures your detector on sessions of its own and belongs after the freeze.

### Read each feature from the rounds

Tour `public/stats.mjs` first, because every feature is one of its functions applied to a list. `median` is `quantile` at one half, and `quantile` sorts the list and interpolates between the two nearest places, so the median of an even-length list is halfway between its middle two values. Both return null for an empty list. `sd` divides by the number of values, the population standard deviation API.md asks for. `correlation` returns null when either list doesn't vary or there are fewer than two pairs. Then, in `detect/features.mjs`, replace the `features` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/features-checkpoint.mjs","region":"features","language":"js","title":"Six features from the shot rounds, two from helpers","change":"Replace the complete features region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/features-checkpoint.mjs","region":"features","title":"Six features from the shot rounds, two from helpers","change":"Replace the complete features region."}
export function features({ record, rounds }) {
  const shotRounds = rounds.filter((r) => r.shot !== null);
  const shots = shotRounds.length;
  const hits = shotRounds.filter((r) => r.result === 'hit').length;
  const fireTimes = shotRounds.map((r) => r.shot.tick - r.start);
  return {
    shots,
    hitRate: shots ? hits / shots : null,
    missMedian: median(shotRounds.map((r) => Math.abs(r.miss))),
    fireMedian: median(fireTimes),
    fireSpread: shots
      ? quantile(fireTimes, 0.75) - quantile(fireTimes, 0.25)
      : null,
    inputsMedian: median(shotRounds.map((r) => r.inputs)),
    cadenceCV: cadenceCV(record.inputs, rounds),
    missLag1: missLag1(rounds),
  };
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

A shot round is a round whose `shot` isn't null, and five of the features are read from those rounds alone. A round without a shot has no fire time, no miss and no result, so leaving it out is what the definitions say, not a shortcut. `hitRate` and `fireSpread` are null for a session with no shots, because a share of nothing and a spread of nothing aren't numbers; `median` already gives null for an empty list. The fire time is `shot.tick - r.start`, measured on the server's clock from the start of the round, so a player far away fires later by their delay, and a client that decides at once fires early. The miss is signed, negative when short, and `missMedian` takes its size, since short and long are equally far from the flag. The other two features need more than one round at a time, so they get helpers. On the type-in route those are still holes, so the probe stops there. The probe plays the first dev session of each kind. It comes in two parts, and the lesson asks for each where it belongs. The first, `run`, only says whether your function runs on all seven sessions and which values are null; the values themselves come after question 14a below:

```sh
node examples/try-features.mjs project run
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/features-partial-output.txt","language":"text","title":"After features: the cadence helper is still a hole"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/features-partial-output.txt","title":"After features: the cadence helper is still a hole"}
cadenceCV: not written yet
```
<!-- /code-example -->

On the supplied route the same part says that `features` ran on all seven sessions with eight values each, and names the one value that is null.

Replace the `cadence-cv` region below `features`:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/features-checkpoint.mjs","region":"cadence-cv","language":"js","title":"Gaps between inputs in the same round","change":"Replace the complete cadence-cv region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/features-checkpoint.mjs","region":"cadence-cv","title":"Gaps between inputs in the same round","change":"Replace the complete cadence-cv region."}
function cadenceCV(inputs, rounds) {
  const gaps = [];
  let previous = null;
  for (const input of inputs) {
    const round = roundAt(rounds, input.tick);
    if (previous && previous.round === round)
      gaps.push(input.tick - previous.tick);
    previous = { round, tick: input.tick };
  }
  if (gaps.length < 5) return null;
  const m = mean(gaps);
  return m > 0 ? sd(gaps) / m : null;
}

function roundAt(rounds, tick) {
  let found = null;
  for (const r of rounds) if (r.start <= tick) found = r.round;
  return found;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The inputs in `record.inputs` carry the tick each was applied, not a round, so `roundAt` finds the round: the last one in the list whose start is at or before the tick, which is the latest round started by then because rounds come in order. A gap is counted only between two inputs of the same round. The gap across a round change is time spent watching the shell land and waiting for the next round, not how fast a player presses keys. `previous` moves on at every input, so each gap is between neighbours. With fewer than five gaps the spread of the gaps says little, and a client that sends one message a round has no gaps at all, so the feature is null. Then replace the `miss-lag1` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/features-checkpoint.mjs","region":"miss-lag1","language":"js","title":"Does one miss predict the next?","change":"Replace the complete miss-lag1 region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/features-checkpoint.mjs","region":"miss-lag1","title":"Does one miss predict the next?","change":"Replace the complete miss-lag1 region."}
function missLag1(rounds) {
  const xs = [];
  const ys = [];
  for (let i = 0; i + 1 < rounds.length; i++) {
    const a = rounds[i];
    const b = rounds[i + 1];
    if (a.shot && b.shot && b.round === a.round + 1) {
      xs.push(a.miss);
      ys.push(b.miss);
    }
  }
  return xs.length < 4 ? null : correlation(xs, ys);
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

A pair is two rounds next to each other that both had a shot, so a round lost to a reconnect breaks the chain instead of pairing two misses far apart. The signed misses go in, because a player who corrects tends to fall short after landing long, which shows as a negative correlation. Fewer than four pairs give a correlation too noisy to use, so the feature is null then.

## The adapted searcher

A cheat whose sessions get flagged adapts. `recordings/` holds sessions of two adapted searchers, recorded once by the course's author with a tool the course doesn't ship. `delay` uses the searcher's aim but sends it the way an expert would, with several inputs a round at a human pace, about two and a half seconds into the round. Its timing and its input counts look like an expert's, and only its aim gives it away. `delay-misses` does the same and also misses on purpose.

The recordings are labelled examples of an adapted cheat, not held-out sessions, so run `node lab.mjs recordings project` whenever you like while you design your score, once your features and score run. Until `detect/settings.json` holds a threshold, it uses the threshold `tune` would choose on the dev split for your current score, says so, and writes nothing. Check `14.recordings` requires your detector to flag at least 12 of the 60 `delay` sessions, so a score built on timing alone won't pass.

For comparison, the course's worked detector, described in the next section, gives this table, in which recall is the share of a set's sessions it flags:

```
  set           sessions           hit rate  flagged  missed  recall
  delay               60    68.1% (490/720)       22      38   0.367
  delay-misses        60    31.1% (224/720)        0      60   0.000
```

It still flags 22 of the 60 `delay` sessions, because they land far closer than experts do. It flags none of the `delay-misses` sessions, because they miss about as often as an expert.

Question 14c: the `delay-misses` sessions hit 31.1% of their shots, and the dev split's experts hit 27.5%. If your detector flags none of them, how many percentage points of hit rate has the cheat bought over an expert, to the nearest whole point?

```
node lab.mjs predict project 14c YOUR_ANSWER
```

Detection falls when the cheat adapts, and so does what the cheat gets for cheating. A defence doesn't have to catch every adapted cheat to work, as long as it makes cheating cost more than it buys.

## A score and a budget

Write `score(features, settings)`. The rule is yours. One rule that works takes, for each feature, how far the session sits from the legal median in units of a robust scale, its robust z-score, signs it so that the suspicious side is positive, caps it so that one wild feature can't decide alone, and sums them. The robust scale is 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of the legal sessions, and the median absolute deviation is the median of their distances from the legal median. The factor makes the scale match the standard deviation when values are normally distributed, and it's robust because a few extreme sessions barely move it, where they'd drag a mean and a standard deviation with them. `node lab.mjs features project` prints the legal median and robust scale of each feature for exactly this, rounded to three decimals, which is precise enough to copy into `detect/settings.json`. Times, counts and distances are skewed (a few very slow players, a few huge misses), so compare them as `Math.log1p(value)`. Leave out a feature whose legal robust scale is 0, such as `shots`. Almost every session fires in all 12 rounds, so the median absolute deviation is 0 and dividing by it means nothing. The course's worked detector gives every feature a weight of 1 and a cap of 10. A much lower cap clips the `delay` sessions' aim scores, the part of their score that gives them away.

### One feature, worked through

The lesson works one feature through that rule, `hitRate`, so that you can see the shape of a score and run it. It is not a detector. In `detect/detector.mjs`, replace the `robust-z` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"robust-z","language":"js","title":"One feature's capped, signed robust z-score","change":"Replace the complete robust-z region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"robust-z","title":"One feature's capped, signed robust z-score","change":"Replace the complete robust-z region."}
function robustZ(value, { transform, direction, median, scale, cap }) {
  if (value === null || value === undefined) return 0;
  const x = transform === 'log' ? Math.log1p(value) : value;
  const z = (direction * (x - median)) / scale;
  return Math.min(cap, Math.max(-cap, z));
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The second argument is one feature's entry in your settings, so everything the rule needs about a feature lives in `detect/settings.json`, where `freeze` will hash it. A null feature adds nothing, which is how the searching client's missing `cadenceCV` is handled: it neither helps nor hurts. With `transform` set to `log`, the value is compared as `Math.log1p(value)`, and the median and scale in the entry must then be the ones `features` prints for `log1p`. `direction` is 1 when a high value is suspicious and −1 when a low one is, so the result is positive on the suspicious side either way. The cap clips the result to between minus and plus `cap`. Then replace the `score` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"score","language":"js","title":"The shape of a score, with one feature","change":"Replace the complete score region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"score","title":"The shape of a score, with one feature","change":"Replace the complete score region."}
export function score(features, settings) {
  return robustZ(features.hitRate, settings.features.hitRate);
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

A score takes the features of one session and your settings and returns one number, higher for more suspicious. This one reads only `hitRate`. It needs that feature's entry in `detect/settings.json`. In the output of `node lab.mjs features project`, under `hitRate`, the line `all legal` gives the legal median, 0.083, and the robust scale, 0.124. A high hit rate is the suspicious side, and the rates are shares, not skewed counts, so no log. Write `detect/settings.json` as:

```json
{
  "budget": 0.002,
  "features": {
    "hitRate": {
      "transform": "none",
      "direction": 1,
      "median": 0.083,
      "scale": 0.124,
      "cap": 10
    }
  },
  "threshold": null
}
```

Then score the same seven sessions:

```sh
node examples/try-score.mjs project
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/score-output.txt","language":"text","title":"The one-feature score of one dev session of each kind"} -->

session             hitRate    score

The expert and the searcher get the same score, because over twelve shots they hit equally often. A hit rate over twelve shots is one of only thirteen values, so this score is too, and on hit rate alone the best experts and the searching client overlap.

A threshold turns a score into a decision, and a session is flagged when its score is at or above the threshold. The decision has a cost, because every flagged legal session is a false flag, a person asked to look at a player who did nothing. So choose the threshold from that cost. The budget here is one false flag in 500 legal sessions. Write `chooseThreshold(legalScores, budget)`: the smallest of the scores such that the share of scores at or above it is at most the budget.

Question 14d: suppose the legal scores on dev were 1, 3, 3, 5, 9, 9, 12, 20, 25, 40, and the budget 0.2. What does `chooseThreshold` return?

```
node lab.mjs predict project 14d YOUR_ANSWER
```

### Choose the smallest threshold within the budget

Replace the `choose-threshold` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"choose-threshold","language":"js","title":"The smallest score that keeps false flags within the budget","change":"Replace the complete choose-threshold region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"choose-threshold","title":"The smallest score that keeps false flags within the budget","change":"Replace the complete choose-threshold region."}
export function chooseThreshold(legalScores, budget) {
  const sorted = [...legalScores].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const n = sorted.length;
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i > 0 && sorted[i] === sorted[i - 1]) continue;
    if ((n - i) / n <= budget) return sorted[i];
  }
  return Infinity;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The scores are copied before sorting, so the caller's list keeps its order. Walking up the sorted list, at place `i` the scores at or above `sorted[i]` are the last `n - i` of them, provided `sorted[i]` is the first of its value. That is what the line that skips a repeated value is for: a threshold flags every session with that score, so the share must be counted from the first copy. The first place whose share fits the budget gives the smallest such threshold, and a smaller threshold flags more cheats, so it's the one to take. When even the highest score alone is too many, no score qualifies, and the answer is `Infinity`, which flags nothing. Check `14.threshold` tests your `chooseThreshold` on lists with ties at the cut.

`tune` scores the dev split's legal sessions with your score and settings and runs your `chooseThreshold` on them. Without `--write` it prints and stores nothing:

```sh
node lab.mjs tune project
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/tune-output.txt","language":"text","title":"node lab.mjs tune project, with the one-feature score"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/tune-output.txt","title":"node lab.mjs tune project, with the one-feature score"}

  legal sessions flagged     2 of 1000: dev-expert-85 5.379, dev-expert-101 5.379

At the budget, the one-feature score flags 29 of the 100 searcher sessions. The threshold has to clear the two experts who hit nine shots in twelve, and most searcher sessions hit fewer. That is as far as one feature goes, and why the score you hand in needs more. Its design comes after the counting below.

## Base rates

Recall is the share of cheat sessions a detector flags, the false positive rate is the share of legal sessions it flags, and precision is the share of flagged sessions that are cheats. Recall and the false positive rate belong to the detector, but precision also depends on how many sessions are cheats. When cheats are rare, even a small false positive rate fills the flagged list with legal players.

Write `count(decisions)`, `evaluate(cases, settings)` and `precisionAt(baseRate, recall, fpr)`. `count` turns one decision per session, `{ label, flagged }`, into the counts tp (flagged cheats, true positives), fn (cheats not flagged, false negatives), fp (flagged legal sessions, false positives) and tn (legal sessions not flagged, true negatives), with the three rates. `evaluate` makes one decision per case with your score and threshold and counts them. `precisionAt` takes the base rate, the share of sessions that are cheats, with the recall and the false positive rate (fpr).

Question 14b: a detector catches 90% of cheats and flags 1% of legal sessions. One session in 100 is a cheat. What share of flagged sessions are cheats, to the nearest whole percent? Commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 14b YOUR_ANSWER
```

### Count sessions, then the rates

Replace the `count` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"count","language":"js","title":"One decision per session, four counts, three rates","change":"Replace the complete count region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"count","title":"One decision per session, four counts, three rates","change":"Replace the complete count region."}
export function count(decisions) {
  let tp = 0;
  let fp = 0;
  let tn = 0;
  let fn = 0;
  for (const { label, flagged } of decisions) {
    if (label === 'cheat') {
      if (flagged) tp++;
      else fn++;
    } else if (flagged) fp++;
    else tn++;
  }
  return {
    total: decisions.length,
    tp,
    fp,
    tn,
    fn,
    recall: tp + fn ? tp / (tp + fn) : null,
    falsePositiveRate: fp + tn ? fp / (fp + tn) : null,
    precision: tp + fp ? tp / (tp + fp) : null,
  };
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

Each decision lands in exactly one of the four counts, so they add up to `total`. Each rate is a count over the sessions it is about: recall over the cheats, the false positive rate over the legal sessions, precision over the flagged sessions. A rate whose denominator is 0 is null, not 0 and not `NaN`: a detector that flagged nothing has no precision, which is different from a precision of 0. Then replace the `evaluate` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"evaluate","language":"js","title":"Flag each case at the frozen threshold","change":"Replace the complete evaluate region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"evaluate","title":"Flag each case at the frozen threshold","change":"Replace the complete evaluate region."}
export function evaluate(cases, settings) {
  return count(
    cases.map((c) => ({
      label: c.label,
      flagged: score(sessionFeatures(c), settings) >= settings.threshold,
    })),
  );
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`evaluate` is given whole cases, because counting needs the labels, but the label goes only into the decision's `label`. The flag comes from your features and score, which the checks call with a session's play alone, so a session sent twice under two labels gets the same flag both times, which check `14.heldout` tests. The comparison is at or above the threshold, the same as `chooseThreshold` assumed. Then replace the `precision-at` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"precision-at","language":"js","title":"Precision at a base rate","change":"Replace the complete precision-at region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/detector-checkpoint.mjs","region":"precision-at","title":"Precision at a base rate","change":"Replace the complete precision-at region."}
export function precisionAt(baseRate, recall, fpr) {
  const denominator = baseRate * recall + (1 - baseRate) * fpr;
  return denominator === 0 ? null : (baseRate * recall) / denominator;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

Out of all sessions, a share `baseRate × recall` are flagged cheats, and the legal share of sessions times `fpr` are flagged legal sessions; precision is the first over both. When nothing is flagged there is nothing to divide by, and the answer is null, as in `count`. Run the probe, which counts five decisions, counts none, and gives the precision of question 14b's detector at four base rates:

```sh
node examples/try-count.mjs project
```

count(five decisions) {"total":5,"tp":1,"fp":1,"tn":2,"fn":1,"recall":0.5,"falsePositiveRate":0.3333333333333333,"precision":0.5}
count([])             {"total":0,"tp":0,"fp":0,"tn":0,"fn":0,"recall":null,"falsePositiveRate":null,"precision":null}
precision of recall 0.9, false positive rate 0.01, when cheats are
  1 session in 2     0.989
  1 session in 10    0.909
  1 session in 100   0.476
  1 session in 1000  0.083
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The same detector, with the same recall and false positive rate, gives a flagged list that is almost all cheats when half the sessions are cheats, and mostly legal players when one in 1,000 is. ## Use the idea on a new case

A budget over all legal sessions says nothing about who the false flags fall on. They tend to fall on the players most like the cheat, experts, as in the worked detector's held-out result. Suppose the team that reviews flags asks for the budget to hold for every kind of legal player separately: within each kind, the share of its dev sessions at or above the threshold must be at most the budget.

The comment at the top of that file gives its contract: `legal` is one `{ kind, score }` per legal dev session, and the answer is the smallest score that keeps every kind within the budget, or `Infinity`. Choosing a threshold per kind uses the kinds of the dev sessions, which you know because you designed on them; the detector itself still never sees a kind.

```md
# 15 · Latency on the courier game

The courier arena is part one's game (README.md, "The two games"). A player steers a courier around a floor in 250 mm steps, picks up a parcel at the core and delivers it to the depot, each with a press of interact within 250 mm of the place, and every delivery scores a point. In part one the courier server and its client shared one machine, so a press reached the server the moment it was made. Here the courier arena is played over a network. A player's screen always shows the past, and a press always arrives late. By the end of this lesson your `courier/rewind.mjs` will judge each interaction at the moment the player saw, no further back than a window (a limit in ticks that you choose) and than that player's measured round trip. You will measure, for each window, how many honest presses are refused and how many lies are accepted, and choose a window against a budget.

The technique is usually called lag compensation. Multiplayer shooters use it to judge a shot against where the target was on the shooter's screen. The server keeps a short history of positions and rewinds to the shooter's moment, up to a limit the server sets. Valve, the game developer, describes one such system in "Source Multiplayer Networking", an article about its Source engine.

## A press, late

`public/courier.mjs` runs part one's rules: the courier moves 250 mm a tick while an admitted input is active (on each of the next 4 ticks), and an interaction needs it within 250 mm of its target, the core without a parcel or the depot with one. After an interaction counts, a cooldown makes the next one wait 4 ticks. The boundary at `k × 50` ms starts tick `k`. At that instant the server admits the inputs that have arrived, runs tick `k` (the courier moves, and a press admitted at that boundary is decided) and sends the view of tick `k`. That view reaches the client one one-way latency later. A press sent at that moment takes another one-way latency to arrive, and the server admits it at the first boundary at or after its arrival. The input's move or stop takes effect in the tick that starts there, before the courier moves, and its press is decided after that move, at the position the ring holds for that tick. So a server judging "now" judges a press about one round trip after the moment the player saw.

The core, where the courier picks up a parcel, is a single point. Walking along the floor, the courier is within 250 mm of it at exactly three positions: one step before, on it, and one step past. At 250 mm a tick, it crosses that zone in three ticks, 150 ms.

Question 15a: the core is at x = 2,000 and the courier walks east at full speed. A player with a one-way latency of 100 ms and no jitter sees the courier at x = 1,750, the first view that shows it in range, and at that moment sends an input that stops and presses interact. The server judges at now. At what x is the courier when the server decides? Commit before reading on:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 15a YOUR_ANSWER
```

## The position ring

To judge a press at an earlier tick, the server must remember where the courier was. `public/courier.mjs` keeps a ring of the last 40 ticks, where slot `tick % size` holds `{ tick, x, y }` for the newest tick written there, with `size` 40, so writing tick 40 overwrites tick 0. Read the size from `history.size`, as API.md says, not from this lesson. Forty ticks is two seconds, longer than any window this lesson will use.

Write `positionAt(history, tick)`: the position at the end of `tick`, or `null` when the slot holds a different tick or nothing. Check `15.position-at` reads rings after overwrites and asks for ticks the ring no longer holds. A ring is bounded retention, as part one's unit M9 taught it, meaning the server keeps what its rule needs and no more.

### Read a tick back from the ring

Tour `public/courier.mjs` first. `createHistory` makes the ring, `{ size, slots }`, with every slot null, and `recordPosition` writes `{ tick, x, y }` into slot `tick % size`, replacing whatever was there. Then find `step` inside `createCourierServer`: each tick it moves the courier, writes the new position into the ring, and only then decides a pending press, so the tick being decided is always in the ring when your judge runs. In `courier/rewind.mjs`, replace the `position-at` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/rewind-checkpoint.mjs","region":"position-at","language":"js","title":"A slot answers only for the tick it holds","change":"Replace the complete position-at region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/rewind-checkpoint.mjs","region":"position-at","title":"A slot answers only for the tick it holds","change":"Replace the complete position-at region."}
export function positionAt(history, tick) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(tick) || tick < 0) return null;
  const slot = history.slots[tick % history.size];
  return slot && slot.tick === tick ? { x: slot.x, y: slot.y } : null;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The slot for a tick is found by arithmetic, but a slot doesn't know which of the many ticks that share it was written last, so the stored `tick` is compared with the one asked for. A slot that holds another tick, or nothing, answers null instead of a position from another moment. A tick that isn't a whole number, or is negative, has no slot at all, and it is refused before the arithmetic, because `-1 % 40` is `-1` in JavaScript and `2.5 % 40` is `2.5`, neither of them a slot. The answer is a new `{ x, y }`, so a caller that changes it can't change the ring.

## Measuring the round trip

The input says which tick the player saw: `seen`. A server that rewinds to `seen` trusts the client's word about its own lateness. A client that wants to interact from out of range can claim to have seen an earlier tick, when the courier was in range.

The server can't see when a client looked at its screen, but it can time a round trip itself. Every 10 ticks it sends a ping, the client answers with a pong, and the server keeps the last 20 round trips in milliseconds. A client can't answer a ping before the ping reaches it, as long as it can't guess the ping, which is why real servers put an unguessable number in each one. (This course's server numbers its pings by tick, and none of its clients exploits that.) So a measured round trip is never shorter than the real one. It can be longer, because a client can hold its pongs.

Write `measureRtt(samples)`: the largest of the last 20 samples, in ticks (milliseconds divided by 50), or 0 with no samples. The largest is the generous choice, because an honest player whose connection hiccups keeps the rewind its worst recent trip needs.

Check `15.measure-rtt` gives your function lists of every length, including more than 20 samples.

### Keep the worst recent trip

Tour `receivePong` in `public/courier.mjs`: a pong for a ping the server is still waiting on becomes one sample, the time it arrived less the time the ping left, and the oldest sample is dropped once there are more than `RTT_SAMPLES`. The server passes your function a copy of that list, oldest first. Replace the `measure-rtt` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/rewind-checkpoint.mjs","region":"measure-rtt","language":"js","title":"The largest of the recent samples, in ticks","change":"Replace the complete measure-rtt region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/rewind-checkpoint.mjs","region":"measure-rtt","title":"The largest of the recent samples, in ticks","change":"Replace the complete measure-rtt region."}
export function measureRtt(samples) {
  const recent = samples.slice(-RTT_SAMPLES);
  return recent.length ? Math.max(...recent) / TICK_MS : 0;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`slice(-RTT_SAMPLES)` keeps the newest samples whatever the list's length, so a slow trip that has dropped out of them no longer counts, and a list shorter than that is kept whole. Dividing by `TICK_MS` gives ticks with the fraction kept: a 210 ms trip is 4.2 ticks, and the judge rounds it up where it needs whole ticks. An empty list gives zero, not `-Infinity`, which is what `Math.max()` of nothing would be. The probe comes in three parts, and the lesson asks for each one at the point where you have what it shows. Its first part, `ring`, reads a ring the way the server's would be read and measures three lists of samples. It calls only the two functions written so far, so it prints the same on both routes:

```sh
node examples/try-rewind.mjs project ring
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/rewind-ring-output.txt","language":"text","title":"After position-at and measure-rtt: the ring and three round trips"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/rewind-ring-output.txt","title":"After position-at and measure-rtt: the ring and three round trips"}
A ring of 40 slots, written for ticks 0 to 44 with x = 1000 + 50 × tick:
  positionAt(ring, 44)   {"x":3200,"y":1000}
  positionAt(ring, 5)    {"x":1250,"y":1000}
  positionAt(ring, 4)    null: slot 4 now holds tick 44
  positionAt(ring, 45)   null: never written
  positionAt(ring, 2.5)  null: not a whole tick
measureRtt([])                                   0
measureRtt([210, 190, 205])                      4.2
measureRtt(25 samples: 400, then 100 24 times)   2
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The ring was written for ticks 0 to 44, so slots 0 to 4 now hold ticks 40 to 44, and asking for tick 4 gets null rather than the position of tick 44. In the last list, the 400 ms sample is the oldest of 25 and has dropped out of the last 20, so the round trip is 2 ticks.

## The judge

`now` is the tick being decided: the tick that starts at the boundary where the press was admitted. Write `judgeInteract(args)` in the order API.md gives: refuse a `seen` in the future, then refuse when the cooldown hasn't run out (judged at now, because the cooldown is the server's own clock), then rewind to `max(seen, now - allowed)` with `allowed = min(window, ceil(rtt) + 1)`, and accept when the courier stood within range there. The extra tick covers a press that lands between two ticks.

A claim older than the rewind allows is judged at the oldest tick allowed rather than refused, which is what an honest player with a bad moment needs.

```

```

```

### Judge at the moment the client may claim

Tour `interact` in `public/courier.mjs`: it is the only place the server decides a press, and it builds your judge's arguments from its own state: `seen` from the input that asked to interact, `now` the tick, `rtt` your `measureRtt` of its samples, `target` the core or the depot, and `readyAt` the cooldown's first free tick. Whatever your judge returns, the server accepts the press only when `accept` is `true`. Replace the `judge-interact` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/rewind-checkpoint.mjs","region":"judge-interact","language":"js","title":"Three refusals, then a rewind bounded twice","change":"Replace the complete judge-interact region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/rewind-checkpoint.mjs","region":"judge-interact","title":"Three refusals, then a rewind bounded twice","change":"Replace the complete judge-interact region."}
export function judgeInteract(args) {
  const { seen, now, window, rtt, history, target, range, readyAt } = args;
  const read = args.positionAt ?? positionAt;
  if (seen > now) return { accept: false, at: now, reason: 'future' };
  if (now < readyAt) return { accept: false, at: now, reason: 'cooldown' };
  const allowed = Math.min(window, Math.ceil(rtt) + 1);
  let at = Math.max(seen, now - allowed);
  let spot = read(history, at);
  if (!spot) {
    at = now;
    spot = read(history, now);
  }
  if (!spot) return { accept: false, at, reason: 'range' };
  const dx = spot.x - target.x;
  const dy = spot.y - target.y;
  const inRange = dx * dx + dy * dy <= range * range;
  return { accept: inRange, at, reason: inRange ? 'ok' : 'range' };
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The two refusals that don't look at the ring come first, and both are judged at `now`. A `seen` after `now` is a client claiming to have drawn a tick the server hasn't run. The cooldown belongs to the server's clock, so rewinding it would let a late press slip in under a cooldown that has already been running. Then the rewind: `Math.ceil` turns the round trip into whole ticks, the extra tick covers a press that lands between two ticks, and `Math.min` with the window means a client's round trip can only shrink the rewind, never stretch it past the limit you set. `Math.max(seen, ...)` means the judge never looks earlier than the tick the client says it saw, and a claim older than the bound is judged at the bound, not refused. If the ring has lost that tick, the press is judged at `now`, which the server always writes first. The range test compares squared distances, so it needs no square root, and a distance exactly at the range counts. `args.positionAt` is the reader the server was given, and the file's own `positionAt` stands in when a caller passes none.

You have committed questions 15a, 15b and 15c, so run the probe's other two parts. The second, `approach`, plays question 15a's approach on the real server at two windows:

```sh

```

Question 15a's approach, played on the real server, gives the answers to 15a and 15b. At window 0 the press is judged where the courier stands when it arrives, past the core, and refused. At window 2 the bound is `min(2, 4 + 1)`, so the judge looks two ticks back, where the courier stood one step past the core, and accepts. The `claim` part is question 15c's client: it claims a tick 6 back, its own round trip of one tick allows 2, so it is judged where it stood 2 ticks ago, out of range. A claim reaches no further back than the client's own round trip, plus a tick, allows.

## The window table

`runCourier` in `public/courier.mjs` plays sessions with three kinds of client:

- honest couriers on connections from 10 to 200 ms each way with up to 40 ms of jitter
- a naive faker on a 20 ms connection that answers pings honestly and claims to have seen up to 12 ticks earlier whenever that would put it in range
- a slow-pong faker on a 20 ms connection that holds its pongs, so its measured round trip looks like 300 to 400 ms, and claims to have seen accordingly

Each interaction comes back with whether it was accepted and two facts from the server's full record: was the courier in range at the tick the client claimed (`inRangeAtSeen`) and at the tick of the decision (`inRangeNow`). Write `tally(outcomes)` to turn them into one row: honest presses refused although the courier was in range at `seen` (legitimate rejections), and fakers' presses accepted although the courier was out of range at the decision (accepted cheats).

### Count one row of the table

Replace the `tally` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/rewind-checkpoint.mjs","region":"tally","language":"js","title":"Two kinds of error, counted per client","change":"Replace the complete tally region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/rewind-checkpoint.mjs","region":"tally","title":"Two kinds of error, counted per client","change":"Replace the complete tally region."}
export function tally(outcomes) {
  const row = {
    honest: 0,
    legit: 0,
    legitRate: 0,
    naive: 0,
    naiveCheats: 0,
    slow: 0,
    slowCheats: 0,
  };
  for (const o of outcomes) {
    const cheat = o.accepted && !o.inRangeNow;
    if (o.who === 'honest') {
      row.honest += 1;
      if (!o.accepted && o.inRangeAtSeen) row.legit += 1;
    } else if (o.who === 'naiveFaker') {
      row.naive += 1;
      if (cheat) row.naiveCheats += 1;
    } else if (o.who === 'slowPongFaker') {
      row.slow += 1;
      if (cheat) row.slowCheats += 1;
    }
  }
  row.legitRate = row.honest ? row.legit / row.honest : 0;
  return row;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

Each outcome counts once, under its client. The two errors are judged by different facts, on purpose. An honest press is a legitimate rejection when it was refused although the courier was in range at the tick the player saw, because that is the moment the player acted on. A faker's press is a cheat when it was accepted although the courier was out of range at the tick of the decision, because the server gave it something its courier wasn't standing close enough to earn. The rate is over all honest presses, and it is zero, not `NaN`, when there are none. Check `15.tally` gives your `tally` crafted outcomes, and check `15.sweep` runs the courier with your functions on its own seeds and compares every decision with the server's record.

Question 15d: here are four rows of the table you will run in a moment:

- window 0, legitimate rate 20.8%, slow-pong cheats 0
- window 4, 4.7%, 4,681
- window 6, 2.0%, 13,279
- window 8, 0.0%, 22,283

### Pick the window that lets the fewest lies through

Replace the `pick-window` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/rewind-checkpoint.mjs","region":"pick-window","language":"js","title":"Within the budget, the fewest slow-pong cheats","change":"Replace the complete pick-window region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/rewind-checkpoint.mjs","region":"pick-window","title":"Within the budget, the fewest slow-pong cheats","change":"Replace the complete pick-window region."}
export function pickWindow(rows, budget) {
  let best = null;
  for (const row of rows) {
    if (row.legitRate > budget) continue;
    const fewer = !best || row.slowCheats < best.slowCheats;
    const tie = best && row.slowCheats === best.slowCheats;
    if (fewer || (tie && row.window < best.window)) best = row;
  }
  return best ? best.window : null;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

A row over the budget is skipped, whatever it costs the faker. Among the rest, a row replaces the best so far when it lets fewer slow-pong cheats through, or as many from a smaller window, so a tie goes to the smaller window and the answer doesn't depend on the order of the rows. When no row is within the budget there is nothing to choose, and the answer is null rather than the least bad window. Only the slow-pong column decides, because the naive faker is already bounded by its own round trip. Check `15.pick` gives your `pickWindow` crafted rows, including ties and a budget nothing meets.

Read it a column at a time.

- At window 0, 20.77% of honest presses are refused although the courier was in range when the player pressed. These are players whose round trip is longer than about 100 to 150 ms and who walk onto the target without slowing down. The rate falls as the window grows: 0.24% at window 7, and 0 at window 8. The slowest honest round trip is 480 ms, nearly 10 ticks, and the in-range zone is three positions wide, so 8 ticks back always reaches it. The number of honest presses changes a little with the window, because a refused player walks back and presses again. Between sets of sessions it changes more, as the last point below says.
- The naive faker gets nothing through, with 0 accepted at every window. It answers pings honestly, so its own round trip bounds its rewind, and every claim older than that bound is judged where the courier was out of range.
- The slow-pong faker's pongs make its round trips look like 300 to 400 ms. The largest of its last 20 is typically about 370 ms, so its own bound allows 8 or 9 ticks, and only the window limits it. From window 3 on it gets claims through: 20,123 of its 22,211 presses at window 7, and 22,283 of 22,311 at window 8.
- The deliveries column shows what accepted claims buy. Both fakers play the same way. They touch the target's range, turn straight back, and press later claiming the tick of the touch. The naive faker's claims are always cut short, so it walks back and delivers 41.2 parcels a session at every window. The slow-pong faker delivers 50.3 at window 0, 105.5 at window 7 and 111.2 at window 8, where nearly all its claims count. The honest column moves most from one set of sessions to the next. This table is one set, seed 1, where honest couriers deliver 33.1 parcels a session at window 0; seeds 2 and 3 give 39.3 and 40.6 there. So compare the honest and slow-pong columns within one seed's table, and read a gain from one table as that seed's.

The last two lines are your `pickWindow`'s answers for two budgets. A budget of 1% refused honest presses allows window 7, and at window 7 the slow-pong faker gets 91% of its claims through. A budget of 2% allows window 6, and the faker still gets 62% through. No window serves every honest player and refuses the faker, because at the server both send a press that claims an old tick, from a client whose pongs say it's far away.

`courses/anti-cheat-engineering-part-two/lessons/16.md`:

```md
# 16 · The duplicated item

Two players agree a trade, in which Ana sells Bo her sword for 40 coins. The server has four things to write: the sword into Bo's inventory, the sword out of Ana's, 40 coins out of Bo's purse, 40 into Ana's. If the server stops between two of those writes, and the client, getting no answer, sends the request again, the world can end up in a state no trade could have produced. Players who find such a crash can make it happen on purpose, as often as they like.

By the end of this lesson your `trade/trade.mjs` will carry out a trade so that a crash after any single write, followed by recovery and the client's retry, leaves every item in exactly one inventory and the coins either where they were or where the trade put them, never between. A request sent twice will be carried out once.

The fixes in this lesson come from outside games. Payment services give each request a key chosen by the client, and answer a repeated key with the stored result instead of charging again. Databases write down what they are about to do before doing it, so that after a restart they can finish it. This is called write-ahead logging.

Only `node lab.mjs crash project --naive`, which runs the store's own naive trade, has anything to show.

**After this unit** your `trade` writes what it will do before doing it, writes absolute values, and marks the trade done with its receipt; a request sent again gets that receipt back; and your `recover` finishes whatever a crash interrupted. `node lab.mjs crash project` then finds nothing wrong at any of its crash points.

## Four writes and a crash

The store in this lesson stands for any game server that keeps items, and it isn't part of Lob or the courier arena. `public/store.mjs` keeps every player's belongings: `inv:ana` is a list of item ids, `coins:ana` a whole number. The operations you need are `get`, `put`, `keys`, `crashAfter` and `restart`, and API.md's unit 16 says what each does. Each `put` is durable the moment it returns, and nothing is bigger than one `put`, meaning there is no transaction across two keys. `crashAfter(n)` makes the n-th put from now apply and then throw, as if the server died the moment that write reached the disk.

Tour `createStore` in `public/store.mjs` now. In `put`, the value is stored and counted before the crash is thrown, so the write that crashes has happened; once the store is down every later `put` throws until `restart`, while `get` keeps working, because the data is on disk and only the server stopped. `naiveTrade` in the same file is a trade as it's often first written: the four puts in a row, in the order above.

The server restarts and the client sends the same request again, and this time it runs to the end. Who holds a sword afterwards? ## Request keys

The first fix is for the retry. Each request carries a `key` the client chose, and when the trade is carried out, the server stores its receipt, `{ key, seller, buyer, item, price }`, under the key. A trade's receipt is its answer to the client and has nothing to do with the lab's receipt (README.md, "Start"). A request whose key was already carried out with the same body gets that receipt back and writes nothing.

Question 16c: a request with key `k1` (Ana sells Bo the sword for 40) has been carried out. The client sends key `k1` again, with price 45. What should `trade` return: `ok`, or a reason from API.md's list?

```
node lab.mjs predict project 16c YOUR_ANSWER
```

A request that reuses a key with a different body is refused `conflict`, because the client has a bug, and guessing which body it meant would be worse.

Keys alone don't fix a crash. If the receipt is written last, a crash before it leaves half a trade and no receipt, and the retry runs the trade again on top of the half.

## Write what you will do first

The second fix is to write the whole trade down before touching anything. Your first write is a journal entry under a key of your own, for example `trade:<key>`, holding the request and the values the trade will change, read before any change: Ana's items, Bo's items, Ana's coins, Bo's coins. Then write the end state, computed from those values. Then mark the entry done with the receipt.

Write absolute values, not changes. "Bo has 40 coins" written twice leaves Bo with 40. "Take 40 from Bo" done twice takes 80. With absolute values computed from the journal, finishing a trade is safe to repeat.

Read each value with care, too, because a key can be missing. A player who has never held coins has no `coins:` key in the store at all, and `store.get` returns `undefined` for a key that was never written. In JavaScript, `undefined` plus or minus a number gives `NaN` ("not a number"), so arithmetic on a missing key writes a value that isn't a number. API.md therefore says to read a missing inventory as an empty list and missing coins as zero. Reading the four values once, before any change, puts that rule in one place, and every write is then computed from those values.

The order of the four writes matters too. Take before you give, removing the sword from Ana before adding it to Bo and taking Bo's coins before paying Ana. Then a crash between two writes leaves the sword or the coins in the journal for a moment, never in two places. The checks look at the world only after recovery, so they don't test this order, but it matters to anything that reads the store between a crash and its recovery.

Question 16b: with the journal written first and absolute writes, a crash happens after the write that adds the sword to Bo. Recovery finishes the trade from the journal. How many coins does Bo have afterwards, starting from 100? Commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 16b YOUR_ANSWER
```

### Finish a trade from its journal entry

The journal entry in this walkthrough is `{ state, body, before }`: `state` is `pending` until the trade is done, `body` is the request without its key, and `before` holds the four values read before any change. One function writes a trade's end state from that entry, and both `trade` and recovery call it. In `trade/trade.mjs`, replace the `finish` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/trade-checkpoint.mjs","region":"finish","language":"js","title":"The end state from the journal, then the done mark","change":"Replace the complete finish region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/trade-checkpoint.mjs","region":"finish","title":"The end state from the journal, then the done mark","change":"Replace the complete finish region."}
function finish(store, key, entry) {
  const { seller, buyer, item, price } = entry.body;
  const { sellerItems, buyerItems, sellerCoins, buyerCoins } = entry.before;
  store.put(
    `inv:${seller}`,
    sellerItems.filter((id) => id !== item),
  );
  store.put(`inv:${buyer}`, [...buyerItems, item]);
  store.put(`coins:${buyer}`, buyerCoins - price);
  store.put(`coins:${seller}`, sellerCoins + price);
  const receipt = { key, ...entry.body };
  store.put(`trade:${key}`, { ...entry, state: 'done', receipt });
  return receipt;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

Every value `finish` writes comes from the entry, never from the store as it is now. Ana's items are her items before the trade without the sword, Bo's coins are his coins before the trade less the price, and so on. A crash can stop `finish` after any of its writes, and running it again from the start writes the same five values, so a write that already happened is written again unchanged. The four moves take before they give: the sword leaves Ana before it reaches Bo, and Bo pays before Ana is paid. The last write keeps the whole entry, marks it `done` and adds the receipt, and only that write makes the trade finished: a crash before it leaves the entry `pending`, so recovery will run `finish` again. The receipt is the request's key with its body, which is what a retry gets back.

## Recovery

After a crash the server restarts and calls `recover(store)` before it serves anything. Recovery reads every journal entry that isn't done and finishes it. A crash can happen during recovery as well. The server restarts and calls it again, and because every write is absolute, finishing twice is the same as finishing once.

### Roll every pending entry forward

Replace the `recover` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/trade-checkpoint.mjs","region":"recover","language":"js","title":"Finish every entry still pending","change":"Replace the complete recover region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/trade-checkpoint.mjs","region":"recover","title":"Finish every entry still pending","change":"Replace the complete recover region."}
export function recover(store) {
  const finished = [];
  for (const name of store.keys('trade:')) {
    const entry = store.get(name);
    if (entry.state !== 'pending') continue;
    const key = name.slice('trade:'.length);
    finish(store, key, entry);
    finished.push(key);
  }
  return finished;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`store.keys('trade:')` lists every journal entry, sorted, so recovery always works in the same order. An entry already `done` is skipped: its trade is finished, and writing it again would only repeat the done mark. Each pending entry is finished from its own `before`, and its request key, the store key without `trade:`, goes in the answer, so the list holds the trades this call finished and no others. A crash during `finish` stops recovery with that entry still pending, so the next call finishes it again, from the same values.

The probe runs your `recover` on the sale as a crash left it right after write 1, when only the journal entry exists, and right after write 5, when only the done mark is missing, and then runs it again. It writes the pending entry itself, in this walkthrough's form. On the type-in route `trade` is still a hole, so the probe stops there:

```sh
node examples/try-trade.mjs project
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/trade-partial-output.txt","language":"text","title":"After finish and recover: trade is still a hole"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/trade-partial-output.txt","title":"After finish and recover: trade is still a hole"}
The sale as a crash right after write 1 left it: ana [sword lamp] 20, bo [bow] 100; trade:sale-1 pending
  recover(store) -> ["sale-1"], writing inv:ana, inv:bo, coins:bo, coins:ana, trade:sale-1 done
  now: ana [lamp] 60, bo [bow sword] 60; trade:sale-1 done
  recover(store) again -> [], writing nothing
The sale as a crash right after write 5 left it: ana [lamp] 60, bo [bow sword] 60; trade:sale-1 pending
  recover(store) -> ["sale-1"], writing inv:ana, inv:bo, coins:bo, coins:ana, trade:sale-1 done
  now: ana [lamp] 60, bo [bow sword] 60; trade:sale-1 done
  recover(store) again -> [], writing nothing
trade: not written yet
```
<!-- /code-example -->

Both crash points end in the same world, the trade wholly done. After write 5 recovery writes all five values again, and only the done mark changes anything. A second `recover` finds nothing pending and writes nothing.

The order of the checks in `trade` is in API.md: shape, a seller selling to themselves, then the key, then whether the seller holds the item and the buyer has the coins. A refusal writes nothing.

### Answer from the key, then write the journal first

Tour `wellFormed` at the top of `trade/trade.mjs` first: it is supplied, and it refuses any request whose keys aren't exactly the five, whose names aren't 1 to 40 of the allowed characters, or whose price isn't a whole number of 0 or more, the same strictness as lesson 12's admission. Then, in `trade`, replace the `trade-key` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/trade-checkpoint.mjs","region":"trade-key","language":"js","title":"Shape, self, then the key","change":"Replace the complete trade-key region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/trade-checkpoint.mjs","region":"trade-key","title":"Shape, self, then the key","change":"Replace the complete trade-key region."}
  if (!wellFormed(request)) return { ok: false, reason: 'shape' };
  if (request.seller === request.buyer) return { ok: false, reason: 'self' };
  recover(store);
  const body = {
    seller: request.seller,
    buyer: request.buyer,
    item: request.item,
    price: request.price,
  };
  const done = store.get(`trade:${request.key}`);
  if (done) {
    if (JSON.stringify(done.body) !== JSON.stringify(body))
      return { ok: false, reason: 'conflict' };
    return { ok: true, receipt: done.receipt };
  }
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The two checks that need nothing from the store come first. Then `recover(store)` finishes any trade a crash left pending, so a key whose trade was interrupted is answered from a finished entry rather than a half-made one. The key is looked up before anything about the items, which is why a retry after the trade went through gets its receipt and not `missing`: Ana no longer holds the sword, because the trade gave it away. The bodies are compared as `JSON.stringify` of objects built in the same field order, so a different price, item or player is a `conflict`, and a conflict writes nothing. Then replace the `trade-journal` region below it:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/trade-checkpoint.mjs","region":"trade-journal","language":"js","title":"Read, refuse, write the journal, finish","change":"Replace the complete trade-journal region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/trade-checkpoint.mjs","region":"trade-journal","title":"Read, refuse, write the journal, finish","change":"Replace the complete trade-journal region."}
  const sellerItems = store.get(`inv:${body.seller}`) ?? [];
  const buyerItems = store.get(`inv:${body.buyer}`) ?? [];
  const sellerCoins = store.get(`coins:${body.seller}`) ?? 0;
  const buyerCoins = store.get(`coins:${body.buyer}`) ?? 0;
  if (!sellerItems.includes(body.item)) return { ok: false, reason: 'missing' };
  if (buyerCoins < body.price) return { ok: false, reason: 'funds' };
  const before = { sellerItems, buyerItems, sellerCoins, buyerCoins };
  const entry = { state: 'pending', body, before };
  store.put(`trade:${request.key}`, entry);
  return { ok: true, receipt: finish(store, request.key, entry) };
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The four values are read once, before any write, with a missing inventory as an empty list and missing coins as zero, as API.md says. A refusal returns before the first `put`, so it writes nothing, and since its key was never stored, a later request with the same key is a new trade. The journal entry is the first write, holding the values just read, and `finish` does the rest from it. Run the probe again:

```sh
node examples/try-trade.mjs project
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/trade-output.txt","language":"text","title":"Recovery, the six writes of a sale, a retry, a conflict and a crash"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/trade-output.txt","title":"Recovery, the six writes of a sale, a retry, a conflict and a crash"}
The sale as a crash right after write 1 left it: ana [sword lamp] 20, bo [bow] 100; trade:sale-1 pending

  now: ana [lamp] 60, bo [bow sword] 60; trade:sale-1 done
  recover(store) again -> [], writing nothing
The sale as a crash right after write 5 left it: ana [lamp] 60, bo [bow sword] 60; trade:sale-1 pending
  recover(store) -> ["sale-1"], writing inv:ana, inv:bo, coins:bo, coins:ana, trade:sale-1 done
  now: ana [lamp] 60, bo [bow sword] 60; trade:sale-1 done

sale-1, Ana sells Bo the sword for 40, with no crash: ok, receipt {"key":"sale-1","seller":"ana","buyer":"bo","item":"sword","price":40}
  write 1: trade:sale-1 pending
  write 2: inv:ana ["lamp"]
  write 3: inv:bo ["bow","sword"]

  write 6: trade:sale-1 done
the same request again: ok, receipt {"key":"sale-1","seller":"ana","buyer":"bo","item":"sword","price":40}, writing nothing
the same key, price 45: conflict, writing nothing
A crash right after write 3: ana [lamp] 20, bo [bow sword] 100; trade:sale-1 pending
  restart, recover(store) -> ["sale-1"]: ana [lamp] 60, bo [bow sword] 60
  the client's retry: ok, receipt {"key":"sale-1","seller":"ana","buyer":"bo","item":"sword","price":40}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The sale is six writes, in the order the next section lists. The retry gets the same receipt and writes nothing, and so does the refused conflict. A crash right after write 3 leaves the sword moved and no coins, with the entry pending; recovery finishes the sale from the journal, and the retry is answered from the key.

## Crash at every write

Check `16.crash-trade` does what an attacker pulling the plug would do, at every place they could pull it. For each write of a trade it runs the trade with a crash after that write, restarts, recovers, sends the client's retry, and then checks the world. Every item in exactly one inventory, the total of all coins unchanged, the trade wholly done or not at all, and the retry's receipt the same as the trade's. Check `16.crash-recover` crashes recovery at each of its writes too.

With a journal entry, the four moves and the done mark, a sale is six writes:

1. `trade:<key>`: pending, with the request and the values read before any change
2. `inv:ana` without the sword
3. `inv:bo` with the sword
4. `coins:bo` less 40
5. `coins:ana` plus 40
6. `trade:<key>`: done, with the receipt

So the command tries six crash points. A crash after write 1 leaves only the journal entry, and recovery does all the rest. A crash after write 5 leaves only the done mark missing, and recovery writes all five again from the journal, which changes nothing but the mark, because every write is absolute. Run it:

```sh
node lab.mjs crash project
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/crash-output.txt","language":"text","title":"node lab.mjs crash project, after unit 16"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/crash-output.txt","title":"node lab.mjs crash project, after unit 16"}
Crash test: your trade and recover.
  start: ana [sword lamp] 20, bo [bow] 100, cy [cap] 60 (coins 180)
  script: 1. sale-1: ana sells bo the sword for 40; 2. sale-2: ana sells cy the sword for 30
  without a crash: sale-1 ok, sale-2 missing; 6 writes in all, so 6 crash points.
  At each crash point the server restarts, runs your recover, and the client sends the interrupted request again.

1     sale-1   ["sale-1"]  sword: bo; coins 180        ok       sword: bo; coins 180        missing  0

<!-- /code-example -->

Your design may use more or fewer writes. The count of crash points changes, but the number of violations may not. Check `16.trade` covers the refusals and the receipt, and check `16.double-sell` sells one item to two buyers, with and without a crash in the first sale, and requires that one sale succeeds, the other is refused as `missing`, and the item's new owner can sell it on.

### Break one rule, then repair it

In your project only, make the buyer's coin write relative: in `finish`, change `` store.put(`coins:${buyer}`, buyerCoins - price); `` to `` store.put(`coins:${buyer}`, store.get(`coins:${buyer}`) - price); ``.

## Use the idea on a new case

Players also want to swap: Ana gives Bo her sword, and Bo gives Ana his bow, with no coins. A swap needs the same guarantees as a sale: after a crash at any write, and after a crash during recovery, each item is in exactly one inventory, the swap happened wholly or not at all, and a retry gets the receipt.

Write `swap(store, request)` and `recoverSwaps(store)` in `trade/swap.mjs`. The comment at the top of that file gives the contract: `request` is `{ key, a, b, itemA, itemB }`, the receipt is the same five fields, and the reasons, in order, are `self`, `conflict` and `missing`. Keep swaps under journal keys of their own, such as `swap:<key>`, so your `recover` for trades never meets one.

Before writing code, answer in `project/report.md`: list your swap's writes in order, as the six writes of a sale are listed above, and for a crash right after each one, say what the world looks like and what `recoverSwaps` will write.

Then run the supplied checker on the unfinished file once, implement, and run it again, describing your help each time:

```sh
node examples/check-swap.mjs project --help-used "first run; swap not written"
node examples/check-swap.mjs project --help-used "describe what helped you"
```

Each run copies your trade and swap files and your report into a new folder under `project/attempts/`, and saves its results beside them in `swap-receipt.json`; a later run never replaces an earlier one, and `node lab.mjs status project` lists every run among your other attempts. The checker runs one swap with no crash and counts its writes, then crashes it after each of them, and also crashes `recoverSwaps` after each of its writes, and after each it checks the world as `16.crash-trade` does. It also sends the same request twice, a conflicting key, and requests that must be refused. `trade/swap.mjs` isn't one of the unit's checked files, so this doesn't change your trade. A pass is not your explanation: in your report, compare the writes the checker counted with your list, and say which of your writes recovery depends on and why.

# 17 · The scoreboard

Five lessons built five defences, each measured on its own. A defence is judged as a whole. A strict admission that refuses an honest player's message, or a detector tuned so tightly that it flags experts, fails as surely as one that lets a cheat through. This lesson runs everything at once.

By the end of it you will have chosen your courier window, run the scoreboard, and met every budget below on sessions you have never seen.

## Start

This lesson builds on your unit 16 project: keep working in the same folder. Run every command from the course's folder, the one that holds `lab.mjs`.

**What is new.** Almost no code. Everything the scoreboard plays is yours already: your admission and recorder from lesson 12, your view from lesson 13, your frozen detector from lesson 14, your judge from lesson 15 and your trade from lesson 16. The one new file is `capstone/defence.json`, which holds the window you chose in lesson 15 and your sentence on why. This lesson is about reading the whole defence's numbers and judging them.

**Before this unit** `capstone/defence.json` is the starter's, so `node lab.mjs scoreboard project` stops before it plays anything, with `capstone/defence.json: not written yet`.
