```mjs
#!/usr/bin/env node
import {readFile, writeFile, mkdir} from 'node:fs/promises';
import {resolve, dirname, join} from 'node:path';
import {fileURLToPath, pathToFileURL} from 'node:url';
import {createHash} from 'node:crypto';
import {Worker} from 'node:worker_threads';
import {readJournal, appendRecord, exportJournal, importJournal, flattenedRecords, latestAttempt, assistanceFor, questionHash} from './lib/journal.mjs';

const ROOT = dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));
// Reliability limit for JavaScript heaps, not an OS memory or security boundary.
const WORKER_LIMITS={maxOldGenerationSizeMb:192,maxYoungGenerationSizeMb:32,stackSizeMb:4};
const hash = source => createHash('sha256').update(source).digest('hex');
const args = process.argv.slice(2);
const command = args.shift() ?? 'help';
function option(name, fallback = undefined) {
  const position = args.indexOf(`--${name}`);
  if (position < 0) return fallback;
  if (position === args.length - 1 || args[position + 1].startsWith('--')) throw new Error(`--${name} needs a value.`);
  return args[position + 1];
}
const journalPath = resolve(option('journal', join(ROOT, 'work', 'attempts.json')));
const print = value => process.stdout.write(typeof value === 'string' ? value + '\n' : JSON.stringify(value, null, 2) + '\n');
const readJSON = async file => JSON.parse(await readFile(file, 'utf8'));

async function catalog() {
  const lessons = [];
  for (const file of ['lesson-index.json', 'advanced-index.json', 'capstone-index.json']) {
    try {
      const value = await readJSON(join(ROOT, 'lessons', file));
      lessons.push(...(Array.isArray(value) ? value : value.lessons));
    } catch (error) { if (error.code !== 'ENOENT') throw error; }
  }
  return lessons.sort((a, b) => a.id.localeCompare(b.id, undefined, {numeric: true}));
}
async function itemById(id) {
  const lessons = await catalog();
  for (const lesson of lessons) {
    if (lesson.id === id && lesson.question) return {...lesson, lessonId: lesson.id};
    const items = [...(lesson.practice ?? []), ...(lesson.items ?? [])];
    if (lesson.prediction && typeof lesson.prediction === 'object') items.push(lesson.prediction);
    const item = items.find(candidate => candidate.id === id);
    if (item) return {...item, lessonId: lesson.id};
  }
  throw new Error(`Unknown practice item ${id}. Use node cli.mjs list and read its lesson.`);
}
async function practiceFeedback(id, kind) {
  const item = await itemById(id);
  const document = await readJournal(journalPath);
  const attempt = latestAttempt(document, id);
  if (!attempt) throw new Error(`Commit your own response first: node cli.mjs attempt ${id} --answer 'your answer'`);
  if (attempt.data.questionHash !== questionHash(item)) throw new Error('This question changed after your saved attempt. Read the current question and commit a new response. The original question and answer remain preserved.');
  const feedback = {};
  for (const file of ['practice-feedback.json', 'advanced-feedback.json', 'capstone-feedback.json']) {
    try { Object.assign(feedback, await readJSON(join(ROOT, file))); }
    catch (error) { if (error.code !== 'ENOENT') throw error; }
  }
  const entry = feedback[id] ?? feedback.items?.[id];
  if (!entry) throw new Error(`Feedback for ${id} is unavailable. Your attempt is saved.`);
  if (kind === 'hint') {
    const level = Number(option('level', '1'));
    if (![1, 2, 3].includes(level)) throw new Error('Hint level must be 1, 2 or 3.');
    const content = entry.hints?.[level - 1];
    if (!content) throw new Error(`No level-${level} hint is available for ${id}.`);
    await appendRecord(journalPath, 'hint', {itemId: id, questionHash: questionHash(item), attemptId: attempt.id, level, content});
    print(`Saved hint exposure (level ${level}). Subsequent attempts record this assistance.\n\n${content}`);
    return;
  }
  await appendRecord(journalPath, 'feedback', {itemId: id, questionHash: questionHash(item), attemptId: attempt.id, feedbackHash: hash(JSON.stringify(entry)),content:entry});
  print(`Your committed response:\n${attempt.data.response}\n\nCompare with:\n${entry.answer}\n\nWhy:\n${entry.reason}`);
  if (entry.rubric?.length) print('Self-check criteria:\n' + entry.rubric.map(line => `- ${line}`).join('\n'));
  print('\nThis is practice feedback, not an automatic grade of your reasoning. Revise with another attempt; your first response remains saved.');
}
async function checkLearner(module) {
  if (module === 'baseline') module = '1';
  if (!['1', '2', '3', '4', '5', '6', 'evaluation', 'search'].includes(module)) throw new Error('Use check 1 through check 6, or baseline/evaluation/search.');
  const fileGroups = {'1':['baseline.mjs'], '2':['evaluation.mjs','search.mjs'], evaluation:['evaluation.mjs'], search:['evaluation.mjs','search.mjs'], '3':['value-model.mjs'], '4':['report.mjs'], '5':['opponent-sampler.mjs'], '6':['vulnerability.mjs']};
  const files = fileGroups[module];
  const snapshots = [];
  for (const file of files) {
    const path = join(ROOT, 'learner', file);
    const source = await readFile(path, 'utf8');
    snapshots.push({file, source, sha256: hash(source)});
  }
  const {captureSourceBundle}=await import('./lib/league-config.mjs');
  const dependencies=await captureSourceBundle(ROOT);
  const committed = await appendRecord(journalPath, 'code-attempt', {module, files: snapshots,dependencyManifest:dependencies.codeManifest,dependencySources:dependencies.codeBundle});
  const result = await new Promise(resolveResult => {
    const worker = new Worker(new URL('./lib/check-worker.mjs', import.meta.url), {workerData: {root: ROOT, module}, stdout: true, stderr: true, resourceLimits:WORKER_LIMITS});
    let settled = false;
    const finish = value => {
      if (settled) return;
      settled = true;
      clearTimeout(timer);
      worker.terminate();
      resolveResult(value);
    };
    const timer = setTimeout(() => finish({ok: false, error: 'The check exceeded 8 seconds and was stopped. Inspect your loops or recursion. This interruption is not a game loss.', interrupted: true}), 8000);
    worker.once('message', finish);
    worker.once('error', error => finish({ok: false, error: error.message}));
    worker.once('exit', code => finish({ok: false, error: `Check worker exited before returning a result (code ${code}).`}));
    worker.stdout.resume();
    worker.stderr.resume();
  });
  for (const snapshot of snapshots) {
    const currentSource = await readFile(join(ROOT, 'learner', snapshot.file), 'utf8');
    if (hash(currentSource) !== snapshot.sha256) {
      result.ok = false;
      result.sourceChanged = `The file ${snapshot.file} changed during the check. This result cannot qualify the saved attempt. Run the check again.`;
    }
  }
  const afterDependencies=await captureSourceBundle(ROOT);
  if(JSON.stringify(afterDependencies.codeManifest)!==JSON.stringify(dependencies.codeManifest)) {
    result.ok=false;
    result.sourceChanged='A captured local dependency changed during the check. Repeat with a stable source version.';
  }
  await appendRecord(journalPath, 'code-feedback', {attemptId: committed.id, module, result});
  print(result);
  print(`\nSource attempt ${committed.id} and actual checker result saved. This is practice feedback, not full-course acceptance.`);
  if (!result.ok) process.exitCode = 1;
}
async function playDemo() {
  const {generateScenario} = await import('./lib/game.mjs');
  const {snapshotPolicy, runMatch} = await import('./lib/runner.mjs');
  const supplied = await import('./lib/supplied-policies.mjs');
  const names = Object.keys(supplied);
  const random = supplied.randomPolicy ?? supplied.random ?? supplied.randomAction;
  const greedy = supplied.greedyPolicy ?? supplied.greedy ?? supplied.greedyAction;
  if (typeof random !== 'function' || typeof greedy !== 'function') throw new Error(`Supplied policy adapter needs review: ${names.join(', ')}`);
  const seed = Number(option('seed', '7'));
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(seed) || seed < 0 || seed > 0xffffffff) throw new Error('Seed must be an unsigned 32-bit integer.');
  const policies = [snapshotPolicy({name: 'supplied-random', decide: random}), snapshotPolicy({name: 'supplied-greedy', decide: greedy})];
  const record = runMatch({policies, scenario: generateScenario(seed, 4), seed, budget: 256, planId: 'supplied-demo-v1'});
  const destination = resolve(option('out', join(ROOT, 'work', 'demo.json')));
  await mkdir(dirname(destination), {recursive: true});
  await writeFile(destination, JSON.stringify(record, null, 2) + '\n', {flag: 'wx'});
  print(`Supplied baseline demonstration saved to ${destination}.\nThis is not learner work. Open index.html and choose this file to inspect the replay.`);
  print(record.result ?? {status: record.status});
}
async function playLeague(configuration) {
  if(!configuration) throw new Error('Provide a league configuration, for example development-league.json.');
  const path=resolve(configuration);
  const configurationText=await readFile(path,'utf8');
  const committed=await appendRecord(journalPath,'league-attempt',{configuration:JSON.parse(configurationText),configurationHash:hash(configurationText)});
  const result=await new Promise(resolveResult=>{
    const worker=new Worker(new URL('./lib/league-worker.mjs',import.meta.url),{workerData:{root:ROOT,configuration:path},stdout:true,stderr:true,resourceLimits:WORKER_LIMITS});
    let settled=false;
    const finish=value=>{if(settled)return;settled=true;clearTimeout(timer);worker.terminate();resolveResult(value);};
    const timer=setTimeout(()=>finish({ok:false,error:'League exceeded the 60-second local run limit and was stopped. This is an incomplete run, not a scored loss. Reduce the development roster or inspect policy code.'}),60000);
    worker.once('message',finish);worker.once('error',error=>finish({ok:false,error:error.message}));worker.once('exit',code=>finish({ok:false,error:`League worker stopped without a complete result (${code}).`}));
    worker.stdout.resume();worker.stderr.resume();
  });
  if(!result.ok){await appendRecord(journalPath,'league-result',{attemptId:committed.id,complete:false,error:result.error});throw new Error(result.error);}
  if(result.season.configurationHash!==hash(configurationText)||hash(await readFile(path,'utf8'))!==hash(configurationText)) {
    const error='League configuration changed during the run. Repeat with a frozen configuration.';
    await appendRecord(journalPath,'league-result',{attemptId:committed.id,complete:false,error});throw new Error(error);
  }
  const destination=resolve(option('out',join(ROOT,'work','season.json')));
  await mkdir(dirname(destination),{recursive:true});
  await writeFile(destination,JSON.stringify(result.season,null,2)+'\n',{flag:'wx'});
  await appendRecord(journalPath,'league-result',{attemptId:committed.id,complete:true,output:destination,seasonHash:hash(JSON.stringify(result.season)),matches:result.season.matches.length});
  print({saved:destination,matches:result.season.matches.length,partition:result.season.plan.partition,note:'Actual match records and source bundle saved. A development run is not final evaluation or full-course completion.'});
}

async function verifyRecord(filename) {
  if(!filename) throw new Error('Provide a match or season JSON file to verify.');
  const path = resolve(filename);
  const bytes = await readFile(path);
  const configuration = option('configuration');
  const result = await new Promise(resolveResult => {
    const worker = new Worker(new URL('./lib/verify-worker.mjs', import.meta.url), {workerData:{root:ROOT,record:path,configuration:configuration?resolve(configuration):null},stdout:true,stderr:true,resourceLimits:WORKER_LIMITS});
    let settled=false;
    const finish=value=>{if(settled)return;settled=true;clearTimeout(timer);worker.terminate();resolveResult(value);};
    const timer=setTimeout(()=>finish({ok:false,error:'Verification exceeded 60 seconds and was interrupted. No successful verification is claimed.'}),60000);
    worker.once('message',finish);worker.once('error',error=>finish({ok:false,error:error.message}));worker.once('exit',code=>finish({ok:false,error:`Verification worker ended without a result (${code}).`}));
    worker.stdout.resume();worker.stderr.resume();
  });
  if(hash(await readFile(path)) !== hash(bytes)) {result.ok=false;result.error='The record changed during verification. Run the check again.';}
  await appendRecord(journalPath,'replay-verification',{input:path,inputHash:hash(bytes),result});
  print(result);
  if(!result.ok) process.exitCode=1;
}

async function makeReport(filename) {
  if(!filename) throw new Error('Provide a completed season JSON file.');
  const path=resolve(filename);
  const bytes=await readFile(path);
  const source=await readFile(join(ROOT,'learner/report.mjs'),'utf8');
  const committed=await appendRecord(journalPath,'report-attempt',{seasonHash:hash(bytes),source,sourceHash:hash(source)});
  const result=await new Promise(resolveResult=>{
    const worker=new Worker(new URL('./lib/report-worker.mjs',import.meta.url),{workerData:{root:ROOT,season:path},stdout:true,stderr:true,resourceLimits:WORKER_LIMITS});
    let settled=false;
    const finish=value=>{if(settled)return;settled=true;clearTimeout(timer);worker.terminate();resolveResult(value);};
    const timer=setTimeout(()=>finish({ok:false,error:'Report exceeded 8 seconds and was interrupted.'}),8000);
    worker.once('message',finish);worker.once('error',error=>finish({ok:false,error:error.message}));worker.once('exit',code=>finish({ok:false,error:`Report worker ended without a result (${code}).`}));
    worker.stdout.resume();worker.stderr.resume();
  });
  if(hash(await readFile(path))!==hash(bytes)||hash(await readFile(join(ROOT,'learner/report.mjs'),'utf8'))!==hash(source)) {result.ok=false;result.error='Report source or season changed during execution. Try again.';}
  if(!result.ok){await appendRecord(journalPath,'report-result',{attemptId:committed.id,...result});throw new Error(result.error);}
  const destination=resolve(option('out',join(ROOT,'work','report.json')));
  await mkdir(dirname(destination),{recursive:true});
  const evidence={schemaVersion:1,type:'learner-league-report',seasonHash:hash(bytes),sourceHash:hash(source),codeManifest:result.codeManifest,codeBundle:result.codeBundle,report:result.report,scope:'Learner-produced interpretation. Passing public checks and independent evidence review are separate requirements.'};
  await writeFile(destination,JSON.stringify(evidence,null,2)+'\n',{flag:'wx'});
  await appendRecord(journalPath,'report-result',{attemptId:committed.id,ok:true,output:destination,reportHash:hash(JSON.stringify(evidence))});
  print({saved:destination,report:result.report,scope:evidence.scope});
}

async function train(configuration) {
  if(!configuration) throw new Error('Provide a training configuration, for example development-training.json.');
  const path=resolve(configuration),source=await readFile(path,'utf8');
  const committed=await appendRecord(journalPath,'training-attempt',{configuration:JSON.parse(source),configurationHash:hash(source)});
  const result=await new Promise(resolveResult=>{
    const worker=new Worker(new URL('./lib/training-worker.mjs',import.meta.url),{workerData:{root:ROOT,configuration:path},stdout:true,stderr:true,resourceLimits:WORKER_LIMITS});
    let settled=false;
    const finish=value=>{if(settled)return;settled=true;clearTimeout(timer);worker.terminate();resolveResult(value);};
    const timer=setTimeout(()=>finish({ok:false,error:'Training exceeded the 60-second local run limit and was interrupted. Reduce the development configuration or inspect your learner code. No completed training is claimed.'}),60000);
    worker.once('message',finish);worker.once('error',error=>finish({ok:false,error:error.message}));worker.once('exit',code=>finish({ok:false,error:`Training worker ended without a result (${code}).`}));
    worker.stdout.resume();worker.stderr.resume();
  });
  if(!result.ok){await appendRecord(journalPath,'training-result',{attemptId:committed.id,complete:false,error:result.error});throw new Error(result.error);}
  if(result.training.configurationHash!==hash(source)||hash(await readFile(path,'utf8'))!==hash(source)) {
    const error='Training configuration changed during the run. Repeat with a frozen configuration.';
    await appendRecord(journalPath,'training-result',{attemptId:committed.id,complete:false,error});throw new Error(error);
  }
  const destination=resolve(option('out',join(ROOT,'work','training.json')));
  await mkdir(dirname(destination),{recursive:true});
  await writeFile(destination,JSON.stringify(result.training,null,2)+'\n',{flag:'wx'});
  await appendRecord(journalPath,'training-result',{attemptId:committed.id,complete:true,output:destination,trainingHash:hash(JSON.stringify(result.training)),generations:result.training.generations.length,totalCredits:result.training.totalCredits});
  print({saved:destination,generations:result.training.generations.length,matches:result.training.matches.length,totalCredits:result.training.totalCredits,note:'Learner functions produced these training artifacts. Qualify them with checks and held-out comparisons; generation count is not a strength score.'});
}

async function fitModel(filename) {
  if(!filename) throw new Error('Provide a completed season JSON file.');
  const path=resolve(filename),bytes=await readFile(path);
  const source=await readFile(join(ROOT,'learner/value-model.mjs'),'utf8');
  const committed=await appendRecord(journalPath,'fit-attempt',{seasonHash:hash(bytes),source,sourceHash:hash(source)});
  const result=await new Promise(resolveResult=>{
    const worker=new Worker(new URL('./lib/fit-worker.mjs',import.meta.url),{workerData:{root:ROOT,season:path},stdout:true,stderr:true,resourceLimits:WORKER_LIMITS});
    let settled=false;
    const finish=value=>{if(settled)return;settled=true;clearTimeout(timer);worker.terminate();resolveResult(value);};
    const timer=setTimeout(()=>finish({ok:false,error:'Value fitting exceeded 15 seconds and was interrupted. Inspect the fit loop.'}),15000);
    worker.once('message',finish);worker.once('error',error=>finish({ok:false,error:error.message}));worker.once('exit',code=>finish({ok:false,error:`Fitting worker ended without a result (${code}).`}));
    worker.stdout.resume();worker.stderr.resume();
  });
  if(!result.ok){await appendRecord(journalPath,'fit-result',{attemptId:committed.id,complete:false,error:result.error});throw new Error(result.error);}
  if(hash(await readFile(path))!==hash(bytes)||result.model.seasonHash!==hash(bytes)||hash(await readFile(join(ROOT,'learner/value-model.mjs'),'utf8'))!==hash(source)) {
    const error='Fitting input or learner source changed during the run. Repeat with a stable version.';
    await appendRecord(journalPath,'fit-result',{attemptId:committed.id,complete:false,error});
    throw new Error(error);
  }
  const destination=resolve(option('out',join(ROOT,'work','value-model.json')));
  await mkdir(dirname(destination),{recursive:true});
  await writeFile(destination,JSON.stringify(result.model,null,2)+'\n',{flag:'wx'});
  await appendRecord(journalPath,'fit-result',{attemptId:committed.id,complete:true,output:destination,modelHash:hash(JSON.stringify(result.model))});
  print({saved:destination,trainingMetrics:result.model.model.trainingMetrics,validationMetrics:result.model.model.validationMetrics,scope:result.model.scope});
}

async function assembleRoster(filename) {
  if(!filename) throw new Error('Provide a fitted value-model or population-training artifact.');
  const destination=resolve(option('out',join(ROOT,'work','candidate-league.json')));
  const {makeDevelopmentRoster}=await import('./lib/roster.mjs');
  const config=await makeDevelopmentRoster(resolve(filename),destination,ROOT);
  await mkdir(dirname(destination),{recursive:true});
  await writeFile(destination,JSON.stringify(config,null,2)+'\n',{flag:'wx'});
  print({saved:destination,policies:config.policies.length,partition:config.partition,next:`node cli.mjs league ${destination} --out ./work/candidate-season.json`,note:config._note});
}

async function main() {
  if (command === 'doctor') {
    const major = Number(process.versions.node.split('.')[0]);
    if (major < 22) throw new Error(`Node 22+ required; found ${process.version}.`);
    print({ok: true, node: process.version, platform: process.platform, architecture: process.arch, dependencies: 'none', course: 'local course candidate 0.1.1', note: 'This validates runtime availability, not your agent or course completion.'});
    return;
  }
  if (command === 'list') {
    for (const lesson of await catalog()) print(`${lesson.id}  ${lesson.title}`);
    print('\nRead: node cli.mjs lesson 1.1\nCode checks: node cli.mjs check 1 through check 6\nAll navigation is unlocked.');
    return;
  }
  if (command === 'lesson') {
    const lesson = (await catalog()).find(value => value.id === args[0]);
    if (!lesson) throw new Error('Unknown lesson. Use node cli.mjs list.');
    print(await readFile(join(ROOT, 'lessons', lesson.file), 'utf8'));
    return;
  }
  if (command === 'question') {
    const item = await itemById(args[0]);
    print(`${item.id}\n${item.question}\n\nCommit: node cli.mjs attempt ${item.id} --answer 'your response'`);
    return;
  }
  if (command === 'attempt') {
    const item = await itemById(args[0]);
    const response = option('answer');
    if (!response?.trim()) throw new Error('Supply a nonempty --answer.');
    if (Buffer.byteLength(response) > 32000) throw new Error('Answer exceeds 32,000 bytes. Save code through check instead.');
    const confidence = option('confidence', 'unspecified');
    if (!['low', 'medium', 'high', 'unspecified'].includes(confidence)) throw new Error('Confidence must be low, medium or high.');
    const current = await readJournal(journalPath);
    const attempt = await appendRecord(journalPath, 'attempt', {itemId: item.id, lessonId: item.lessonId, question: item.question, questionHash: questionHash(item), response, confidence, assistanceBefore: assistanceFor(current, item.id)});
    print(`Attempt saved: ${attempt.id}\nYour answer and prior assistance are preserved.\nNext: node cli.mjs feedback ${item.id}`);
    return;
  }
  if (command === 'feedback' || command === 'hint') return practiceFeedback(args[0], command);
  if (command === 'check') return checkLearner(args[0]);
  if (command === 'demo') return playDemo();
  if (command === 'league') return playLeague(args[0]);
  if (command === 'verify') return verifyRecord(args[0]);
  if (command === 'report') return makeReport(args[0]);
  if (command === 'train') return train(args[0]);
  if (command === 'fit') return fitModel(args[0]);
  if (command === 'roster') return assembleRoster(args[0]);
  if (command === 'history') {
    const records = flattenedRecords(await readJournal(journalPath));
    print(records.map(record => ({id: record.id, type: record.type, createdAt: record.createdAt, item: record.data.itemId ?? record.data.module, response: record.data.response, assistanceBefore: record.data.assistanceBefore})));
    return;
  }
  if (command === 'export') {
    if (!args[0]) throw new Error('Provide a new destination file. Existing exports are never overwritten.');
    const count = await exportJournal(journalPath, resolve(args[0]));
    print(`Exported ${count} top-level records to ${resolve(args[0])}.`);
    return;
  }
  if (command === 'import') {
    if (!args[0]) throw new Error('Provide an exported journal file.');
    print(await importJournal(journalPath, resolve(args[0])));
    return;
  }
  print(`Agent League — local course candidate

Read and practice:
  node cli.mjs doctor
  node cli.mjs list
  node cli.mjs lesson 1.1
  node cli.mjs question 1.1-p1
  node cli.mjs attempt <item> --answer "your response" --confidence medium
  node cli.mjs feedback <item>
  node cli.mjs hint <item> --level 1
  node cli.mjs check <1|2|3|4|5|6|evaluation|search>

Play, learn and inspect:
  node cli.mjs demo --seed 7 --out ./work/demo.json
  node cli.mjs league development-league.json --out ./work/season.json
  node cli.mjs verify ./work/season.json --configuration development-league.json
  node cli.mjs fit ./work/season.json --out ./work/model.json
  node cli.mjs train development-training.json --out ./work/training.json
  node cli.mjs roster ./work/training.json --out ./work/population-league.json
  node cli.mjs report ./work/season.json --out ./work/report.json

Keep work:
  node cli.mjs history
  node cli.mjs export ./my-attempts.json
  node cli.mjs import ./my-attempts.json

Use --journal /path/to/journal.json for a separate work history.
Output files must be new names; existing work is never overwritten.
No server, account, model API or package installation is needed.`);
}

main().catch(error => { process.stderr.write(`Error: ${error.message}\n`); process.exitCode = 1; });
```

```html
<article id="lesson-1.1" class="lesson" hidden><h1>1.1 Read the decision contract</h1>
<p>A pawn reaches the far edge, yet a program reports that the other player won. Before improving the program's strategy, you need to know which part of the system owns that result. In this lesson you will identify the actor, legal actions and terminal return for a supplied game state, then implement a policy that respects that contract.</p>
<p>You need arrays, functions and zero-based indexing. Read time is approximately 5–7 minutes, with 20–35 minutes of practice and coding; these are targets awaiting learner trials.</p>
<h2>A move is a request to the referee</h2>
<p>The supplied game is a small version of Breakthrough. Player 0 begins on row 0 and moves toward row 4. Player 1 begins on row 4 and moves toward row 0. Each player starts with five pawns. A turn moves one pawn one row forward. A straight move needs an empty destination. A diagonal move may enter an empty square or capture an opposing pawn. A friendly occupied destination is illegal.</p>
<p>Reaching the opposite edge or removing all opposing pawns wins immediately. If the player to move has no legal action, it loses. Official terminal returns are <code>+1</code> for the winner and <code>-1</code> for the loser. Capturing an ordinary pawn does not itself earn a game point. A policy may prefer captures as a useful heuristic, but it cannot change the referee's objective.</p>
<p>For a worked position, suppose player 0 has a pawn at <code>(1,2)</code>. The cell <code>(2,2)</code> is empty, <code>(2,1)</code> holds an opponent and <code>(2,3)</code> holds a friendly pawn. Moving straight is legal. Moving diagonally left is a legal capture. Moving diagonally right is illegal. The relevant facts are the actor, direction and destination occupancy; a visually attractive route has no authority over those rules.</p>
<p>Before proceeding, commit this application. <strong>Item <code>1.1-p1</code>:</strong> Player 1 has a pawn at <code>(3,1)</code>. Its forward cell <code>(2,1)</code> contains an opponent, <code>(2,0)</code> is empty, and <code>(2,2)</code> contains a friendly pawn. Which destinations are legal, and what rule excludes each other destination?</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 1.1-p1 --answer 'Your destinations and reasons' --confidence medium
node cli.mjs feedback 1.1-p1</code></pre>
<p>The feedback displays your saved answer beside the reference and its reasoning. This is self-assessed practice, not an automatic grade for the quality of your explanation.</p>
<h2>The board is only part of the state</h2>
<p><code>context.state.board</code> is a flat array of 25 cells. An empty cell is <code>-1</code>; a pawn contains its player ID, <code>0</code> or <code>1</code>. Cell index is <code>row * 5 + column</code>. The state also includes <code>currentPlayer</code>, <code>ply</code>, rule identity, terminal status and terminal returns. <code>returns</code> is <code>null</code> before the game ends. Two identical boards can allow different actions when different players are to move.</p>
<p>An action is an integer identifying its source and destination. For this board, the encoding is <code>fromCell * 25 + toCell</code>. The supplied engine already performs this conversion and validates moves. For example, source cell 6 and destination cell 11 encode as 161. An integer can have the right shape while still describing an illegal move: encoding is not validation.</p>
<p>The policy receives <code>context.legalActions</code>, an ordered list of actions the referee permits at the current state. Your first policy's job is to select from that list. It should not modify the board, invent a different action format, or turn the observation into a result record. The observation is information for making a decision; the referee remains responsible for applying the decision.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>1.1-p2</code>:</strong> An action moves from cell 8 to cell 13. What is its encoded ID? Does knowing that ID establish legality? Name two additional facts you would inspect.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 1.1-p2 --answer 'ID; legality explanation; two facts'
node cli.mjs feedback 1.1-p2</code></pre>
<h2>Build the smallest honest policy</h2>
<p>Open <code>learner/baseline.mjs</code>. Implement <code>chooseAction(context)</code> so that it returns a legal action ID. Choose a simple documented rule: a fixed position in the legal list is enough to establish the contract. A later lesson will make randomized choices reproducible. You do not need to implement movement, capture detection, game storage or a user interface.</p>
<p>The copied state is not a scratch board. For hypothetical moves, later search code will use the supplied simulation oracle. Mutating an observation would make the program's reasoning difficult to reproduce and could make one branch of a search affect another. A policy should return a decision; it should not try to make that decision happen by editing state.</p>
<p>Run the actual policy checker:</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs check 1</code></pre>
<p>A passing code check establishes the finite behaviors it reports. It does not establish playing strength. If a check fails, identify the violated requirement before changing code. Fix that requirement and rerun; preserve the earlier attempt in your history instead of rewriting its result.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>1.1-p3</code>:</strong> A policy returns a valid-looking action ID and also sets the opponent's last pawn to empty in its copied observation. Which part should the referee use to determine the next state, and why must the modified observation not establish victory?</p>
<h2>Transfer and repair</h2>
<p><strong>Item <code>1.1-transfer</code>:</strong> A cache stores decisions using only the 25 board cells. The same board is later queried with the other player to move. Describe the failure this can cause and the additional identity the cache must preserve. You are diagnosing the policy, not redesigning the game.</p>
<p>Commit each item with <code>attempt</code>, then request its feedback. If your answer is incomplete, use <code>node cli.mjs hint &lt;item-id&gt; --level 1</code>; later hints become more specific. Record a revision as another attempt so that your first reasoning remains visible. You are ready to continue when your policy passes its public checks and you can explain why a legal decision and a winning decision are different claims.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. The local CLI preserves the original question, first response, assistance and revisions. This reading view does not grade your reasoning.</div></article>
<article id="lesson-1.2" class="lesson" hidden><h1>1.2 Make one policy reproducible</h1>
<p>Your policy wins, but a rerun of the same match loses. That may reflect a different random choice, changed code or a different game—not a change in strength. In this lesson you will make a policy's decisions reproducible and identify the evidence needed to rerun them.</p>
<p>You need lesson 1.1 and the idea of a deterministic function. Allow approximately 5–7 minutes to read and 25–40 minutes to implement and investigate; these are unmeasured targets.</p>
<h2>Randomness can be controlled</h2>
<p>A deterministic game has no random state transition once its state and action are fixed. Its policies can still make random choices. A random policy is useful as a baseline because it produces varied legal behavior without pretending to understand the position. To study that policy, the runner must be able to reproduce its sequence of random decisions.</p>
<p>The supplied <code>context.rng()</code> returns the next number in a private seeded pseudorandom sequence. The same seed and same sequence of calls produce the same values. Values lie in <code>[0,1)</code>. A policy chooses from a legal-action list using this stream, not the current time or JavaScript's ambient <code>Math.random()</code>.</p>
<p>For a worked choice, take three legal actions in the order <code>[40,42,66]</code> and a random value of <code>0.62</code>. Divide the unit interval into three equal slots. The value lies in the second slot, so this choice uses the second action. The order matters. Sorting the same actions differently after drawing the number changes the decision even though the set of legal actions is unchanged.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>1.2-p1</code>:</strong> The legal actions are <code>[27,30,54,55]</code> and the next private random value is <code>0.76</code>. Which action does equal-width sampling select? What changes if the program consumes one extra random value before selecting?</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 1.2-p1 --answer 'Action and consequence of the extra draw'
node cli.mjs feedback 1.2-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Freeze what “the same policy” means</h2>
<p>A name such as <code>challenger</code> is a display label. The policy's behavior also depends on its source, parameters, seed handling and configuration. A source hash identifies bytes; a parameter hash identifies the associated data. The runner records both. Changing a weight while retaining the name creates a new snapshot.</p>
<p>The experiment also needs a game identity, starting state, side assignment and compute budget. If one program receives 256 simulated moves and another receives 1,024, a difference in results does not isolate policy logic. Similarly, repeating the same seed after changing the move order is a new experiment. Reproducibility requires the relevant conditions, not just one familiar number in the report.</p>
<p>Consider two archived records named <code>runner-up</code>. Their source hashes agree, but one uses a parameter vector from Tuesday and the other from Wednesday. It is entirely possible for both records to be genuine and for them to choose different moves. The correct repair is to retain both parameter identities. Renaming one record would make it easier to read, but would not replace that evidence.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>1.2-p2</code>:</strong> Two runs have the same policy name and random seed. The second run has different parameter bytes and twice the simulation budget. Can their disagreement establish nondeterminism? List what would have to be held fixed for that diagnosis.</p>
<h2>Replaying moves is weaker than rerunning a policy</h2>
<p>A trajectory replay starts from the recorded state and applies the recorded actions. It asks whether those actions produce the recorded states and result under the stated rules. It is valuable: an edited winning score should disagree with the referee's calculation.</p>
<p>A policy rerun asks a further question: given the recorded policy, parameters, observations, seed and budget, does the policy choose those actions again? A person could attach the wrong policy name to a perfectly legal action trace. That trace could pass trajectory replay while failing policy rerun.</p>
<p>This distinction helps you localize a problem. If policy decisions differ before any state difference, inspect policy identity, random-call order and configuration. If actions agree but states differ, inspect the rule/runtime identity and transition record. Do not begin by tweaking strategic weights; that would change the object you are trying to diagnose.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>1.2-p3</code>:</strong> Every recorded action replays to the recorded final state. The reported policy, rerun with its frozen inputs, chooses a different first action. Which reproducibility claim passed, which failed, and what should the report avoid claiming?</p>
<h2>Revise your policy and retain the evidence</h2>
<p>In <code>learner/baseline.mjs</code>, make your choice rule explicit. You may keep a deterministic rule or use the private random stream. A valid deterministic policy does not need artificial randomness. A valid randomized policy must draw only from its supplied stream and return a legal action.</p>
<p>Run <code>node cli.mjs check 1</code>. The checker exercises legality and declared reproducibility behavior; inspect the individual results. Keep your first failed version in your own version history or exported record. The course journal records your written attempts and assistance; it does not magically preserve every edit to a JavaScript file. Save code snapshots when you want to compare versions.</p>
<p>Use <code>node cli.mjs history</code> to inspect attempts and <code>node cli.mjs export ./my-attempts.json</code> to create a portable journal. Export is useful evidence of your reasoning history, not proof that a policy produced a tournament trace.</p>
<p><strong>Item <code>1.2-transfer</code>:</strong> A program logs a random number for debugging by calling <code>context.rng()</code> and then calls it again to choose its move. Debug logging is later disabled, and decisions change. Explain the cause and propose a repair that preserves the intended choice sequence without removing useful diagnostics.</p>
<p>Commit the transfer answer before feedback. After a miss, request a hint, revise the specific explanation and rerun the relevant check. You are ready to proceed when you can reproduce the decision and explain exactly which frozen inputs make that claim meaningful.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. The local CLI preserves the original question, first response, assistance and revisions. This reading view does not grade your reasoning.</div></article>
<article id="lesson-1.3" class="lesson" hidden><h1>1.3 Separate playing strength from harness failure</h1>
<p>A tournament says your agent won six games, but two planned matches are missing. A clean percentage would conceal whether the agent played well, returned illegal moves or never ran. In this lesson you will classify those outcomes and preserve enough evidence to make the result interpretable.</p>
<p>You need lessons 1.1–1.2. Allow about 5–7 minutes to read and 20–35 minutes to examine records and complete the module; these times are design targets.</p>
<h2>A legal loss is useful evidence</h2>
<p>A completed game has a sequence of legal actions and a terminal outcome from the referee. Your agent may lose because its evaluation was poor or it missed an adversarial reply. Those are strategic failures. They belong in the result. Deleting them would remove precisely the observations that can improve your policy.</p>
<p>A policy forfeit has a different cause. The program may return an illegal action or exceed the deterministic simulation quota. It did not satisfy the decision contract. The league records the forfeit and its reason instead of silently substituting another policy's move. A strong fallback would award the program competence it had not demonstrated.</p>
<p>For a worked record, suppose a policy is allowed 12 simulation calls but makes a thirteenth and then returns a legal move. The final action's legality does not erase the quota violation. The program used a decision process outside the agreed contract. Compare that with a policy that uses only four of the allowed 12 calls and loses legally: using less than the maximum is permitted, and its loss remains a game result.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>1.3-p1</code>:</strong> Classify these three cases as legal game loss, policy forfeit, or unresolved infrastructure failure: (A) the opponent reaches the final row after legal play; (B) the policy returns an action absent from the current legal list; (C) the host process stops before a result is committed. Explain why they must not be collapsed into one label.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 1.3-p1 --answer 'A: ...; B: ...; C: ...; explanation'
node cli.mjs feedback 1.3-p1</code></pre>
<h2>An interrupted host has not supplied a game result</h2>
<p>A host crash, failed write or watchdog interruption can leave the result unknown. It does not establish that either policy won. Keep the partial record and classify the planned game as incomplete. The report cannot quietly replace the unknown outcome with a draw; the default game has no draw rule that says “the computer stopped.”</p>
<p>An exact rerun can resolve an incomplete game when its inputs are retained. Link the retry to the same planned match, its snapshot identities and the reason for rerunning. Do not count the original partial record and the retry as two independent games. If an apparently identical completed record arrives twice, the system should recognize the duplicate. If their results conflict, it should expose the conflict rather than choosing whichever result arrived last.</p>
<p>Suppose a plan contains ten matches. Seven complete legally, one policy forfeits, and two are interrupted. There are eight resolved outcomes and two unresolved entries. A win rate among the seven legal games answers a narrower question than a score over all resolved outcomes. Neither denominator turns the two unknown entries into evidence. Later modules will specify the comparison before running it; for now, preserve the categories so that comparison remains possible.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>1.3-p2</code>:</strong> A report has four wins, three legal losses, one forfeit by the evaluated policy and two host interruptions in ten planned games. Give the counts of resolved and unresolved matches. Is “four wins out of ten completed games” an accurate description? Explain the correction.</p>
<h2>Diagnose the first disagreement</h2>
<p>Use the earliest reliable divergence to decide what to inspect. If the policy returns a forbidden action, examine the decision contract and current observation. If a legal action produces an unexpected state, inspect the rules/version and transition evidence. If a complete action trace agrees but a displayed score differs, recompute the score from the referee result. If the trace stops before completion, do not reason backward from a guessed winner.</p>
<p>The CLI's <code>verify</code> command checks recorded evidence; run <code>node cli.mjs help</code> for its required file argument and supported verification modes. Read whether a report verifies the action trajectory or also reruns the policy. Those are the distinct claims from lesson 1.2.</p>
<p>This is why the supplied runner owns records and transitions while you own strategy. It keeps a policy's claim separate from the evidence used to judge that claim. A policy cannot make itself a winner by returning <code>{winner: 0}</code>. Your function returns an action ID; the referee determines what happens next.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>1.3-p3</code>:</strong> A dashboard says “player 0 won,” but replaying its recorded legal actions ends with player 1 reaching the target row. Which evidence should decide the official result? Identify the first two things you would compare before changing either policy.</p>
<h2>Complete the first cumulative artifact</h2>
<p>Your module artifact is a small legal, reproducible policy in <code>learner/baseline.mjs</code>, plus written reasoning that distinguishes strategy from execution failure. Run:</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs check 1
node cli.mjs history</code></pre>
<p>Read failures by requirement. Repair a legal-action problem with the contract in lesson 1.1; repair a changing decision with the frozen inputs in lesson 1.2. A passing check is engineering evidence for those finite behaviors. Your explanations remain self-assessed practice until reviewed separately. Neither result says the policy is strong.</p>
<p><strong>Item <code>1.3-transfer</code>:</strong> A developer removes every record with a nonzero error count before ranking policies. One policy has many illegal-action forfeits; another has no forfeits but loses strategically. Explain how this filter can reverse the apparent ranking, and state which records or counts the report must retain.</p>
<p>Commit your answer, inspect feedback, and make a new attempt after any repair. Do not replace an inconvenient first answer. Continue to module 2 when your baseline passes its checks and you can trace a reported loss to either a legal game outcome, a policy-contract violation, or a genuinely unresolved execution problem.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. The local CLI preserves the original question, first response, assistance and revisions. This reading view does not grade your reasoning.</div></article>
<article id="lesson-2.1" class="lesson" hidden><h1>2.1 Value a position from the correct player's perspective</h1>
<p>A search program gives a winning position a negative score because the turn changed. It can examine many moves and still choose badly if its values switch meaning. In this lesson you will implement an evaluation whose player perspective stays explicit and whose estimates never override a known terminal result.</p>
<p>You need module 1, signed numbers and simple arithmetic. Plan for approximately 5–7 minutes of reading and 25–40 minutes of practice and implementation; these targets are not measured learner times.</p>
<h2>A value needs an owner</h2>
<p>An evaluation estimates how favorable a state is to a named player. In this course, larger values mean better outcomes for that player. The argument <code>player</code> in <code>evaluate(state, player)</code> is that owner. It is not automatically the player whose turn comes next.</p>
<p>Suppose player 0 has a clear advantage. An evaluator may give that state <code>+0.4</code> from player 0's perspective and <code>-0.4</code> from player 1's. The board did not become worse when you asked the second question. You changed whose interests the number describes. This game is zero-sum: one player's terminal gain is exactly the other's loss.</p>
<p>For a worked heuristic, imagine counting only a material difference in a different small position. Player 0 has four pawns and player 1 has two. A coefficient of <code>0.1</code> per extra pawn gives <code>+0.2</code> for player 0 and <code>-0.2</code> for player 1. That is an estimate, not a proof. Two advanced enemy pawns might be more dangerous than four poorly placed pawns. The feature is useful only to the extent that it guides decisions toward winning.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>2.1-p1</code>:</strong> A nonterminal state has heuristic value <code>+0.35</code> for player 1 under an antisymmetric evaluation. What value should the same evaluator give player 0? If <code>currentPlayer</code> changes but the question still asks for player 1's prospects, should the sign automatically change? Explain.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 2.1-p1 --answer 'Value; sign decision; reason'
node cli.mjs feedback 2.1-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Known outcomes outrank estimates</h2>
<p>A terminal state is no longer a prediction problem. The referee's <code>returns</code> array contains the outcome for both players. If player 0 won, <code>returns[0]</code> is <code>+1</code> and <code>returns[1]</code> is <code>-1</code>. Asking from player 1's perspective must not retrieve the first entry merely because player 0 started the game.</p>
<p>Terminal handling comes before any depth limit or heuristic. A search that reaches a terminal win on its final allowed edge should return the known win, not call a rough material estimator because its depth counter reached zero at the same moment. The order of those decisions changes what the number means.</p>
<p>Nonterminal heuristic scores in this course lie between <code>-0.99</code> and <code>+0.99</code>. Terminal outcomes remain exactly <code>-1</code> and <code>+1</code>. The separation prevents an overconfident estimate such as <code>1.4</code> from outranking an actual win. Later learned values will retain their raw predictions for analysis, but the search boundary will keep this score contract.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>2.1-p2</code>:</strong> A search reaches a terminal state with <code>returns=[-1,+1]</code> exactly at its depth limit. The requested perspective is player 1, and the material heuristic would give <code>-0.2</code>. Which value belongs in the search, and which condition must be checked first?</p>
<h2>Build an estimator you can explain</h2>
<p>Open <code>learner/evaluation.mjs</code> and implement <code>evaluate(state, player)</code>. Handle terminal values from the referee first. For nonterminal states, choose a small set of visible features that you can explain. Material and progress toward the target row are possible starting ideas. Keep your output finite and within the heuristic range. Do not read final-game labels, hidden scenario names or future moves.</p>
<p>Changing a feature's direction when the player changes needs care. Player 0 advances toward larger row numbers; player 1 advances toward smaller ones. Raw row number therefore does not mean the same progress for both players. A useful representation converts geometry into a player's distance or advancement before combining features. Check the interpretation on one pawn near each player's target edge.</p>
<p>An all-zero nonterminal evaluation is a meaningful reference: it expresses no preference before a terminal result is found. It can support exact search when the whole relevant tree is explored, but it is weak guidance when search stops early. You may compare against it; do not call it a trained value or claim it understands positions.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>2.1-p3</code>:</strong> Player 0 has a pawn on row 3; player 1 has a pawn on row 1. Each is one move from its target row. A feature uses raw row number and therefore assigns greater advancement to player 0. Explain the representation error and describe a perspective-consistent replacement without writing the whole evaluator.</p>
<h2>Check meaning before strength</h2>
<p>Run <code>node cli.mjs check 2</code> after implementing your evaluator and, in the next lesson, your search function. Early failures may include unfinished search. Read the individual requirement results rather than treating one overall failure as evidence that every component is wrong.</p>
<p>For your own inspection, retain three cases: a known terminal win, the same terminal result from the losing player's perspective, and a nonterminal state evaluated for both players. Those checks test the meaning of scores. They do not prove that your heuristic is strategically good. That requires matched games and tactical cases after the search works.</p>
<p><strong>Item <code>2.1-transfer</code>:</strong> A future rule gives the same player another turn after a particular move. A programmer flips the sign whenever one move is simulated, assuming that each edge changes the player. Explain why this can fail and which explicit state information should determine the backup's role.</p>
<p>Commit before viewing feedback. If you miss a perspective question, mark the player who owns each value on a tiny tree and then try a fresh item. Preserve the first attempt. You are ready for search when your evaluator's sign, range and terminal behavior have a single consistent meaning.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. The local CLI preserves the original question, first response, assistance and revisions. This reading view does not grade your reasoning.</div></article>
<article id="lesson-2.2" class="lesson" hidden><h1>2.2 Search adversarial replies under a node budget</h1>
<p>A move wins a pawn immediately but lets the opponent reach the far edge next turn. Looking at only your move rewards the wrong consequence. In this lesson you will implement bounded adversarial search that chooses a move by accounting for the opponent's reply.</p>
<p>You need lesson 2.1, recursion and the difference between a maximum and a minimum. Allow approximately 5–7 minutes to read and 45–75 minutes to implement and repair; these are design estimates.</p>
<h2>Back up the consequence the opponent can force</h2>
<p>Keep every value in one named player's perspective—the root player for this decision. At a state where that player acts, it chooses the largest child value. At a state where its opponent acts, the opponent can choose the smallest value for the root player. Propagating these choices back through the tree is minimax search.</p>
<p>Consider a worked sibling tree. You choose between <code>north</code> and <code>south</code>. After <code>north</code>, the opponent can force values <code>-0.2</code> or <code>+0.7</code>; after <code>south</code>, it can force <code>+0.1</code> or <code>+0.3</code>. The backed-up value of <code>north</code> is <code>-0.2</code>, because the opponent need not cooperate. The backed-up value of <code>south</code> is <code>+0.1</code>. You select <code>south</code>. Selecting the largest leaf anywhere in the tree would assume the opponent chooses the outcome you want.</p>
<p>This calculation depends on the player's identity at each state. The ordinary game alternates turns, but the interface tells you <code>currentPlayer</code> explicitly. Use that fact. A generic tree or a later rule change can give the same player consecutive decisions; the backup should follow the actor, not the recursion level's parity.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>2.2-p1</code>:</strong> At a root where player 0 acts, move A lets player 1 choose between <code>+0.8</code> and <code>-0.4</code> for player 0. Move B lets player 1 choose between <code>+0.2</code> and <code>0</code>. What are the two backed-up values, and which root move should player 0 select?</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 2.2-p1 --answer 'A value; B value; chosen move; reason'
node cli.mjs feedback 2.2-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Stop a branch for the right reason</h2>
<p>At each state, first ask whether it is terminal. If so, use the requested player's exact return. Otherwise, if the declared depth is exhausted, use <code>context.evaluate(state, player)</code>. A depth counts simulated transition edges: depth one examines the states after one move; it does not mean one complete pair of turns.</p>
<p>For a nonterminal state below the limit, inspect its legal actions, simulate children and combine their values according to the actual actor. The supplied oracle exposes <code>terminal</code>, <code>returns</code>, <code>currentPlayer</code>, <code>legal</code> and <code>next</code>. The search implementation owns traversal and choice. It does not own game rules. In particular, <code>context.oracle.next(state, action)</code> returns the hypothetical child <strong>State</strong>; it does not apply an action to the actual match.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>2.2-p2</code>:</strong> A root move leads to another decision by the root player. Its two possible children have values <code>-0.6</code> and <code>+0.25</code> from that player's perspective. What value should this intermediate state back up? Explain why “always minimize on the second level” gives the wrong answer.</p>
<h2>A budget is part of the algorithm's contract</h2>
<p><code>context.oracle.remaining</code> reports unused simulation credits, and <code>used</code> reports consumed credits. Every call to <code>next</code> consumes a credit. Asking for an extra child after the budget is exhausted violates the contract even if your code catches the resulting error. Choosing a legal move afterward does not undo that extra work.</p>
<p>Select a legal fallback before expanding children. With no simulation credits, a policy still has to return a legal action from <code>context.legalActions</code>. When there are credits, avoid claiming an unfinished branch's partial result as if every relevant reply had been examined. A partial opponent node can look unusually strong simply because its dangerous reply has not yet been visited.</p>
<p>A clear initial policy can restrict itself to work it can finish at its chosen depth, or use a documented safe result from an earlier completed search. More sophisticated methods are welcome, but their treatment of incomplete work must be explicit. The next lesson develops iterative deepening as one way to retain a complete earlier result.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>2.2-p3</code>:</strong> A search fully checks candidate A and finds value <code>0</code>. It starts candidate B, sees one favorable reply worth <code>+0.7</code>, and runs out of credits before examining B's other replies. Why is selecting B as a proved <code>+0.7</code> move unjustified? State what evidence is missing.</p>
<h2>Implement and test your search</h2>
<p>Open <code>learner/search.mjs</code> and implement <code>search(context)</code>. It returns one legal action ID. The context supplies <code>state</code>, <code>player</code>, <code>legalActions</code>, <code>parameters.maxDepth</code>, <code>evaluate</code>, the seeded <code>rng</code>, and the counted <code>oracle</code>. Keep values in the explicit root player's perspective. Any documented tie choice among equally best legal moves is acceptable.</p>
<p>Run <code>node cli.mjs check 2</code>. The checker includes small independently understood cases; it does not merely demand that your code resemble a reference implementation. Unpruned minimax and correct alpha-beta search can both meet the contract. If a tiny endgame fails, keep its state, predicted action and actual returned action. Trace one branch by hand before adding more search depth.</p>
<p><strong>Item <code>2.2-transfer</code>:</strong> A tree contains two different states with the same board layout but different players to move. A transposition cache returns the first stored value for both. Describe how this can change the selected root move and which information the cache key must include.</p>
<p>Commit, obtain feedback and record your repair as a new attempt. Finish with a legal search policy that respects credits and explains its fallback. Finding a winning move once is weaker evidence than choosing correctly on the targeted adverse and valid-alternative cases.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. The local CLI preserves the original question, first response, assistance and revisions. This reading view does not grade your reasoning.</div></article>
<article id="lesson-2.3" class="lesson" hidden><h1>2.3 Use deeper search without changing the experiment</h1>
<p>Your revised policy wins more often after you add pruning and raise its budget fourfold. The result is real, but it does not tell you which change helped. In this lesson you will compare search changes under matched conditions and preserve a defensible result when deeper search runs out of work.</p>
<p>You need lesson 2.2 and the distinction between a code change and an experiment change. Allow approximately 5–7 minutes of reading and 35–60 minutes of coding and comparison; these are targets awaiting trials.</p>
<h2>Count work, not the label on the algorithm</h2>
<p>A depth limit and a compute budget answer different questions. The depth limit restricts how many transitions a branch may contain. The budget restricts the total number of simulated transitions across the whole decision. Two searches with the same depth can use very different numbers of transitions because positions have different legal actions or because one algorithm prunes branches.</p>
<p>For a worked tree with branching factor three, a complete depth-one expansion uses three transitions. Extending every branch one more edge adds nine, for 12 in total. Extending to depth three adds another 27, for 39. These numbers count edges actually simulated, including the root's outgoing edges. A large depth setting does not promise that the budget can complete that tree.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>2.3-p1</code>:</strong> In a full tree with two actions at every nonterminal node, how many simulated transitions are required to complete depth three from the root? Can a budget of ten complete that expansion? Explain your counting unit.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 2.3-p1 --answer 'Transition count; budget decision; counting unit'
node cli.mjs feedback 2.3-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Keep a completed answer while looking deeper</h2>
<p>Iterative deepening runs a shallow search, retains its completed result, then attempts a deeper one. If the new iteration finishes, its result replaces the earlier result. If it cannot finish under the remaining credits, the previous complete result remains available. The repeated shallow work has a cost; it buys a well-defined answer at interruption points.</p>
<p>For example, a policy completes depth one, then depth two, and begins depth three. When the credit limit is reached during the third iteration, it should not silently label a partially explored move as a depth-three optimum. It can return the depth-two result and report the completed depth honestly. That choice may be weaker than an unlimited search, but it is a comprehensible bounded policy.</p>
<p>Other safe partial-search schemes are possible. The requirement is not “use this exact loop.” It is to preserve the meaning of the returned result, respect the budget, and avoid treating a missing hostile reply as evidence of safety. All work through the supplied oracle counts, including repeated expansions between iterations.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>2.3-p2</code>:</strong> A policy completed depth two and selected move C. Its depth-three iteration saw a promising move D before exhausting its credits halfway through D's opponent replies. What result can it safely describe as a completed search result, and which claim about D remains unsupported?</p>
<h2>Pruning changes the work, not perfect minimax's answer</h2>
<p>Alpha-beta pruning avoids exploring branches that cannot change the minimax choice given bounds already established elsewhere. The bounds describe what the maximizing player can already guarantee and what the minimizing player can already enforce. A cutoff is justified by those bounds—not by a branch merely looking unattractive.</p>
<p>Consider a root maximizing player with one completed option worth <code>0.3</code>. In another option, the minimizing opponent already has a reply worth <code>0.1</code>. Any further reply can only leave that option at <code>0.1</code> or make it worse for the root. That option cannot beat <code>0.3</code>, so its remaining replies need not be evaluated to choose the root action. This is a proof about the current search tree, not a heuristic prediction that all remaining moves look similar.</p>
<p>Move ordering can make useful bounds appear earlier and therefore reduce work. With enough resources to complete the same finite-depth search, correct pruning preserves its value and set of optimal moves. Under a tight budget, ordering can change how much is completed and thus the chosen action. Record the tie rule and ordering when reproducing a bounded result.</p>
<p>Commit <strong>item <code>2.3-p3</code>:</strong> A maximizing root already has a completed option worth <code>0.4</code>. In a second option, its minimizing opponent has an inspected reply worth <code>0.2</code>. Does exploring more replies allow that second option's minimax value to become greater than <code>0.4</code>? Explain whether a cutoff is justified.</p>
<h2>Compare one change at a time</h2>
<p>To test an ordering or pruning change, hold fixed the rules, starting states, sides, evaluator, random seeds, maximum transition budget and result definition. Record actual credits as well as outcomes. If two algorithms return equally good moves but one uses fewer credits, that is useful evidence even when the win rate does not change.</p>
<p>To test a larger budget, change the budget deliberately and describe that as a compute comparison. Do not attribute its gain solely to a new heuristic. Retain both source/parameter identities and the exact plan. A result on a selected tactical set establishes behavior on that set; broader claims will need the paired tournament and uncertainty work in module 4.</p>
<p>Complete <code>learner/search.mjs</code>, then run <code>node cli.mjs check 2</code>. Your module artifact includes the evaluator, legal budgeted search, one retained failure/repaired explanation, and a comparison plan. A passing check does not require alpha-beta if a correct unpruned search meets the finite contract. Extra sophistication earns no credit when the underlying value or budget handling is wrong.</p>
<p><strong>Item <code>2.3-transfer</code>:</strong> Version A searches with a hand-built evaluator and 256 credits. Version B uses a new evaluator, a different move order and 1,024 credits, then wins more games on newly chosen positions. Propose the smallest set of matched comparisons that can separate evaluator, ordering and compute effects. State which claim the original comparison cannot support.</p>
<p>Commit this plan before feedback. Use the hint ladder only after recording your reasoning, and label assisted revisions honestly. You now have the agent substrate for later learning: a policy whose score meaning, adversarial backup, resource use and comparison conditions can be inspected rather than guessed.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. The local CLI preserves the original question, first response, assistance and revisions. This reading view does not grade your reasoning.</div></article>
<article id="lesson-3.1" class="lesson" hidden><h1>3.1 Build outcome-labelled training examples</h1>
<p>A search policy can play a complete game without knowing whether its position scores were useful. You will turn completed games into training examples whose labels mean the same thing from either player's seat.</p>
<h2>Decide what the prediction means</h2>
<p>A value estimate predicts a future result from a particular player's perspective. In this course, a terminal win is +1 and a loss is -1. A training example contains a feature vector <code>x</code>, a <code>target</code>, an <code>episodeId</code>, and a <code>scenarioId</code>. Before fitting anything, write down which player the target belongs to. “Good position” is too ambiguous to debug.</p>
<p>Consider a completed game won by player 1. An observation represented from player 1's perspective receives target +1; the same observation represented for player 0 receives -1. The label does not change merely because the next row in your dataset represents a later move. Player identity and perspective determine the sign. This also works if a future game allows the same player to move twice.</p>
<p>The label describes what happened under the policies that generated the game. It is not a certificate of the position's optimal minimax value. A strong position may receive a losing label because the continuation contained a mistake. Several games and informative features help the learner discover a pattern, but cannot turn a finite sample into a proof.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 3.1-p1.</strong> A game ends with returns <code>[-1,+1]</code>. Its stored observations have perspectives <code>[1,1,0]</code>. Give the three outcome labels and explain why alternating signs by row number would be wrong.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 3.1-p1 --answer 'your labels and reason'
node cli.mjs feedback 3.1-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Keep information available at decision time</h2>
<p>Features are measurements of the current observable state: material, advancement, threatened paths, or another quantity your policy can compute before the outcome. The supplied <code>features(state, player)</code> interface in <code>learner/value-model.mjs</code> makes the perspective explicit. It returns at most 32 finite numbers. A bias feature is a constant input that lets the model learn an offset.</p>
<h2>Separate board information from perspective</h2>
<p>A representation has two different obligations. First, hold the requested player, actor and move count fixed and compare different boards. Some feature vectors must change when a relevant board fact changes. A vector containing only a bias, player ID or move count cannot distinguish those positions. Second, compare the requested players on feature-relevant positions: the representation must preserve whose outcome it describes. Passing one check does not establish the other.</p>
<p>There is no required author feature vector, bias term or sign convention. A material difference is a valid simple representation. It can remain unchanged after a quiet move because the pawn counts have not changed. It should distinguish appropriate boards with different material. Advancement-based features can notice a quiet forward move; arrangement-based features can notice a positional change with equal material. A pair of own/opponent counts is also valid, without expressing the pair as one signed difference.</p>
<p>Likewise, balanced material can produce the same material-difference vector for both players even on a visually asymmetric board. Check perspective on several relevant imbalanced positions instead of demanding different numbers on every position. Keep the vector's order and dimension fixed and its entries finite within <code>[-1,1]</code>. Extraction must be reproducible and leave the input unchanged.</p>
<p>The practice checker varies material, advancement and arrangement while holding actor and ply fixed. It requires a board distinction somewhere in that set for each requested player and a perspective distinction somewhere in the set. It does not demand sensitivity to every feature family. These are finite behavior checks, not proof that a representation is strategically useful: explain what each measurement means and inspect its effect on actual decisions.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 3.1-p4.</strong> Feature A returns only a bias and the requested player's ID. Feature B returns a material difference and is unchanged after a non-capturing move. Explain why A is insufficient and why that one unchanged move does not invalidate B. Describe separate board and perspective comparisons that would provide relevant evidence.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 3.1-p4 --answer 'your board and perspective comparisons'
node cli.mjs feedback 3.1-p4</code></pre>
<h2>Exclude information from the future</h2>
<p>A completed episode record contains much more information than a decision observation. Its final winner, future captures, and final score are legitimate labels or analysis fields. They are not decision-time features. Including the winner in <code>x</code> can make validation look excellent while creating an impossible deployed policy.</p>
<p>The supplied transport produces candidate examples. You remain responsible for inspecting their labels and deciding which completed episodes belong in the fit. An interrupted episode has no terminal outcome. Do not manufacture a loss merely because its process stopped. Preserve and quarantine it, then repair the data source or use a separately justified partial-return method outside this exercise's default contract.</p>
<p>Generate actual behavior records with the supplied development configuration:</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs league development-league.json --out ./work/behavior.json</code></pre>
<p>This small development season is an inspectable data source, not the final league benchmark. Keep its policy identities and completed records for the fit in 3.2.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 3.1-p2.</strong> A dataset column named <code>eventualWinner</code> reduces validation error nearly to zero. Another column is current pawn count. Explain which can enter <code>features</code>, which belongs elsewhere, and how you would detect this leakage in a code review.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 3.1-p2 --answer 'your feature audit'
node cli.mjs feedback 3.1-p2</code></pre>
<h2>Split games, not adjacent rows</h2>
<p>Suppose a 20-move game supplies 20 similar positions. Randomly assigning individual rows to training and validation can put neighboring states from that same game on both sides. Validation then tests familiar trajectories more than the intended change of situation.</p>
<p>Group by episode and declared scenario family before splitting. Keep reflected sibling starting positions together. Record the generator and behavior-policy versions so you can reproduce the partition. Different trajectories can naturally reach the same internal state; record such overlap instead of claiming that every validation state is entirely novel.</p>
<p>Your retained artifact is an example audit: two correctly labelled seats, the feature definition and version, rejected/incomplete episodes, and the train/validation groups. This prepares the fitting exercise in 3.2. No model performance claim is needed yet.</p>

<article id="lesson-3.2" class="lesson" hidden><h1>3.2 Fit and inspect a small value model</h1>
<p>Your examples have meaningful labels, but fixed hand-written weights cannot learn from them. You will fit a small linear model and show that its predictions respond to relevant training data.</p>
<h2>Predict with a declared feature order</h2>
<p>A linear model predicts a value with a dot product: multiply each feature by its corresponding weight and add the products. With features <code>[1, advancement]</code> and weights <code>[0.1, 0.4]</code>, advancement 0.5 produces <code>0.1 + 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.3</code>. The first feature is the bias. Reordering features without reordering weights changes the model even when the weight file is unchanged.</p>
<p>Keep the feature version, coefficient order, training input identity and configuration beside the weights. Normalize quantities whose scales differ greatly. For example, a bounded material difference and a raw byte-sized state identifier should not be treated as equally meaningful measurements. An identifier is generally a poor feature here: it encourages recognition of named cases rather than reasoning from the board.</p>
<p>The learner file exports <code>features(state, player)</code> and <code>fit(examples, {seed, epochs, learningRate})</code>. The fit returns <code>{weights}</code>. You may choose a suitable fitting method; the checker evaluates behavior rather than requiring one particular loop.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 3.2-p1.</strong> A saved model expects <code>[bias, materialDifference, advancement]</code>, but a refactor returns <code>[bias, advancement, materialDifference]</code>. Both vectors contain finite numbers and the same length. Explain why shape validation cannot catch the full error and what identity must change.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 3.2-p1 --answer 'your diagnosis and repair'
node cli.mjs feedback 3.2-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Fit a prediction error, not a preferred answer</h2>
<p>Squared error measures the distance between a prediction and its labelled outcome. For a single example, use half the squared difference, <code>(prediction - target)² / 2</code>; the half simplifies its derivative. Gradient descent adjusts weights opposite the loss gradient. For a linear prediction, each coordinate's gradient is the prediction error multiplied by that feature. Batch fitting averages gradients across the chosen examples; stochastic fitting updates from individual examples in a declared order.</p>
<p>As a worked sibling, suppose one example has feature 0.5, target 1, and current weight 0. The prediction is 0, the error is -1, and the gradient is -0.5. A small step opposite that gradient increases the weight. It should move the prediction toward 1, not away from it. This sign check is useful before running thousands of updates.</p>
<p>A learning rate controls step size. A rate that is too large can make loss oscillate or explode. A constant or redundant feature may make some fitting formulations singular. Handle these cases explicitly; do not allow NaN weights to reach search. A stable regularized fit or an appropriate gradient method can both be valid.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 3.2-p2.</strong> Training loss grows every epoch, and doubling the learning rate makes growth faster. Name two checks that distinguish a wrong gradient sign from an excessively large correct step. Explain why running more epochs is not the first repair.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 3.2-p2 --answer 'your diagnostic experiments'
node cli.mjs feedback 3.2-p2</code></pre>
<h2>Demonstrate that the model learned from its inputs</h2>
<p>Complete the two functions and run:</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs check 3
node cli.mjs fit ./work/behavior.json --out ./work/value-model.json</code></pre>
<p>Inspect the saved source and checker messages. A genuine fitter changes appropriately when relevant targets change. Returning a copied constant vector is not training, even if it happens to score well on one fixture. Test a small dataset whose expected relationship you can calculate independently before trusting game data.</p>
<p>The <code>fit</code> command supplies episode transport and grouped splitting, then calls your feature and fitting functions. Inspect the resulting weights and metrics. This command does not require the opponent sampler from module 5.</p>
<p>Compare training and validation prediction error, retaining the initial weights and configuration. Lower training loss with worse validation loss is a useful finding, not a reason to move validation examples into training without recording the change. Predictive accuracy also differs from playing strength: a model can reduce error on common easy positions yet mishandle a rare decisive move.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 3.2-p3.</strong> A fitter reduces training error, barely changes validation error, and chooses worse moves. Give one data explanation and one feature/model explanation. State the next controlled comparison you would run rather than declaring learning a success or failure from one number.</p>
```
