```html
<article id="lesson-3.3" class="lesson" hidden><h1>3.3 Put learned values inside search</h1>
<p>A new agent wins more games, but it also searches four times as many positions. You will compare learned and hand-written evaluations while keeping computation and evaluation conditions visible.</p>
<h2>Keep known outcomes stronger than guesses</h2>
<p>Search uses an evaluation when it stops before a terminal state. A terminal result is different: it is an outcome established by the game rules. The course keeps terminal returns exactly at -1 or +1 and bounds nonterminal heuristic scores to <code>[-0.99,+0.99]</code>. A learned raw prediction of 1.4 must not outrank a proved win.</p>
<p>The bound is applied at the search boundary. Keep the raw prediction separately for regression diagnostics; otherwise clipping can hide a badly calibrated model. Feature computation must use the requested player's perspective, and terminal checks still happen before depth truncation.</p>
<p>For a worked sibling, imagine two available actions. One reaches a terminal win. The other reaches an unexplored position whose regression prediction is 1.2. The search adapter bounds the second estimate below 1, preserving the distinction between a forecast and an established result. This is an interface guarantee, not proof that the forecast is otherwise good.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 3.3-p1.</strong> A model predicts -1.7 for a nonterminal position. Should the training-error report, the search score and the terminal-return field all contain the same number? Explain the purpose of each field.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 3.3-p1 --answer 'your three-field explanation'
node cli.mjs feedback 3.3-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Change one cause at a time</h2>
<p>An ablation is a comparison that removes or changes one component while retaining the others. To study learned values, compare the same search procedure with a hand-written evaluation and with the learned evaluation. Use the same scenarios, seats, policy seeds, transition budget and evaluation protocol. Record actual credits used: equal upper limits do not guarantee equal consumption.</p>
<p>Then compare the learned evaluation with and without the added search. This asks a different question: how much does planning contribute once the value function is fixed? A four-cell comparison—hand-written/learned crossed with shallow/deeper search—can reveal interactions. Learning might help at shallow depth and matter less when search reaches terminal outcomes.</p>
<p>For example, agent A uses a hand-written value at 64 credits, while agent B uses a learned value at 256. Their win-rate difference measures the combined change. You cannot attribute it solely to fitting. A new comparison with the same credit budget is needed; relabeling the old table does not repair the design.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 3.3-p2.</strong> You can afford only one additional comparison after observing B beat A under different budgets. Specify the comparison that best isolates the learned value's contribution, including which settings you freeze.</p>

<article id="lesson-4.1" class="lesson" hidden><h1>4.1 Pair positions and swap seats</h1>
<p>Your candidate wins every game in one starting seat and loses every game in the other. You will construct a complete paired comparison that separates a policy's result from the opportunities its seat received.</p>
<h2>Name the quantity you are measuring</h2>
<p>An estimand is the quantity a comparison is intended to estimate. Here, a simple estimand is policy A's mean utility against B over a declared distribution of starting scenarios, giving both seats equal weight. Utility is +1 for a win and -1 for a loss. A win fraction of 0.75 corresponds to mean utility 0.5 when every scored game is a win or loss.</p>
<p>For each starting scenario, run A in seat 0 against B in seat 1, then swap policies on the same starting state. Do not quietly replace the state when swapping. Geometry and side-to-move can make a seat favorable; pairing ensures both policies receive it.</p>
<p>As a worked sibling, A wins as seat 0 and loses as seat 1 on a particular scenario. Its paired mean utility is <code>(1 + -1) / 2 = 0</code>. Reporting only the first game would say +1 and answer a different question. The paired average does not prove the starting game is balanced; it removes that one-sided allocation from this comparison.</p>

<article id="lesson-4.2" class="lesson" hidden><h1>4.2 Quantify uncertainty at the right unit</h1>
<p>A report claims certainty because it contains thousands of moves, although those moves came from eight starting scenarios. You will choose a sampling unit that matches the question and interpret an interval without overstating what it measures.</p>
<h2>Count independent variation, not rows</h2>
<p>Moves inside one game are linked. The same initial scenario also links its seat-swapped games and randomness replicates. Treating every move as an independent observation creates a large apparent sample while adding little independent information about different situations.</p>
<p>For this course's scenario-distribution claim, a block is one scenario with all of its planned seats and replicates. Compute one mean utility for each block, then analyze variation across blocks. If you compare two methods, keep their paired results together. Destroying pairing can either increase or decrease the apparent uncertainty; it changes the sampling experiment.</p>
<p>Suppose six scenarios each produce four games. There are 24 scored games but six scenario blocks. The report should show both numbers. If all four games on one scenario are duplicates in effect, repeating them 100 times still does not provide 100 new scenarios.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 4.2-p1.</strong> A report has 16 scenarios, two seats and two randomness replicates per scenario. It resamples its 64 games independently. Identify the sampling unit the planned scenario-distribution claim requires and explain what structure the resampling must preserve.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 4.2-p1 --answer 'your sampling unit and repair'
node cli.mjs feedback 4.2-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Build and label a block bootstrap</h2>
<p>A bootstrap constructs new samples by sampling observed units with replacement. For each resample, draw as many scenario blocks as the original report contains, allowing a block to appear more than once. Compute the statistic again. The distribution of those resampled statistics approximates sampling variation under the procedure's assumptions.</p>
<p>The supplied <code>blockBootstrap</code> utility uses the declared seed and interval settings. The course default is a nominal 95% percentile interval from 2,000 resamples. The paired reducer in your report must create complete blocks before calling it. More bootstrap resamples make the numerical approximation smoother; they do not create new game evidence.</p>
<p>A 95% confidence procedure aims to cover the underlying quantity in about 95% of repeated experiments under its assumptions. It does not assign a 95% probability that this particular fixed interval contains a fixed parameter. With few scenarios or strongly discrete outcomes, nominal coverage can be poor. Show counts, method and limits, and be willing to say the evidence is inconclusive.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 4.2-p2.</strong> Your interval crosses zero. A teammate writes “the policies are equally strong.” Explain what is missing from that conclusion. Then explain why raising bootstrap resamples from 2,000 to 20,000 does not by itself solve the evidence problem.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 4.2-p2 --answer 'your corrected interpretation'
node cli.mjs feedback 4.2-p2</code></pre>
<h2>Separate a checkpoint from a training algorithm</h2>
<p>One fitted policy can play thousands of games. Those games characterize that frozen checkpoint under the declared evaluation distribution. They do not reveal how much the training algorithm varies across independently trained models.</p>
<p>To compare training methods, retain multiple independent training seeds. The course uses five as a bounded starting target, not a theorem of adequacy. Evaluate each trained model on a matched scenario plan. Training run is the upper level of variation; scenario blocks sit within it. Keep failed and weak training runs, rather than selecting the lucky one before computing the method's mean.</p>
<p>There is also a simpler legitimate claim: the exact average over this fixed finite roster. That average is an observed fact once all results are valid. An interval is useful only when you identify the broader sampling target; it does not automatically generalize the roster to every opponent or rule.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 4.2-p3.</strong> You have one trained checkpoint, 1,000 evaluation games and no other training runs. Write one supported claim and one unsupported algorithm-level claim. Describe the additional evidence needed for the latter.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 4.2-p3 --answer 'your claims and evidence plan'
node cli.mjs feedback 4.2-p3</code></pre>

<article id="lesson-4.3" class="lesson" hidden><h1>4.3 Freeze selection before final evaluation</h1>
<p>After seeing a final evaluation loss, you repair the policy and run the same cases again. You will distinguish useful development from confirmation and preserve the history that makes the distinction visible.</p>
<h2>Give each partition a job</h2>
<p>Training data changes parameters. Selection data helps choose among features, budgets, checkpoints or policies. Final evaluation measures a candidate chosen before its results are inspected. These are roles in a workflow, not magical properties of filenames.</p>
<p>If you use a final result to decide what to change, that result has become selection evidence. This does not make the improvement worthless. It changes what you can claim. Label the follow-up exploratory and use fresh, separately specified final evidence for a confirmatory claim.</p>
<p>As a worked sibling, a designer compares three feature sets on a selection roster, chooses the second, freezes its source and parameters, and runs a distinct final roster once. That final report evaluates the chosen version. If the designer instead picks whichever feature set scored highest on the final roster, the apparent winner benefits from selection on the very evidence being reported.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 4.3-p1.</strong> A policy fails final scenario Q. You add a feature targeting Q and rerun all final scenarios. Which results can still be retained, how should the new report be labelled, and what would support a new confirmatory claim?</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 4.3-p1 --answer 'your evidence disposition'
node cli.mjs feedback 4.3-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Freeze a concrete comparison</h2>
<p>A useful plan identifies the exact policy snapshots and parameters, game/rules hash, scenario roster, seed schedule, seat assignments, budgets, score, uncertainty procedure, missing-game handling and intended claim. A label such as “candidate-v2” is insufficient if its file can change between games.</p>
<p>The supplied plan and snapshot machinery preserve identities. Your responsibility is to choose the comparison before inspecting its final outcomes. Record why the comparison answers the decision you need to make. A plan might ask whether a specific candidate improves mean utility against a declared opponent mixture while keeping old-opponent regressions visible.</p>
<p>Predeclaring a plan does not rescue an invalid metric or buggy runner. Run correctness controls first. If a genuine infrastructure defect forces a repair, retain the old failed run and explain which records are invalid. Do not disguise a policy edit as an infrastructure repair so that it inherits the old untouched-test label.</p>

<h2>Avoid choosing the story after seeing the noise</h2>
<p>If you inspect many pairwise comparisons, some may look favorable by chance. Reporting only the most attractive nominal interval hides this search. Likewise, repeatedly checking an ordinary interval and stopping at the first favorable result does not preserve its original fixed-sample interpretation.</p>
<p>For this course, choose one primary contrast and sample plan before final evaluation. Other pairwise results may be shown as descriptive evidence with that label. If your decision needs many simultaneous claims or adaptive stopping, use a separately justified statistical procedure. Do not improvise one after the results arrive.</p>
<p>“No clear improvement” is an acceptable conclusion when evidence is limited. It does not mean your implementation is correct automatically; code checks and experimental validity remain separate. Preserve negative results because they help the next controlled decision and stop future you from rediscovering the same failed idea.</p>

<article id="lesson-5.1" class="lesson" hidden><h1>5.1 See what latest-only self-play forgets</h1>
<p>The newest policy defeats yesterday's checkpoint but loses to a policy from several generations ago. You will diagnose that regression without assuming that each generation has become generally stronger.</p>
<h2>A changing opponent changes the learning problem</h2>
<p>Self-play generates experience by having policies compete against themselves or related policies. It can produce a useful training curriculum: a new opponent exposes a weakness, the learner adapts, and the resulting games offer new situations. But the distribution of experience changes as the opponent changes.</p>
<p>With latest-only self-play, training concentrates on the newest opponent. A response that wins this narrow contest may neglect a defense that mattered against older policies. This is not necessarily a software bug or catastrophic parameter forgetting in the strict machine-learning sense. It can be a strategic distribution shift: the current objective no longer rewards that defense.</p>
<p>Consider this explicitly synthetic comparison. Snapshot C scores +0.6 against latest snapshot B but -0.5 against older snapshot A. Snapshot B had scored +0.3 against A. C's improvement against B is real on those measured matchups; it does not imply that C is the best choice against a population containing A. The missing comparison matters more than the generation number.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 5.1-p1.</strong> Your new snapshot wins against its immediate predecessor but its aggregate score against a frozen three-opponent roster decreases. Give two distinct explanations to investigate, one strategic and one experimental, before concluding that self-play caused forgetting.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 5.1-p1 --answer 'your two explanations'
node cli.mjs feedback 5.1-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Compare on a common roster</h2>
<p>Keep a historical archive of immutable snapshots. Evaluate new and old candidates against the same frozen opponents, scenarios, seats, seeds and compute conditions. A history graph should show individual matchups as well as any aggregate score. A rising training reward can coexist with a falling score against the old archive.</p>
<p>Recall module 4: a missing difficult game must not become a zero, a duplicate retry must not add weight, and games from one checkpoint do not become independent training runs. Before explaining a regression strategically, verify snapshot identities and complete coverage. A changed parameter file under an old name can manufacture a false learning story.</p>
<p>When a genuine regression remains, inspect a losing trace. Identify a concrete behavior: the new agent advances too quickly into a threat, overvalues material, or repeatedly assumes a reply that the old opponent does not make. A useful diagnosis connects a change in experience or evaluation to an observed decision. It does not need to tell an anthropomorphic story about the agent's intentions.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 5.1-p2.</strong> A chart shows performance at generations 1–5, but each point used a different opponent roster. What can the chart legitimately show? Design a second chart that can reveal regression against historical opponents.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 5.1-p2 --answer 'your chart interpretation and redesign'
node cli.mjs feedback 5.1-p2</code></pre>
<h2>Preserve a weakness before repairing it</h2>
<p>Choose one historical regression and save the old/new snapshot hashes, fixed comparison plan and a representative replay. That evidence becomes a regression test for your league design. A later repair should face the same disclosed development case and fresh cases selected under the next evaluation plan.</p>
<p>Adding old opponents to training can help retain useful defenses, but it is not guaranteed to improve every objective. A limited training budget spread across many opponents may learn more slowly against any one of them. This is why module 5 compares latest-only, uniform-history and a declared learner-chosen distribution under the same training budget.</p>

<article id="lesson-5.2" class="lesson" hidden><h1>5.2 Sample opponents from an archive</h1>
<p>You want half your training games against a recent rival and the rest against older weaknesses. You will implement a reproducible discrete sampler whose actual choices match the declared archive weights.</p>
<h2>A distribution is part of the training objective</h2>
<p>An archive entry has an immutable snapshot <code>id</code> and a nonnegative <code>weight</code>. Weights describe how often each opponent should be selected. The runtime contract requires probabilities summing to one; your implementation validates this representation and rejects an unnormalized roster. Do not silently include unknown IDs or a renamed duplicate as if it added a new strategy.</p>
<p>The learner function is <code>sampleOpponent(archive, rng)</code> in <code>learner/opponent-sampler.mjs</code>. It returns one existing snapshot ID. The supplied <code>rng()</code> returns a value in <code>[0,1)</code>. Using ambient randomness instead would break replay even if the long-run frequencies looked reasonable.</p>
<p>A worked sibling is a bag with one red ticket, two blue tickets and one green ticket. Their probabilities are one quarter, one half and one quarter. You can divide <code>[0,1)</code> into intervals of those lengths and select the interval containing a random value. Boundaries must be assigned consistently so that no value falls into two intervals or a gap. This illustrates the sampling operation; your archive may contain a different number of entries and zero weights.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 5.2-p1.</strong> An archive has weights <code>[0,2/3,1/3]</code>. Explain which IDs may be returned, what their probabilities should be, and why an all-zero archive needs an explicit error rather than an arbitrary choice.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 5.2-p1 --answer 'your distribution and error policy'
node cli.mjs feedback 5.2-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Test behavior at boundaries and over a sequence</h2>
<p>Validate numbers before sampling: negative weights, NaN, infinity and an empty archive do not define the intended finite distribution. Duplicate IDs also need a declared policy; this exercise rejects ambiguous duplicate entries rather than accidentally doubling their probability. A zero-weight item must never be selected, including when the random value is exactly zero.</p>
<p>Two useful tests answer different questions. Repeating a fixed seed should reproduce the same sequence of choices. A sufficiently long sequence should have frequencies compatible with the probabilities, allowing sampling variation. It should not be forced to contain exactly the expected counts unless you intentionally implement a different balanced scheduling method and name it as such.</p>
<p>Run the practice checker on your sampler:</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs check 5</code></pre>
<p>If a boundary fails, retain the offending random value and archive in your attempt record. Repair the interval handling, then test a new archive shape. Hardcoding a special answer for the observed ID does not fix the sampling rule.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 5.2-p2.</strong> A sampler reproduces its sequence for a fixed seed, but the last archive item is never chosen. Why does reproducibility alone not establish correctness? Describe a boundary test and a distribution test that would expose different causes.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 5.2-p2 --answer 'your two tests'
node cli.mjs feedback 5.2-p2</code></pre>
<h2>Choose once per game</h2>
<p>The league's population mixture selects one snapshot at the start of a game and keeps that opponent for the whole game. Selecting a new snapshot every move creates a different policy. It can combine moves that no archived program would make consistently, and it changes what the empirical matchup matrix means.</p>
<p>The opponent's chosen ID is not included in the acting policy's observation. A learner may infer tendencies from ordinary play, but a privileged roster label is not a legal board feature. The core policies are stateless apart from their seeded randomness and immutable parameters, so claims about unrestricted adaptation to a hidden opponent identity remain outside this response class.</p>

<article id="lesson-5.3" class="lesson" hidden><h1>5.3 Admit a new policy without erasing history</h1>
<p>A candidate has the highest average score but reopens a weakness your league had already repaired. You will make an admission decision using a declared objective, comparable evidence and preserved historical snapshots.</p>
<h2>Admission answers a product question</h2>
<p>Admitting a policy means making it available for future sampling or selection. It does not have to mean replacing every older policy. A league may value broad coverage, low vulnerability to a tested responder, strong performance against a target population, or a useful counter-strategy. State the objective before evaluating the candidate.</p>
<p>A synthetic example illustrates the distinction. Candidate C gains substantially against a recent aggressive rival but loses a defense against an older cautious rival. If your declared objective is average return against a population dominated by the aggressive rival, admitting C may be reasonable. If preserving the cautious-rival defense is a mandatory constraint, the same evidence may justify rejection or retaining both policies. There is no context-free “highest score wins” rule.</p>
<p>Any empirical thresholds must be declared before the relevant selection experiment and interpreted with uncertainty. They should not be repeatedly adjusted until the preferred candidate passes. You can revise the policy for the next experiment, but record that revision.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 5.3-p1.</strong> A candidate improves average utility by 0.08 but loses 0.4 against a previously important opponent. Give two defensible admission decisions under different explicitly stated objectives. Explain why the raw average alone cannot choose between them.</p>

<h2>Compare like with like</h2>
<p>Use frozen selection evidence with common game rules, scenarios, seats and compute budgets. A candidate evaluated with four times the search budget is a different system; its result can be useful, but does not demonstrate that the policy logic alone improved. An incomplete result cannot silently pass because the finished games look favorable.</p>
<p>Snapshot identity includes source, learned parameters and relevant configuration. A new display name does not create a new policy. Conversely, an unchanged source file with different learned weights may represent a genuinely different policy. Retain parent IDs, training data/configuration and actual credit usage so the ancestry can be audited.</p>
<p>The final league requires six distinct roles: supplied random and greedy baselines, your search policy, your learned-value/search policy, an earlier snapshot and a counter-strategy. It allows up to two additional variants. Diversity here must have a behavioral or parameter basis; eight aliases of the same source and weights do not provide eight strategies.</p>

<h2>Retention is not deletion</h2>
<p>An active sampling roster can have a size limit. Removing a snapshot from active sampling means assigning it no current training probability or excluding it from a particular run. It does not require deleting its source, parameters, failed experiments or historical reports. Those records explain how the current league reached its decision.</p>
<p>Keep at least one historical policy in evaluation even when it is no longer sampled for training. Save the exact admission evidence and decision. If a later generation regresses, you can reproduce the older comparison instead of relying on a remembered headline.</p>
<p>A candidate can be correctly rejected. A weak training run should remain a recorded run rather than disappear from an algorithm comparison. An inconclusive admission decision may justify collecting more preplanned evidence; it should not trigger unbounded retries until a lucky result appears.</p>

<article id="lesson-6.1" class="lesson" hidden><h1>6.1 Build an approximate best response</h1>
<p>A cautious policy protects against the worst possible reply, but a particular rival rarely makes that reply. You will build a response to a fixed opponent model and test whether its advantage survives fresh games against the actual opponent.</p>
<h2>Decide which opponent you are optimizing against</h2>
<p>Minimax protects against an adversary that selects the worst legal reply. A best response to a fixed stochastic policy instead maximizes expected return against that policy's action probabilities. These are different objectives. Neither calculation should be silently reported as the other.</p>
<p>Consider a worked sibling with two choices. A safe choice always returns 0.2. A risky choice returns +1 with probability 0.8 and -1 with probability 0.2 under the stated opponent. Its expectation is <code>0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × -1 = 0.6</code>, so a response to that model favors it. A worst-case calculation sees -1 and prefers the safe choice. If the rival changes its behavior, the exploit can disappear.</p>
<p>The learner's <code>responsePolicy(context)</code> lives in <code>learner/vulnerability.mjs</code>. Its context supplies <code>opponentPolicy(state)</code>, returning legal action/probability pairs for a known fixed model, as well as the counted oracle, your evaluation and <code>parameters.maxDepth</code>. At your own turn, maximize. At a modeled opponent turn, average over its declared probabilities. Terminal returns and resource limits still apply.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 6.1-p1.</strong> A response implementation always takes the minimum child value at opponent turns, even though a fixed probability model was supplied. What problem does it solve, and why can it miss a profitable counter-strategy? State the appropriate backup operation without assuming the modeled opponent is perfect.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 6.1-p1 --answer 'your objective and backup diagnosis'
node cli.mjs feedback 6.1-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Validate the model and keep the budget</h2>
<p>Probabilities must be finite, nonnegative and sum to one within the declared tolerance. Every action must be legal in that state. An invalid distribution is a model error, not permission to silently use a favorable replacement. The model describes behavior observable or explicitly supplied for training; it must not reveal a hidden evaluation policy ID.</p>
<p>Use the same transition-credit discipline as your robust search. Exploring an opponent distribution can be expensive. A depth limit or approximate evaluation creates an approximate response, even if the expectation over each expanded node is exact. Record its policy family, depth, budget and training/selection conditions.</p>
<p>Run the practice checker after implementing the response and the gap function introduced in 6.2:</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs check 6</code></pre>
<p>The supplied exact tiny-tree utility is an independent comparison instrument. Your learner code still chooses the counter-policy. Passing tiny controls does not prove that your model matches the real rival throughout a game.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 6.1-p2.</strong> Your counter-policy performs well against its model but poorly against fresh games from the real opponent. Give one model explanation, one search-budget explanation and an experiment that distinguishes them while preserving the original failure.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 6.1-p2 --answer 'your explanations and experiment'
node cli.mjs feedback 6.1-p2</code></pre>
<h2>Evaluate a frozen response independently</h2>
<p>Training or selecting the responder against one set of games can overfit it. Freeze the response before testing it on fresh scenarios and randomness. Compare both seats. Retain failed restarts and the total response budget; selecting the luckiest of many attempts and reporting only its training score is not an independent test.</p>
<p>The actual opponent may be a hidden per-game mixture of archived policies. Choosing one policy for the whole game is not the same as averaging their original action probabilities independently at every state. Observed actions can change beliefs about which policy was chosen. The course's stateless response family does not implement an unrestricted history-dependent best response, so name that limitation.</p>

<article id="lesson-6.2" class="lesson" hidden><h1>6.2 Distinguish measured exploitability from a proof</h1>
<p>Your responder found no winning strategy, and the report calls the champion “unexploitable.” You will compute a precisely defined gap on a finite matrix and limit larger-game claims to the response space actually tested.</p>
<h2>Define the game and the normalization</h2>
<p>Let matrix A contain the row player's payoff. A row distribution <code>x</code> and column distribution <code>y</code> describe mixtures over the listed strategies. Their probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one. The column player's payoff is the negative of A because this is a zero-sum game.</p>
<p>Holding y fixed, the best listed pure row response obtains <code>max_i (A y)_i</code>. Holding x fixed, the column player wants the smallest row payoff, <code>min_j (x^T A)_j</code>. Their difference is the Nash gap:</p>
<p><code>gap(x,y) = max_i (A y)_i - min_j (x^T A)_j</code>.</p>
<p>The current value <code>x^T A y</code> cancels when you add the two players' unilateral improvement opportunities. Some conventions report two-player exploitability as half this gap. Neither label is useful without stating its normalization.</p>
<p>As a worked sibling, the matching-pennies payoff matrix has rows <code>[1,-1]</code> and <code>[-1,1]</code>. Uniform x and y make every listed response worth zero, so the gap is zero. This certifies the specified finite matrix calculation. It says nothing about an unlisted action that changes the game.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 6.2-p1.</strong> One report calls a value of 0.4 the Nash gap; another calls 0.2 exploitability for the same x, y and matrix. Can both be correct? State the convention that would reconcile them and one additional identity you must verify before comparing the numbers.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 6.2-p1 --answer 'your normalization check'
node cli.mjs feedback 6.2-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Implement the restricted calculation honestly</h2>
<p>Implement <code>nashGap(matrix, x, y)</code> in <code>learner/vulnerability.mjs</code>. The matrix may be rectangular. Validate its shape, finite entries and the distributions' dimensions and probabilities. Do not assume a square symmetric matrix merely because the league's common-roster display is square. The function returns the gap as defined above, not its half.</p>
<p>The practice checker uses independently calculable cases and invalid-input controls:</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs check 6</code></pre>
<p>If A contains estimated rather than exact payoffs, your computed number inherits estimation uncertainty. A solver ending after a fixed number of iterations also does not automatically establish zero gap. Report its measured residual and the response class represented by the rows and columns.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 6.2-p2.</strong> A zero-gap result was computed on a matrix containing three archived policies. A new fourth policy defeats every member of that archive. Explain which earlier statement remains correct and which broader statement the new evidence refutes.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 6.2-p2 --answer 'your restricted-game interpretation'
node cli.mjs feedback 6.2-p2</code></pre>
<h2>A discovered exploit and a failed search are asymmetric evidence</h2>
<p>A valid counter-policy that achieves a positive advantage on independent evidence demonstrates a weakness against that responder and evaluation distribution. It need not be the strongest possible response. A search that finds no advantage only establishes that this procedure failed to find one under its budget; a stronger or different response class may succeed.</p>
<p>Exact full-game exploitability requires a genuinely exhaustive or otherwise certified best-response calculation for the game's policy space. Our larger 5×5 experiments do not promise that. They report empirical vulnerability to a declared learned/search responder. Tiny enumerable fixtures can support stronger exact claims because their response space is explicitly bounded and exhausted.</p>
<p>Preserve the response's source, training/selection history, budget, model and held-apart evaluation. For a two-sided gap, you need both players' unilateral response opportunities; one bad matchup is not automatically the complete metric.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 6.2-p3.</strong> Three response searches with different seeds find no advantage within 256 credits per move. Write a defensible headline and a short limitation. Then name one additional experiment that would probe the limitation without pretending to prove it away.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 6.2-p3 --answer 'your headline, limit and probe'
node cli.mjs feedback 6.2-p3</code></pre>
<p>Keep exact matrix quantities and empirical game findings in separate fields. Lesson 6.3 uses the matrix to expose strategic structure that a single rank cannot preserve.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. The local CLI preserves the original question, first response, assistance and revisions. This reading view does not grade your reasoning.</div></article>
<article id="lesson-6.3" class="lesson" hidden><h1>6.3 Read cycles that a single ranking hides</h1>
<p>Agent A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. You will recognize this nontransitive structure and explain why a single ordered leaderboard cannot capture every matchup.</p>
<h2>Read the pairwise relation first</h2>
<p>A relation is transitive when A being above B and B above C implies A above C. Competitive policies need not satisfy that property. Different strategies can expose different weaknesses. Nontransitivity therefore concerns interactions, not merely uncertainty in a scalar skill number.</p>
<p>Consider an explicitly synthetic exact matrix with zeros on its diagonal: A earns +1 against B and -1 against C; B earns +1 against C and -1 against A; C earns +1 against A and -1 against B. Against a uniform mixture of the other listed strategies, no one is a universal champion. Yet choosing any single policy leaves a clear counter-policy in the set.</p>
<p>A directed graph makes this structure visible. Draw an edge from a policy to one it defeats under the declared comparison rule. The three edges above form a directed cycle. Retain the underlying matrix: a graph alone can hide the size and uncertainty of each advantage.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 6.3-p1.</strong> A scoreboard sorts the synthetic cycle by policy name after all three receive the same average. Explain what the order means and why calling the first row the strongest policy would be misleading. Identify the information a reader needs beside the scalar score.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 6.3-p1 --answer 'your leaderboard interpretation'
node cli.mjs feedback 6.3-p1</code></pre>
<h2>Do not manufacture a cycle from missing or noisy results</h2>
<p>In the real league, pairwise payoffs are estimates from finite games. An unplayed pair is unknown, not a tie. A tiny positive mean is not automatically a reliable directional edge. Show the complete count, interval procedure, comparison status and any missing games for each pair.</p>
<p>If you inspect many potential edges, recall the selection problem from 4.3. A cycle found after searching many noisy comparisons is descriptive unless the simultaneous inference or confirmation plan supports a stronger claim. Do not choose the edge threshold after looking at the plot merely to make a dramatic loop appear.</p>
<p>The course includes an exact analytic cycle control so that you can demonstrate correct reasoning even if your particular game population does not develop a natural cycle. A genuinely transitive-looking population is a valid observation. Failing to produce a dramatic cycle is not a reason to alter results.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 6.3-p2.</strong> A beats B in complete paired evidence and B beats C, but A versus C was never run. What graph can you draw? What claim must remain open, and which missing comparison would resolve it under the same plan?</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 6.3-p2 --answer 'your graph and missing evidence'
node cli.mjs feedback 6.3-p2</code></pre>
<h2>Choose a population for a declared opponent distribution</h2>
<p>A mixture can reduce the weakness of committing to one predictable policy. In the exact cyclic example, a uniform mixture has zero restricted gap against those three strategies. That conclusion depends on the complete specified matrix. Adding a stronger unlisted response can change it.</p>
<p>The league samples a member once per game. Its average payoff against an independently sampled opposing mixture is the corresponding weighted matrix average when the matrix describes those same frozen policies and conditions. Mixing policies anew at every turn changes the policy and requires new evaluation; the old matrix is no longer sufficient.</p>
<p>A single scalar remains useful for a specific decision—for example, expected utility against a stated opponent mixture. Label that mixture and keep the payoff structure visible. A policy can be best for today's target distribution without being generally best or safe against every response.</p>
<p><strong>Commit 6.3-p3.</strong> A deployment expects one opponent 90% of the time and the other two only 5% each. Explain why the best expected-return choice may differ from a low-gap mixture. Propose a report that shows the tradeoff and a test for what happens if the opponent distribution changes.</p>
<pre><code>node cli.mjs attempt 6.3-p3 --answer 'your objective tradeoff and test'
node cli.mjs feedback 6.3-p3</code></pre>

Module 7 uses these artifacts to assemble and defend a replayable season rather than simply naming its highest-scoring row.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. <article id="lesson-7.1" class="lesson" hidden><h1>7.1 Assemble a replayable season</h1>
<p>Your newest policy has beaten every opponent you tried yesterday, but yesterday's files do not say which parameters or starting positions were used. Assemble a season whose claim can be checked by rerunning the same decisions and games.</p>
<h2>The season is a declared experiment</h2>
<p>A season starts with an evaluation plan. The plan names the rules, the exact policy snapshots, the starting scenarios, both seat assignments, the random seeds and the budget. Freeze those fields before the first scored game. A friendly display name such as <code>champion</code> is not enough: changing its parameters changes the policy even when the name stays the same.</p>
<p>The six required roles are a supplied random baseline, a supplied greedy baseline, your search policy, your learned-value search policy, an older learned snapshot and a counter-policy. They should differ in behavior or learned parameters. Merely giving the same program six names does not create a league. You may add two more variants if you have a reason to compare them.</p>
<p>For every unordered pair of policies, play both seat assignments on the same starting scenario. Repeat using the declared policy-randomness seeds. This arrangement makes the roster explicit and preserves useful pairing. The two seat games are related observations; they are not two independent draws of a new scenario.</p>
<p><strong>Commit before continuing:</strong> item <code>7.1-p1</code> asks you to calculate the complete match count for a declared small season. Use <code>node cli.mjs attempt 7.1-p1 --answer 'your count and reasoning'</code>, then request feedback.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 7.1-p1:</strong> A season has six policies, three scenarios, both seats and two randomness replicates. How many games are planned? Explain the unit you counted.</p>
<h2>From a missing result to a complete denominator</h2>
<p>Suppose a three-policy season uses two scenarios, both seats and one randomness replicate. There are three unordered policy pairs and four games per pair. The plan therefore expects twelve uniquely identified games. If eleven records exist, the report does not silently redefine the season as eleven games. It identifies the missing key.</p>
<p>A policy that returns an illegal action can legitimately forfeit under the declared rules. A host process that crashes before it records a result does not establish that either policy lost. Preserve that failure and retry the same planned game with a linked reason. A duplicate retry must not count twice. Two different outcomes for the same supposedly deterministic match identity are an inconsistency to investigate, not an invitation to keep the favorable one.</p>
<p>Coverage is part of the result. Before computing a headline, reconcile expected keys, completed results, policy failures and unresolved infrastructure failures. This work is evaluation logic, not a demand that you build a database or job scheduler; the supplied host owns storage and execution.</p>
<p><strong>Apply it:</strong> commit item <code>7.1-p2</code> before viewing feedback. Decide what a report should do with one missing game and one duplicate result.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 7.1-p2:</strong> Your planned twelve-game season has eleven distinct results and a duplicate of one of those results. May you report twelve completed games? What should happen next?</p>
<h2>Two different kinds of replay</h2>
<p>Trajectory replay starts from the recorded initial state and applies the recorded actions through the supplied game engine. It checks the next state and the official result at every step. This establishes that the actions form the reported game. It does not establish that the named policy chose those actions.</p>
<p>Policy rerun goes further. It loads the same policy code and parameters, gives them the same observations and private random stream, enforces the same budget and compares the decisions. Then trajectory replay checks the consequences. Both identities matter. A correct board animation can display a fabricated attribution.</p>
<p>The viewer is a way to inspect where a game changed. It displays data; it does not certify that the data is authentic. Use the command-line verifier for the recorded rules and source identity. If a later rule patch changes the game's semantics, keep the old rule identity with old records. Never recompute an old match with new rules while retaining the old label.</p>
<p><strong>Transfer:</strong> item <code>7.1-p3</code> gives a replay that is legal but has the wrong policy hash. Explain the strongest claim it still supports and the claim it cannot support.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 7.1-p3:</strong> A recorded action sequence replays legally to the reported winner, but its named policy hash differs from the supplied policy file. What can you claim?</p>
<h2>Build and retain</h2>
<p>Assemble a development season through the supplied league runner using your actual learner functions. Inspect a loss, trace its first consequential decision and link that game ID in your notes. Then freeze the final plan and execute its entire roster. Keep the plan, snapshots, raw matches, coverage report and your written claim together. If your learner functions are unfinished, finish their earlier checks first; a supplied demonstration is useful for learning the interface but does not replace your season.</p>
<p>The module's evidence is a complete reproducible season, not a particular champion. Record the first report and any repaired report as different attempts.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. The local CLI preserves the original question, first response, assistance and revisions. This reading view does not grade your reasoning.</div></article>
<article id="lesson-7.2" class="lesson" hidden><h1>7.2 Choose a population rather than one lucky winner</h1>
<p>Your highest-scoring policy loses consistently to an older opponent that the training loop nearly discarded. Choose a retained population and a deployment distribution using the opponents and evidence you actually have.</p>
<h2>A policy's score depends on who it meets</h2>
<p>An average score is an expectation under an opponent distribution. Changing that distribution can change the ordering of policies. If a league contains many copies of an easy opponent, a specialist against that opponent may look impressive. Its score does not establish robustness against a different pool.</p>
<p>Begin with the pairwise payoff matrix. Each entry states how one frozen policy performs against another under the same scenario and seat schedule. Missing entries remain missing. They are not draws. Look for large weaknesses, not just the row with the largest average. If the confidence intervals are broad, distinguish an apparent advantage from a supported one.</p>
<p>As a worked comparison, imagine two candidates. Candidate A scores well against the most frequent training opponents but has a large loss against a rare archived one. Candidate B is slightly worse against the frequent opponents and much better against the rare one. Under the current frequency weighting, A can have the larger average. Under a policy that protects against the worst measured matchup, B can be preferable. Neither conclusion is meaningful until the selection objective is stated.</p>
<p><strong>Commit:</strong> item <code>7.2-p1</code> asks which information is missing from a claim that one candidate is simply “better.” State the objective and evidence you would need, then inspect feedback.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 7.2-p1:</strong> Policy A has the higher mean score while policy B has the better worst measured matchup. What is missing from the statement that A is better?</p>
<h2>Retaining a policy can have experimental value</h2>
<p>An archived policy can be useful even when it is not selected for deployment. It can expose a weakness in newer policies. Removing it from active training may save computation, but removing its records destroys evidence about forgetting. Keep the immutable snapshot and its results even when its active sampling weight becomes zero.</p>
<p>Retention therefore has two decisions: what remains in the archive, and what receives current training probability. The supplied host retains history. You choose active opponents and weights. A fixed budget forces tradeoffs: spreading samples over more policies improves coverage but leaves fewer samples per matchup. Repeatedly sampling only the newest rival can produce fast local improvement and miss older failures.</p>
<p>Use your earlier sampler and admission rule. Compare the candidate against the same frozen evaluation pool used for its predecessor. If a new policy improves one family and harms another, preserve both facts. A defensible admission rule can retain the candidate for its complementary behavior while keeping the predecessor. It need not pretend that every accepted policy dominates all earlier ones.</p>
<p><strong>Apply it:</strong> commit item <code>7.2-p2</code> about retaining a losing historical policy before revealing the answer.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 7.2-p2:</strong> An old policy loses to most of the pool but exposes a reproducible weakness in the newest candidate. Give a defensible reason to retain it.</p>
<h2>A mixture has precise semantics</h2>
<p>In this course, a mixture chooses one frozen policy at the start of each game and uses it throughout that game. The choice is private to that side. This produces a distribution over complete policies. Choosing a different policy at every move is a different strategy: moves that make sense as part of one plan may interact badly with another policy's continuation.</p>
<p>A matrix-distribution helper may suggest mixture weights. Inspect its reported restricted gap, numerical tolerance and iteration budget. An optimizer stopping is not a certificate of exact equilibrium. More importantly, even an exact solution of the measured policy matrix protects only against the strategies represented by that matrix. A new opponent can still expose a weakness.</p>
<p>Uniform weights are a useful baseline, not a universal solution. A nonuniform distribution is acceptable when you state what it optimizes and evaluate the actual resulting policy-selection procedure. Keep its random seed and weights with the deployment snapshot. Avoid choosing weights after seeing the final test results and then reporting those same results as independent confirmation.</p>
<p><strong>Transfer:</strong> item <code>7.2-p3</code> compares per-game and per-move switching. Explain why the old matrix cannot automatically certify the new behavior.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 7.2-p3:</strong> You evaluated a mixture that chooses one policy per game. You now choose a fresh policy each move using the same weights. Does the old payoff matrix certify the new policy?</p>
<h2>Your deliverable</h2>
<p>Retain six distinct policy roles and state which ones receive training and deployment weight. Explain one inclusion and one exclusion or reduced weight using observed matchups. Compare your choice with uniform historical sampling under equal budgets. A negative or inconclusive comparison is allowed; the artifact must still contain a valid distribution, complete evaluation and honest interpretation.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. The local CLI preserves the original question, first response, assistance and revisions. This reading view does not grade your reasoning.</div></article>
<article id="lesson-7.3" class="lesson" hidden><h1>7.3 Audit the evidence behind the headline</h1>
<p>A report says the league has become harder to exploit, but its newer run used more search and omitted two failed games. Audit the evidence before accepting the headline.</p>
<h2>Start with the claim's subject</h2>
<p>“This frozen policy scored higher on these sixteen scenarios” is a different claim from “this training method produces stronger policies.” The first concerns one set of code and parameters. The second concerns a distribution over training runs. Replaying many games from one trained policy does not create independent training runs.</p>
<p>Name the subject, comparison and domain. Include the game/rule version, opponent pool, scenario-generation process, training replicas, evaluation replicas and compute budget. The final report can be concise because those details live in linked manifests. It cannot omit them from the evidence entirely.</p>
<p>As a worked audit, consider a new checkpoint compared with an older checkpoint at the same rules and scenario roster. The new checkpoint receives twice as many simulation calls per decision. A higher score supports a comparison between those two deployed configurations. It does not isolate the contribution of training. To investigate learning, compare them at a matched budget or report the combined configuration change explicitly.</p>
<p><strong>Commit:</strong> item <code>7.3-p1</code> asks you to rewrite an overbroad result into a claim the supplied evidence can support.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 7.3-p1:</strong> One trained checkpoint beats its predecessor on a fixed roster, but used twice the search budget. Rewrite the claim without attributing the gain to learning alone.</p>
<h2>Check identity, coverage and independence</h2>
<p>First verify identity. The policy source, parameter file and rule hashes in the report must match the executed records. Second verify coverage. Every expected game has one qualified result or a visible unresolved failure. Third inspect independence and selection. Did the reported final scenarios influence feature choice, training duration, opponent weights or checkpoint selection?</p>
<p>If they did, the run is useful exploratory evidence. It is no longer untouched confirmation of the final choice. Preserve it, label it and use a fresh confirmation set for a new confirmatory claim. Rewriting filenames or reseeding the same disclosed tiny roster does not necessarily create a genuinely new test.</p>
<p>The same care applies to intervals. Show the resampling unit and count. Correlated moves are not independent samples. A narrow interval produced by resampling thousands of moves from a few games can be very precise about the wrong experiment. Repeatedly checking an ordinary interval and stopping when it looks favorable also changes its interpretation.</p>
<p><strong>Apply it:</strong> commit item <code>7.3-p2</code> about a final set used to choose between three model variants. Then compare your disposition with the feedback.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 7.3-p2:</strong> You chose the best of three feature variants after looking at final-test scores. How should those scores now be labeled, and what would confirmation require?</p>
<h2>Search for a reason your interpretation could fail</h2>
<p>An audit is stronger when it contains a counterexample. Inspect the policy's worst measured matchup, a failed or low-performing training run, and a scenario where the apparent improvement reverses. Ask whether the mechanism in your explanation predicts these cases too.</p>
<p>If you claim lower exploitability, identify the responder family and its search/training budget. A responder finding no profitable deviation does not prove that none exists. For a tiny game you can enumerate, exact best-response evidence can support an exact gap. For the larger league, your result normally remains empirical vulnerability to tested responders.</p>
<p>Include a valid alternative explanation. Perhaps a value model improved tactical ordering rather than its numerical accuracy. Perhaps a population helped because it retained a particular counter, not because more opponents are always better. An ablation can distinguish these explanations. If it was not run, record the uncertainty rather than inventing a mechanism from the outcome alone.</p>
<p><strong>Transfer:</strong> item <code>7.3-p3</code> asks what to report when the counter-policy fails to find a win. The correct level of confidence depends on what was searched, not on the desired story.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 7.3-p3:</strong> A responder searched for ten minutes and found no winning policy. Is the champion unexploitable? State a defensible conclusion.</p>
<h2>Evidence to retain</h2>
<p>Keep your frozen plan, source and parameter identities, complete match roster, failures, interval configuration, first report and revised report. Link at least one replay supporting your diagnosis. Have another person or a fresh process rerun from those artifacts without relying on your working directory's unnamed current files.</p>
<p>Passing the audit means your claims match your evidence. It does not mean your policy must win, that your method is universally best, or that the course has proved a learning effect.</p><div class="callout">Commit your work in the terminal. The local CLI preserves the original question, first response, assistance and revisions. This reading view does not grade your reasoning.</div></article>
<article id="lesson-8.1" class="lesson" hidden><h1>8.1 Freeze a prediction before the patch</h1>
<p>Your league is about to receive a rule change, and you want to know whether its design transfers. Commit a prediction and evaluation plan before learning the exact change.</p>
<h2>Prediction creates a comparison with your earlier understanding</h2>
<p>A useful prediction names an assumption and a consequence. “Something might break” cannot distinguish insight from hindsight. “My route planner's proof needs every edge cost to be nonnegative, so I expect its greedy search can return a wrong route once a change makes an edge negative” can be checked. It also names what would show it wrong: the greedy route still matching an exhaustive search on every test map built around a negative edge. The worked example below develops this case.</p>
<p>Your prediction is not a scored guess of a secret answer. It records what your current model of the system implies. If it is wrong, retain it and explain why. Editing the prediction after seeing the patch removes the evidence of that change in understanding.</p>
<p>As a worked example from another domain, a route planner assumes all edges have nonnegative cost. A new discount can introduce a negative edge. Before seeing the map, the author predicts that a greedy shortest-path implementation may fail and names the condition needed by its proof. The value lies in connecting the algorithm's premise to its behavior, not in guessing the exact discounted road.</p>
<p><strong>Commit:</strong> item <code>8.1-p1</code> asks for a testable transfer prediction about an assumption your own agent makes. Save it before you open lesson 8.2, this item's feedback or any challenge text. Navigation is open, so keeping this order is your own discipline. The item also asks you to declare what you had read before predicting. If you have already read 8.2, say so: that is an exposure record, not a fault, and the prediction then counts as assisted practice.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 8.1-p1:</strong> Write a testable prediction about one assumption your current search or value model makes. Name the consequence you expect and an observation that would show the prediction was wrong. Then declare what you had read before predicting: lesson 8.2, this item's feedback, or any rule-change or challenge text.</p>
<h2>Freeze the experiment as well as the prose</h2>
<p>Save the old policy source and parameters, ordinary-game results, responder configuration, training budget and evaluation plan. Do not overwrite the champion in place. A before/after comparison needs a real before artifact.</p>
<p>The plan should separate adaptation from evaluation. Allocate the same allowed simulation credits to the methods being compared. Name the ordinary-rule checks you will rerun as well as the new-rule checks. Otherwise an adaptation that handles the patch by breaking ordinary play could be called an unqualified improvement.</p>
<p>Decide how you will treat an incomplete adaptation run. A host interruption is not a loss. An illegal policy action is a policy failure under the declared contract. Preserve those distinctions, as in the earlier season. They do not disappear because this is the capstone.</p>
<p><strong>Apply it:</strong> commit item <code>8.1-p2</code> about an old checkpoint overwritten by the adaptation process. Identify what evidence was lost and what can still be recovered honestly.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 8.1-p2:</strong> You overwrote the old champion parameters while adapting. Why is this a problem, and what can you honestly do now?</p>
<h2>A practice patch is not a held-out assessment</h2>
<p>This package ships worked examples and analysis items. It ships no patched game simulator and no runnable practice patch. The rule change discussed in lesson 8.2 is hypothetical, and because every learner can read it, it is not a secret assessment item. The independently administered capstone uses a new instance issued separately from the public package. Its exact rule, starting positions and scoring controls should not have appeared in your worked examples.</p>
<p>For that separately issued challenge, the instructor supplies the changed simulator and its written rules. You are not expected to guess hidden rules or implement a new engine. Your work is to reason about the changed assumptions and adapt the policy, learned representation or experiment where needed.</p>
<p>If you have already seen the challenge's private controls or reference answer, label that attempt assisted and use a fresh independently issued instance for a claim of unassisted transfer. Do not hide prior exposure. That record helps distinguish a learning exercise from measurement.</p>
<p><strong>Transfer:</strong> item <code>8.1-p3</code> asks whether a new seed for a publicly disclosed worked patch automatically creates a held-out test, and which kind of novelty would matter.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 8.1-p3:</strong> A learner has read a worked solution to a public rule patch. They rerun it with a new random seed. Is this automatically an unassisted held-out transfer assessment? Which kind of novelty would matter?</p>
<h2>Your before artifact</h2>
<p>Export the prediction, old snapshots and plan. Record assistance used in reaching the prediction. Then stop changing the before artifact. When the challenge arrives, keep the instructor's rule version and challenge identity with your new work. The final lesson compares your prediction with the actual failure or success; it does not erase the first answer.</p>
<h2>What you can complete now, and where to stop</h2>
<p>All nine analysis items in this module, <code>8.1-p1</code> to <code>8.3-p3</code>, can be completed now. They ask for reasoning about worked examples and hypothetical cases, and none of them needs a patched simulator. Commit <code>8.1-p1</code> first, then work through lessons 8.2 and 8.3.</p>

<article id="lesson-8.2" class="lesson" hidden><h1>8.2 Adapt under the original compute budget</h1>
<p>This lesson uses a hypothetical rule change to practise diagnosis. No patched game simulator ships in this package. Answer the three analysis items using the worked examples below. The executable adaptation steps apply after an instructor supplies a versioned challenge.</p>
<h2>Read the new contract before changing the code</h2>
<p>The base game alternates players, but your search interface exposes the actual current player. Those facts were deliberately separate. If a new rule sometimes gives the same player another move, a recursion that simply negates every returned value may apply the wrong perspective. A recursion that asks who acts next has a chance to remain correct without a structural rewrite.</p>
<p>When an instructor supplies a challenge, do not infer its rules from an animation. Read the instructor's written rules, inspect the supplied conformance examples and check the state fields. Keep the rule version and challenge identity with your work. New counters can matter to future legal moves. Two equal boards with different remaining privileges are different states and need different cache identities.</p>
<p>As a worked diagnostic on a generic tree, suppose the root and its child are both controlled by the maximizing player. At the child, the player can select between two outcomes. Treating that child as an opponent turn predicts the wrong choice. The mistake concerns who owns the decision, not the arithmetic sign of the terminal reward. Use an explicit actor trace to identify where your implementation's assumption diverges.</p>
<p><strong>Commit:</strong> item <code>8.2-p1</code> asks you to locate the kind of component that can fail even when the visible board and legal-action encoding stay the same.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 8.2-p1:</strong> The board and action IDs look unchanged, but a new visible phase field changes who moves next. Name two components that may still be wrong.</p>
<h2>Reproduce one failure before making a broad repair</h2>
<p><strong>Conditional on an instructor-supplied challenge:</strong> the steps in this section are executable work. They apply once an instructor has supplied the rules and the simulator. Until then, read them as the method that item <code>8.2-p2</code> asks you to reason about.</p>
<p>Run the frozen old policy under the instructor-supplied rules and the fixed evaluation plan. Find one small failing trace. Record its initial state, rule identity, action sequence and first consequential decision. A smaller witness is easier to reason about than an average season score.</p>
<p>State a hypothesis before editing. Perhaps the search backup assumes alternation, the transposition key omits a new counter, or the learned feature representation collapses strategically different states. Make the narrow change that addresses the hypothesis. Reproduce the witness, then test fresh positions. A patch that hardcodes the observed action can fix one replay while leaving the actual assumption unchanged.</p>
<p>If your generic policy already handles the changed rule, do not add a meaningless edit to look busy. Demonstrate that it obeys the new contract, explain why, and test the new state field and actor cases. Transfer can be preservation of a valid abstraction.</p>
<p><strong>Apply it:</strong> commit item <code>8.2-p2</code> comparing a hardcoded trace repair with a state-representation repair. Then inspect feedback and revise your diagnosis if needed.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 8.2-p2:</strong> A repair returns the known winning move whenever the failing board appears. Another repair includes the new phase in the state representation and follows the actual actor. Which better addresses the hypothesis, and what must still be tested?</p>
<h2>Learning and evaluation can break independently of search</h2>
<p><strong>Conditional on an instructor-supplied challenge:</strong> refitting a model and running the evaluations described below are executable work. Item <code>8.2-p3</code> can be answered now from the reasoning alone.</p>
<p>A value model may have learned returns under the ordinary rule distribution. Correct search does not make those estimates automatically calibrated under the patch. New counters may need representation; different move sequences can change which training examples occur. If you refit the model, retain its new training provenance and count its computation against the adaptation budget.</p>
<p>Evaluate both ordinary and changed rules. Keep the original budget, opponent identities and declared scenario process for each comparison. If you choose among multiple adaptation candidates using a selection set, freeze the choice before final evaluation. A patch does not excuse test-set tuning.</p>
<p>For response search, distinguish a responder's limited failure from the absence of any exploit. The new game may enlarge the set of relevant strategies. Your old response family might simply be too narrow to detect the new weakness.</p>
<p><strong>Transfer:</strong> item <code>8.2-p3</code> asks what you can conclude when the ordinary policy's score holds but its new-rule feature errors grow. Keep prediction quality, playing strength and uncertainty separate.</p>
<p><strong>Practice 8.2-p3:</strong> After a patch, win rate appears unchanged but value prediction error increases. Does unchanged win rate prove the model still represents the game equally well?</p>

<article id="lesson-8.3" class="lesson" hidden><h1>8.3 Defend what transferred and what did not</h1>
<p>Suppose your adapted policy wins more often under the changed rules but regresses on ordinary play. These gains and regressions are hypothetical until an instructor-supplied challenge produces actual results. Defend a conclusion that preserves both results and the limits of the experiment.</p>
<h2>Compare the prediction with the actual mechanism</h2>
<p>Retrieve your pre-patch prediction without rewriting it. Identify the assumptions that survived, the ones that failed and the evidence supporting each judgment. <p>Use a causal explanation proportional to the evidence. If changing one cache key fixes the minimal witness and several fresh structurally similar positions, that supports the cache hypothesis. <p>Show the old and adapted configurations on ordinary and changed rules. Name the opponent pool, scenario set, seeds, budgets and unresolved failures for each cell. Do not omit ordinary-rule regression because the headline concerns adaptation. A deployment decision can legitimately prefer the adapted policy for the new rules while keeping the earlier one for the old rules.</p>
<p>As a worked decision, imagine an adaptation that fixes every issued conformance case but has an uncertain tournament difference. You can conclude that it satisfies those contract cases. Correctness and empirical performance answer different questions.</p>
```

`courses/game-playing-agent-league/learner/counter-policy.mjs`:

```mjs
/** Supplied adapter for a declared opponent model, not hidden opponent access. */
import {responsePolicy} from './vulnerability.mjs';
import {evaluate} from './evaluation.mjs';
import {greedyPolicy} from '../lib/supplied-policies.mjs';
export function decide(context) {
  const model=context.parameters.opponentModel??'greedy';
  if(!['greedy','uniform'].includes(model)) throw new Error('Supported declared opponent models are greedy and uniform.');
  function opponentPolicy(state) {
    const actions=context.oracle.legal(state);
    if(model==='uniform') return actions.map(actionId=>({actionId,probability:1/actions.length}));
    const selected=greedyPolicy({state,player:context.oracle.currentPlayer(state),legalActions:actions});
    return actions.map(actionId=>({actionId,probability:actionId===selected?1:0}));
  }
  return responsePolicy({...context,evaluate,opponentPolicy});
}
```
