<p>Ghidra imports machine code, identifies possible functions and produces a C-like explanation called <strong>decompilation</strong>. That explanation is a hypothesis about behavior. It does not recover the author&#x27;s original names or source text. Keep using native probes to test it.</p>
<p>Use this companion after saving the prediction required by the milestone and reaching its instruction-inspection step. The existing M1 v0.6 and M2 v0.5 archives remain unchanged. Their setup notes describe the earlier build; this page records the later tool validation. Do not copy a decompilation into an earlier record and present it as your first prediction.</p>
<h2 id="tool-identity-and-installation">Tool identity and installation</h2>
<p>The tested toolchain is Apple Silicon macOS, Ghidra <strong>12.1.4</strong>, Temurin JDK <strong>21.0.12.1+1</strong>, Python <strong>3.14.6</strong>, and Apple clang <strong>21.0.0</strong>. The Java runtime and Ghidra were extracted into a dedicated directory. No global Java registration, shell-profile edit, driver, VM or OS-security change was required.</p>
<p>Use the official <a href="https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/releases/tag/Ghidra_12.1.4_build">Ghidra release</a>, <a href="https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/blob/Ghidra_12.1.4_build/GhidraDocs/GettingStarted.md">version-pinned setup guide</a>, and <a href="https://github.com/adoptium/temurin21-binaries/releases/tag/jdk-21.0.12.1%2B1">Temurin JDK release</a>. Download the named release assets, not the source-code archives. Before extracting, compare their SHA-256 hashes:</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Asset</th><th scope="col">SHA-256</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC_20260921.zip</code></td><td><code>ddac49f903da9d5bac833e5cc79395098b9c33cfd3279be5f31bd00387d2d4db</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>OpenJDK21U-jdk_aarch64_mac_hotspot_21.0.12.1_1.tar.gz</code></td><td><code>3623232f33a9c3baadf304480b2535f9a3cba8a58d42ecbb438ba267315d9998</code></td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>The archives total approximately 770 MB and expand to approximately 1.26 GB together. Allow additional room for the native build, Gradle, projects and your records. Extract into new directories; never overwrite another installation. On this JDK distribution, the Java home is the extracted <code>jdk-21.0.12.1+1/Contents/Home</code> directory.</p>
<p>Ghidra&#x27;s release requires a native-component build for Apple Silicon. In its <code>support/gradle</code> directory, the official procedure is <code>./gradlew buildNatives</code>. Give that process the JDK21 <code>JAVA_HOME</code>; the tested run used <code>--no-daemon --max-workers=2</code> and a separate <code>GRADLE_USER_HOME</code>. The shipped wrapper uses Gradle <strong>9.7.1</strong>. Its official distribution SHA-256 is <code>acd53f1edaf02f1a8ff99879f8a34b302661a057d9b063ae9e35b552f804d20a</code>; pin it as <code>distributionSha256Sum</code> in that installation&#x27;s wrapper properties before the first download. The native build must finish successfully before you proceed.</p>
<p>To apply that setup, first check the JDK by running its <code>bin/java -version</code>. In a terminal, enter the extracted Ghidra <code>support/gradle</code> folder. Open its <code>gradle-wrapper.properties</code> in a text editor and add this line if it is absent:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-properties">distributionSha256Sum=acd53f1edaf02f1a8ff99879f8a34b302661a057d9b063ae9e35b552f804d20a
</code></pre>
<p>An environment variable is a named setting passed to a program. <code>JAVA_HOME</code> tells this build where the JDK is; <code>GRADLE_USER_HOME</code> chooses its download/cache folder. The <code>env</code> command below sets them for this one command, without editing a shell profile. Replace both paths with your actual JDK directory and a new cache folder:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">env JAVA_HOME=&quot;/path/to/jdk-21.0.12.1+1/Contents/Home&quot; GRADLE_USER_HOME=&quot;/path/to/new-gradle-cache&quot; ./gradlew --no-daemon --max-workers=2 buildNatives
</code></pre>
<p>The first run downloads the pinned Gradle distribution. Stop on a checksum failure or build failure and preserve the output. Continue only after <code>BUILD SUCCESSFUL</code>; the tested build produced the ARM64 decompiler, sleigh, demanglers and file-format helper. This is a compiler/setup checkpoint, not a successful target import yet.</p>
<p>If an OS permission or security dialog prevents launch, preserve the error and stop that route. Do not disable protections or remove quarantine attributes as a course step. Use the supplied listing while arranging the tool issue separately.</p>
<h2 id="run-the-command-line-inspection">Run the command-line inspection</h2>
<p><strong>Headless</strong> means that Ghidra runs without its graphical window. This route performs real import, analysis and decompilation. It does not test graphical navigation, screen-reader access or your interpretation.</p>
<p>From the complete student bundle&#x27;s top-level folder, use <code>tools/inspect_ghidra.py</code>. In the private source checkout, first enter <code>courses/re-lab</code> to use the same relative path. This helper and its adjacent <code>CourseEvidence.java</code> contain export plumbing, not the target&#x27;s answer. It writes logs, a Ghidra project, decompilation and an exact-target receipt to new paths. It never installs tools or replaces earlier evidence.</p>
<p>For the already-investigated M1 <code>cart</code>, replace the four example paths below with your extracted tool directories, target and a new private output directory. Quotes keep spaces in a path together. You can drag a directory into Terminal to obtain its path. <code>--symbol</code> names the function seen in the supplied listing.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 tools/inspect_ghidra.py \
  --ghidra &quot;/path/to/ghidra_12.1.4_PUBLIC&quot; \
  --java-home &quot;/path/to/jdk-21.0.12.1+1/Contents/Home&quot; \
  --target &quot;/path/to/m1-student/cart&quot; \
  --symbol lab_step \
  --out &quot;/path/to/new-cart-evidence&quot;
</code></pre>
<p>Ghidra refuses a project path containing a hidden component such as <code>.tmp</code> or <code>.claude</code>. If your output is inside one, add <code>--project-root &quot;/tmp/re-lab-project-01&quot;</code>, using a new name for each run. The helper records that external project location in <code>run.json</code>; keep it with the evidence. <code>/tmp</code> can be cleared by the operating system, so copy a finished project into your own durable storage before relying on it long-term. Do not reuse or delete an older project to silence a refusal.</p>
<p>The successful command prints the path to <code>run.json</code>. Open it and <code>evidence.json</code> in a text editor. Verify <code>status</code> is <code>passed</code>, the target hash matches your manifest, and all requested functions appear. Ghidra reports the supplied targets as <code>Mac OS X Mach-O</code>, with language <code>AARCH64:LE:64:AppleSilicon</code>.</p>
<p>For M1&#x27;s other two targets, change <code>--target</code> and use a new output/project name; <code>lab_step</code> remains the function. For M2&#x27;s <code>parcel</code> and <code>parcel-shifted</code>, replace the symbol argument with four arguments:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-text">--symbol initialize_parcel --symbol adjust_credit --symbol score_parcel --symbol process_parcel
</code></pre>
<p>For M6, inspect <code>quote-O0</code> and <code>quote-O2</code> with <code>--symbol quote</code>; the separate worked targets <code>fee-O0</code> and <code>fee-O2</code> use <code>--symbol fee_example</code>. For M7, inspect <code>reserve</code>, <code>reserve-atomic</code> and <code>reserve-opt</code> with <code>--symbol decode_record --symbol apply_record --symbol replay</code>. Use a new output and project name every time. M3/M4 work directly with file bytes and a Python parser, and M5 traces Python processes; their exercises do not require Ghidra.</p>
<h2 id="compare-representations-before-accepting-a-claim">Compare representations before accepting a claim</h2>
<ol>
<li><p>Choose a short instruction range already traced in your notebook. Find its address and text in <code>evidence.json</code>, then compare them with the supplied <code>.asm</code> listing. Leading underscores in function names are normal for these targets.</p></li>
<li><p>Identify the same input, arithmetic operation, branch or memory update in <code>decompiled_c</code>. Temporary names such as <code>local_18</code>, <code>param_1</code> and types such as <code>undefined4</code> are generated labels. They are not evidence of the original source spelling, field names or intended signedness.</p></li>
<li><p>Write a claim and a competing explanation. Predict a native input that would distinguish them, save that prediction, then execute the target. Keep the result beside the prediction. A clean-looking decompilation does not replace this check.</p></li>
<li><p>Add the target hash, tool versions, function entry, relevant addresses and observed result to a new notebook record. If you opened a hint or answer, use the milestone&#x27;s assistance field. Keep the old record unchanged.</p></li>
</ol>
<p>This is the same evidence habit as the supplied-listing route. The additional tool helps you move between representations; it does not certify a correct model or an independent attempt.</p>
<p><strong>M2 caution: machine evidence and a reported decompilation.</strong> In the supplied <code>parcel</code> listings, <code>_process_parcel</code> calls <code>_score_parcel</code> and then restores the frame and returns without changing <code>w0</code>. Four selected author probes of the exact delivered targets agree with the score calculation. This review did not recover the historical generated-C export, so the reported <code>void</code> return type and shifted <code>undefined2 *</code> pointer example remain unverified tool observations; do not infer either from the assembly alone. Follow the register value across the call instead of treating the guessed <code>void</code> type as proof that no result returns. Compare actual load/store widths and byte offsets before accepting a field map.</p>
<h2 id="diagnose-a-failed-run">Diagnose a failed run</h2>
<p>An existing output/project directory is a preservation refusal: choose a new name. A missing Java or launcher path means the directory argument is wrong or setup is incomplete. A missing function can mean the symbol was mistyped or the target does not match the listing. Do not guess a result from a partially written file.</p>
<p>Keep <code>run.json</code>, <code>console.log</code>, <code>analysis.log</code> and <code>script.log</code>. A zero Ghidra process exit alone is insufficient: the helper also requires a complete export of every requested function. If no successful evidence receipt exists, label the run failed and continue with the supplied listing until the concrete error is resolved.</p>
<h2 id="graphical-route-and-remaining-limits">Graphical route and remaining limits</h2>
<p>The <a href="https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra/blob/Ghidra_12.1.4_build/GhidraDocs/GhidraClass/Beginner/Introduction_to_Ghidra_Student_Guide.html">official introductory guide</a> describes CodeBrowser. Launch <code>ghidraRun</code>, create a non-shared project, import the owned target, confirm its format/language, open it and allow analysis. In the Symbol Tree, find the function named above; compare the Listing and Decompiler and save your addresses. Keep the project in a path without hidden components.</p>
<p>The released M1 cart has also opened in native CodeBrowser with its Listing and Decompiler visible. Selected API-driven navigation and font changes from 12 to 24 points and back were checked against actual window captures. Those checks do not establish physical keyboard/pane operation, VoiceOver, native browser/OS zoom or first-time human follow-along; these remain unverified. Earlier M1/M2 setup notes describe their original validation scope. Windows, Linux, Intel Mac, live-process debugging and other tool versions remain unsupported by these execution receipts.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#tool-identity-and-installation">Tool identity and installation</a></li><li><a href="#run-the-command-line-inspection">Run the command-line inspection</a></li><li><a href="#compare-representations-before-accepting-a-claim">Compare representations before accepting a claim</a></li><li><a href="#diagnose-a-failed-run">Diagnose a failed run</a></li><li><a href="#graphical-route-and-remaining-limits">Graphical route and remaining limits</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>Work from an observation to a reproducible explanation · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="course.css"><script defer src="course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. Bytes between processes</span><div><a href="learning/m05.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="m05/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>6. Compiled forms and behavior</span><div><a href="learning/m06.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="m06/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>7. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="m07/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><article><h1 id="work-from-an-observation-to-a-reproducible-explanation">Work from an observation to a reproducible explanation</h1>
<p>Your aim is to make a claim that another person can test. A result becomes useful evidence when you retain the input, the command, the observed output and the reason that observation favors one explanation over another.</p>
<h2 id="learn-a-procedure-then-use-it-on-your-program">Learn a procedure, then use it on your program</h2>
<p>Each guided lesson introduces a mechanism, works through a smaller example and asks you to complete or apply the same reasoning. Use Check to see an explanation of your chosen answer. The first answer remains in your practice history when you try again. A later correct answer after feedback is a revision, not an unseen first success.</p>
<p>For text-only practice, each lesson links to a questions-only worksheet and a separate feedback page. Write the first choice and reason in your notes before opening feedback; keep any correction separately. These notes do not automatically import into the browser practice record.</p>
<p>Then open the original project procedure. Its target differs from the worked example. Choose a probe on which two plausible explanations disagree. If both explanations predict the same output, that probe may confirm a calculation but cannot choose between the explanations. Include the inputs and complete prediction before running the target.</p>
<h2 id="keep-prediction-and-observation-separate">Keep prediction and observation separate</h2>
<p>Edit <code>response.json</code>, validate its syntax, and use that module&#x27;s recorder command at the named stage. A successful save creates a new record path. Opening a page, typing an answer or receiving a save error is not a committed prediction. A new <code>record</code> command creates a new submission rather than changing the old one.</p>
<p>After the run, retain the exact output, identify the earliest difference from your prediction and explain its consequence. A wrong guess is useful evidence; do not overwrite it with what you now know. When the first implementation passes, challenge a plausible alternative and make a fresh prediction as the project directs. You do not need to manufacture a failed implementation.</p>
<p>Follow each project&#x27;s assistance categories and describe help accurately. Hints, checker output, other people&#x27;s code and worked solutions can change what you know. Ordinary lesson teaching and the target&#x27;s observed behavior are distinct sources; name them when explaining a claim. Keep the versioned whole-course packet because its new guided lessons are outside the older module&#x27;s manifest. For every project, retain and cite that exact whole-course packet or guide beside your export. M5 and M7 additionally support <code>--evidence</code>; use only the syntax shown by that module&#x27;s <code>record --help</code>. The other project recorders do not have this option.</p>
<h2 id="diagnose-before-repairing">Diagnose before repairing</h2>
<p>Classify the failure first. A missing file or unsupported architecture is a setup problem. Malformed JSON is a save-input problem. A native <code>refused:</code> response is a parser outcome, not a valid replay event. A checker disagreement can be a wrong model, missing corpus coverage or changed target bytes. Read the full message before editing the algorithm.</p>
<p>For a real model mismatch, preserve the offending bytes and both outputs. Locate the first contradicted value, propose one change that explains it, save the revised source, then rerun that case and a different case. A successful patch on one input can still encode the wrong rule. The projects&#x27; public checkers supply broader finite feedback; retain their exact scope rather than claiming every possible input is correct.</p>
<h2 id="back-up-the-work-you-can-actually-resume">Back up the work you can actually resume</h2>
<p>A useful backup includes the model or decoder, response, raw probes, target manifest and the entire notebook-record directory. Each project gives concrete copy/export commands. Use a new destination; do not clear an old folder to make an export succeed. Compare copied records with the originals and open an older copied JSON file to confirm that its question, response, code and evidence remain readable.</p>
<p>To resume in a fresh extraction of the same version, restore your own working code, response, probes and records. List the records before saving another. Keep the original ZIP beside the export. Changing a course version does not reinterpret an old question or make its original target identical to a new one.</p>
<p>Guided browser practice is a separate notebook: Export practice downloads its original and later checks with the lesson/question identities. Restore it on the matching lesson. Browser storage is a convenience, not the portable backup, and project-code notebooks do not automatically enter that browser export.</p>
<h2 id="judge-the-finished-project-at-the-right-level">Judge the finished project at the right level</h2>
<p>Use the module checkpoint and <a href="CAPSTONE.html">capstone handoff</a>. Check code behavior with the shipped tools, trace factual claims to the actual bytes or instructions, and review the explanation for what follows and what remains uncertain. Passing a public check does not grade arbitrary prose or authenticate assistance. Project 7&#x27;s public checker covers finite behavior, decoder shape and bounds; its richer private field/behavior assessment is separate and is not included in the learner packet.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#learn-a-procedure-then-use-it-on-your-program">Learn a procedure, then use it on your program</a></li><li><a href="#keep-prediction-and-observation-separate">Keep prediction and observation separate</a></li><li><a href="#diagnose-before-repairing">Diagnose before repairing</a></li><li><a href="#back-up-the-work-you-can-actually-resume">Back up the work you can actually resume</a></li><li><a href="#judge-the-finished-project-at-the-right-level">Judge the finished project at the right level</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>

<p>Use the symptom to choose the next small check. Preserve the working folder and the complete error before changing anything. Most failures below concern location, format or an unfinished starter rather than the native rule you are trying to infer.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Symptom</th><th scope="col">What to inspect</th><th scope="col">Safe next action</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>No such file</code>, <code>can&#x27;t open file</code></td><td>Run <code>pwd</code>, then <code>ls</code> for the exact named file.</td><td>Change to the intended <code>mNN</code> folder; quote a path containing spaces or drag it after <code>cd </code>.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Python prints a JSON line/column error</td><td>Open the named response at that location.</td><td>Use double-quoted keys/strings, commas between entries and no trailing comma; rerun <code>python3 -m json.tool response.json</code>. This is syntax feedback, not a factual grade.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Python reports <code>SyntaxError</code></td><td>Run <code>python3 -m py_compile</code> on your model.</td><td>Fix the named syntax while preserving the earlier source/record; no native experiment is needed to diagnose punctuation.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Untouched code raises <code>NotImplementedError</code></td><td>Check which starter was run.</td><td>Implement the requested function; an intentionally incomplete starter is not a broken installation.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Native executable says <code>Permission denied</code></td><td>Confirm the path, then inspect <code>ls -l</code> and the module setup.</td><td>If the execute bit was lost, restore it only for the named supplied target using the module&#x27;s <code>chmod u+x</code> command.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Wrong architecture or an OS security warning</td><td>Keep <code>uname -sm</code>, the exact message and target fingerprint.</td><td>Use the supported native profile. Do not remove quarantine or disable OS security. Listing-only work can continue but cannot be reported as native execution.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Target hash mismatch</td><td>From the course root use <code>python3 check_packet.py --targets-only</code>.</td><td>Keep the changed copy and extract the original version into a new folder. Do not edit the manifest to hide a changed target.</td></tr>
<tr><td>A corpus lacks accepted/rejected coverage</td><td>Read the complete checker diagnostic and your selected raw inputs.</td><td>Add a predicted discriminating input of the missing kind; keep earlier cases and do not tune expected answers to silence the check.</td></tr>
<tr><td>A native file is <code>refused:</code></td><td>Compare its size, count and byte bounds with your inferred format.</td><td>Preserve it as a malformed control; make a separate well-formed file to test an operation&#x27;s state effect.</td></tr>
<tr><td>A run/output directory already exists</td><td>Inspect the previous output before doing anything else.</td><td>Choose a new name such as <code>first-2</code>; never delete earlier evidence to make a run appear fresh.</td></tr>
<tr><td>A notebook save fails</td><td>Keep the response and read the complete validation error.</td><td>Repair that input and retry; confirm a new record path before considering it saved. Existing records remain evidence.</td></tr>
<tr><td>A prediction was saved too late</td><td>Retain the actual order and which answer or run you saw.</td><td>Label the observation honestly. Make a different fresh prediction for later work; changing the timestamp cannot restore unseen history.</td></tr>
<tr><td>A stream decoder fails at EOF</td><td>Separate an empty <code>feed</code> call from <code>finish()</code>, and inspect pending bytes.</td><td>Preserve the exact partial header/payload; compare the intended EOF rule before changing the framing loop.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Browser progress did not persist</td><td>Read the save-status message; file-URL storage can vary.</td><td>Export this lesson&#x27;s practice before closing. Terminal project notebooks remain separate and are not lost by a browser storage failure.</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<h2 id="restore-only-what-you-mean-to-restore">Restore only what you mean to restore</h2>
<p>A fresh archive contains the original starter, not your completed work. Copy your own preserved model, response, probes and records into the new same-version working folder before resuming. Keep the older folder. For the cumulative revisit, restore your own M5 decoder first; substituting a supplied author solution would change what the revisit establishes.</p>
<p>If you need help, a useful report names the project/version, platform, Python version, exact command, complete error, and relevant target hash. Supply the smallest synthetic input that reproduces the problem. Do not post your entire private notebook, unrelated files or credentials. A small reproduction makes diagnosis possible without reproducing your whole computer setup.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#restore-only-what-you-mean-to-restore">Restore only what you mean to restore</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>

<p>Prepare one working folder in which the supplied native programs, Python checkers and your saved files remain together. The main route uses the assembly listings already in the download; it does not require Ghidra, Java, Clang, LLDB, Node.js or the Ivy game source.</p>
<h2 id="check-the-computer-before-starting">Check the computer before starting</h2>
<p>The native targets are Mach-O ARM64 programs for Apple Silicon macOS. The full CLI learner route has been exercised on macOS 26.6.2 arm64 with Python 3.14.6. Module manifests also retain their original author-build details. Other Python versions or operating systems are not established by that run. The guided reading remains available elsewhere, but it does not make the native binaries portable.</p>
<p>In Terminal run:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">uname -sm
python3 --version
</code></pre>
<p>The supported architecture response is <code>Darwin arm64</code>; the recorded Python profile is <code>Python 3.14.6</code>. Python functions, lists, dictionaries, integer arithmetic and editing a plain-text file are prerequisites. No assembly knowledge is assumed. If the command is missing, Python must be available before the coding route can run; the archive does not install software. Keep the actual interpreter version with your work rather than changing global aliases to make a version line look right.</p>
<h2 id="extract-once-into-a-new-folder">Extract once into a new folder</h2>
<p>Keep the downloaded ZIP and its adjacent <code>.sha256</code> file. A SHA256 fingerprint identifies bytes; it does not by itself authenticate an unknown sender. Compare the download with the fingerprint supplied alongside this course before extracting. On a Mac, the following command prints the fingerprint of a named file:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">shasum -a 256 re-lab-course-macos-arm64-v0.6.0.zip
</code></pre>
<p>Use the actual filename if your delivered version differs. Extract into a new writable folder, not over an older attempt. In Terminal, type <code>cd </code> with a trailing space, drag the extracted folder onto the window, then press Return. Dragging supplies the folder&#x27;s real path, including spaces. Check your location:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">pwd
ls START-HERE.md index.html check_packet.py m01 m07
python3 check_packet.py
</code></pre>
<p>The packet check reads the listed files and compares their bytes with the course manifest. Before editing, expect <code>Packet files match the manifest.</code> An added notes folder is allowed. A changed supplied file is reported by name. Preserve a mismatching download and use an untouched copy rather than repairing its manifest to match the error.</p>
<p>Open <code>index.html</code> in a browser for the offline reader. It needs no server or connection. Its practice answers are saved locally when browser storage is available; export each lesson&#x27;s practice to keep a portable copy. The raw Markdown instructions and original project tools are also present.</p>
<h2 id="start-project-1-from-its-own-directory">Start Project 1 from its own directory</h2>
<p>All seven project procedures run commands inside their respective <code>m01</code> through <code>m07</code> folders. The complete packet is already extracted; ignore an older standalone setup&#x27;s instruction to find a second module ZIP. From the course root:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">cd m01
pwd
ls START-HERE.md response.json model.py cart manifest.json
python3 -m json.tool response.json
python3 -m py_compile model.py notebook.py
</code></pre>
<p>JSON syntax success prints the worksheet; Python syntax success is silent. Neither means the starter is finished. <code>NotImplementedError</code> is intentional in an untouched model. Read the guided lesson and the original first-prediction step before running a behavioral checker.</p>
<p>A module&#x27;s <code>setup.md</code> describes its original standalone author environment. This complete-course setup governs extraction and navigation; the module&#x27;s target manifest governs that target&#x27;s identity. Some retained standalone notes call the first project a foundation under development or describe tools not yet installed. Those statements describe that earlier module edition, not a missing step in this seven-project route. Use this edition&#x27;s shared setup and project map; the original project recording and checking instructions still apply. Optional Ghidra has its own guide and distinct validation scope.</p>
<h2 id="separate-work-from-inspection">Separate work from inspection</h2>
<p>Edit the named starter and <code>response.json</code>. Keep native executables, listings, checkers and original manifests unchanged. After intentional model edits, the full baseline packet check will correctly name changed files; it is not your progress checker. From the course root, <code>python3 check_packet.py --targets-only</code> verifies supplied native/listing assets without treating your model edits as damaged targets.</p>
<p>If a copied executable lost permission, the module setup names the exact files for <code>chmod u+x</code>; this changes only that working copy&#x27;s execute bit. An OS security warning is a different issue. Do not disable protections or bypass quarantine as a course step. Keep the exact warning and target identity; reading the listing can continue, but an unrun target must remain unrun in your evidence. See <a href="RECOVERY.html">recovery</a>.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a rel="prev" href="../index.html">Previous: Course start</a><a rel="next" href="learning/m01.html">Next: Prepare M01</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#check-the-computer-before-starting">Check the computer before starting</a></li><li><a href="#extract-once-into-a-new-folder">Extract once into a new folder</a></li><li><a href="#start-project-1-from-its-own-directory">Start Project 1 from its own directory</a></li><li><a href="#separate-work-from-inspection">Separate work from inspection</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. `courses/inside-the-shot/reader/course.js`:

```js
/* Offline authored practice. No network, dynamic code, or learner Python execution. */
(function (root) {
  "use strict";
  const SCHEMA = "re-lab-reader-attempts-v1";
  const clone = value => JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value));
  const own = (value, key) => Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(value, key);
  const object = value => value !== null && typeof value === "object" && !Array.isArray(value);
  function canonical(value) {
    if (Array.isArray(value)) return "[" + value.map(canonical).join(",") + "]";
    if (object(value)) return "{" + Object.keys(value).sort().map(key => JSON.stringify(key) + ":" + canonical(value[key])).join(",") + "}";
    return JSON.stringify(value);
  }
  function emptyWork(config) {
    return {
      schema: SCHEMA, course_id: config.course_id, course_version: config.course_version,
      page: config.page, question_version: config.question_version,
      questions: clone(config.questions),
      responses: Object.fromEntries(config.questions.map(question => [question.id, {first: null, later: [], imported_first: []}]))
    };
  }
  function validateImport(value, config) {
    if (!object(value) || value.schema !== SCHEMA) throw new Error("This is not a reader lesson export.");
    for (const field of ["course_id", "course_version", "page", "question_version"]) {
      if (value[field] !== config[field]) throw new Error("The " + field + " does not match this exact lesson. Open the original packet/version to read it.");
    }
    if (canonical(value.questions) !== canonical(config.questions)) throw new Error("Question wording or choices differ from this lesson.");
    const ids = config.questions.map(question => question.id);
    if (!object(value.responses) || canonical(Object.keys(value.responses).sort()) !== canonical(ids.slice().sort())) {
      throw new Error("The saved question identities do not match this lesson.");
    }
    const clean = emptyWork(config);
    const seen = new Set();
    for (const question of config.questions) {
      const record = value.responses[question.id];
      if (!object(record) || !own(record, "first") || !Array.isArray(record.later) || !Array.isArray(record.imported_first)) {
        throw new Error("A question's first/later attempt history is malformed.");
      }
      if (record.first === null && (record.later.length || record.imported_first.length)) throw new Error("Later attempts require a preserved first attempt.");
      function attempt(value) {
        if (!object(value) || typeof value.id !== "string" || !value.id || typeof value.choice !== "string" ||
            !question.choices.some(choice => choice.id === value.choice) || typeof value.checked_at !== "string" ||
            !Number.isFinite(Date.parse(value.checked_at))) throw new Error("An attempt has an invalid identity, choice, or check time.");
        if (seen.has(value.id)) throw new Error("An attempt identity occurs more than once.");
        seen.add(value.id);
        return {id: value.id, choice: value.choice, checked_at: value.checked_at};
      }
      clean.responses[question.id] = {
        first: record.first === null ? null : attempt(record.first),
        later: record.later.map(attempt), imported_first: record.imported_first.map(attempt)
      };
    }
    return clean;
  }
  function mergeWork(current, incoming, config) {
    // Validate both entirely before constructing a merged value. Neither input is mutated.
    const result = validateImport(current, config);
    const restored = validateImport(incoming, config);
    const seen = new Map();
    for (const question of config.questions) {
      const record = result.responses[question.id];
      for (const attempt of [record.first, ...record.later, ...record.imported_first].filter(Boolean)) {
        seen.set(attempt.id, {question: question.id, attempt});
      }
    }
    for (const question of config.questions) {
      const target = result.responses[question.id];
      const source = restored.responses[question.id];
      function add(attempt, role) {
        if (!attempt) return;
        if (seen.has(attempt.id)) {
          const previous = seen.get(attempt.id);
          if (previous.question !== question.id || canonical(previous.attempt) !== canonical(attempt)) {
            throw new Error("An existing attempt identity has different contents. Current work was kept.");
          }
          return;
        }
        if (role === "first" && target.first === null) target.first = clone(attempt);
        else if (role === "later") target.later.push(clone(attempt));
        else target.imported_first.push(clone(attempt));
        seen.set(attempt.id, {question: question.id, attempt});
      }
      add(source.first, "first");
      source.later.forEach(attempt => add(attempt, "later"));
      source.imported_first.forEach(attempt => add(attempt, "imported_first"));
    }
    return validateImport(result, config);
  }
  function recordCheck(current, config, questionId, choice, id, checkedAt) {
    const result = validateImport(current, config);
    const question = config.questions.find(item => item.id === questionId);
    if (!question || !question.choices.some(item => item.id === choice)) throw new Error("Select one of this question's choices.");
    const record = result.responses[questionId];
    const attempt = {id, choice, checked_at: checkedAt};
    if (record.first === null) record.first = attempt;
    else record.later.push(attempt);
    return validateImport(result, config);
  }
  function persistWork(storage, key, work) {
    try {
      if (!storage) throw new Error("Storage unavailable");
      storage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(work));
      return true;
    } catch (_) {
      return false;
    }
  }
  const api = {SCHEMA, canonical, emptyWork, validateImport, mergeWork, recordCheck, persistWork};
  if (typeof module !== "undefined" && module.exports) module.exports = api;
  if (!root.document) return;

  function boot() {
    const document = root.document;
    const sidebar = document.querySelector(".course-sidebar details");
    if (sidebar && root.matchMedia && root.matchMedia("(max-width:760px)").matches) sidebar.open = false;
    const embedded = document.getElementById("lesson-data");
    if (!embedded) return;
    const config = JSON.parse(embedded.textContent);
    const key = [SCHEMA, config.course_id, config.course_version, config.page, config.question_version].join(":");
    let work = emptyWork(config);
    let storage = null;
    let loadProblem = false;
    try {
      storage = root.localStorage;
      const saved = storage.getItem(key);
      if (saved !== null) work = validateImport(JSON.parse(saved), config);
    } catch (_) {
      loadProblem = true;
    }
    const storageStatus = document.getElementById("storage-status");
    const importStatus = document.getElementById("import-status");
    function reportStorage(saved) {
      storageStatus.textContent = saved
        ? "Checked attempts are saved in this browser. Export JSON to keep a portable copy."
        : "Unsaved in browser storage: your checked work remains in memory on this open page. Export JSON before closing or changing pages.";
    }
    if (loadProblem) {
      storageStatus.textContent = "Browser storage was unavailable or could not be read. Any existing stored data was left unchanged. New checked work can still be exported from this page.";
    } else {
      storageStatus.textContent = "Checked attempts can be kept in this browser. Export JSON after the lesson: file:// storage varies across browsers.";
    }
    function textElement(tag, text, parent) {
      const element = document.createElement(tag);
      element.textContent = text;
      parent.appendChild(element);
      return element;
    }
    function showFeedback(section, question, attempt) {
      const feedback = section.querySelector("[data-feedback]");
      feedback.replaceChildren();
      textElement("p", attempt.choice === question.answer ? "This choice agrees with the worked reasoning." : "This choice needs revision. Compare the explanation with your reasoning.", feedback);
      textElement("p", question.feedback[attempt.choice], feedback);
      textElement("p", "Derivation: " + question.derivation, feedback);
      feedback.hidden = false;
    }
    function renderHistory(section, question) {
      const record = work.responses[question.id];
      const details = section.querySelector("[data-history]");
      const history = section.querySelector("[data-attempts]");
      history.replaceChildren();
      details.hidden = record.first === null;
      if (!record.first) return;
      const label = attempt => {
        const choice = question.choices.find(item => item.id === attempt.choice);
        return choice.id + ": " + choice.text + " — checked " + attempt.checked_at;
      };
      textElement("p", "First checked attempt: " + label(record.first), history);
      if (record.later.length) {
        textElement("p", "Later checked attempts (the first stays unchanged):", history);
        const list = textElement("ol", "", history);
        record.later.forEach(attempt => textElement("li", label(attempt), list));
      }
      if (record.imported_first.length) {
        textElement("p", "Other first attempts preserved from merged exports (your existing first stays above):", history);
        const list = textElement("ul", "", history);
        record.imported_first.forEach(attempt => textElement("li", label(attempt), list));
      }
    }
    const sections = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll("[data-question]"));
    function restoreDisplay() {
      for (const section of sections) {
        const question = config.questions.find(item => item.id === section.dataset.question);
        const record = work.responses[question.id];
        renderHistory(section, question);
        if (record.first) {
          const last = record.later.length ? record.later[record.later.length - 1] : record.first;
          section.querySelectorAll('input[type="radio"]').forEach(input => { input.checked = input.value === last.choice; });
          showFeedback(section, question, last);
          section.querySelector("[data-status]").textContent = "A previously checked answer was restored. A new Check adds a separate attempt.";
        }
      }
    }
    let counter = 0;
    function attemptId() {
      if (root.crypto && typeof root.crypto.randomUUID === "function") return root.crypto.randomUUID();
      counter += 1;
      return Date.now().toString(36) + "-" + counter + "-" + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2);
    }
    for (const section of sections) {
      const question = config.questions.find(item => item.id === section.dataset.question);
      const status = section.querySelector("[data-status]");
      section.querySelector("[data-check]").addEventListener("click", () => {
        const selected = section.querySelector('input[type="radio"]:checked');
        if (!selected) {
          status.textContent = "Choose an answer before checking. Nothing has been saved for this check.";
          section.querySelector('input[type="radio"]').focus();
          return;
        }
        try {
          const wasFirst = work.responses[question.id].first === null;
          work = recordCheck(work, config, question.id, selected.value, attemptId(), new Date().toISOString());
          const record = work.responses[question.id];
          showFeedback(section, question, wasFirst ? record.first : record.later[record.later.length - 1]);
          renderHistory(section, question);
          const saved = persistWork(storage, key, work);
          status.textContent = (wasFirst ? "Your first checked attempt is preserved." : "A later attempt was added; your first attempt is unchanged.") +
            (saved ? "" : " Browser storage failed; export JSON before leaving this page.");
          reportStorage(saved);
        } catch (error) {
          status.textContent = "This check could not be saved: " + error.message;
        }
      });
      section.querySelectorAll('input[type="radio"]').forEach(input => input.addEventListener("change", () => {
        section.querySelector("[data-feedback]").hidden = true;
        status.textContent = "Choice selected. Check to preserve this attempt and reveal its explanation.";
      }));
    }
    restoreDisplay();
    document.getElementById("export-progress").addEventListener("click", () => {
      const exported = {...clone(work), exported_at: new Date().toISOString()};
      const contents = JSON.stringify(exported, null, 2) + "\n";
      const fallback = document.getElementById("export-fallback");
      document.getElementById("export-text").value = contents;
      fallback.hidden = false;
      try {
        const url = root.URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([contents], {type: "application/json"}));
        const anchor = document.createElement("a");
        anchor.href = url;
        anchor.download = "inside-the-shot-" + config.page.split("/").pop().replace(/\.md$/, "") + "-v" + config.course_version + "-practice.json";
        document.body.appendChild(anchor);
        anchor.click();
        anchor.remove();
        root.setTimeout(() => root.URL.revokeObjectURL(url), 1000);
        importStatus.textContent = "JSON export prepared. Keep the downloaded file; a readable copy is also available below.";
      } catch (_) {
        fallback.open = true;
        importStatus.textContent = "The download could not open. Copy the readable JSON backup below into a private .json file.";
      }
    });
    document.getElementById("import-progress").addEventListener("change", async event => {
      const input = event.target;
      const file = input.files && input.files[0];
      if (!file) return;
      try {
        const parsed = JSON.parse(await file.text());
        const candidate = mergeWork(work, parsed, config);
        // Only assign after parsing, exact identity/wording validation and a complete merge.
        work = candidate;
        const saved = persistWork(storage, key, work);
        restoreDisplay();
        reportStorage(saved);
        importStatus.textContent = "Matching lesson history merged. Existing first attempts and later checks were kept; repeated records were not duplicated." +
          (saved ? "" : " The merged work is in memory; export it before leaving.");
      } catch (error) {
        importStatus.textContent = "Restore rejected: " + error.message + " Current work and browser storage were left unchanged.";
      } finally {
        input.value = "";
      }
    });
  }
  if (root.document.readyState === "loading") root.document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", boot);
  else boot();
})(typeof window !== "undefined" ? window : globalThis);

This separate help page is not a secure exam or evidence of mastery.</aside><article><h1 id="stream-review-feedback-open-after-saving">Stream review feedback — open after saving</h1>
<p>The first frame occupies byte offsets <code>[0,8)</code>: a two-byte header declares six bytes, <code>sync:5</code>. The second occupies <code>[8,17)</code>: a two-byte header declares seven bytes, <code>note:12</code>.</p>
<p>The three delivered chunks end at offsets 3, 10 and 17. After the first, the header and one payload byte are present, so the decoder returns <code>[]</code>. After the second, it returns <code>[&#x27;sync:5&#x27;]</code> and retains the next frame&#x27;s two-byte header. After the third, it returns <code>[&#x27;note:12&#x27;]</code> and retains nothing. <code>finish()</code> accepts that empty remainder.</p>
<p>Use the actual <code>os_read</code> rows in the supplied trace for the read-boundary question; do not copy delivery offsets as if they were OS observations. A read can stop before a frame ends or span a frame boundary. The valid reconstruction comes from the length headers and complete payload bytes, independent of how the OS grouped reads.</p>
<p>Sequence numbers order observations within one process. The same pipe preserves its byte order. A sorted timestamp log does not by itself prove which application event caused a different process&#x27;s event or measure exact transport latency: scheduling and instrumentation intervene. Name your chosen events and measured time difference, then state that limit. An answer that says “the nearest timestamp must be its cause” needs repair even if all decoded strings are correct.</p>
<p>Preserve the first explanation, add the actual output and feedback to a new record, and explain the precise correction if needed. This return to an earlier skill is practice; one successful later attempt does not establish durable human retention.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>Practice feedback for Project1 · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. Follow the original project’s save-before-reveal order. This separate help page is not a secure exam or evidence of mastery.</aside><article><h1 id="practice-feedback-for-project1">Practice feedback for Project1</h1>
<p>Open after choosing on <a href="m01-practice.html">m01-practice.md</a>. Preserve the original answer and any later correction.</p>
<h2 id="m01-receipt-trace">m01-receipt-trace</h2>
<p>Correct choice: b.</p>
<p>w8 = 10; w9 = 10 + 4 = 14; memory[P] = w9 = 14; w0 = w8 = 10.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> The addition puts 14 in w9, then str copies w9 to memory at P. The final mov reads w8, which still contains 10. Follow the destination on each line instead of swapping memory and return.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> The load retains old count 10 in w8. Addition produces 14 in w9; the store makes memory 14. Nothing replaces w8, so mov w0,w8 returns 10.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> The store changed memory, not w8. The add destination is w9, so the final mov reads the old 10. Returning 14 would require a different source for that mov.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m01-practice.html#m01-receipt-trace">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m01-register-width">m01-register-width</h2>
<p>Correct choice: c.</p>
<p>An ARM64 W-register write zero-extends its 32-bit result into the matching X register: x8 = zero_extend_64(2) = 2.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> A write to w8 does more than replace the low bits: ARM64 also zeros x8&#x27;s upper 32 bits. Revisit the shared x8/w8 storage rule before carrying an old pointer forward.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> w8 names the low 32 bits of x8. They are not independent storage locations, so a write to w8 changes x8.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> Writing w8 puts 2 in the low 32 bits and zero in the upper 32 bits of x8. The entire x8 is therefore 2; the previous 64-bit value is gone.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m01-practice.html#m01-register-width">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m01-repeat-state">m01-repeat-state</h2>
<p>Correct choice: a.</p>
<p>receive(2,5) = (7,2); receive(7,5) = (12,7). Receipts are [2,7] and retained state is 12.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> The first call returns (7, 2). Feeding its new state 7 to the second returns (12, 7). The receipts report each call&#x27;s input state.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> This repeats a call starting at 2 instead of carrying state 7 into the second call. Write the next input beside the first returned pair before updating again.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> The final count is right, but these receipts report the updated states. The function&#x27;s second component is the old count, so read the pair&#x27;s roles separately.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m01-practice.html#m01-repeat-state">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m01-distinguishing-probe">m01-distinguishing-probe</h2>
<p>Correct choice: b.</p>
<p>For start 9 and delivery 2: both stored states are 11, while A returns 9 and B returns 11. For delivery 0 both returns are 9.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> With delivery zero, old and new are both 9. The receipt agrees under both explanations, so this run cannot choose between them.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> The old-count explanation predicts receipt 9 and the new-count explanation predicts 11. Observing the receipt can reject one explanation for this case.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> Both explanations store 9 + 2 = 11. They differ in the return&#x27;s source, so the final stored count is the wrong observation to separate them.</p></li>
</ul>

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>Preparation 1: follow a value from input to stored state · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. Native state updates</span><div><a href="m01.html" aria-current="page">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m01/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>2. Records across calls</span><div><a href="m02.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m02/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>3. Bytes between processes</span><div><a href="m05.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m05/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>6. Compiled forms and behavior</span><div><a href="m06.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m06/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>7. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="m01.html" aria-current="page">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="../m01/START-HERE.html">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="preparation-1-follow-a-value-from-input-to-stored-state">Preparation 1: follow a value from input to stored state</h1>
<p>The first project asks you to explain one cart tick, then decide what transfers to two related targets. Before investigating those targets, practise the smaller task underneath: keep an old state, a calculated value, a stored value and a return value distinct. This lets you support a Python model with a trace rather than with matching outputs alone.</p>
<p>You need Python variables, integer addition, functions and an <code>if</code> statement. A <strong>state</strong> is the information retained between updates. An input can affect an update without becoming part of the retained state. A function&#x27;s return value reports something to its caller; it need not equal the state left in memory. You do not need to memorize assembly.</p>
<p>This preparation uses a completely declared receipt counter. Its rule and instructions are unrelated to the cart. Keep the project&#x27;s existing <a href="../m01/START-HERE.html">marker trace</a>, <a href="../m01/methods.html">probe and tracing method</a> and <a href="../m01/follow-along.html">follow-along checkpoints</a>: they remain part of the original route, including saving the marker answer before opening its feedback.</p>
<h2 id="read-number-notation">Read number notation</h2>
<p>A <strong>bit</strong> is one binary digit, 0 or 1; a <strong>byte</strong> contains eight bits. A 32-bit pattern therefore occupies four bytes. <strong>Unsigned</strong> interpretation treats the pattern as zero or a positive number. Hexadecimal writes four bits per digit, using 0–9 and a–f; the prefix <code>0x</code> marks that notation, so <code>0x0a</code> is decimal 10 and a full 32-bit pattern uses eight hexadecimal digits. The <strong>low</strong> bits are the least-significant positions; the <strong>upper</strong> bits are the more-significant positions. Python&#x27;s <code>**</code> means exponentiation: <code>2**32</code> counts the possible 32-bit patterns.</p>
<h2 id="a-complete-example-update-a-counter-return-a-receipt">A complete example: update a counter, return a receipt</h2>
<p>A delivery counter retains one unsigned 32-bit count. Its function adds the delivered quantity to that count and returns the <strong>old</strong> count as a receipt. Use small nonnegative values here, so no arithmetic wraps.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">def receive(count, delivered):
    old = count
    count = old + delivered
    return count, old
</code></pre>
<p>The first component is the new state; the second is the receipt. With count 14 and delivery 3, the new count is 17 and the receipt is 14.</p>
<p>Here is a short ARM64 version written for this example. It is not a listing from a course target. Let <strong>P</strong> name the memory address of the count. On entry <code>x0 = P</code>, memory at P holds 14, and <code>w1 = 3</code>. An address tells you where a value lives; it is not the value itself.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-asm">ldr w8, [x0]
add w9, w8, w1
str w9, [x0]
mov w0, w8
ret
</code></pre>
<p>The destination comes first. <code>ldr</code> loads from memory, <code>add</code> computes into a register, <code>str</code> stores to memory, <code>mov</code> copies, and <code>ret</code> returns. Brackets mean “memory at this address.” A register is a processor&#x27;s working storage. The caller reads this function&#x27;s receipt from <code>w0</code> after the return.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Instruction</th><th scope="col">Values read</th><th scope="col">Result</th><th scope="col">Count in memory at P</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>ldr w8, [x0]</code></td><td>Address P, then its four-byte count</td><td><code>w8 = 14</code></td><td>14</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>add w9, w8, w1</code></td><td>14 and 3</td><td><code>w9 = 17</code></td><td>14</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>str w9, [x0]</code></td><td>17 and address P</td><td>Four bytes at P become 17</td><td>17</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>mov w0, w8</code></td><td>The still-retained 14</td><td>Receipt register <code>w0 = 14</code></td><td>17</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ret</code></td><td>Return address</td><td>Caller receives 14</td><td>17</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>Addition does not change memory: there are no brackets on its destination. Nor does it replace <code>w8</code>: its destination is <code>w9</code>. The store is the point at which the retained state changes. The final copy still reads the old count. This chain of “which produced value does the next operation read?” is <strong>dataflow</strong>.</p>
<p>A near miss translates the last two lines as “return the new count because the store already happened.” It predicts receipt 17. The store changed memory at P, not <code>w8</code>, so it cannot justify that prediction. Another near miss changes memory in the addition row and then treats the store as a second addition. A store copies bits; it does no addition.</p>
<p>Complete this same trace with a new starting count and delivery. Track the memory column separately from the register columns before checking.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m01-receipt-trace" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Distinguish a register calculation, a stored next state and an old-value return.</p><fieldset><legend>Complete the receipt-counter trace with memory at P initially 10 and w1 = 4. The instructions are ldr w8,[x0]; add w9,w8,w1; str w9,[x0]; mov w0,w8; ret, with x0 initially P. What are the final count in memory and the returned receipt?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-1-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-1-0" name="practice-1" value="a"><span>Count 10; receipt 14.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-1-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-1-1" name="practice-1" value="b"><span>Count 14; receipt 10.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-1-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-1-2" name="practice-1" value="c"><span>Count 14; receipt 14.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m01-practice.html#m01-receipt-trace">question</a> · <a href="m01-practice-feedback.html#m01-receipt-trace">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="width-belongs-to-the-operation-signedness-belongs-to-the-interpretation">Width belongs to the operation; signedness belongs to the interpretation</h2>
<p>ARM64&#x27;s <code>x8</code> and <code>w8</code> are two names for parts of the same register, not independent boxes. <code>x8</code> names all 64 bits. <code>w8</code> names the low 32 bits. Writing <code>w8</code> also makes the upper 32 bits of <code>x8</code> zero. Reading <code>w8</code> reads only its low 32 bits. The same relationship holds for <code>x0/w0</code> and the other numbered pairs.</p>
<p>In the example, <code>ldr w8, [x0]</code> reads <strong>four</strong> bytes from the address held in the 64-bit <code>x0</code>. The address width does not make that a load of eight bytes. <code>str w9, [x0]</code> likewise writes four bytes. Writing the receipt to <code>w0</code> replaces the address previously held in <code>x0</code> with the zero-extended receipt bits. This is safe in the example because no later instruction needs that address. In a longer trace, using <code>x0</code> as P after that write would be an error.</p>
<p>For a separate width example, if <code>x8</code> holds <code>0x0000000100000007</code> and <code>mov w8, #2</code> runs, <code>x8</code> becomes 2. <code>#2</code> is the literal number 2. It does not mean “memory at address 2,” and the instruction has not stored anything to memory.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m01-register-width" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Track the shared x/w register storage and the effect of a 32-bit destination.</p><fieldset><legend>A separate instruction sequence starts with x8 = 0x0000000100000007, then executes mov w8,#2. What does x8 hold afterward?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-2-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-0" name="practice-2" value="a"><span>0x0000000100000002: the old upper half is preserved.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-2-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-1" name="practice-2" value="b"><span>0x0000000100000007: w8 is a separate register.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-2-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-2" name="practice-2" value="c"><span>0x0000000000000002: the write also clears the upper half.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m01-practice.html#m01-register-width">question</a> · <a href="m01-practice-feedback.html#m01-register-width">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<p>A 32-bit register holds one of <code>2**32</code> bit patterns. Unsigned interpretation gives 0 through 4294967295. Under signed two&#x27;s-complement interpretation, patterns from <code>0x80000000</code> upward represent negative values: subtract <code>2**32</code> from the unsigned reading. Thus <code>0xfffffffe</code> has unsigned value 4294967294 and signed value −2. A load into a <code>w</code> register alone does not choose which interpretation your Python model needs.</p>
<p>A 32-bit addition retains the low 32 result bits. For example, the bit pattern for −2 plus 5 becomes <code>0x00000003</code>. Python integers do not have that fixed width automatically. This explains the notation; it is not a request to add overflow behavior outside the original project&#x27;s input and output contract. In the cart project, use its signed values, supported domains and observed instructions to justify your model.</p>
<h2 id="carry-the-returned-state-into-the-next-update">Carry the returned state into the next update</h2>
<p>Run the receipt counter twice, starting at count 2 and delivering 5 each time. The first call returns new state 7 and receipt 2. The second call starts from <strong>7</strong>, so it returns state 12 and receipt 7. Feeding 2 to both calls would model two separate deliveries to a reset counter. Keeping the receipt as the next state would also be wrong: the receipt reports the old value.</p>
<p>This distinction is useful when one tick works but a later tick fails. Compare the first differing row, then check which returned component became the next input. You cannot diagnose the cause by looking only at the final number.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m01-repeat-state" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Use each returned next state as the following update&#x27;s input.</p><fieldset><legend>Apply receive(count, delivered), which returns (count + delivered, count), twice. Start with count 2 and use delivery 5 on both calls, carrying the new state forward. Which sequence is produced?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-3-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-0" name="practice-3" value="a"><span>Receipts 2 then 7; final count 12.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-3-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-1" name="practice-3" value="b"><span>Receipts 2 then 2; final count 7.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-3-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-2" name="practice-3" value="c"><span>Receipts 7 then 12; final count 12.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m01-practice.html#m01-repeat-state">question</a> · <a href="m01-practice-feedback.html#m01-repeat-state">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="choose-an-observation-that-distinguishes-the-explanations">Choose an observation that distinguishes the explanations</h2>
<p>Suppose you had not been told whether this receipt function returns the old or new count. With delivery zero, both explanations return the same number. Agreement there leaves the ambiguity intact. Starting at count 9 and delivering 2 predicts receipt 9 under the old-count explanation and 11 under the new-count explanation. Observing the receipt now separates them; inspecting the final count alone does not, because both explanations update it to 11.</p>
<p>Before probing an unfamiliar program, write down both predictions. Name the output field on which they disagree. This gives a matching result a purpose and gives a mismatch somewhere to lead.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m01-distinguishing-probe" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Select an observation on which two candidate dataflow explanations disagree.</p><fieldset><legend>Two candidate counter functions both add the delivery to the stored count. A returns the old count; B returns the new count. Which single observation distinguishes them?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-4-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-4-0" name="practice-4" value="a"><span>Start at 9, deliver 0, and inspect the receipt.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-4-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-4-1" name="practice-4" value="b"><span>Start at 9, deliver 2, and inspect the receipt.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-4-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-4-2" name="practice-4" value="c"><span>Start at 9, deliver 2, and inspect only the final stored count.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m01-practice.html#m01-distinguishing-probe">question</a> · <a href="m01-practice-feedback.html#m01-distinguishing-probe">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="apply-the-method-to-the-original-cart-project">Apply the method to the original cart project</h2>
<p>Open <a href="../m01/START-HERE.html">Milestone 1: explain one tick</a>. Follow its original order: setup, marker trace, saved first prediction, native probes, instruction trace, model and the two transfer investigations. The receipt example has supplied its own rule; it supplies no cart rule.</p>
<p>For your cart instruction trace, keep a row for the instruction, the values it reads, the destination and what that value supports. Label an address P or Q until you have evidence for what is stored there. When an arithmetic destination overwrites a register, cross out its old value. When a store occurs, update the memory state. When a branch is taken, follow the instruction address selected by the actual comparison; do not keep tracing the untaken path as if it also ran.</p>
<p>If Python reports a syntax error, use the named line and <code>python3 -m py_compile model.py</code> to check the file before comparing behavior. If the native program cannot execute, use <a href="../m01/setup.html">setup</a> and the <a href="../m01/follow-along.html">follow-along troubleshooting</a>; a platform or working-directory failure is not a counterexample to your rule. If output runs but disagrees with your model, preserve it, find the first different value in the trace, and only then revise the model. A checker result cannot identify which instruction you misunderstood.</p>
<p>Your carried artifact is your own <code>model.py</code> together with saved predictions, native observations and the instruction evidence that explains it. Keep <code>transfer_model.py</code> and <code>crossing_model.py</code> as separate revisions for the related targets, following the project&#x27;s save-before-feedback procedure. M2 uses this same retained evidence and dataflow habit to connect memory bytes to a function call; the models remain your record of what was learned about these particular targets.</p></article><aside class="progress-tools" aria-label="Lesson progress"><h2>Your practice record</h2><p>These are authored exercises, with answers available in this packet. <h2 id="m02-complete-fields">m02-complete-fields</h2>
<p>Correct choice: b.</p>
<p>bias_unsigned = 0x80 + 0xff<em>256 = 65408; bias_signed = 65408 - 65536 = -128; cycles = 0x00 + 0x01</em>256 = 256; code = 0x7f = 127.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> 65408 is the unsigned value of 80 ff. The bias is signed and its top bit is set, so subtract 65536. The cycle and code readings in this choice use the stated rules.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> Bias bits give 128 + 255 × 256 = 65408, then signed interpretation gives -128. Cycles 00 01 give 0 + 1 × 256 = 256. Code 7f is 127.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> 00 01 means 256 in little-endian order. A value of 1 reverses its byte weights. Keep the slice correct while checking the byte-order decision separately.</p></li>

<h2 id="m02-probe-width">m02-probe-width</h2>
<p>Correct choice: a.</p>
<p>Two-byte little-endian 255 = ff 00 and 256 = 00 01. Reading only byte 4 yields 255 and 0 instead of 255 and 256.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> At 255 to 256, the low byte wraps from ff to 00 and the next becomes 01. A predicts cycle values 255 and 0; B predicts 255 and 256. The held-fixed fields make the changed byte easier to attribute.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> Both hypotheses read 1 and 2 for these bytes because the high byte remains zero. This ordinary pair does not reject the one-byte explanation.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> Changing bias can help locate bias bytes, but the cycle value remains 1 under both cycle-width hypotheses. Choose a probe whose cycle predictions disagree.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m02-practice.html#m02-probe-width">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m02-call-versus-layout">m02-call-versus-layout</h2>
<p>Correct choice: c.</p>
<p>bias_after = -3 + 5 = 2. Return source is memory[P+4:P+6] = 01 02 = 513. T+8 = S-8, whereas caller slot is S+8; neither is P+8.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> The updated bias is 2, but the final load overwrites w0 with the cycle count 513. Follow the return register&#x27;s last producer rather than the most recent memory update.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> The store base is sp, so its address is S+8 or T+8. A record offset would use P as the base. Equal displacement text does not make these addresses equal.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> The signed load and addition produce -3+5=2, stored at P. The final halfword load reads cycles 513 into w0, which the caller leaves unchanged. Since T=S-16, the two pointer slots are 16 bytes apart.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m02-practice.html#m02-call-versus-layout">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m02-reordered-record">m02-reordered-record</h2>
<p>Correct choice: b.</p>
<p>code = 0x81 = 129; cycles = 1 + 2<em>256 = 513; bias_unsigned = 0 + 128</em>256 = 32768; bias_signed = 32768 - 65536 = -32768. New total length is 6.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> This reads both two-byte fields in big-endian order. With the declared little-endian order, 01 02 is 513 and 00 80 has unsigned value 32768, then signed value -32768.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> The revised ranges locate code 81, cycles 01 02 and bias 00 80. Apply the surviving interpretations to those new slices: 129, 513 and -32768.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> The old exact-length guard rejects six bytes, and its field offsets refer to different locations. Types can survive while the layout and guard must change.</p></li>
</ul>
