<h2 id="work-a-complete-framed-stream">Work a complete framed stream</h2>
<p>The display protocol has a one-byte unsigned length from 1..3, followed by that many printable ASCII bytes. One byte <code>02</code> means length 2; the hex pairs <code>4f 4b</code> spell <code>OK</code>. There is no separator or implied newline. This is deliberately different from the original project&#x27;s two-byte header.</p>
<p>The stream below contains three frames. Offsets are positions in this direction of the stream, not times.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-text">bytes:    02 4f 4b | 01 3f | 03 52 55 4e
payload:     OK   |   ?   |    RUN
interval: [0,3)   | [3,5) | [5,9)
</code></pre>
<p>Use the invented capture&#x27;s application deliveries: one byte, then three, then five. A <strong>pending buffer</strong> retains the incomplete suffix between decoder calls.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Delivery</th><th scope="col">Bytes added</th><th scope="col">Reasoning</th><th scope="col">Returned messages</th><th scope="col">Pending bytes</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>[0,1)</code></td><td><code>02</code></td><td>Length is known, but neither body byte is present.</td><td>none</td><td><code>02</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>[1,4)</code></td><td><code>4f 4b 01</code></td><td>Finish the first frame and remove exactly three bytes. The next header remains.</td><td><code>OK</code></td><td><code>01</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>[4,9)</code></td><td><code>3f 03 52 55 4e</code></td><td>Finish <code>?</code>, remove its two bytes, then finish <code>RUN</code> and remove its four bytes.</td><td><code>?</code>, <code>RUN</code></td><td>empty</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>The middle delivery finishes an old frame and begins another. The last finishes two frames, so a decoder must loop rather than check for only one message per call. At each step, pending bytes plus newly added bytes are the unconsumed suffix; removing anything beyond the complete frame would lose the next header. Keeping an already consumed prefix would emit the same message again.</p>
<p>The framing calculation is separate from character decoding. First find a complete body using byte counts; only then validate its allowed byte values and decode ASCII. Three body bytes are six displayed hex characters. Counting the spaces or hex digits would produce a different, incorrect size.</p>
<p>Complete the same stream under a new delivery grouping before checking the explanation.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m05-regroup-completion" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Complete an incremental frame trace when a delivery finishes two messages and starts another header.</p><fieldset><legend>Regroup the same toy stream 02 4f 4b 01 3f 03 52 55 4e into deliveries of 2, 4 and 3 bytes. After the SECOND delivery, what has that call returned and what remains pending? Toy lengths use one byte and allow 1..3.</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-2-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-0" name="practice-2" value="a"><span>Return only OK; retain 01 3f 03 because one delivery can return at most one message.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-2-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-1" name="practice-2" value="b"><span>Return OK and ?; retain 03, the next frame&#x27;s header.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-2-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-2" name="practice-2" value="c"><span>Return OK, ? and RUN; the final length byte proves the remaining letters are available.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m05-practice.html#m05-regroup-completion">question</a> · <a href="m05-practice-feedback.html#m05-regroup-completion">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<p>With a wider header there is an earlier waiting stage. In a two-byte big-endian variant, <code>00 03</code> means <code>0*256+3=3</code>. Receiving only <code>00</code> has not declared zero: the header is incomplete, and its missing second byte could change the length. Wait for the whole header before interpreting or bounding its value, then separately wait for the body. These are two different reasons to retain pending bytes.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m05-split-header" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Accumulate a split multi-byte header before decoding its length, then distinguish incomplete body from incomplete header.</p><fieldset><legend>Use a two-byte big-endian variant of the toy protocol, allowing lengths 1..4. A fresh decoder receives 00, then 02 41. After those two feeds, what is known?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-3-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-0" name="practice-3" value="a"><span>The first feed declared forbidden length 0, so it had to fail before the second header byte arrived.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-3-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-1" name="practice-3" value="b"><span>The complete header declares length 2; one body byte A is present, so retain 00 02 41 and wait for one more body byte.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-3-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-2" name="practice-3" value="c"><span>The second feed starts a new header 02 41, declaring length 577; previous pending bytes should be discarded.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m05-practice.html#m05-split-header">question</a> · <a href="m05-practice-feedback.html#m05-split-header">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="waiting-refusal-and-eof-are-distinct">Waiting, refusal and EOF are distinct</h2>
<p>A correct incremental decoder needs enough memory to distinguish “not enough bytes yet” from “these bytes cannot form an allowed frame.” In the toy display protocol, pending <code>02 41</code> promises two body bytes but has only <code>A</code>: wait for another delivery. Pending <code>04</code> already declares a forbidden length: reject immediately instead of waiting for four bytes. A complete body with a disallowed character is invalid when that body is available for validation.</p>
<p>EOF means no later bytes will arrive. On the project&#x27;s blocking pipe, a zero-byte OS read signals EOF after the sending side has closed and buffered bytes are exhausted. A decoder&#x27;s <code>feed(b&quot;&quot;)</code> is an API call with no new bytes; it does not announce EOF. The project uses a separate <code>finish()</code> call to do that. If bytes are still pending at <code>finish()</code>, the stream is truncated, even if its earlier frames were valid. If nothing is pending, EOF is clean. Closing the request pipe and closing the response pipe are also separate events: label the direction.</p>
<p>For example, feed toy bytes <code>01 41 02 42</code>. The decoder returns <code>A</code> and retains <code>02 42</code>. An empty feed changes neither the buffer nor the open lifecycle. A subsequent <code>43</code> would complete <code>BC</code>. Calling <code>finish()</code> before that byte arrives must refuse the incomplete suffix. Calling it after that byte arrives can close successfully.</p>
<p>The original project&#x27;s lifecycle contract adds another distinction: failed, open and successfully closed decoders allow different calls. Read those exact rules when implementing. Do not use one boolean “buffer empty” as a substitute for lifecycle state; an empty open decoder can accept more bytes, whereas a closed one cannot. A raised <code>feed</code> returns no list from that call, even if its internal loop had encountered a complete frame first; events already returned by earlier successful calls remain earlier events.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m05-eof-application" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Distinguish an empty feed from EOF and diagnose an incomplete suffix after earlier successful output.</p><fieldset><legend>Fresh application: feed toy bytes 01 58 03 59 5a. This returns X and retains 03 59 5a (length 3, only YZ present). Then call feed(b&#x27;&#x27;) and finally finish(), with no further bytes. What should happen?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-4-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-4-0" name="practice-4" value="a"><span>The empty feed closes the stream successfully because it contains zero bytes.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-4-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-4-1" name="practice-4" value="b"><span>finish succeeds because X was already emitted, so all later bytes may be ignored.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-4-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-4-2" name="practice-4" value="c"><span>The empty feed emits nothing and leaves the suffix; finish refuses truncation because one body byte is missing.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m05-practice.html#m05-eof-application">question</a> · <a href="m05-practice-feedback.html#m05-eof-application">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m05-invalid-header" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Reject a fully known invalid length without confusing it with an incomplete valid frame.</p><fieldset><legend>A fresh toy display decoder accepts lengths 1..3. Its first feed is the single byte 04, with no body. <h2 id="explain-order-without-inventing-timings">Explain order without inventing timings</h2>
<p>Suppose a writer logs intent, enters its write loop, and later logs its return. The reader can receive bytes and log a read while the writer is waiting to run its return-logging statement. A sorted timestamp list may therefore place the read before the write return. That does not reverse the byte flow.</p>
<p>Use each process&#x27;s sequence numbers for its local order and stream offsets for byte order. A monotonic timestamp difference is elapsed time between recorded observations on this host; it includes scheduling, buffering, Python work and logging. It does not isolate transport latency. Actual PIDs, read grouping and timing may differ between repeats even when prescribed decoder deliveries match. If a particular pair of runs has the same reads, report that observation without generalizing it into an OS guarantee.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m05-causal-order" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Interpret cross-process observations without equating logging order or a measured gap with transport causality.</p><fieldset><legend>One saved trace records writer intent at 100 ns, a peer read at 130 ns, and the writer&#x27;s write-loop return at 160 ns. All are relative observations from one host run. Which interpretation is supported?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-6-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-6-0" name="practice-6" value="a"><span>The peer caused the write, since its read was logged before the writer&#x27;s return.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-6-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-6-1" name="practice-6" value="b"><span>The read observation lies 30 ns after intent and 30 ns before return; scheduling and logging are included, so this is not an isolated transport-latency measurement.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-6-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-6-2" name="practice-6" value="c"><span>Exactly 60 ns of network latency occurred, and the same gap must recur under the fixed delivery schedule.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m05-practice.html#m05-causal-order">question</a> · <a href="m05-practice-feedback.html#m05-causal-order">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="enter-the-original-exchange">Enter the original exchange</h2>
<p>Follow <a href="../m05/START-HERE.html">M5 START-HERE</a> from its first save, then do its separate printer example in the stated order. The original wire contract has two big-endian length bytes, bounded printable ASCII bodies, and explicit failure/lifecycle rules. Use those rules rather than copying the toy display format. Compute the original baseline&#x27;s frame intervals and messages per application delivery yourself, save successfully, then run the supervisor and inspect the saved trace.</p>
<p>If a live run fails, inspect the named child logs before interpreting a partial trace as a complete exchange. Keep a refused existing output folder and choose a new run path. If your decoder disagrees, first identify the layer: missing or changed trace bytes, incorrect pending-suffix arithmetic, premature ASCII decoding, header bounds, or EOF/lifecycle handling. A <code>finish()</code> failure with pending bytes is a different diagnosis from a refused length during <code>feed</code>.</p>
<p>Carry forward the existing project&#x27;s own decoder, interval timeline, raw trace, saved first attempt, feedback and revisions. For each claim, cite the direction, interval and event that supplies its evidence. Preserve the changed-request prediction before the transfer run. These artifacts support a bounded explanation of how this exchange was decoded; neither repeatable deliveries nor a finite decoder check establishes universal correctness.</p></article><aside class="progress-tools" aria-label="Lesson progress"><h2>Your practice record</h2><p>These are authored exercises, with answers available in this packet. <h2 id="m06-value-correspondence">m06-value-correspondence</h2>
<p>Correct choice: a.</p>
<p>enabled=0 implies Z=1 and bonus=2. Branch base=3<em>6=18; adjusted result=18+2=20. Selected form chooses w8=2 and computes madd=6</em>3+2=20.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> The branch takes off and adds 2 to base 18. The selected form has Z=1, chooses its first source 2, then madd combines 6*3+2. Different intermediate roles converge on return 20.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> The branch w8 holds base 18 before adjustment; selected-form w8 holds the chosen bonus 2. Follow definitions and uses rather than equating register labels.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> Comparing enabled 0 with zero sets Z=1. eq is true, so csel chooses its first source, not its second. Bonus 5 would apply to a nonzero input.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m06-practice.html#m06-value-correspondence">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m06-flags-survive-move">m06-flags-survive-move</h2>
<p>Correct choice: b.</p>
<p>cmp(0,0) yields zero and Z=1. mov w9,99 leaves Z=1. eq therefore holds, and csel copies first input w2=9.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> An ordinary mov changes a register without setting arithmetic flags. Look for cmp, subs or another actual flag producer before changing Z in your trace.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> cmp computes flags for 0-0, so Z=1. No later instruction replaces them before csel; its true eq arm copies w2=9 into w8.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> csel selects one of two values using existing flags; it does not compare its sources or produce a boolean. cset is the form that writes 0 or 1.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m06-practice.html#m06-flags-survive-move">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m06-conditional-compare">m06-conditional-compare</h2>
<p>Correct choice: c.</p>
<p>2&gt;3 is false. ccmp uses literal NZCV=0100, hence Z=1. ne=(Z=0) is false and cset result is 0.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> The nonzero test happens only when the preceding signed-greater condition holds. Here it does not, so flag=-1 is not compared by ccmp.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> Fallback 4 encodes the four flags, not a register result. cset writes 1 or 0 based on ne; inspect the fallback&#x27;s Z bit.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> The first comparison makes gt false. Fallback binary 0100 gives Z=1; ne requires Z=0, so cset writes 0 despite the nonzero second input.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m06-practice.html#m06-conditional-compare">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m06-discriminating-probe">m06-discriminating-probe</h2>
<p>Correct choice: a.</p>
<p>n=5: min(4<em>5,30)=20 and min(4</em>5+2,30)=22. n=8 gives min(32,30)=min(34,30)=30; n=9 similarly caps 36 and 38 to 30.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> At 5, raw values 20 and 22 are both below 30, so the displays preserve their difference. This probe can reject at least one candidate if the observation matches only the other.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> At 9, raw values are 36 and 38, both capped to 30. Agreement there leaves both hypotheses possible; it does not choose A.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> A repeat may check repeatability, but both candidates already predict 30 at 8. More observations of the same nondiscriminating case do not identify which raw value was computed.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m06-practice.html#m06-discriminating-probe">Return to this question</a>.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#m06-value-correspondence">m06-value-correspondence</a></li><li><a href="#m06-flags-survive-move">m06-flags-survive-move</a></li><li><a href="#m06-conditional-compare">m06-conditional-compare</a></li><li><a href="#m06-discriminating-probe">m06-discriminating-probe</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. <h2 id="m06-value-correspondence">m06-value-correspondence</h2>
<p>Complete the display example for n=6, enabled=0. It computes 3*n plus bonus 2 for zero enabled, otherwise 5. Which trace agrees in both schematic forms?</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> Branch w8 reaches 20; selected-form w8 is bonus 2 before madd, whose return is 6*3+2=20.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> Both w8 registers must hold 18 at the selection stage, because equal register names identify equal source values.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> The selected form returns 23 because csel always chooses its second source after any comparison.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m06-practice-feedback.html#m06-value-correspondence">Feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m06-flags-survive-move">m06-flags-survive-move</h2>
<p>Fresh register trace: initially w1=0, w2=9, w3=14. Execute cmp w1,#0; mov w9,#99; csel w8,w2,w3,eq. What is w8, and why?</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> 14: mov of nonzero 99 must clear the zero flag.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> 9: cmp sets Z=1, mov leaves flags unchanged, and eq selects the first source w2.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> 0: csel compares w2 with w3 and returns a boolean equality result.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m06-practice-feedback.html#m06-flags-survive-move">Feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m06-conditional-compare">m06-conditional-compare</h2>
<p>Apply cmp w0,#3; ccmp w1,#0,#4,gt; cset w8,ne to n=2, flag=-1. Fallback #4 is NZCV=0100. What does w8 become?</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> 1, because flag=-1 is nonzero, regardless of the first comparison.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> 4, because cset copies the fallback number directly.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> 0: signed 2 is not greater than 3, so ccmp supplies Z=1 and ne is false.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m06-practice-feedback.html#m06-conditional-compare">Feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m06-discriminating-probe">m06-discriminating-probe</h2>
<p>An indicator returns min(raw,30). Candidate A uses raw=4<em>n; candidate B uses raw=4</em>n+2. You observed display 30 at n=8. Which new input best separates these candidates?</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> n=5: candidate A predicts 20, candidate B 22.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> n=9: candidate A predicts 30, candidate B 30, so equal outputs prove A.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> n=8 again: repeating the same saturated result identifies the hidden raw value.</p></li>
</ul>

<p>M6 asks you to explain one calculation in two compiled forms. Your model predicts behavior; your correspondence map explains how both listings produce that behavior. Bring M1&#x27;s prediction/probe/revision routine, M2&#x27;s argument/return and stack vocabulary, and Python comparisons. You need to follow a register write and the later instruction that uses its value. You do not need to recover the exact spelling of the original C source.</p>
<p>Do this separate practice before the original fee example. It uses different arithmetic and supplies none of the fee completion, fee practice or <code>quote</code> answers. At <a href="../m06/START-HERE.html">M6 START-HERE</a>, preserve P0&#x27;s original prediction before opening the original worked example or running its programs. Later, save hypotheses and a first model before the original target checks.</p>
<h2 id="a-complete-unrelated-correspondence-example">A complete unrelated correspondence example</h2>
<p>A display computes <code>3*n + bonus</code>, where <code>n</code> is in 0..20 and <code>bonus</code> is 2 when <code>enabled</code> equals zero, otherwise 5. A negative <code>enabled</code> is nonzero. This tiny rule is supplied, so the task is to explain its representations rather than infer its rule.</p>
<p>Here are two <strong>schematic</strong> ARM64 fragments for that rule. They illustrate value flow; they are authored examples, not captured compiler listings or runnable project files. Inputs enter <code>w0=n</code>, <code>w1=enabled</code>, and the integer result leaves <code>w0</code>. <code>mul d,a,b</code> multiplies its two source values. <code>madd d,a,b,c</code> multiplies a and b and adds c. All example arithmetic fits in signed 32 bits, so overflow is not involved.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-text">Branch form                       Selected-value form
mov w8, #3                        mov w8, #2
mul w8, w0, w8                    mov w9, #5
cbz w1, off                       cmp w1, #0
add w8, w8, #5                    csel w8, w8, w9, eq
b done                            mov w9, #3
off: add w8, w8, #2                madd w0, w0, w9, w8
done: mov w0, w8                   ret
ret
</code></pre>
<p><code>cbz</code> branches only when its tested register is zero. <code>cmp a,b</code> records flags from a-b. The <strong>zero flag</strong>, Z, is 1 when that result is zero. The condition <code>eq</code> tests Z=1; <code>ne</code> tests Z=0. <code>csel d,a,b,condition</code> writes a when the condition is true, otherwise b. It chooses a value without jumping to another instruction address. Source values are read before the destination is overwritten, even when the register names overlap.</p>
<p>For <code>n=4, enabled=-2</code>, the branch form calculates <code>3*4=12</code>. Its <code>cbz</code> is not taken because -2 is not zero. Adding 5 gives 17, which moves to the return register. The selected form first prepares candidate bonuses 2 and 5. Comparing -2 with zero gives Z=0, so <code>eq</code> is false and <code>csel</code> writes the second candidate, 5, into <code>w8</code>. It next overwrites <code>w9</code> with multiplier 3; the previously selected 5 remains in <code>w8</code>. <code>madd</code> reads old <code>w0=4</code>, <code>w9=3</code>, <code>w8=5</code>, then writes <code>w0=4*3+5=17</code>.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Role</th><th scope="col">Branch form for this input</th><th scope="col">Selected-value form for this input</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>Input n</td><td>Entry <code>w0=4</code></td><td>Entry <code>w0=4</code>, retained until <code>madd</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Conditional fact</td><td><code>cbz</code> sees -2 and falls through</td><td><code>cmp</code> sets Z=0; <code>csel ... eq</code> chooses 5</td></tr>
<tr><td>Running arithmetic</td><td><code>w8=12</code>, then <code>w8=17</code></td><td>Bonus <code>w8=5</code>, combined with multiplication in <code>madd</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Return value</td><td>Move 17 to <code>w0</code></td><td><code>madd</code> writes 17 directly to <code>w0</code></td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>Matching <code>w8</code> to <code>w8</code> would equate 12 with 5 at the arithmetic stage. Match their roles and consumers instead. A destination register is reusable storage, not a permanent source variable. Likewise, the selected form still has conditional behavior despite having no conditional branch.</p>
<p>Complete another trace before checking it.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m06-value-correspondence" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Complete a value-role correspondence across branch and conditional-selection forms.</p><fieldset><legend>Complete the display example for n=6, enabled=0. It computes 3*n plus bonus 2 for zero enabled, otherwise 5. Which trace agrees in both schematic forms?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-1-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-1-0" name="practice-1" value="a"><span>Branch w8 reaches 20; selected-form w8 is bonus 2 before madd, whose return is 6*3+2=20.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-1-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-1-1" name="practice-1" value="b"><span>Both w8 registers must hold 18 at the selection stage, because equal register names identify equal source values.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-1-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-1-2" name="practice-1" value="c"><span>The selected form returns 23 because csel always chooses its second source after any comparison.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>

<h2 id="trace-the-flag-producer-separately-from-value-producers">Trace the flag producer separately from value producers</h2>
<p>Flags are state too. A later conditional instruction reads the most recent flags, not the old value of its destination. Ordinary <code>mov</code>, <code>ldr</code>, <code>str</code> and <code>add</code> without the <code>s</code> suffix do not set arithmetic flags. <code>cmp</code>, <code>subs</code> and <code>adds</code> do. If a flag-setting instruction intervenes, the consumer uses those newer flags. On the original listings, write down the instruction address that produced the flags used at each <code>csel</code>, branch or conditional comparison.</p>
<p>For example, <code>cmp w1,#0; mov w9,#99; csel w8,w2,w3,eq</code> still selects using the comparison with zero. The move makes <code>w9=99</code> but does not replace Z. Do not read <code>eq</code> as “the two source registers are equal”; <code>csel</code> does not compare them. It consumes a condition already represented in flags.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m06-flags-survive-move" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Identify the flag-setting instruction consumed by a conditional selection despite an intervening value write.</p><fieldset><legend>Fresh register trace: initially w1=0, w2=9, w3=14. Execute cmp w1,#0; mov w9,#99; csel w8,w2,w3,eq. What is w8, and why?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-2-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-0" name="practice-2" value="a"><span>14: mov of nonzero 99 must clear the zero flag.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-2-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-1" name="practice-2" value="b"><span>9: cmp sets Z=1, mov leaves flags unchanged, and eq selects the first source w2.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-2-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-2" name="practice-2" value="c"><span>0: csel compares w2 with w3 and returns a boolean equality result.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m06-practice.html#m06-flags-survive-move">question</a> · <a href="m06-practice-feedback.html#m06-flags-survive-move">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<p>Signed and unsigned conditions also answer different questions. <code>gt</code> means signed greater; <code>lo</code> means unsigned lower. A negative 32-bit value has a large unsigned interpretation. Use the specific condition and its flag producer; establish nonnegativity before replacing an unsigned comparison with a signed one in your model.</p>
<h2 id="conditional-comparison-can-combine-questions">Conditional comparison can combine questions</h2>
<p>A <strong>conditional comparison</strong>, <code>ccmp</code>, either performs a comparison or supplies literal fallback flags. That lets later code test a combined condition without a separate branch for each question.</p>
<p>Consider another supplied toy question: “Is n greater than 3, and is flag nonzero?”</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-text">cmp  w0, #3
ccmp w1, #0, #4, gt
cset w8, ne
</code></pre>
<p><code>cset</code> writes 1 when its condition is true, otherwise 0. Here <code>ccmp</code> compares <code>w1</code> with zero only if the preceding flags say signed greater. Otherwise it sets NZCV to the fallback integer 4, binary <code>0100</code>: N=0, Z=1, C=0, V=0. N, Z, C and V are the negative, zero, carry and signed-overflow flags. The fallback therefore makes the final <code>ne</code> false.</p>
<p>With n=6, flag=0, the first comparison makes <code>gt</code> true, so the second comparison runs. Zero minus zero gives Z=1, and <code>cset ... ne</code> writes 0. With n=6, flag=-2, the second comparison instead gives Z=0 and the result is 1. With n not greater than 3, the second input is not compared at all: the fallback Z=1 forces result 0. Reading only the last comparison would lose the first question&#x27;s gate.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m06-conditional-compare" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Use conditional comparison&#x27;s gate and fallback flags to derive a combined condition.</p><fieldset><legend>Apply cmp w0,#3; ccmp w1,#0,#4,gt; cset w8,ne to n=2, flag=-1. Fallback #4 is NZCV=0100. What does w8 become?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-3-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-0" name="practice-3" value="a"><span>1, because flag=-1 is nonzero, regardless of the first comparison.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-3-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-1" name="practice-3" value="b"><span>4, because cset copies the fallback number directly.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-3-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-2" name="practice-3" value="c"><span>0: signed 2 is not greater than 3, so ccmp supplies Z=1 and ne is false.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m06-practice.html#m06-conditional-compare">question</a> · <a href="m06-practice-feedback.html#m06-conditional-compare">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="choose-probes-that-can-separate-explanations">Choose probes that can separate explanations</h2>
<p>Two equal outputs can hide unequal intermediate values. Suppose a separate indicator displays <code>min(raw,30)</code>. Candidate A computes <code>raw=4*n</code>; candidate B computes <code>raw=4*n+2</code>. At n=8, raw values are 32 and 34, but both displays are 30. This observation cannot tell you which raw rule ran. At n=5, displays are 20 and 22, so that input separates the candidates.</p>
<p>The <strong>limit</strong> is where an intermediate becomes capped; a <strong>boundary probe</strong> chooses an input around a suspected condition. A good probe has predictions that differ under the competing models. Pair one changed input with two otherwise identical inputs to isolate a condition, and inspect the listing when a final cap conceals earlier changes. Agreement in sampled outputs supports those cases; it does not establish source identity or prove a rule for every input.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m06-discriminating-probe" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Select a probe that separates raw-value hypotheses despite a shared output cap.</p><fieldset><legend>An indicator returns min(raw,30). Candidate A uses raw=4*n; candidate B uses raw=4*n+2. You observed display 30 at n=8. Which new input best separates these candidates?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-4-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-4-0" name="practice-4" value="a"><span>n=5: candidate A predicts 20, candidate B 22.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-4-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-4-1" name="practice-4" value="b"><span>n=9: candidate A predicts 30, candidate B 30, so equal outputs prove A.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-4-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-4-2" name="practice-4" value="c"><span>n=8 again: repeating the same saturated result identifies the hidden raw value.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m06-practice.html#m06-discriminating-probe">question</a> · <a href="m06-practice-feedback.html#m06-discriminating-probe">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="enter-the-original-compiled-comparison">Enter the original compiled comparison</h2>
<p>Follow <a href="../m06/START-HERE.html">M6 START-HERE</a>, beginning with its P0 save. The original fee exercise teaches its own supplied rule; the larger <code>quote</code> function remains an investigation. Predict the original completion and practice cases before their linked feedback. For <code>quote</code>, use the original paired probes and add a pair when two explanations remain compatible.</p>
<p>When tracing either original listing, keep a row for each definition: address, new value or expression, the role it serves, next consumer, and any flags set or consumed. Track the input through loads, stack slots, combined arithmetic and returns. Give both listings&#x27; actual addresses in the final correspondence map; the schematic fragments above do not supply address evidence for your binaries.</p>
<p>A surprising selection is often a trace problem before it is a compiler mystery. Recheck operand order, the exact condition, its flag producer and any overwrite between definition and use. If program launch fails or the checker reports a target hash mismatch, follow the original setup and re-extract matching artifacts; that is not evidence for a different calculation. If a behavioral check disagrees, preserve its input, both native results, your first model and the false assumption before changing one rule.</p>
<p>Carry forward the original Python model, input/output table, correspondence report, fresh saved prediction and revision records. <p>Open after choosing on <a href="m07-practice.html">m07-practice.md</a>. Preserve the original answer and any later correction.</p>
<h2 id="m07-distinct-layouts">m07-distinct-layouts</h2>
<p>Correct choice: b.</p>
<p>Entry address=0x7000+2=0x7002. Direction=0x44=68; packed=68+256*2=580=0x0244. State pointer is independently supplied as 0x9000.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> The file buffer and mutable state are separate objects. The decoder reads at entry address 0x7002; the operation receives state pointer 0x9000 plus the decoded value, not the state pointer as record bits.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> Direction is 0x44=68 and amount is 2, so packed value is 68+2*256=580=0x0244. The stated state pointer remains 0x9000 regardless of the entry&#x27;s file offset.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> Offset 2 must be added to the file base to form an entry address. The declared packing puts direction in the low byte, yielding 0x0244; neither an offset nor byte order can be substituted by guess.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m07-practice.html#m07-distinct-layouts">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m07-competing-hypotheses">m07-competing-hypotheses</h2>
<p>Correct choice: a.</p>
<p>Start (2,0). U3: (2+3,0+3)=(5,3). D6 proposes 5-6=-1&lt;0, so state remains (5,3). Continue U1: (5+1,3+1)=(6,4), 3 events. Stop after D6: (5,3), 2 events.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> U3 reaches (5,3). D6 proposes -1 and is rejected, retaining (5,3). Continuing evaluates U1 and reaches (6,4); stopping records the rejection as event 2 and never evaluates U1.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> D6 is well-formed but would exceed the floor bound. The supplied toy rule leaves both state values unchanged on rejection; it does not add the rejected six units to travel.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> The explicit difference between hypotheses is whether U1 is evaluated after rejection. Its accepted change from (5,3) to (6,4) makes this sequence discriminating.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m07-practice.html#m07-competing-hypotheses">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m07-invariant-diagnosis">m07-invariant-diagnosis</h2>
<p>Correct choice: c.</p>
<p>u,d&gt;=0 imply u+d&gt;=abs(u-d). For floor 4 from floor 1, abs(displacement)=3. Travel 1&lt;3 is impossible. Controls: U3 gives (4,3); U4,D1 gives (4,5), both respecting bounds.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> U3 alone reaches floor 4 with travel 3, staying inside the bounds. No downward move is required; this is a valid example satisfying the ledger.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> U4 then D1 stays within floors 0..6 and reaches floor 4 with travel 5. Opposite-direction travel can exceed net displacement.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> The exact ledger gives travel=u+d and displacement=u-d, with u,d nonnegative. Therefore travel must be at least abs(4-1)=3. A reported travel of 1 violates this necessary condition.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m07-practice.html#m07-invariant-diagnosis">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m07-published-state">m07-published-state</h2>
<p>Correct choice: b.</p>
<p>Speculative accepted movement: u=3+1=4,d=0, so f=2+4=6,t=4. Published no-commit history has u=d=0, so f=2,t=0. Both satisfy their own ledger; substituting u=4 into final f=2 mixes state versions.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> The snapshots explicitly describe changing working state. A final reset can coexist with internal updates to a working copy; the output alone cannot establish absence of stores.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> Accepted speculative moves total 3+1=4, reaching floor 6. The reported final retains initial (2,0). An invariant must name whether it describes speculative accepted movement or committed movement.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> That equivalence is the hypothesis under investigation, not an interface guarantee. These supplied observations distinguish event snapshots from the final publication result.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m07-practice.html#m07-published-state">Return to this question</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m07-evidence-boundary">m07-evidence-boundary</h2>
<p>Correct choice: a.</p>
<p>Output equality on a set S constrains the composition replay(decode(raw)) for raw in S. It does not uniquely identify decode: a reversible relabeling P can be canceled by replay composed with inverse(P). Required keys and bounds do not rule out every such semantic error.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> Shape constrains structure, while six matches support end-to-end behavior on six cases. Cite offsets, widths, byte order, discriminating mutations and actual value flow to support each field meaning independently.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> A well-shaped dictionary can attach a label to the wrong byte. If replay compensates for that mismatch, final outputs can agree while the decoder boundary remains wrong.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> Repeated cases can check repeatability but do not create a new distinction between equivalent end-to-end explanations. Design evidence that observes or separates the claimed field boundary.</p></li>
</ul>

<h2 id="m07-distinct-layouts">m07-distinct-layouts</h2>
<p>Complete a new lift entry. File bytes are 45 01 44 02 at file-buffer base 0x7000. The two-byte entry starts at file offset 2. Toy packing is direction + 256*amount; state is separately allocated at 0x9000. Which call values are justified?</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> x0=0x7002 and w1=0x9000, because the entry pointer is the mutable state.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> x0=0x9000 and w1=0x0244 (580); 0x7002 is the entry&#x27;s address, not its packed value.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> x0=2 and w1=0x4402, because file offsets are pointers and the first byte is the most significant byte.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m07-practice-feedback.html#m07-distinct-layouts">Feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m07-competing-hypotheses">m07-competing-hypotheses</h2>
<p>Fresh toy sequence: start at floor 2, travel 0; moves U3, D6, U1; floors must remain 0..6. Rejected moves leave working state unchanged. How do continue-after-rejection and stop-at-rejection differ?</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> Continue produces 3 events and ends (6,4); stop produces 2 events and ends (5,3).</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> Both produce 3 events and end (0,10), because every amount changes travel even when the move is rejected.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> Both produce 2 events and end (5,3), so including a later U1 cannot distinguish them.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m07-practice-feedback.html#m07-competing-hypotheses">Feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m07-invariant-diagnosis">m07-invariant-diagnosis</h2>
<p>For a lift starting at floor 1 with travel 0, which reported (floor, travel) is impossible under the supplied accepted-move rules? Amounts are nonnegative, and rejected moves change neither value.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> (4,3), because arriving above the start requires at least one downward move.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> (4,5), because travel must equal displacement even when both directions occur.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> (4,1), because displacement 3 exceeds total accepted travel 1.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m07-practice-feedback.html#m07-invariant-diagnosis">Feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m07-published-state">m07-published-state</h2>
<p>A hypothetical run starts at (floor 2, travel 0), evaluates U3, D6, U1, and reports event snapshots (5,3), (5,3), (6,4), then final (2,0) with publication=false. Which interpretation is supported?</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> No internal state changes occurred, because final equals the initial state.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> The event history records speculative travel 4, while the published state retains travel 0; applying the speculative movement ledger to final would mix histories.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> Final must be wrong because the last event snapshot is always the published state.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><a href="m07-practice-feedback.html#m07-published-state">Feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="m07-evidence-boundary">m07-evidence-boundary</h2>
<p>A model returns dictionaries with the required keys and bounded integers, and its final outputs match native results on six saved files. You want to claim that each decoded field has the correct meaning. What is still needed?</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>a.</strong> Separate byte/extraction and call evidence for field meanings; two compensating decoder/replay mistakes could still match those six final outputs.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>b.</strong> Nothing: correct dictionary shape proves every label refers to the correct input bytes on every file.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>c.</strong> Only more repetitions of the same six outputs; repetition necessarily identifies each hidden field independently.</p></li>
</ul>

<p>The reservation capstone combines earlier work: infer a bounded file format, connect bytes to native calls, model state changes, compare compiled forms and defend a fresh prediction. The useful outcome is a reproducible argument with preserved counterevidence. It is not a collection of outputs that happen to match.</p>
<p>Bring your byte-order and bounds notes, M4&#x27;s cause tracing, M5&#x27;s distinction between observations and inferred events, and M6&#x27;s value/flag correspondence method. You need Python functions and exceptions, state traces and caller/callee notation. A <strong>state</strong> is the set of values needed to predict subsequent behavior. An <strong>invariant</strong> is a stated relation that should hold over a specified kind of state under stated assumptions.</p>
<p>This preparation works a separate lift-display example. Its layout and rules are supplied solely to make the method visible. They say nothing about the reservation program&#x27;s operation codes, fields or transition rules. Use scratch notes for these checks; the capstone retains its original deliverables and probe requirements. Keep the original count practice and target hypotheses saved before their respective reveals in <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">M7 START-HERE</a>.</p>
<h2 id="separate-syntax-from-an-operation-s-acceptance">Separate syntax from an operation&#x27;s acceptance</h2>
<p>The toy lift file begins with magic byte <code>45</code>, then an unsigned one-byte count 0..4. Each entry has two bytes: direction <code>55</code> (<code>U</code>) or <code>44</code> (<code>D</code>), then amount 0..6. Its exact size is <code>2 + 2*count</code>. Validate the entire file before replay. Thus <code>45 01 55 03</code> is one well-formed upward entry of amount 3. Removing its last byte makes the file malformed, so no operation is attempted. Appending a byte also violates the exact-size rule.</p>
<p>Toy state has floor <code>f</code> in 0..6 and total accepted travel <code>t</code>. An accepted U amount a sets <code>f=f+a</code> and <code>t=t+a</code>; an accepted D sets <code>f=f-a</code> and <code>t=t+a</code>. A move whose proposed floor lies outside 0..6 is rejected and leaves this toy state unchanged. A well-formed D entry can therefore be rejected at floor zero. That is a replay result, not a file-parser error. These are supplied toy rules, not discoveries about the capstone.</p>
<p>For a real probe, retain separate columns for file validity, process exit, operation acceptance, event state and published final state. If the process refuses malformed bytes before producing events, do not describe that as a rejected operation in a valid replay. If the process succeeds and reports an event as rejected, do not infer that its file was invalid.</p>
<h2 id="draw-three-layouts-before-tracing-a-call">Draw three layouts before tracing a call</h2>
<p>The same logical entry can have different representations on disk, in an argument and in mutable state. Here are declared layouts for the toy; their addresses are illustrative, not addresses from the capstone.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Representation</th><th scope="col">Toy facts</th><th scope="col">Example for U amount 3</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>File bytes</td><td>Magic at file offset 0, count at 1, first two-byte entry at 2</td><td><code>45 01 55 03</code>; entry bytes <code>55 03</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>By-value call argument</td><td>Entry packed as <code>direction + 256*amount</code> in low 32 bits of <code>x1</code> (<code>w1</code>)</td><td><code>0x0355</code> = 853; not an address</td></tr>
<tr><td>Mutable state</td><td><code>x0</code> points to an eight-byte object: four-byte floor at state offset 0, four-byte travel at state offset 4</td><td>At address <code>0x9000</code>, floor 2 and travel 0 before the move</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>If the file buffer begins at <code>0x7000</code>, the first entry&#x27;s address is <code>0x7002</code>. Decoding reads its two bytes and produces integer 853. A later call receives state address <code>x0=0x9000</code> and record bits <code>w1=853</code>. For the accepted U3 move, state becomes floor 5, travel 3. The file offset 2, entry address <code>0x7002</code>, packed integer 853 and state address <code>0x9000</code> have four distinct roles.</p>
<p>Follow each pointer through saves and reloads rather than treating every load as a fresh input. A stack displacement locates temporary storage relative to that function&#x27;s stack/frame reference. It is neither a file offset nor automatically an object-field offset. A callee&#x27;s <code>[sp,#8]</code> is not the caller&#x27;s <code>[sp,#8]</code>. Likewise, a four-byte load establishes an access width, not the source-level name of the value.</p>
<p>Complete another entry&#x27;s file-to-call trace.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m07-distinct-layouts" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Complete a byte-to-call trace without confusing file offsets, packed values, object offsets or pointers.</p><fieldset><legend>Complete a new lift entry. File bytes are 45 01 44 02 at file-buffer base 0x7000. The two-byte entry starts at file offset 2. Toy packing is direction + 256*amount; state is separately allocated at 0x9000. Which call values are justified?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-1-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-1-0" name="practice-1" value="a"><span>x0=0x7002 and w1=0x9000, because the entry pointer is the mutable state.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-1-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-1-1" name="practice-1" value="b"><span>x0=0x9000 and w1=0x0244 (580); 0x7002 is the entry&#x27;s address, not its packed value.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-1-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-1-2" name="practice-1" value="c"><span>x0=2 and w1=0x4402, because file offsets are pointers and the first byte is the most significant byte.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m07-practice.html#m07-distinct-layouts">question</a> · <a href="m07-practice-feedback.html#m07-distinct-layouts">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="choose-an-input-on-which-hypotheses-disagree">Choose an input on which hypotheses disagree</h2>
<p>Suppose the toy move rule is known, but how a sequence is processed and published is not. Three plausible runners are:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Continue after a rejected move and publish the resulting state.</p></li>
<li><p>Stop at the first rejected move and publish the state reached so far.</p></li>
<li><p>Continue using a working copy, record every event, but publish the original state if any move was rejected.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>A <strong>working</strong>, or speculative, state is what the runner uses while evaluating a sequence. The <strong>published</strong> state is the one it exposes as final. They can differ. Do not decide publication merely from an intermediate event.</p>
<p>Start the toy at floor 1, travel 0 and choose U2, D4, U1. This is discriminating: it includes a rejection, a later move, and a net change from the initial state.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Entry under continued evaluation</th><th scope="col">Proposed floor</th><th scope="col">Accepted?</th><th scope="col">Working floor, travel after entry</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>U2</td><td>3</td><td>yes</td><td>3, 2</td></tr>
<tr><td>D4</td><td>-1</td><td>no</td><td>3, 2</td></tr>
<tr><td>U1</td><td>4</td><td>yes</td><td>4, 3</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>The first runner predicts three events and final <code>(4,3)</code>. The stop runner predicts two events and final <code>(3,2)</code>. The working-copy runner predicts three events with the table&#x27;s snapshots, but final <code>(1,0)</code> and unsuccessful publication. If a hypothetical observation has those three snapshots and final <code>(1,0)</code>, it rejects the first two hypotheses on this input and supports the third. It does not establish that every detail of the third runner is correct.</p>
<p>An all-accepted control U2, D1 from the same start reaches <code>(2,3)</code> under all three candidates. It cannot distinguish their rejection policies, but it can refute a model that always resets final state. An empty sequence checks initialization. A sequence whose net change is zero may conceal publication differences; calculate both predictions before selecting the input.</p>
<p>For the original program, write your own two competing hypotheses before the first run and choose observations that can disagree. “Maybe it works differently” is not a predictive hypothesis. State what each candidate expects for event count, acceptance, snapshots and final state. Keep observations that fit neither; they are reasons to revise, not discard the input.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m07-competing-hypotheses" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Derive different predicted event counts and states for continuation and stop-on-rejection hypotheses.</p><fieldset><legend>Fresh toy sequence: start at floor 2, travel 0; moves U3, D6, U1; floors must remain 0..6. Rejected moves leave working state unchanged. How do continue-after-rejection and stop-at-rejection differ?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-2-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-0" name="practice-2" value="a"><span>Continue produces 3 events and ends (6,4); stop produces 2 events and ends (5,3).</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-2-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-1" name="practice-2" value="b"><span>Both produce 3 events and end (0,10), because every amount changes travel even when the move is rejected.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-2-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-2-2" name="practice-2" value="c"><span>Both produce 2 events and end (5,3), so including a later U1 cannot distinguish them.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m07-practice.html#m07-competing-hypotheses">question</a> · <a href="m07-practice-feedback.html#m07-competing-hypotheses">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<h2 id="use-an-invariant-as-a-diagnostic-with-its-limits">Use an invariant as a diagnostic, with its limits</h2>
<p>For the toy, let u be the sum of accepted upward amounts and d the sum of accepted downward amounts in a particular state history. Starting at floor <code>f0</code>, travel zero, the exact ledger equations are:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-text">f = f0 + u - d
t = u + d
</code></pre>
<p>For the worked continued evaluation, u=3 and d=0: rejected D4 contributes nothing under the supplied toy rule. Thus f=1+3=4 and t=3. The equations imply <code>t &gt;= abs(f-f0)</code> and that <code>t-(f-f0)</code> is even. These weaker consequences can flag an impossible state, but they cannot establish the exact history. From start 1, <code>(f=4,t=3)</code> fits U3; <code>(f=4,t=5)</code> fits U4 followed by D1. Both satisfy the inequalities and parity, despite different paths.</p>
<p>Name the state version to which an invariant applies. The speculative ledger for the three-entry example ends at <code>(4,3)</code>. If the runner publishes its initial state instead, the published ledger has no committed movement and ends at <code>(1,0)</code>. Plugging speculative u and d into a published-state equation would manufacture a contradiction by mixing histories.</p>
<p>Your capstone needs an invariant justified from its own inferred operations. Label any quantity entering or leaving the modeled system and each separately indexed state component. Do not copy the lift&#x27;s equation or collapse multiple slots into one aggregate unless the evidence justifies that abstraction. A violated invariant points to a false assumption, bad trace, lost component or wrong state version; a satisfied invariant is a consistency check, not a proof of the entire model.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m07-invariant-diagnosis" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Use a derived invariant to reject an impossible state while recognizing that passing it does not identify a unique history.</p><fieldset><legend>For a lift starting at floor 1 with travel 0, which reported (floor, travel) is impossible under the supplied accepted-move rules? Amounts are nonnegative, and rejected moves change neither value.</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-3-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-0" name="practice-3" value="a"><span>(4,3), because arriving above the start requires at least one downward move.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-3-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-1" name="practice-3" value="b"><span>(4,5), because travel must equal displacement even when both directions occur.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-3-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-3-2" name="practice-3" value="c"><span>(4,1), because displacement 3 exceeds total accepted travel 1.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>

<section class="practice" data-question="m07-published-state" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Distinguish speculative event history from final published state and avoid inferring absence of internal writes from rollback.</p><fieldset><legend>A hypothetical run starts at (floor 2, travel 0), evaluates U3, D6, U1, and reports event snapshots (5,3), (5,3), (6,4), then final (2,0) with publication=false. <h2 id="give-each-claim-evidence-at-the-right-boundary">Give each claim evidence at the right boundary</h2>
<p>Keep four kinds of claim separate: supplied interface facts, byte-field interpretations, instruction-derived transitions, and behavior observed on specific probes. A dictionary with the required keys and bounded values can have its field labels attached to the wrong bytes. Even end-to-end output agreement can hide two compensating mistakes: a decoder swaps two meanings and a replay function swaps them back. Shape checks and native result comparisons do not independently validate every isolated decoded field.</p>
<p>Support a field claim with byte offsets, width, byte order, controlled changes and the actual extraction or call trace. Support a transition with pre-state, input, guard, stores or lack of stores, returned acceptance and post-state. Support publication with the relation between event snapshots and final state, plus the relevant caller/return/selection path. Use actual addresses from the supplied listings; a plausible source reconstruction is not address evidence.</p>
<section class="practice" data-question="m07-evidence-boundary" aria-label="Authored practice"><p class="eyebrow">Authored practice · no score gate</p><p class="practice-objective">Practice goal: Identify what output/shape agreement can establish and what additional evidence an isolated decoded-field claim needs.</p><fieldset><legend>A model returns dictionaries with the required keys and bounded integers, and its final outputs match native results on six saved files. You want to claim that each decoded field has the correct meaning. What is still needed?</legend><label class="choice" for="practice-5-0"><input type="radio" id="practice-5-0" name="practice-5" value="a"><span>Separate byte/extraction and call evidence for field meanings; two compensating decoder/replay mistakes could still match those six final outputs.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-5-1"><input type="radio" id="practice-5-1" name="practice-5" value="b"><span>Nothing: correct dictionary shape proves every label refers to the correct input bytes on every file.</span></label><label class="choice" for="practice-5-2"><input type="radio" id="practice-5-2" name="practice-5" value="c"><span>Only more repetitions of the same six outputs; repetition necessarily identifies each hidden field independently.</span></label></fieldset><button type="button" data-check>Check and save attempt</button><p class="practice-status" data-status role="status" aria-live="polite"></p><div class="practice-feedback" data-feedback hidden></div><details class="practice-history" data-history hidden><summary>Preserved attempts</summary><div data-attempts></div></details></section>
<p>Text version: <a href="m07-practice.html#m07-evidence-boundary">question</a> · <a href="m07-practice-feedback.html#m07-evidence-boundary">feedback after choosing</a>.</p>
<p>When optimized code looks different, choose one representation change and explain the values that survive it. M6&#x27;s method still applies: follow definitions, flag producers and consumers, and return values. Fewer visible branches do not prove that rejection disappeared. If an instruction is unfamiliar, name the unknown and use the provided reference rather than filling the gap with a guessed rule.</p>
<h2 id="enter-the-reservation-investigation">Enter the reservation investigation</h2>
<p>Follow <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">M7 START-HERE</a> from setup and the separate count example. Save that practice before its feedback, then save two target hypotheses before the first target run. Use the original route&#x27;s supplied specimens and required small probe set; preserve each raw input, prediction, command and output. Establish file bounds and field claims before treating a replay model as an explanation of the file.</p>
<p>Do not run the transfer binary until its original prediction is saved. Compare speculative events with published state, test controls that distinguish candidate policies, and preserve any counterexample before repair. If your first model agrees with the public checks, challenge a plausible alternative rather than inventing a failure. Public agreement supports the checked behaviors and shape constraints; it cannot independently certify all decoded fields or the argument you wrote.</p>
<p>Diagnose a malformed probe by checking your proposed exact-size relation and reversible hex bytes first. A writer helper&#x27;s success confirms that it created bytes, not that the target accepts their format. A hash mismatch or launch error belongs to setup recovery, not a new state-rule hypothesis. If outputs disagree, locate the first layer that differs: file decoding, argument packing, operation acceptance, state update, event capture, or final publication. Preserve that version and input before changing the smallest supported part.</p>
<p>Carry forward the original <code>investigation.py</code>, field/call/state diagrams, discriminating probe corpus, invariant with assumptions, instruction evidence, fresh combined-case prediction and exported records. These are parts of the original capstone handoff, not a new project. Another person should be able to rerun a claim and see what could disprove it, including the limits of finite checks and supplied facts.</p></article><aside class="progress-tools" aria-label="Lesson progress"><h2>Your practice record</h2><p>These are authored exercises, with answers available in this packet.
