<p>A compiled program moves a cart, but you do not have its update rule. Build a Python model that predicts its next state, support the model with native output and instructions, then decide what must change for a second target.</p>
<p>Start in the extracted student bundle, using <a href="setup.html">setup</a>. Keep the <a href="follow-along.html">follow-along checkpoints and troubleshooting</a> available as you work. All commands below run from that bundle&#x27;s root. You need Python functions, integer arithmetic, <code>if</code> statements and a terminal; no assembly knowledge is assumed. This is one local investigation, not a complete reverse-engineering course.</p>
<p>The deliverable is <code>model.py</code> plus saved prediction, model and transfer records. Keep your learner workspace outside the source repository. The recorder preserves new records; it does not grade their reasoning.</p>
<h2 id="1-describe-the-state">1. Describe the state</h2>
<p>An <strong>integer</strong> is a whole number such as <code>-3</code>, <code>0</code> or <code>4</code>. The cart&#x27;s <strong>state</strong> is its position and velocity at one moment. Position names a location on a line; velocity is signed movement per tick. Positive movement goes right and negative movement goes left. A <strong>tick</strong> is one update, not a measured second.</p>
<p>The command is an input to that update. You will discover what it does. For now, <code>cart</code> is a <strong>black box</strong>: you supply inputs and observe outputs without reading its implementation.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-text">./cart POSITION VELOCITY COMMAND TICKS
</code></pre>
<p>Use integers in these input ranges:</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Argument</th><th scope="col">Accepted inputs</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>POSITION</code></td><td><code>-1000</code> through <code>1000</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>VELOCITY</code></td><td><code>-6</code> through <code>6</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>COMMAND</code></td><td><code>-1</code>, <code>0</code> or <code>1</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>TICKS</code></td><td><code>1</code> through <code>8</code></td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>One invocation repeats the same command for every tick. The JSON output is a list of states <strong>after</strong> each tick, with keys <code>tick</code>, <code>position</code> and <code>velocity</code>. Input limits tell you what the command line accepts; they are not evidence of the internal update rule. Invalid inputs return an error instead of a state list.</p>
<h2 id="2-follow-a-smaller-worked-example">2. Follow a smaller worked example</h2>
<p>First use this different rule for a marker. It is a teaching example, not the cart&#x27;s hidden rule:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">def marker_step(p, v, flip):
    if flip == 1:
        v = -v
    p = p + v
    return p, v
</code></pre>
<p>Variables hold the current values. An assignment replaces a value; the next line reads its replacement. Starting with <code>p = 4</code>, <code>v = -3</code>, <code>flip = 1</code>:</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Step</th><th scope="col">Position</th><th scope="col">Velocity</th><th scope="col">Why</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>Read inputs</td><td>4</td><td>-3</td><td>These are the old state.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Test <code>flip == 1</code> and negate <code>v</code></td><td>4</td><td>3</td><td>The condition is true.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Add current <code>v</code> to <code>p</code></td><td>7</td><td>3</td><td>This line reads the updated velocity.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Return</td><td>7</td><td>3</td><td>The new state is <code>(7, 3)</code>.</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>The order matters: adding the old velocity would produce a different position. When you inspect the cart, establish its order from evidence instead of borrowing the marker&#x27;s rule.</p>
<p><strong>Your short trace:</strong> for this marker only, start with <code>p = -2</code>, <code>v = 4</code>, <code>flip = 0</code>. Put the returned position, velocity and a one-sentence reason in <code>response.json</code> under <code>miniature</code>. Keep <code>marker-feedback.md</code> closed until you save this answer with your first cart prediction.</p>
<h2 id="3-save-a-prediction-before-running-the-cart">3. Save a prediction before running the cart</h2>
<p>Choose a one-tick input within the table&#x27;s ranges. Write a concrete possible rule in <code>claim</code>, and explain why you chose it in <code>reason</code>. It can be wrong; “unknown” alone is not a prediction. In <code>probe</code>, enter the four arguments and the exact output row you predict. Also state one different rule that this input could distinguish from yours in <code>alternative</code>.</p>
<p>For example, a command might choose a velocity, modify a velocity, or change position directly. These are possibilities to investigate, not an announced answer. Choose inputs on which your two possibilities disagree.</p>
<p><code>response.json</code> is a plain-text JSON document. Keys and text use double quotes; numbers do not. Separate entries with commas, but do not put a comma after the last entry. For example, <code>&quot;claim&quot;: &quot;I expect position to stay fixed&quot;</code> stores text, while <code>&quot;position&quot;: -2</code> stores a number. Replace the template&#x27;s empty strings and <code>null</code> values with your response; leave unrelated later fields alone. You can check the syntax without changing or grading it:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 -m json.tool response.json
</code></pre>
<p>If it reports a line/column error, repair the punctuation in your working file before saving. This does not change an earlier recorded attempt.</p>
<p>Save the completed response before running <code>cart</code>, reading <code>cart.asm</code>, or opening the checkers:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m01 --stage prediction --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none
python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m01
</code></pre>
<p>Use the assistance you actually had: <code>none</code>, <code>hint-1</code>, <code>hint-2</code>, <code>hint-3</code> or <code>solution</code>. Use the most revealing level already seen and describe other help in <code>assistance_details</code>. A blank template is not a completed prediction. The manifest identifies the exact target files for your record.</p>
<p>After saving the marker trace, open <a href="marker-feedback.html">its separate feedback</a>. Keep that file closed before your first save; even a plain-text reader will then show the question separately from its answer.</p>
<h2 id="4-run-a-probe-and-challenge-the-explanation">4. Run a probe and challenge the explanation</h2>
<p>Run <code>./cart</code> with your saved four arguments. Copy the actual output into <code>observations</code> alongside its inputs. Compare each predicted field with the observed field. Write whether the observation supports or contradicts your claim; one matching result can fit several rules.</p>
<p>Change one input at a time for the next probe. Before each run, add its expected result and what disagreement it would resolve, then save another prediction record. Seek evidence about command direction, the effect of the old velocity, repeated ticks and what happens near the accepted velocity endpoints. Do not infer a rule from a single zero input. If choosing probes or following a branch is new to you, <a href="methods.html">work through this different example</a> before selecting the next cart probe.</p>
<p>Use <a href="hints.html">the hints</a> if you cannot select the next probe. You may edit the working <code>response.json</code>; save each change as a new record and leave the earlier saved records intact.</p>
<h2 id="5-connect-output-to-instructions">5. Connect output to instructions</h2>
<p><strong>Disassembly</strong> is a readable list of the processor instructions encoded in an executable. An <strong>instruction</strong> is a small operation such as adding values, comparing them or reading memory. A <strong>register</strong> is a small working storage location inside the processor; names differ between processor types. A <strong>branch</strong> chooses which instruction runs next, often after a comparison. Some processors can choose between values without a branch, so a condition need not appear as an obvious jump.</p>
<p>A <strong>load</strong> reads a value from memory into a register. A <strong>store</strong> writes a value back to memory. An argument may contain a value or the address of its memory location. The useful question is which value an instruction reads, not whether a register has a familiar name.</p>
<p>Here is a notation bridge for the supplied ARM64 listing. It is an illustrative memory update, <strong>not</strong> a capture from the cart:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-text">ldr w8, [x0]       // read a 32-bit value at the address held in x0
add w9, w8, #1     // add the immediate (literal) value 1
str w9, [x0]       // store that result at the same address
</code></pre>
<p>If the memory value starts at 4, the first line puts 4 in <code>w8</code>, the next puts 5 in <code>w9</code>, and the last leaves 5 in memory. <code>x0</code> holds an address, not that memory value. <code>xN</code> is a 64-bit register; <code>wN</code> names its low 32 bits. A destination appears first. Brackets mean “memory at this address”; <code>#</code> marks a literal, and <code>0x</code> introduces a hexadecimal number.</p>
<p>In this compiled function the first two arguments, <code>x0</code> and <code>x1</code>, are addresses of the position and velocity; the third, <code>w2</code>, is the command value. This argument convention is supplied scaffolding, not something you have already inferred. <code>sp</code> is the stack pointer, and <code>[sp, #0x10]</code> is a temporary slot 16 bytes from it. Stores of an address and loads through that address are different operations. <code>mov</code> copies a literal or register value into its destination. <code>mul</code> multiplies; <code>add</code> adds; <code>sub</code> subtracts. <code>adds</code> and <code>subs</code> also set condition flags: a record of the arithmetic result that the next conditional branch reads. A later <code>b.le</code> follows a signed less-or-equal result and <code>b.ge</code> follows a signed greater-or-equal result; plain <code>b</code> jumps unconditionally. These conditional branches test the preceding flags, not their jump-address operand. Follow the address shown on the taken branch. <code>ret</code> returns to the caller. Use these facts to build your table; you do not need to memorize register names.</p>
<p>Open <code>cart.asm</code> in a text editor and search for <code>lab_step</code> (some platforms show <code>_lab_step</code>). This function performs one update. The rest of the program handles arguments and printing. The supplied names are intentional help.</p>
<p>Trace one of your observed one-tick runs through that function. In <code>static_evidence</code>, record instruction addresses or quoted lines for:</p>
<ol>
<li><p>Where the old state and command enter the calculation.</p></li>
<li><p>Arithmetic or comparisons that affect a returned value.</p></li>
<li><p>Which value feeds the position calculation, and where each result is stored.</p></li>
</ol>
<p>Use a small table with “instruction or address / value before / value after / what this supports.” You do not have to translate the entire executable. If a line is unclear, label it uncertain and design a native probe that could resolve the question.</p>
<p>There is also a <a href="setup.html">Ghidra route in setup</a>: import this same <code>cart</code>, analyze it, find <code>lab_step</code> and compare its listing and decompiled view with your trace. <strong>The Ghidra route has not been executed for this milestone.</strong> Use the supplied assembly route here; report a missing symbol, tool or import failure instead of claiming a completed Ghidra analysis. A decompiled view is a tool&#x27;s reconstruction, so support its interpretation with the listing and native output.</p>
<h2 id="6-implement-and-save-the-model">6. Implement and save the model</h2>
<p>Complete <code>step(p, v, c)</code> in <code>model.py</code>. It must accept one valid input state and command, return a pair of integers <code>(new_position, new_velocity)</code>, and match <strong>one</strong> cart tick. Return signed values. Do not print, invoke <code>cart</code>, read files or keep state between calls. The caller supplies the old state every time.</p>
<p>Before running a checker, update <code>response.json</code> with your rule, supporting observations, static evidence and any change from the first claim. Save the code with it:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m01 --stage model --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact model.py
python3 check_basic.py
</code></pre>
<p>Use your actual assistance level in the record command. The basic checker exposes two ordinary cases after your attempt. It reports inputs, expected state and actual state if they differ. It does not test every command, endpoint, repeated tick or explanation.</p>
<p>On a failure, compare the named case with your own instruction trace before editing. Record what the mismatch changes in your explanation, revise the code and save a <strong>new</strong> model record. After these basic checks, the wider public check is:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 check_model.py model.py --target baseline
</code></pre>
<p>The wider check includes the named cases plus 24 generated public probes. You can choose another set with <code>--seed 41</code>; the seed is visible, not a held-out exam. A lookup table that fits a few displayed cases is not an explanation of the update.</p>
<p>Both checkers execute your Python code locally. They are not sandboxes; run only code you wrote or trust. Passing public checks supports the model on those cases. It does not show that your reasoning is sound or measure independent mastery.</p>
<h2 id="7-decide-whether-the-model-transfers">7. Decide whether the model transfers</h2>
<p>Keep the baseline model. The second executable, <code>cart-transfer</code>, accepts the same command-line interface. Its behavior may differ. Your task is to decide whether the baseline model can be reused, must change, or still lacks enough evidence.</p>
<p>Before running the second executable or opening <code>cart-transfer.asm</code>, record a predicted output from your baseline model for a probe <strong>you select</strong>, and state why that probe could reveal a difference. Set <code>probe.target</code> to <code>cart-transfer</code>, then save:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m01 --stage transfer --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact model.py
</code></pre>
<p>Do this part without the hints or source solution; record assistance if you use any.</p>
<p>Then investigate the new target. Use your own probes and its <code>lab_step</code> listing. Preserve the original baseline code by putting any new implementation in <code>transfer_model.py</code>. Explain each proposed change with a native observation and an instruction reference; “the checker passed” is not an explanation.</p>
<p>Finally, choose a start state and a command for a run of several ticks that you have not used while fitting the transfer model. Predict the complete state list, save it with <code>--stage transfer</code> and <code>--artifact transfer_model.py</code>, then run that exact native case. Remember that an invocation keeps its command constant; its internal later states need not be valid starting arguments for a separate invocation.</p>
<p>You can check your new model after saving the attempt:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 check_model.py transfer_model.py --target transfer
</code></pre>
<p>In <code>transfer_decision</code>, state your decision, the most useful counterexample or confirming probe, and one remaining uncertainty. Save the observed result as a new transfer record. This is practice on a fresh artifact, not evidence of broad reverse-engineering ability.</p>
<h2 id="8-investigate-a-different-control-structure">8. Investigate a different control structure</h2>
<p>The second target gives practice with changed arithmetic. Continue to <a href="crossing.html">the crossing investigation</a>, where a third target asks you to identify when a different control path runs. Keep both earlier models. You will build <code>crossing_model.py</code>, save competing predictions, and test a new multi-tick forecast. Its separate hints remain optional.</p>
<h2 id="keep-or-deliberately-reveal-your-work">Keep or deliberately reveal your work</h2>
<p>The milestone&#x27;s evidence is a first prediction, observed results, saved models with instruction traces, a recorded repair if needed, and fresh transfer predictions checked against native output. Complete the crossing investigation before treating this milestone&#x27;s learning path as finished. <code>notebook.py list</code> shows the retained records. Keep them with the bundle&#x27;s manifest so later work can be tied to these exact targets. This is a learner artifact checklist, not a claim that the course&#x27;s human, tool and accessibility acceptance gates have closed.</p>
<p>The repository&#x27;s <code>courses/re-lab/solutions/01-cart.md</code> and <code>courses/re-lab/source/</code> are deliberate answer-reveal material, omitted from this student bundle. After committing an attempt, you may request them for a walkthrough. Save later work with <code>--assistance solution</code>; it remains useful assisted practice. No score or tool blocks you from moving on.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a rel="prev" href="../learning/m01.html">Previous: Prepare M01</a><a rel="next" href="../learning/m02.html">Next: Prepare M02</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#1-describe-the-state">1. <p>Read one level at a time after saving your current prediction. Record the highest level seen as <code>hint-1</code>, <code>hint-2</code> or <code>hint-3</code>; retain the earlier attempt. These hints help select evidence. The worked implementation is separate.</p>
<h2 id="hint-1-challenge-a-symmetry">Hint 1 — challenge a symmetry</h2>
<p>In the baseline model, shifting the input position shifts the output position by the same amount. Velocity does not change just because you chose another starting location. Test that prediction with positions on different parts of the line while keeping velocity, command and one tick fixed.</p>
<p>Before running, calculate both baseline outputs. If the new target disagrees, write exactly which field breaks the assumption. If it agrees, that pair has not established the assumption for other positions.</p>
<h2 id="hint-2-keep-old-and-proposed-values-apart">Hint 2 — keep old and proposed values apart</h2>
<p>Take a case your current model misses. Write the old position, the velocity your ordinary update would compute, and the position that velocity would propose. Compare this with a nearby case that follows ordinary movement. Ask whether their locations at the beginning and end of the proposed move matter.</p>
<p>Choose cases that approach a boundary from different directions. Include an exact endpoint, not only values well beyond it. Predict the result under each candidate rule before running. Follow the comparisons in <code>lab_step</code> using those same values.</p>
<h2 id="hint-3-trace-all-tests-and-both-returned-fields">Hint 3 — trace all tests and both returned fields</h2>
<p>Build a small table: old position, proposed position, comparison outcomes, selected position, selected velocity. Compare a negative starting position that stays negative, one whose proposed move reaches zero, and a start exactly at zero. Include movement in the opposite direction too. This separates several superficially plausible conditions; it does not license treating every arrival at one coordinate alike.</p>
<p>Trace all tests that select the surprising path. Then inspect <strong>both</strong> final writes. A changed position does not tell you whether velocity was retained or replaced. For a multi-tick forecast, use the returned pair as the next input and reassess the conditions; do not assume a selected path becomes permanent.</p>

<p>Complete the baseline and <code>cart-transfer</code> practice first. You now have models that can be reused or revised. This challenge asks whether that familiar kind of revision is enough for a third target. Your decision must come from evidence.</p>
<p><code>cart-crossing</code> is another original local toy. It accepts the same <code>POSITION VELOCITY COMMAND TICKS</code> arguments and ranges as <code>cart</code>, repeats one command, and returns the same JSON state rows. Its one-tick function is still named <code>lab_step</code>. The target&#x27;s name is not a specification of its behavior.</p>
<p>Keep <code>model.py</code> and <code>transfer_model.py</code>. Your new deliverables are <code>crossing_model.py</code> and saved <code>challenge</code> records: two candidate rules, predictions, native observations, an instruction trace, an attempted model, any repairs, and a fresh multi-tick forecast. Use the existing <code>response.json</code> fields below; each save preserves a new copy. Work from the extracted bundle&#x27;s root.</p>
<h2 id="1-make-the-old-assumptions-visible">1. Make the old assumptions visible</h2>
<p>Read <a href="methods.html">the probe and tracing method</a>, including its different dispenser example. In your baseline model, a change in starting position shifts the returned position by the same amount without changing returned velocity. That is a consequence of your model, <strong>not</strong> a promise about this target.</p>
<p>Write your best candidate rule in <code>claim</code> and a different plausible rule in <code>alternative</code>. Give enough detail to calculate a returned position and velocity for both. You might retain a previous model, alter its arithmetic, change its order, or propose a different decision. Do not simply label them “same” and “different.” In <code>reason</code>, name the old assumption you intend to test.</p>
<p>Choose a one-tick input on which your candidates disagree. Set <code>probe.target</code> to <code>cart-crossing</code>, put the four integers in <code>probe.args</code>, and put your claim&#x27;s exact predicted row in <code>probe.predicted_rows</code>. Put the alternative&#x27;s predicted row and why they differ in <code>probe.distinguishes</code>. Keep <code>observations</code> empty until you run it.</p>
<p>Before running the new target, reading its assembly or opening its checker, save:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 -m json.tool response.json
python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m01 --stage challenge --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact crossing_model.py
</code></pre>
<p>The starter is deliberately unfinished. Saving it now preserves the starting point, not a correct implementation. Replace <code>none</code> with the highest assistance you have actually used. List the records and confirm the new file exists before proceeding.</p>
<h2 id="2-choose-evidence-not-just-more-outputs">2. Choose evidence, not just more outputs</h2>
<p>Run your saved case, substituting its four integers:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-text">./cart-crossing POSITION VELOCITY COMMAND TICKS
</code></pre>
<p>Add the actual rows to <code>observations</code> beside their inputs. Say which candidate each field supports or contradicts. If both candidates fail, retain that result and propose a third explanation.</p>
<p>For each next run, save its prediction first. Begin with one tick. Include a pair with the same starting velocity and command but different positions; this tests the position assumption above. Also choose a pair that changes just velocity or command. Explain what each pair can distinguish. Do not run a large grid before writing down what a useful difference would mean.</p>
<p>If nearby inputs produce different kinds of outcome, find the boundary. Predict a case on each side and the exact boundary value. “Below” and “at” may follow different paths. A rule that fits ordinary movement can still be wrong there. If you see no difference, record that limitation and try a probe selected to challenge your current rule.</p>
<p>Stuck selecting a probe? The separate <a href="crossing-hints.html">ordered hints</a> offer increasing help. Record the highest level seen and describe other help in <code>assistance_details</code>.</p>
<h2 id="3-explain-a-path-through-the-instructions">3. Explain a path through the instructions</h2>
<p>Open <code>cart-crossing.asm</code> and find <code>lab_step</code>. Use the instruction vocabulary in the first lesson. Trace one ordinary observation and one that best distinguishes your candidates. Record this in <code>static_evidence</code>:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>instruction addresses or exact lines, with the input values they read;</p></li>
<li><p>arithmetic results and comparisons that affect the selected path;</p></li>
<li><p>which values finally become position and velocity.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>The supplied ARM64 listing adds three useful spellings. <code>tbz w8, #0x1f, ADDRESS</code> tests bit 31 of <code>w8</code> and jumps to <code>ADDRESS</code> if that bit is zero; <code>tbnz</code> jumps if it is one. A bit is a binary digit, and bit numbers start at zero; hexadecimal <code>0x1f</code> is decimal 31. For a signed 32-bit integer in two&#x27;s-complement form, bit 31 distinguishes negative values from zero or positive values. Thus a register holding <code>3</code> has that bit clear, while one holding <code>-3</code> has it set. These instructions test the named register directly, rather than the condition flags described in the first lesson. First find which value the register holds at that point. <a href="https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ddi0602/2026-03/Base-Instructions/TBNZ--Test-bit-and-branch-if-nonzero-">Arm&#x27;s instruction reference</a></p>
<p><code>wzr</code> is a special register that reads as zero. For example, <code>str wzr, [x9]</code> writes a 32-bit zero to the memory address held in <code>x9</code>; it does not change the address itself. This notation explains the operations, not which cart values they affect. <a href="https://support.arm.com/documentation/dui0801/l/Overview-of-AArch64-state/Registers-in-AArch64-state">Arm&#x27;s register reference</a></p>
<p>Distinguish an old input from a value calculated during the tick. If several tests select a path, trace every relevant test; one matching comparison is not an explanation of the whole path. Consult the compound-condition example in <code>methods.md</code>. Mark uncertain instructions and name a native probe that could resolve the uncertainty. Do not count a checker result as instruction evidence.</p>
<h2 id="4-build-forecast-then-check">4. Build, forecast, then check</h2>
<p>Complete <code>step(p, v, c)</code> in <code>crossing_model.py</code>. It returns one pair of integers after one tick. It must not print, call the native target, read files or retain state between calls. Explain why each part of your rule exists. Save the attempted code and reasoning with the <code>challenge</code> record command above before feedback.</p>
<p>Now choose a fresh run of three to eight ticks that you have not used to fit the model. Keep its command constant. Calculate <strong>every</strong> row by feeding each returned state into the next tick. Put the prediction and inputs in <code>probe</code>, explain why this sequence challenges your rule, and save again before running it. Compare the entire native result, not only the last position.</p>
<p>After preserving the forecast and observed result, run:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 check_model.py crossing_model.py --target crossing --ticks 4
</code></pre>
<p>The checker executes your local Python; it is not a sandbox. Use only your own or trusted code. It compares behavior on public cases, including generated ones. With <code>--ticks 4</code> it compares four consecutive states and names the first mismatching tick. It does not assess your explanation or establish broad RE skill.</p>
<p>If a case fails, retain the failed model record. In <code>revision</code>, identify the first place your predicted values or path disagree with the evidence. Revise your explanation and model, then save a new record before checking again. Avoid a special case keyed only to the displayed test input. If all checks pass, still examine your trace and counterexamples for an unsupported assumption.</p>
<h2 id="5-hand-off-an-explanation-someone-can-test">5. Hand off an explanation someone can test</h2>
<p>In <code>transfer_decision</code>, state what you reused, what you changed, the strongest evidence rejecting an alternative, and one remaining uncertainty with a proposed next probe. Include the boundary and fresh multi-tick evidence. A claim such as “only the constants changed” must explain all your observations, not just an ordinary case.</p>
<p>Your challenge handoff contains:</p>
<ol>
<li><p>A saved prediction preceding target output, including both candidate outputs.</p></li>
<li><p>Paired probes, a boundary investigation, and their observed results.</p></li>
<li><p>Instruction evidence for two informative paths.</p></li>
<li><p>Saved attempted code, feedback and any revised code.</p></li>
<li><p>A fresh multi-tick forecast, its comparison, and your transfer decision.</p></li>
</ol>
<p>Use <code>python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m01</code> to inspect the record list. Copy the entire <code>work/m01/</code> directory, all three model files and <code>manifest.json</code> to your chosen backup location. Keep the same bundle with them for resume; these local tools upload nothing. Preserve assistance and the earlier baseline/transfer records. The source repository&#x27;s <code>solutions/03-crossing.md</code> is an optional answer reveal after your attempt, outside the student bundle.</p>
<p>This completes a challenge submission, not course acceptance. Technical checks, independent reading, supported-platform rehearsal and the unresolved acceptance gates still apply.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M01)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#1-make-the-old-assumptions-visible">1. Make the old assumptions visible</a></li><li><a href="#2-choose-evidence-not-just-more-outputs">2. Choose evidence, not just more outputs</a></li><li><a href="#3-explain-a-path-through-the-instructions">3. Explain a path through the instructions</a></li><li><a href="#4-build-forecast-then-check">4. Build, forecast, then check</a></li><li><a href="#5-hand-off-an-explanation-someone-can-test">5. <p>This companion helps you tell whether a step worked and how to recover. Use it with <code>START-HERE.md</code> in the student bundle. It supplies no cart rule. Save your own attempt before opening a worked solution.</p>
<h2 id="before-the-first-command">Before the first command</h2>
<p>Use the Mac ARM64 bundle on an Apple Silicon Mac. You need Python 3 for the notebook and model, a terminal, and a text editor. Ghidra is a separately documented route, still unverified for this milestone. Do not install it to solve a problem with one of these basic commands.</p>
<p>Open a terminal in the <strong>extracted bundle folder</strong>. A quick location check is:</p>

Do not bypass an OS security warning.</p>
<h2 id="checkpoint-a-the-starter-has-valid-python-syntax">Checkpoint A — the starter has valid Python syntax</h2>
<p>The starter intentionally has no rule. Before your prediction, check only that Python can read its syntax:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 -m py_compile model.py
</code></pre>
<p>Success produces no output. This command compiles the file without calling <code>step</code>; it does not show that the rule is implemented. If it reports a syntax error, restore the unchanged starter from your bundle. Save your first prediction before running either checker: their feedback reveals expected states.</p>
<h2 id="checkpoint-b-your-first-prediction-is-retained">Checkpoint B — your first prediction is retained</h2>
<p>Follow the lesson&#x27;s marker trace and first cart prediction. Fill <code>response.json</code>, check its JSON syntax, then save with the command in the lesson. The success message names a newly created file under <code>work/m01/</code>. List it:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m01
</code></pre>
<p>Open the saved JSON in your editor. It contains the original response, assistance, full lesson wording and target manifest. If the save says <code>Not saved</code>, fix the reported input or storage problem and retry. A failed save must not be counted as a committed prediction. Do not delete earlier records or replace them with a corrected answer.</p>
<h2 id="checkpoint-c-evidence-and-a-model-then-feedback">Checkpoint C — evidence and a model, then feedback</h2>
<p>Run only the native probes you chose and recorded. Compare their output with your prediction, then inspect the matching assembly. Complete <code>model.py</code>, save it with <code>--artifact model.py</code>, and run the two public checkers. A mismatch names the input, observed native state and your model&#x27;s state. Decide which part of your explanation that case contradicts before revising.</p>
<p>If you run the checkers on the unchanged starter at this point, both should report that <code>step</code> is unfinished. The wider check should also point back to section 6 of the lesson. That expected failure shows that an empty implementation is rejected; it does not count as a completed model.</p>
<p>Save the revision as another record. The old record must still appear in the list. If Python reports syntax or import errors, repair those before interpreting the result as a wrong cart rule. The <a href="https://github.com/itsHabib/free-to-learn/blob/main/courses/re-lab/solutions/01-cart.md">baseline worked walkthrough</a> is an optional, explicit answer reveal; record <code>--assistance solution</code> if you open it. It does not contain the changed-target solution.</p>
<h2 id="checkpoint-d-changed-target-practice">Checkpoint D — changed-target practice</h2>
<p>Keep <code>model.py</code> unchanged and write any changed model in <code>transfer_model.py</code>. Predict a distinguishing case before running the changed target. Save the prediction and later actual result separately. Passing its public checks shows agreement on those cases; it does not show that the checker judged your instruction trace or explanation. The lesson asks for both.</p>
<p>A maintainer&#x27;s named checkpoints are indexed separately in the source repository. The baseline and changed-target implementations are worked solutions, not hidden learner work or files the student runtime imports.</p>
<h2 id="checkpoint-e-explain-a-different-control-path">Checkpoint E — explain a different control path</h2>
<p>Open <code>crossing.md</code> after the earlier models. Save two competing rules and their predicted observations before running <code>cart-crossing</code> or its checker. The deliverable is <code>crossing_model.py</code>, instruction evidence, and a fresh multi-tick forecast. Use <code>--stage challenge</code> to keep these attempts separate from earlier transfer practice. The <a href="methods.html">methods example</a> explains how to select a discriminating probe without giving this target&#x27;s rule.</p>
<p>After saving the model, run <code>python3 check_model.py crossing_model.py --target crossing --ticks 4</code>. A failure at a later tick means the first update may match while its resulting state leads to a later disagreement. Check the reported tick in your saved forecast before changing the code. Preserve the failing implementation and any repair as different records.</p>
<h2 id="checkpoint-f-copy-resume-and-inspect">Checkpoint F — copy, resume and inspect</h2>
<p>Stop before changing branches or replacing a bundle. Copy the entire <code>work/m01/</code> directory, your model files and <code>manifest.json</code> to a separate backup location you choose. Those files are your export; they are not uploaded by these tools. Keep private responses outside Git.</p>
<p>Open the copied record and confirm its original response and source snapshot are present. To resume, use a copy of the <strong>same bundle</strong>, restore your files, and point <code>notebook.py list --workspace</code> at the restored work directory. Make the next save as a new record. The earlier records and IDs should remain unchanged. If you upgrade the bundle, keep its old copy and manifest so you can distinguish the two targets.</p>
<h2 id="what-to-send-with-a-bug-report">What to send with a bug report</h2>
<p>Include the milestone version, OS/architecture, Python version, command, exit/error text and relevant target hashes. Share a minimal synthetic example rather than private notes. Do not include a full notebook containing information you do not want to disclose.</p>

<p>These hints apply to the baseline investigation, not the transfer task. Record the highest hint level you read in your next notebook record and name any other help in <code>assistance_details</code>. Keep your first prediction and code attempt.</p>
<h2 id="hint-1-make-one-update-visible">Hint 1: make one update visible</h2>
<p>Use one tick and write two columns: the input state and the state after that tick. Ask which value changed and which stayed the same before naming a rule. Reason: several updates can hide the order of a single update.</p>
<p>Next action: choose two one-tick runs that differ in exactly one argument. Predict both outputs before running them.</p>
<h2 id="hint-2-separate-competing-rules">Hint 2: separate competing rules</h2>
<p>If you think the command chooses a velocity, compare runs with the same command and position but different starting velocities. If you think it changes velocity, ask whether your rule still explains both signs and inputs near the accepted endpoints. Reason: rival rules often agree at a convenient starting value and disagree elsewhere.</p>
<p>Next action: write both rules in words, then pick an input where they predict different output. Use the observed output to reject or retain each rule. The accepted input endpoints alone do not establish output limits.</p>
<h2 id="hint-3-trace-a-sibling-update">Hint 3: trace a sibling update</h2>
<p>Read this level after saving a prediction or model attempt. It uses the marker from the lesson, whose rule is different from the cart&#x27;s.</p>
<p>For the marker, start with <code>p = -4</code>, <code>v = 2</code>, <code>flip = 1</code>. The true condition negates velocity, so the current <code>v</code> becomes <code>-2</code>. The later addition reads that current value: <code>p = -4 + -2 = -6</code>. The returned pair is <code>(-6, -2)</code>. Reason: tracking the value after each assignment reveals which version a later operation uses.</p>
<p>Next action: choose one native cart observation and annotate its <code>lab_step</code> instructions in the same way. Mark the first calculation where your model and the trace disagree. Keep uncertainty explicit if you cannot yet identify the value.</p>
<p>If repeated model attempts still fail, request the separately marked source walkthrough after preserving an attempt. Record that later work as <code>solution</code> assistance. The student bundle intentionally contains no source walkthrough.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M01)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#hint-1-make-one-update-visible">Hint 1: make one update visible</a></li><li><a href="#hint-2-separate-competing-rules">Hint 2: separate competing rules</a></li><li><a href="#hint-3-trace-a-sibling-update">Hint 3: trace a sibling update</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="../learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="../learning/m01.html">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="from-an-output-to-an-explanation">From an output to an explanation</h1>
<p>Use this page when you can run a program but are unsure what to try next. A useful model explains how an input produces an output. A list of matching examples is only a start.</p>
<h2 id="choose-a-probe-that-can-change-your-mind">Choose a probe that can change your mind</h2>
<p>A <strong>hypothesis</strong> is a candidate explanation. A <strong>probe</strong> is an input chosen to test one. Before running it, calculate what at least two hypotheses predict. If they predict the same output, that run cannot distinguish them, even if it succeeds.</p>
<p>Here is a different, fully revealed teaching example. A toy dispenser holds <code>stock</code> items, receives a <code>request</code>, and has a <code>closed</code> switch. The counts are nonnegative integers; <code>closed</code> is <code>1</code> for closed or <code>0</code> for open. It dispenses only when its lid is closed <strong>and</strong> enough items remain. Otherwise it keeps the stock unchanged. These are not the cart&#x27;s rules.</p>
<p>Consider two explanations:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>A:</strong> enough stock alone permits dispensing.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>B:</strong> both enough stock and a closed lid are required.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>With stock <code>5</code>, request <code>2</code>, and closed <code>1</code>, both predict stock <code>3</code>. That is a useful ordinary case, but a poor discriminator. Keep stock and request fixed and change only closed to <code>0</code>: A predicts <code>3</code>; B predicts <code>5</code>. One observed value can now reject one explanation for that case.</p>
<p>Changing one input at a time makes a difference easier to attribute. It is not a law: some hypotheses require a carefully chosen combination. State why the combination distinguishes them instead of changing everything and guessing which change mattered.</p>
<h2 id="trace-a-compound-condition-without-skipping-values">Trace a compound condition without skipping values</h2>
<p>A compound condition combines smaller tests. Here <strong>and</strong> means that both must be true. Trace the actual input values before following the selected path:</p>
<p>The input column gives <code>(stock, request, closed)</code> in that order. In the test column, the stock comparison comes first and the lid comparison second.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Input</th><th scope="col">Tests and combined result</th><th scope="col">New stock</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>5,2,0</code></td><td>true and false → false</td><td><code>5</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>5,2,1</code></td><td>true and true → true</td><td><code>3</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>2,2,1</code></td><td>true and true → true</td><td><code>0</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>1,2,1</code></td><td>false and true → false</td><td><code>1</code></td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>The last two rows locate an equality boundary: enough includes exactly the requested amount. Samples far from that boundary would not distinguish <code>&gt;=</code> from <code>&gt;</code>.</p>
<p>In an instruction listing, follow each comparison&#x27;s operands and the path it selects. Do not infer the whole condition from one comparison. The compiler may arrange two tests as separate branches or select between values without an obvious source-style <code>if</code>. The evidence you need is which values reach the final write on each path.</p>
<h2 id="find-the-first-disagreement">Find the first disagreement</h2>
<p>Write a short trace with four columns: operation, inputs it reads, computed value, destination. Keep the old state separate from replacements. If your model and the program disagree, compare those traces from the start. A wrong early value can cause both wrong arithmetic and a wrong later branch. Patching only the last output can hide the cause.</p>
<p>For a multi-step run, feed each returned state into the next step. Do not reset to the original state between rows. A rule can match the first row and fail when its own output becomes the next input.</p>
<h2 id="state-what-transfers">State what transfers</h2>
<p>When a related program changes, separate three questions: Which old assumptions still predict observations? Which specific observation rejects one? What new rule explains both the old ordinary case and the counterexample? Try the simplest candidate that fits your evidence, then seek a case that could refute it. “Simplest” is a starting preference, not proof.</p>
<p>Save predictions before output, and code before checker feedback. A correction made after seeing an answer is useful practice; preserve the earlier attempt and record the help. Public checker passes support the tested behavior. Your explanation still needs native observations, instruction evidence and an honest remaining uncertainty.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M01)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#choose-a-probe-that-can-change-your-mind">Choose a probe that can change your mind</a></li><li><a href="#trace-a-compound-condition-without-skipping-values">Trace a compound condition without skipping values</a></li><li><a href="#find-the-first-disagreement">Find the first disagreement</a></li><li><a href="#state-what-transfers">State what transfers</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>Milestone 2 — recover a record layout · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. Native state updates</span><div><a href="../learning/m01.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m01/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>2. <p>Two owned native programs print the bytes of a record before and after a function call. You will recover the fields from those bytes, trace the call through an ARM64 listing, and write a decoder that survives a changed layout.</p>
<p>This is a private course milestone under development, not an accepted course. It follows M1&#x27;s prediction, probe and revision workflow. You need a terminal, a text editor, and enough Python to edit a function and dictionary. <a href="setup.html">Setup</a> covers the verified Mac route. <a href="worked-example.html">The worked example</a> teaches the new byte-reading operations before you use them here. No Ghidra installation is required.</p>
<p>The end artifacts are your <code>decoder.py</code>, <code>decoder_shifted.py</code>, and a folder of saved predictions, evidence and revisions. This milestone covers these two programs and their supplied listings; it does not teach arbitrary binary analysis or establish Ghidra proficiency.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Stage</th><th scope="col">Your decision</th><th scope="col">Saved evidence</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>Prediction</td><td>What will one native call change, and what result will distinguish two explanations?</td><td>A prediction saved before its output</td></tr>
<tr><td>Layout</td><td>Which bytes hold each field, and how does the pointer reach those bytes?</td><td>Paired probes, instruction trace, first decoder and repairs</td></tr>
<tr><td>Transfer</td><td>Which parts of the old decoder still fit the reordered record?</td><td>A new prediction and a separate decoder</td></tr>
<tr><td>Handoff</td><td>Can you predict a new case and resume without losing earlier attempts?</td><td>Fresh prediction, result, limitations and export</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<h2 id="1-prepare-a-record-before-revealing-results">1. Prepare a record before revealing results</h2>
<p>Complete <a href="setup.html">setup.md</a>, then <a href="worked-example.html">worked-example.md</a>. Keep the bundle folder open in your terminal. All commands below run there. Keep your private <code>work/</code> folder outside a source checkout or public upload.</p>
<p>Open <code>response.json</code> in a text editor. It is a worksheet, not an answer key. <code>claim</code> is your current explanation; <code>reason</code> is its evidence; <code>alternative</code> is a competing explanation. <code>probe</code> holds an experiment&#x27;s arguments and predicted result. Use <code>observations</code>, <code>layout</code> and <code>static_evidence</code> for later results. <code>revision</code> records what changed and why. Keep <code>question_version</code> unchanged.</p>
<p>To save any attempt, edit the response, check its JSON syntax, then run the relevant record command. JSON uses double quotes, has no comments, and does not allow a comma after the final field.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 -m json.tool response.json
python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m02 --stage prediction --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none
</code></pre>
<p>The first command displays the parsed response. The second prints the path of a <strong>new</strong> record. An unsuccessful save says <code>Not saved</code>; repair the named problem before revealing the result. Editing <code>response.json</code> later does not change a saved record. The recorder captures the question, this lesson, both worked examples, the manifest, your response and declared assistance. It preserves work; it does not grade reasoning.</p>
<p>The command examples use <code>none</code> for a first attempt without optional help. After checker feedback, use <code>checker</code> if that is your only help for the revision. For baseline hints use <code>hint-1</code>, <code>hint-2</code> or <code>hint-3</code>; for changed-layout hints use <code>transfer-hint-1</code>, <code>transfer-hint-2</code> or <code>transfer-hint-3</code>. Record the highest level read for the current task. Use <code>solution</code> after reading a worked answer or the checker implementation. Every assisted save requires nonempty <code>assistance_details</code>: name the hint files/levels, the checker cases and what they revealed, or the solution material used. Include both hint files if applicable and replace the example&#x27;s flag accordingly. The byte and temperature examples are normal lesson teaching, not parcel solutions. Preserve the first attempt before help; assistance does not prevent continuing. The recorder checks that details are present, not that the disclosure is truthful or complete.</p>
<p>Run <code>check_decoder.py</code> as a tool after saving your own layout and decoder. Its source contains a native-probe inference procedure. Failure messages can print valid bytes beside expected fields; one run with a decoder that raises on valid records can reveal the complete byte layout without opening the checker source. Reading that implementation can also guide the solution even though it contains no table of the two layouts. Keep it closed until your first attempts are saved; record <code>solution</code> if you inspect it, and preserve checker feedback used in later repairs. This local bundle manages spoilers; it cannot enforce an answer-hidden examination.</p>
<h2 id="2-predict-one-native-update">2. Predict one native update</h2>
<p>The command shape is <code>./parcel KIND UNITS CREDIT DELTA</code>. The four inputs are decimal integers: kind 0–255, units 0–65535, credit −1000000–1000000, and delta −10000–10000. An optional leading <code>+</code> or <code>-</code> is allowed; fractions, extra text and missing arguments are rejected. A valid call prints one JSON object with <code>before</code> and <code>after</code> hex strings and an integer <code>total</code>. These are snapshots of the same record around one call, not instructions to execute.</p>
<p>Use kind <strong>7</strong>, units <strong>513</strong>, credit <strong>−300</strong>, delta <strong>12</strong> for the first case. Before running it, write the expected field values before and after the call and your predicted total. Propose two explanations: for example, does the total use a field before its update or after it? Say what result would reject your alternative. If you cannot yet predict the exact hex, predict field values and which bytes might change; mark unknown offsets as unknown.</p>
<p>Save this as a new <code>prediction</code> record with the command in section 1. Only after the save succeeds, run:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">./parcel 7 513 -300 12
</code></pre>
<p>Put its actual output in <code>observations</code> without replacing your prediction. Compare the observed total and byte changes with your own expected result. A correct total alone does not identify a field layout: several arrangements can hold the same numbers. Save your comparison as another <code>prediction</code> record. The byte procedure below resolves that uncertainty.</p>
<h2 id="3-separate-field-evidence-from-padding">3. Separate field evidence from padding</h2>
<p>An <strong>offset</strong> counts bytes from the start of this record, beginning at zero. Each pair of hex digits is one byte; <code>01 02</code> occupies two bytes even though four characters are printed. Add spaces between pairs in your notes and number the bytes. On this target, multi-byte integer fields use little-endian order, as in the worked example.</p>
<p>Compare two calls that change one input. That input&#x27;s bytes can move while unrelated fields remain fixed. A value crossing 255 to 256 is useful because it changes from <code>ff 00</code> to <code>00 01</code> in a two-byte little-endian field; a one-byte-only guess will fail. Negative values help distinguish signed interpretation from an unsigned reading of the same bits. One pair is evidence, not a proof of width: the listing and further cases must agree.</p>
<p>Write the expected differences for these paired probes in <code>response.json</code> and save a new <code>prediction</code> record with the command from section 1 before running them. Run each row&#x27;s first and second command separately. Preserve the raw outputs in <code>observations</code> and record which offsets changed.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Purpose</th><th scope="col">First command</th><th scope="col">Second command</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>Isolate kind with ordinary values</td><td><code>./parcel 7 513 -300 12</code></td><td><code>./parcel 8 513 -300 12</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Distinguish kind&#x27;s signed interpretation</td><td><code>./parcel 127 513 -300 12</code></td><td><code>./parcel 128 513 -300 12</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Cross a low-byte boundary in units</td><td><code>./parcel 7 255 -300 12</code></td><td><code>./parcel 7 256 -300 12</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Cross a low-byte boundary in credit</td><td><code>./parcel 7 513 255 0</code></td><td><code>./parcel 7 513 256 0</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Compare negative and zero credit</td><td><code>./parcel 7 513 -1 0</code></td><td><code>./parcel 7 513 0 0</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Isolate the effect of delta</td><td><code>./parcel 7 513 -1 0</code></td><td><code>./parcel 7 513 -1 1</code></td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>Some bytes may stay unchanged in every probe. A native record can contain <strong>padding</strong>: space between or after fields so that fields meet the compiler&#x27;s alignment rules. Alignment places a field at a suitable byte boundary for its type. These programs zero the whole record before assigning fields, so their padding starts at zero. That is a property of these programs, not a general rule for C records. Do not invent a field for every zero byte or reject other padding values in your decoder.</p>
<p>The kind boundary separates interpretation from width. The CLI accepts the positive value 128; its one-byte pattern is <code>80</code>. A signed one-byte decode would call that −128 and disagree with the supplied input contract. The byte itself has no signedness label, and <code>strb</code> alone cannot prove a signed or unsigned C declaration. Cite the accepted positive input as evidence for this decoder&#x27;s unsigned interpretation.</p>
<p>In <code>layout</code>, propose each field&#x27;s offset, width in bytes and signedness, and list the remaining padding offsets. In <code>reason</code>, explain what the paired observations support and what they leave uncertain. Save a <code>layout</code> record now, even if a hypothesis remains incomplete:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m02 --stage layout --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none
</code></pre>
<h2 id="4-follow-the-pointer-through-the-listing">4. Follow the pointer through the listing</h2>
<p>Open <code>parcel.asm</code> in your editor. A <strong>pointer</strong> is an address of data. The <strong>caller</strong> invokes a function; the <strong>callee</strong> is the invoked function. Here <code>process_parcel</code> calls <code>adjust_credit</code>, then <code>score_parcel</code>. The supplied calling convention puts the record pointer in <code>x0</code>, delta in <code>w1</code>, and an integer result in <code>w0</code>. A calling convention is the agreement about where arguments and results go. The earlier <code>initialize_parcel</code> call receives the pointer in <code>x0</code>, kind in <code>w1</code>, units in <code>w2</code> and credit in <code>w3</code>; use its stores to check all three field widths.</p>
<p>The listings contain only the four named functions, not <code>main</code>. Treat this setup as supplied information: <code>main</code> zeroes the record, calls <code>initialize_parcel</code>, captures <code>before</code>, then calls <code>process_parcel</code> and captures <code>after</code> and its total. You cannot trace <code>main</code>&#x27;s calls or snapshots in these focused listings. In the shown build, field stores touch only their own bytes; zero padding in its snapshots is an observed build property, not a general C guarantee.</p>
<p><code>x0</code> and <code>w0</code> are 64-bit and 32-bit views of the same register. A <strong>register</strong> is a small CPU working location; its contents can change during a function. Trace what it holds at each instruction instead of assuming <code>x0</code> always remains a pointer. Other numbered <code>x</code> and <code>w</code> registers follow the same size pattern.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Listing notation</th><th scope="col">What to track</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>ldr xN, [...]</code> / <code>str xN, [...]</code></td><td>Load / store an eight-byte value, such as a saved pointer</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ldr wN, [...]</code> / <code>str wN, [...]</code></td><td>Load / store four bytes</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ldrh wN, [...]</code></td><td>Load two bytes as an unsigned value; the rest of the register becomes zero</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>strh wN, [...]</code> / <code>strb wN, [...]</code></td><td>Store the low two bytes / low one byte of the register</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>[xN, #0xK]</code></td><td>Memory at the address in <code>xN</code> plus the hex displacement <code>K</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>[sp, #0xK]</code></td><td>A location in this function&#x27;s stack storage, not automatically a field in the record</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>add wD, wA, wB</code></td><td>Add two register values and put the result in <code>wD</code></td></tr>
<tr><td><code>bl ... &lt;_name&gt;</code> / <code>ret</code></td><td>Call the named function / return to the caller</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p><code>sp</code> is the stack pointer. The listing saves working values on the <strong>stack</strong>, a memory area used for function calls. Stack setup and restoration keep the calls working; they do not describe the parcel&#x27;s field order. Follow a saved pointer from <code>x0</code> to stack storage, back to a register, and only then to a load or store through that pointer. A four-byte load identifies width; it does not by itself prove whether your Python decoder should interpret the bits as signed.</p>
<p>Work through <a href="call-example.html">one pointer, two stack frames</a> now. It traces a different program completely, then asks you to fill in a new starting state before checking it. Return here for the parcel investigation afterward.</p>
<p>Write four short traces in <code>static_evidence</code>, quoting the relevant instructions and addresses from your own listing:</p>
<ol>
<li><p>In <code>initialize_parcel</code>, follow each incoming value through any stack storage to its store through the record pointer. What offsets and widths do those stores support?</p></li>
<li><p>In <code>process_parcel</code>, where is the original record pointer saved, and how is the same pointer supplied to each call? Where does delta go?</p></li>
<li><p>In <code>adjust_credit</code>, which load, arithmetic instruction and store describe the update? Which address is stack storage and which is within the record?</p></li>
<li><p>In <code>score_parcel</code>, which two loads feed the return value? Compare their widths with your byte evidence. Which field does this calculation leave unused?</p></li>
</ol>
<p>Use the first native case&#x27;s field values in your trace, not just register names. Identify the <code>ret</code> lines in <code>score_parcel</code> and <code>process_parcel</code>, and state the value that <code>w0</code> carries back through each return. You can call the record&#x27;s address <code>P</code>: this route does not print its numeric memory address. Keep that symbolic pointer separate from the numeric field values loaded through it.</p>
<p>Do not claim that a register name or a zero byte proves a type. Combine the native input values, observed bytes, access widths and arithmetic. Resolve your layout proposal and save a new <code>layout</code> record. <a href="hints.html">hints.md</a> gives baseline help in three levels if you need it.</p>
<h2 id="5-implement-and-check-the-baseline-decoder">5. Implement and check the baseline decoder</h2>
<p>Edit <code>decoder.py</code>; keep its function named <code>decode(raw)</code>. A completed decoder takes <code>bytes</code> of exactly <strong>12 bytes</strong> and returns exactly <code>{&#x27;kind&#x27;: int, &#x27;units&#x27;: int, &#x27;credit&#x27;: int}</code>. Return real Python integers, not booleans or strings. Raise <code>ValueError</code> for a non-<code>bytes</code> input or any other length. Accept arbitrary values in padding bytes. The function must use only its argument: do not invoke the target, read files or carry state between calls.</p>
<p>Use the guard, slicing and <code>int.from_bytes</code> procedure from the worked example with your inferred layout. The decoder must cover the full field ranges: unsigned 8-bit kind (0–255), unsigned 16-bit units (0–65535), and signed 32-bit credit (−2147483648–2147483647). The native CLI accepts a smaller credit range to keep its update and total safe. Rejecting a raw record just because its credit is outside the CLI range would violate the decoder contract.</p>
<p>Before checking, save your implementation with your explanation:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 -m py_compile decoder.py
python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m02 --stage layout --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact decoder.py
python3 check_decoder.py decoder.py --target baseline --seed 20261017
</code></pre>
<p><code>py_compile</code> checks syntax and does not call <code>decode</code>. The unchanged starter is deliberately unfinished; the checker must reject it. A completed checker run tests finite public cases, including native before/after snapshots, boundary field values, arbitrary padding and malformed inputs. A passing run establishes agreement on those cases, not universal correctness or a sound instruction trace.</p>
<p>On a failure, copy the actual message into <code>observations</code>. Explain which assumption the case contradicts, edit your code, then save another record before checking again. Use <code>--assistance checker</code> for a revision using only that feedback; include the case and what it revealed in <code>assistance_details</code>. A mutated-padding failure can reveal unused offsets, so that revision is checker-assisted. A syntax/import error is a file problem; a decoded-value mismatch is evidence about your decoder. Keep earlier implementations in their saved records.</p>
<p>If the message instead starts <code>Target evidence check could not complete</code>, the native calibration failed before your decoder was tested. Keep your work and re-extract the original bundle into a new folder; compare its target hashes with <code>manifest.json</code>. Preserve the error. A target refusal is not evidence that your decoding rule is wrong.</p>
<h2 id="6-adapt-to-the-reordered-record">6. Adapt to the reordered record</h2>
<p>Keep <code>decoder.py</code> as your baseline implementation. <code>parcel-shifted</code> exposes the same command and field-value contract, but its record is <strong>8 bytes</strong> long. A change in length is evidence that the byte layout needs investigation; it does not tell you the new field offsets.</p>
<p>Before running <code>parcel-shifted</code>, use <code>transfer_decision</code> to predict which old assumptions may survive and which may fail. In <code>probe</code>, use the same arguments as one saved baseline case so you can separate a layout change from a value change. Predict field values, total and the byte positions you expect. Save the prediction without a decoder artifact:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m02 --stage transfer --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none
./parcel-shifted 7 513 -300 12
</code></pre>
<p>Compare that output with your saved prediction and baseline output. Then make at least one ordinary one-input pair and one boundary pair on <code>parcel-shifted</code>; predict their differences first. Inspect <code>parcel-shifted.asm</code> and update your field table from evidence. Explain which access changed and which call/update relationship stayed the same. <a href="transfer-hints.html">transfer-hints.md</a> is optional help for this stage only.</p>
<p>Edit <code>decoder_shifted.py</code>. Its contract is the same as the baseline decoder except that it requires exactly <strong>8 bytes</strong> and uses the new layout. Save the first implementation before checking it:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m02 --stage transfer --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact decoder_shifted.py
python3 check_decoder.py decoder_shifted.py --target shifted --seed 20261017
</code></pre>
<p>Retain any failure and repair as separate records. Explain why applying the baseline offsets unchanged is wrong, even if one field or the computed total happens to match. The required transfer is the changed layout plus this explanation, not just different numbers in an old test.</p>
<h2 id="7-predict-a-new-case-then-hand-off-your-work">7. Predict a new case, then hand off your work</h2>
<p>Use kind <strong>129</strong>, units <strong>4097</strong>, credit <strong>−65537</strong>, delta <strong>257</strong> for a fresh <code>parcel-shifted</code> case. Before running it, save the expected before/after fields, the total, and the exact hex strings your decoder layout implies in a <code>handoff</code> record. Explain one carry or signed-byte pattern in your predicted bytes. Do not obtain the prediction by calling the target or checker.</p>
<p>The command below uses <code>checker</code> because this stage follows your earlier conformance checks. Describe that prior feedback in <code>assistance_details</code>; use a different flag and details if you used hints or solutions too. A fresh prediction after feedback is useful evidence, but it is not an unaided first attempt.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m02 --stage handoff --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance checker --artifact decoder_shifted.py
./parcel-shifted 129 4097 -65537 257
</code></pre>
<p>Compare the actual output with the saved prediction and explain any difference. Save a second <code>handoff</code> record with the actual result. In that record, state your two supported layouts, pointer evidence, treatment of padding, assistance, and one limitation of the public checks. Someone should be able to distinguish your first guess, observations, first implementation and repairs.</p>
<p>To export, use a new backup folder name if <code>m02-export-01</code> already exists. These commands copy files locally; they upload nothing.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m02
mkdir ../m02-export-01
cp -R work/m02 ../m02-export-01/records
cp response.json decoder.py decoder_shifted.py manifest.json ../m02-export-01/
diff -rq work/m02 ../m02-export-01/records
</code></pre>
<p><code>diff</code> prints nothing when the saved records match byte for byte. Keep the original bundle alongside this backup: its executable, listings and teaching belong to the captured manifest. To resume in the same bundle without altering the first records:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">cp -R ../m02-export-01/records work/m02-resumed
python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m02-resumed
python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m02-resumed --stage handoff --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance checker --artifact decoder_shifted.py
</code></pre>
<p>Use a new <code>m02-resumed</code> name if that folder already exists. Open an earlier copied record and confirm its response, teaching snapshot and code are readable; confirm the new save added a record. If resuming in a fresh copy of the same bundle, restore the backed-up response and decoders first. Keep old records and the old bundle when upgrading: a new manifest must not silently reinterpret an old attempt.</p>
<p>Stop with your artifacts and unanswered questions preserved. Passing the public checks does not certify a first-time human learning outcome, accessibility, arbitrary native targets or the full course.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a rel="prev" href="../learning/m02.html">Previous: Prepare M02</a><a rel="next" href="../learning/m03.html">Next: Prepare M03</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#1-prepare-a-record-before-revealing-results">1. <!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>One pointer, two stack frames · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1.
