Compiled forms and behavior</span><div><a href="../learning/m06.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m06/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>7. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="../learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="../learning/m02.html">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="one-pointer-two-stack-frames">One pointer, two stack frames</h1>
<p>This separate temperature example shows how to trace a call. It does not use the parcel record or reveal its layout. Read the register vocabulary in section 4 of <code>START-HERE.md</code> first.</p>
<p>Memory at address <strong>P</strong> holds the integer <strong>6</strong>. <code>visit_cell</code> receives P in <code>x0</code>, then calls <code>warm_cell</code> with P in <code>x0</code> and the increment <strong>1</strong> in <code>w1</code>. <code>warm_cell</code> updates the integer through P and returns the updated value. P is a symbolic address, not the number 6.</p>
<p>These are actual instructions from the course&#x27;s separately compiled demonstration. You do not need another executable. Addresses label instructions in this build; they are not the data address P.</p>
<h2 id="follow-the-caller-into-the-call">Follow the caller into the call</h2>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-asm">0000000100000494 &lt;_visit_cell&gt;:
100000494: sub sp, sp, #0x20
100000498: stp x29, x30, [sp, #0x10]
10000049c: add x29, sp, #0x10
1000004a0: str x0, [sp, #0x8]
1000004a4: ldr x0, [sp, #0x8]
1000004a8: mov w1, #0x1
1000004ac: bl 0x100000460 &lt;_warm_cell&gt;
1000004b0: ldp x29, x30, [sp, #0x10]
1000004b4: add sp, sp, #0x20
1000004b8: ret
</code></pre>
<p>The first instruction reserves 32 bytes (<code>0x20</code>) of stack storage. Call the resulting stack address <strong>S</strong>. The store at <code>1000004a0</code> copies P to memory at S + 8; it does not copy the integer 6 there. The following load restores that pointer to <code>x0</code>. <code>mov</code> puts 1 in <code>w1</code>. The call at <code>1000004ac</code> therefore passes a pointer and a number, not two numbers describing temperatures.</p>
<p><code>bl</code> also records where execution should resume in <code>x30</code>: here, instruction <code>1000004b0</code>. The caller saved its own incoming <code>x30</code> before making that call. <code>stp</code> and <code>ldp</code> store and load a pair of registers; the saved <code>x29</code> supports this function&#x27;s stack frame. For this trace, follow the pointer and argument first, while checking that the saved registers and stack are restored before returning.</p>
<h2 id="follow-the-callee-s-separate-storage">Follow the callee&#x27;s separate storage</h2>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-asm">0000000100000460 &lt;_warm_cell&gt;:
100000460: sub sp, sp, #0x10
100000464: str x0, [sp, #0x8]
100000468: str w1, [sp, #0x4]
10000046c: ldr x8, [sp, #0x8]
100000470: ldr w8, [x8]
100000474: ldr w9, [sp, #0x4]
100000478: add w8, w8, w9
10000047c: ldr x9, [sp, #0x8]
100000480: str w8, [x9]
100000484: ldr x8, [sp, #0x8]
100000488: ldr w0, [x8]
10000048c: add sp, sp, #0x10
100000490: ret
</code></pre>
<p>The callee reserves another 16 bytes (<code>0x10</code>). Its stack pointer is now <strong>T = S − 16</strong>. Both functions use <code>[sp, #0x8]</code>, but the caller means S + 8 and the callee means T + 8. Those are different memory locations containing copies of the same P. Match addresses and values; matching offset text alone cannot connect two stack slots.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Instruction</th><th scope="col">State after the instruction</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>100000464</code>, <code>100000468</code></td><td>Callee memory at T + 8 holds P; T + 4 holds the increment 1. Memory at P still holds 6.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>10000046c</code></td><td><code>x8</code> holds P, an address.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>100000470</code></td><td><code>w8</code> holds 6, loaded from P. Writing <code>w8</code> replaces the prior pointer in <code>x8</code>; do not keep treating that register as P.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>100000474</code>, <code>100000478</code></td><td><code>w9</code> holds 1; addition makes <code>w8</code> hold 7. Memory at P still holds 6 until the store.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>10000047c</code>, <code>100000480</code></td><td><code>x9</code> reloads P; the four-byte store changes memory at P to 7. The stack copy of P is unchanged.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>100000484</code>, <code>100000488</code></td><td><code>x8</code> reloads P; <code>w0</code> receives 7 from that address.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>10000048c</code>, <code>100000490</code></td><td>The callee restores <code>sp</code> to S and returns to <code>1000004b0</code>, carrying 7 in <code>w0</code>.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>1000004b0</code> through <code>1000004b8</code> in the caller</td><td>The caller restores its saved registers and stack, then returns 7 in <code>w0</code>. It does not perform another temperature update.</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>The demonstration prints <code>temperature=7 return=7</code>. A sound trace connects that output to the store and both returns. Simply listing <code>ldr</code>, <code>add</code> and <code>ret</code> would not explain which memory changed or what returned.</p>
<h2 id="complete-a-different-starting-state">Complete a different starting state</h2>
<p>Now suppose memory at P starts at <strong>4</strong>, with the same call and increment. Before running the check below, write four missing trace entries in your notes: the contents of <code>x8</code> after <code>10000046c</code>, of <code>w8</code> after <code>100000478</code>, of memory at P after <code>100000480</code>, and of <code>w0</code> at each <code>ret</code>. Also explain why the caller and callee&#x27;s <code>[sp, #0x8]</code> slots differ.</p>
<p>Save the notes before checking. The first entry is an address; the remaining entries are integer values. This Python model checks only the arithmetic and returned value, not your explanation of registers or stack frames:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">old, increment = 4, 1
updated = old + increment
print(&quot;stored:&quot;, updated, &quot;callee return:&quot;, updated, &quot;caller return:&quot;, updated)
</code></pre>
<p>If your numbers disagree, locate the addition and store again. If the numbers agree but your pointer or stack explanation is unclear, retrace S, T and P separately. Then return to section 4 of <code>START-HERE.md</code> and apply the same procedure to the parcel listing.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M02)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#follow-the-caller-into-the-call">Follow the caller into the call</a></li><li><a href="#follow-the-callee-s-separate-storage">Follow the callee&#x27;s separate storage</a></li><li><a href="#complete-a-different-starting-state">Complete a different starting state</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. <p>Open this page after saving the three completion answers in <a href="worked-example.html">the worked example</a>. Keep the original record and record this feedback in <code>assistance_details</code>.</p>
<p>The values are reading <strong>512</strong>, drift <strong>−32767</strong> and width <strong>2</strong>. <code>00 02</code> means zero plus two times 256. <code>01 80</code> is unsigned 32769; its top bit is set, so subtracting 65536 gives −32767. The slice <code>[5:7]</code> contains positions 5 and 6 and excludes 7. If an answer differs, identify whether byte order, signed interpretation or slice width caused it before saving a repair.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M02)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. Preserve the first attempt before reading the help that resolves it, and declare the assistance used as the original project instructs.</aside><article><h1 id="optional-baseline-hints">Optional baseline hints</h1>
<p>These hints concern <code>parcel</code> and <code>decoder.py</code>. They do not describe the changed layout. Save your current prediction or implementation before reading more, then record the highest level used as <code>--assistance hint-1</code>, <code>hint-2</code> or <code>hint-3</code>. In <code>assistance_details</code>, name <code>hints.md</code> and that level; the recorder refuses a hint-assisted save without details. A hint-assisted revision remains useful work; it is not an unaided first attempt.</p>
<h2 id="hint-1-change-one-cause">Hint 1 — change one cause</h2>
<p>Start with two calls differing only in kind. Put spaces between hex pairs and number bytes from zero. Compare <code>before</code> with <code>before</code> across the calls, rather than comparing only one call&#x27;s <code>before</code> and <code>after</code>. Repeat for units and credit. A field that does not change during processing still belongs in the decoder.</p>
<p>If you are stuck on values, return to the <code>2c 01</code> example in <a href="worked-example.html">worked-example.md</a>. Work from bytes toward values before writing slices.</p>
<h2 id="hint-2-use-a-boundary-and-the-pointer-path">Hint 2 — use a boundary and the pointer path</h2>
<p>A 255/256 pair carries into a second byte, so it helps reject an undersized field guess. A −1/0 pair exposes the signed pattern. Then use the access widths in <code>parcel.asm</code> to test your proposed sizes. A load through a register containing the record pointer refers to the record; a load through <code>sp</code> refers to stack storage. Trace the pointer rather than copying the first displacement you see.</p>
<p>Compare <code>process_parcel</code> immediately before each <code>bl</code>: what puts the original pointer back in <code>x0</code>? In the callee, follow that pointer until a load or store uses it. Then follow <code>initialize_parcel</code>&#x27;s incoming values to its one-, two- and four-byte stores. Record each link in your own words.</p>
<h2 id="hint-3-assemble-the-decoder-from-evidence">Hint 3 — assemble the decoder from evidence</h2>
<p>Make a table of three fields with offset, width, signedness and supporting observation or instruction. There should be one one-byte unsigned field, one two-byte unsigned field and one four-byte signed field. Mark bytes not covered by these fields as padding; ignore their contents.</p>
<p>Use a guard for <code>bytes</code> and exact record length before any slice. A slice ends just after the field: <code>raw[start:start + width]</code>. Use <code>int.from_bytes</code> with explicit little-endian order and the field&#x27;s signedness. An unchanged unsigned decode of negative credit often produces a huge positive integer; changing offsets cannot repair a signedness error. Test the repaired assumption with a new saved attempt, not by overwriting the old one.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M02)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#hint-1-change-one-cause">Hint 1 — change one cause</a></li><li><a href="#hint-2-use-a-boundary-and-the-pointer-path">Hint 2 — use a boundary and the pointer path</a></li><li><a href="#hint-3-assemble-the-decoder-from-evidence">Hint 3 — assemble the decoder from evidence</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>

<h2 id="verified-scope">Verified scope</h2>
<p>The author route ran on Apple Silicon macOS, Darwin 25.6.0 arm64, with Python <strong>3.14.6</strong>, Apple clang <strong>21.0.0</strong> (<code>clang-2100.1.1.101</code>) and Apple LLVM objdump <strong>21.0.0</strong>. <h2 id="enter-the-extracted-bundle">Enter the extracted bundle</h2>

<p><code>pwd</code> should name your extracted bundle folder. <code>ls</code> should find all twenty files. <h2 id="prepare-files-without-running-an-answer-reveal">Prepare files without running an answer reveal</h2>

<h2 id="hint-1-hold-values-fixed">Hint 1 — hold values fixed</h2>
<p>Run a shifted case with the same arguments as one saved baseline case. Equal field values and total do not imply equal byte positions. Compare record length, then compare the location of each distinctive byte pattern. Write what you can keep and what needs new evidence.</p>
<h2 id="hint-2-revisit-untouched-fields">Hint 2 — revisit untouched fields</h2>
<p>The update can leave fields unchanged even when their locations move. Repeat an ordinary one-input pair to locate those fields, then a boundary pair to check width and byte order. <p>Keep the same three keys, types, byte order and error behavior. Re-derive the offsets and required length from the shifted target. Draw eight numbered byte slots and place each field once, using the probes and access widths as evidence. Leave the remaining slot unassigned and accept any value in it. Keep the new decoder in <code>decoder_shifted.py</code>, then save and check it independently.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M02)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#hint-1-hold-values-fixed">Hint 1 — hold values fixed</a></li><li><a href="#hint-2-revisit-untouched-fields">Hint 2 — revisit untouched fields</a></li><li><a href="#hint-3-separate-the-contract-from-the-layout">Hint 3 — separate the contract from the layout</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>

<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>Worked example — read a seven-byte sensor record · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="../learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="../learning/m02.html">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="worked-example-read-a-seven-byte-sensor-record">Worked example — read a seven-byte sensor record</h1>
<p>A sensor sends seven bytes, but a display needs three integers. You will turn that record into a Python dictionary while keeping byte positions, byte order and signed values distinct. The first example is worked through below. Each later exercise has its own feedback page; open only that exercise&#x27;s feedback after saving its prediction.</p>
<p>This invented wire format is a teaching example, not the native parcel&#x27;s layout. It has a one-byte channel at offset 0, a two-byte unsigned reading at offset 1, two padding bytes at offsets 3–4, and a two-byte signed drift at offset 5. <strong>Unsigned</strong> integers represent zero and positive values; <strong>signed</strong> integers also represent negative values. Padding is unused space that the decoder ignores. A <strong>byte</strong> contains eight binary digits, or bits; two hexadecimal digits represent one byte. Hexadecimal counts 0–9 then a–f, so <code>ff</code> represents 255.</p>
<h2 id="read-positions-before-values">Read positions before values</h2>
<p>An offset counts from zero. A Python slice <code>raw[1:3]</code> takes byte 1 and byte 2; the end position 3 is excluded. That makes the two-byte reading occupy <code>[1:3]</code>, not <code>[1:2]</code>.</p>
<p>Little-endian means the byte with the smallest place value comes first. <code>2c 01</code> represents 44 + 1 × 256 = 300. Reversing those bytes gives 1 + 44 × 256 = 11265. Width and byte order are separate choices: both examples still contain two bytes.</p>
<p>This record&#x27;s bytes are <code>07 2c 01 aa 55 fe ff</code>. Before reading the next section, write the three values you expect in <code>response.json</code>, using an extra field named <code>sensor_prediction</code>. If signed drift is unfamiliar, record it as unknown for now. Use <code>claim</code> to explain which bytes belong to each field. Save before revealing the decoded result:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m02 --stage prediction --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none
</code></pre>
<h2 id="interpret-the-sign-and-decode-the-record">Interpret the sign and decode the record</h2>
<p>Your prediction should use <code>07</code> for channel and <code>2c 01</code> for reading. The padding <code>aa 55</code> belongs to neither value. Drift uses <code>fe ff</code>, with the low byte first.</p>
<p><strong>Two&#x27;s complement</strong> is the signed-integer encoding used here. For two bytes, first read the bits as an unsigned integer. The top bit is the bit with the largest place value; in little-endian order it belongs to the last byte. If the top bit is zero, the signed value is the same. If the top bit is one, subtract 65536, the number of possible two-byte patterns. <code>fe ff</code> is unsigned 65534, so its signed value is 65534 − 65536 = −2. The nearby <code>ff 7f</code> is 32767, while <code>00 80</code> is −32768. One bit pattern can have different values under signed and unsigned interpretation.</p>
<p><code>bytes.fromhex</code> turns readable pairs into Python bytes. <code>int.from_bytes</code> reads a slice with an explicit order and signedness. This complete example checks the type and exact length first, because a short slice can otherwise decode successfully while silently omitting bytes.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">def decode_sensor(raw):
    if not isinstance(raw, bytes) or len(raw) != 7:
        raise ValueError(&quot;sensor record must be bytes of length 7&quot;)
    return {
        &quot;channel&quot;: raw[0],
        &quot;reading&quot;: int.from_bytes(raw[1:3], &quot;little&quot;, signed=False),
        &quot;drift&quot;: int.from_bytes(raw[5:7], &quot;little&quot;, signed=True),
    }

sample = bytes.fromhex(&quot;07 2c 01 aa 55 fe ff&quot;)
print(decode_sensor(sample))
</code></pre>
<p>Save this code as <code>sensor_example.py</code> in the bundle folder and run <code>python3 sensor_example.py</code>. It prints:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-text">{&#x27;channel&#x27;: 7, &#x27;reading&#x27;: 300, &#x27;drift&#x27;: -2}
</code></pre>
<p>Compare that result with <code>sensor_prediction</code>, then add the actual result and your explanation under <code>sensor_observation</code>. Save a new <code>prediction</code> record. The saved original remains your first attempt; the output resolves it without erasing it.</p>
<h2 id="complete-one-case-then-decode-a-new-one">Complete one case, then decode a new one</h2>
<p>First complete these three values without running Python: <code>reading = int.from_bytes(bytes.fromhex(&quot;00 02&quot;), &quot;little&quot;, signed=False)</code>, <code>drift = int.from_bytes(bytes.fromhex(&quot;01 80&quot;), &quot;little&quot;, signed=True)</code>, and the number of bytes in the slice <code>[5:7]</code>. Put your answers in <code>sensor_completion</code>, then save a <code>prediction</code> record with the earlier command.</p>
<p>After saving, add this below the example code and run it. Each comparison prints whether your recorded numeric answer matches the computed value; replace the three <code>None</code> placeholders with your own numbers before running.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">my_reading, my_drift, my_width = None, None, None
reading = int.from_bytes(bytes.fromhex(&quot;00 02&quot;), &quot;little&quot;, signed=False)
drift = int.from_bytes(bytes.fromhex(&quot;01 80&quot;), &quot;little&quot;, signed=True)
width = len(sample[5:7])
print(&quot;completion:&quot;, my_reading == reading, my_drift == drift, my_width == width)
print(&quot;actual:&quot;, reading, drift, width)
</code></pre>
<p>After saving your answers, run the checks and use <a href="completion-feedback.html">the completion feedback</a> to diagnose a difference. Add the result and any repair to your response.</p>
<p>Now independently predict all three decoded fields for <code>09 ff 00 00 00 00 80</code>. Also decide whether <code>09 ff 00 00 00 00</code> should produce a dictionary or an error. Put both decisions and their reasons in <code>sensor_practice</code>, and save before using the following checks:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">practice = bytes.fromhex(&quot;09 ff 00 00 00 00 80&quot;)
print(&quot;practice:&quot;, decode_sensor(practice))
for invalid in (practice[:-1], practice + b&quot;\x00&quot;, &quot;09 ff 00 00 00 00 80&quot;):
    try:
        decode_sensor(invalid)
    except ValueError as error:
        print(type(error).__name__, str(error))
</code></pre>
<p>After saving and running the practice checks, compare with <a href="practice-feedback.html">the practice feedback</a>. Keep the initial answer even if you revise it.</p>
<p>Finally, predict whether replacing padding <code>aa 55</code> with <code>00 ff</code> changes the first dictionary. Save that prediction, then check it with:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">print(&quot;padding ignored:&quot;, decode_sensor(sample) == decode_sensor(bytes.fromhex(&quot;07 2c 01 00 ff fe ff&quot;)))
</code></pre>
<p>After saving and checking your padding prediction, read <a href="padding-feedback.html">the padding feedback</a>. Native programs can contain padding too, but their offsets come from their actual layout. Return to <a href="START-HERE.html">START-HERE.md</a> and infer those offsets from the parcel&#x27;s probes and listing; do not copy the sensor offsets.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M02)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#read-positions-before-values">Read positions before values</a></li><li><a href="#interpret-the-sign-and-decode-the-record">Interpret the sign and decode the record</a></li><li><a href="#complete-one-case-then-decode-a-new-one">Complete one case, then decode a new one</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. <html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>M3 — Read an unfamiliar file · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. <p>You can explain a record across a call from M2. Now infer a bounded file format and build an inspector another person can use without silently accepting missing data. Your outputs are a field map, a robust <code>inspector.py</code>, two saved fresh predictions, an application explanation and an export of your evidence.</p>
<p>Prerequisites: M2&#x27;s offsets, widths, signedness and byte order; Python functions, dictionaries, lists and exceptions; terminal commands. If a term is uncertain, begin at worked-example.md. Plan for several focused sessions; duration has not been tested with first-time learners. Navigation is open and hints are optional.</p>
<h2 id="1-set-up-and-learn-the-method">1. Set up and learn the method</h2>
<p>Follow setup.md, then worked-example.md before the trail investigation. All commands here run <strong>inside the extracted student folder</strong>. <code>trail</code> is the original native executable. A <code>.trail</code> file is data, not a command to execute. <code>response.json</code> is your editable answer; <code>work/m03</code> contains immutable saved copies. The filenames supplied in the archive are already present; never regenerate them over themselves.</p>
<p>The native command is <code>./trail write NEW_FILE TICK DELTA TAG OPAQUE ...</code>, with four decimal integers per entry. Tick is 0–65535, delta −32768–32767, tag 0–255, opaque 0–16777215. These are supplied value domains, not inferred widths or offsets. The last argument is a controllable three-byte marker of <strong>unknown meaning</strong>. Choosing 0 makes comparisons easier; choosing nonzero later tests your assumptions. The writer refuses existing output files. To retry, choose a new filename.</p>
<p>The Python API must return <code>{&#x27;count&#x27;: N, &#x27;entry_size&#x27;: W, &#x27;payload_bytes&#x27;: P, &#x27;entries&#x27;: [...]}</code>. Each entry has exactly <code>tick</code>, <code>delta</code>, <code>tag</code>, and <code>unknown_hex</code>, a lowercase raw hex string for the three unexplained bytes. This output contract supplies names and representations. You must infer their locations, the header length and its size relation. Files contain at most 1024 entries and 8204 bytes. A malformed file must raise ValueError. No recovery or best-effort partial output is requested.</p>
<p>Before <strong>every reveal or probe</strong>, write a prediction in response.json: a nonempty <code>claim</code>, <code>reason</code>, an alternative and what would distinguish it. The notebook copies the current question, teaching, manifest and optional artifacts into a new UUID-named record. It never edits old records.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m03 --stage prediction --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact inspector.py
</code></pre>
<p>After a run, add its actual result in response.json and save again. That edit changes only your scratch response; the earlier record remains. <code>--assistance</code> must describe help already used: none, hint-1, hint-2, hint-3, checker or solution. Every non-none value requires <code>assistance_details</code> naming the help and what it revealed. Use the highest exposure and mention all others. Opening check.py, worker.py or native <code>trail read</code> output can reveal the complete format; classify that as solution. Running the checker is checker assistance, even when its result is green. Native <code>write</code> and a raw hex view are intended investigation tools.</p>
<h2 id="2-make-the-first-comparison">2. Make the first comparison</h2>
<p>Do not open hints or use native <code>read</code> yet. Predict which bytes change if only tick changes. Give an alternative: if tick is one byte, what would happen at 255 → 256? Save first, then generate these new files:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">./trail write probe-a.trail 255 -300 7 0
./trail write probe-b.trail 256 -300 7 0
python3 -c &quot;from pathlib import Path; print(Path(&#x27;probe-a.trail&#x27;).read_bytes().hex(&#x27; &#x27;)); print(Path(&#x27;probe-b.trail&#x27;).read_bytes().hex(&#x27; &#x27;))&quot;
</code></pre>
<p>Read the hex output left to right, numbering the first byte zero. A change in two bytes at a numeric boundary is stronger evidence than “one changed byte means a one-byte field.” Save both outputs and identify offsets that changed. Open feedback.md only for the section you have attempted.</p>
<p>Next choose one-variable pairs for delta −1/0, delta 255/256, and tag 127/128. The positive tag domain crosses its high bit: this distinguishes an unsigned field from interpreting <code>80</code> as −128. Use unused filenames, predict first and retain actual output. Choose a second distinctive tick such as 513 to distinguish little-endian from big-endian. Do not infer the original author&#x27;s C type; infer an interpretation consistent with the supplied domain and observations.</p>
<h2 id="3-find-the-envelope-and-build-incrementally">3. Find the envelope and build incrementally</h2>
<p>Predict what changes between zero, one and two entries; generate each with <code>trail write</code>. With no fields after the filename the file has zero entries. Compare the fixed prefix and the growing suffix. <code>one.trail</code>, <code>markers.trail</code> and <code>empty.trail</code> are prebuilt controls; inspect their raw bytes when useful. Ask whether each header number counts bytes or entries. Test your claim on <strong>both</strong> one and two entries: a mistaken count-as-byte-length can fit the empty case.</p>
<p>Create format-note.md with a table: byte range, proposed meaning, width, byte order/signedness, supporting probe, and competing hypothesis rejected. Mark unexplained bytes explicitly. A sequence of zero bytes is not proof that those bytes may be discarded. Explain how you will handle nonzero values without inventing meaning.</p>
<p>Edit inspector.py in stages: reject too-short input; read the proposed header; cap count; check fixed width; check count × width against declared payload; check total length exactly; only then decode entries. <code>LIMIT</code> is supplied safety policy. Keep <code>inspect_file</code>&#x27;s bounded read. An exact-size check rejects both missing entries and extra trailing data. Before checking, predict how your implementation handles empty, truncated-header, truncated-entry, inconsistent-count and enormous-declaration inputs. Save code and note under stage layout:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m03 --stage layout --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact inspector.py --artifact format-note.md
python3 check.py inspector.py
</code></pre>
<p>The starter deliberately fails with NotImplementedError and exit 2. Completed behavior yields agreement on finite cases. A mismatch names a case and a contract rule, and points to a newly saved feedback folder containing the exact input, expected native result, observed-result summary and original submitted source. Use its printed replay command and save feedback.json plus the relevant input as notebook artifacts before editing. Set <code>--evidence-dir NEW_FOLDER</code> to choose the location; an existing folder is refused. The checker generates fresh native files, mutates bytes and asks native <code>read</code> whether each is valid. It contains no stored layout table, but its code and feedback can expose the answer. It is practice assistance, not a private exam. It cannot grade your inference or prove behavior for every input. See feedback.md for repairs tied to common failures.</p>
<h2 id="4-apply-the-model-to-nonzero-unknown-bytes">4. Apply the model to nonzero unknown bytes</h2>
<p>Before viewing transfer.trail, predict what would break if bytes you called padding were nonzero. Save under transfer. Now inspect the file with your implementation:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 inspector.py transfer.trail
</code></pre>
<p>Compare the output with raw hex. Explain which layout claims survive and whether your implementation retained all three unknown bytes. This practice changes their values and crosses numeric boundaries; it does not establish new semantics for them. Report the bytes without naming them flags, a checksum or padding unless you have evidence for that interpretation.</p>
<p>Generate <strong>two</strong> files from new tuples of your choosing. Before each <code>write</code>, predict the full output dictionary and the total file size from your map. One must be empty or multi-entry, the other must combine a negative delta, a tick over 255 and nonzero opaque bytes. Save separate predictions and actual results; another person must be able to compare them without relying on your memory.</p>
<h2 id="5-deliver-and-resume">5. Deliver and resume</h2>
<p>Run check.py again after repair, label checker assistance, and save the exact final source, note and feedback under handoff. State which claims came from observations, the supplied contract or assistance. Readable errors and preserved unknowns matter as much as plausible happy-path values.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m03
python3 notebook.py export --workspace work/m03 --out exported-m03
python3 notebook.py list --workspace exported-m03
</code></pre>
<p><code>exported-m03</code> must not exist. Its sibling <code>exported-m03-hashes.txt</code> lists SHA256 hashes for verification. Copy your inspector, note and the extracted original student files with your export; records already include attached source and binary snapshots. To resume, use <code>--workspace exported-m03</code> for the next save and keep question_version at this lesson&#x27;s version. Compare old hashes with <code>shasum -a 256 exported-m03/*.json</code>: saving a new record adds one file and does not change old ones.</p>
<p>M4 relies on your validated envelope and field model, then provides a deliberately faulty parser of this same format. A checker pass alone does not establish a sound format explanation; compare your note with the rubric through your reviewer before claiming completion. Keep original records outside a public repository.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a rel="prev" href="../learning/m03.html">Previous: Prepare M03</a><a rel="next" href="../learning/m04.html">Next: Prepare M04</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#1-set-up-and-learn-the-method">1. Follow the original project’s save-before-reveal order. This separate help page is not a secure exam or evidence of mastery.</aside><article><h1 id="investigation-feedback-use-after-your-own-attempt">Investigation feedback — use after your own attempt</h1>
<h2 id="tick-boundary">Tick boundary</h2>
<p>Between 255 and 256 the low byte changes from ff to 00 while the adjacent high byte changes from 00 to 01. If your “one-byte tick” predicts wrap to zero, the second change contradicts it. Find those two bytes in your output; no offset answer is needed to use this rule. A 513 marker separates byte order because its bytes are unequal.</p>
<h2 id="lengths">Lengths</h2>
<p>The invariant prefix is not all one number. A count increases by one per added entry; a byte length increases by a whole entry. Test the proposed header length by subtracting the payload from the total in more than one file. Empty input alone cannot distinguish a zero count from a zero payload size. In an inspector, validate the declarations before a loop. Python slicing accepts an early end, so a loop that decodes slices without a global exact-length check can return invented zeros.</p>
<h2 id="checker-failures">Checker failures</h2>
<p>A negative delta mismatch suggests signedness; a 255/256 mismatch suggests width or byte order. An opaque-byte mutation that rejects an otherwise valid file suggests an unjustified zero requirement. A truncated or changed-header input that returns plausible entries suggests trusting an unvalidated declaration. A trailing-byte input that succeeds suggests you used “at least long enough” where the format requires exact length. Verify the inference with a fresh native probe, save the feedback and your next hypothesis, then patch one rule.</p>
<h2 id="transfer">Transfer</h2>
<p>Nonzero unexplained bytes need preservation, not guessed meaning. Correct output records their hex string. If you intentionally ignore their semantics, say so; “unknown” is a justified result. A passing checker supports tested behavior, while the format-note evidence supports the interpretation. These are separate claims.</p>
<h2 id="valid-decode-contract">Valid-decode contract</h2>
<p><code>VALID-DECODE</code> means the native reader accepts the saved input. Your implementation must return all entries and their complete field values, preserving signed values and uninterpreted bytes. A ValueError on this input is also a mismatch. Compare the saved input with the expected native result in feedback.json. Review the START-HERE section on building/repairing your implementation and preserving valid cases; do not fix this by ignoring entries or returning an empty list.</p>
<h2 id="malformed-input-contract">Malformed-input contract</h2>
<p><code>MALFORMED-REJECTION</code> means the native reader rejects the saved input. Your implementation must raise ValueError rather than returning plausible partial values. Check magic, supported count/entry width, count × width versus declared payload, and exact total size before reading entries. Keep the bounded-file read as well. Review START-HERE&#x27;s envelope or malformed-input procedure; do not weaken a size check to accommodate trailing data.</p>
<p>The checker retains <strong>every</strong> failing input plus a snapshot of the submitted source and native target manifest in a new check-feedback-* folder (or your new --evidence-dir). It prints a replay command and reports expected native results in feedback.json. Those files are checker assistance. Attach feedback.json and the relevant .trail file to a new notebook record, with assistance_details explaining what the feedback revealed, before changing your implementation. Copy the feedback folder with your exported workspace. Its replay requests use the saved bytes or filenames inside that folder. Run the printed command from that folder. If you move the feedback folder, update its cd path; if you also move the original bundle, update the command&#x27;s worker.py path to that bundle. Previous folders and records remain unchanged.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M03)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#tick-boundary">Tick boundary</a></li><li><a href="#lengths">Lengths</a></li><li><a href="#checker-failures">Checker failures</a></li><li><a href="#transfer">Transfer</a></li><li><a href="#valid-decode-contract">Valid-decode contract</a></li><li><a href="#malformed-input-contract">Malformed-input contract</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>

<p>Tested candidate platform: macOS arm64, Python 3.14.6, Apple clang 21.0.0. The delivered native executable is specific to macOS arm64. The author rebuild uses clang; learners need only the delivered binary, Python and a text editor. Linux, Windows, other Python versions and x86 macOS have not been rehearsed for this package. file trail

python3 -m json.tool response.json

A missing-file error usually means the working directory differs; use pwd and ls before changing code. A writer “New output file required” error means choose a fresh filename. A checker target-integrity error means re-extract the original package; do not update its manifest to conceal a changed fixture.</p>

<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>Before trail: a two-reading badge · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="../learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="../learning/m03.html">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="before-trail-a-two-reading-badge">Before trail: a two-reading badge</h1>
<p>Goal: explain why a count, a byte length and an absolute end position are different numbers. Read this short example, then do the practice before opening its feedback. This page teaches a <em>different</em> format; its offsets are not trail offsets.</p>
<p>A byte is an integer from 0 to 255. Hexadecimal writes a byte with two base-16 digits: <code>7f</code> is 127, <code>80</code> is 128, <code>fe</code> is 254. A byte offset counts from zero. A slice <code>raw[2:4]</code> includes offsets 2 and 3, stopping before 4. Its length is two, not four. Multi-byte values need a byte order: little-endian stores the least significant byte first, so <code>01 02</code> means 513, while <code>02 01</code> means 258. <code>signed=True</code> interprets the high bit as part of a two&#x27;s-complement signed number; <code>fe</code> is then −2.</p>
<p>Our badge format begins with <code>42</code> (ASCII B), then a one-byte count, then that many signed one-byte readings. The format accepts at most four readings. The sample <code>42 02 7f fe</code> has a two-byte header and two readings. Its total length is <code>2 + 2 = 4</code>. The second byte means <em>two readings</em>, not offset two or total size two.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Offset</th><th scope="col">Byte</th><th scope="col">Meaning in this declared badge format</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>0</td><td>42</td><td>Signature B</td></tr>
<tr><td>1</td><td>02</td><td>Two readings</td></tr>
<tr><td>2</td><td>7f</td><td>Reading 127</td></tr>
<tr><td>3</td><td>fe</td><td>Reading −2</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>The complete worked implementation is <code>badge.py</code>. Read its five validation lines and run it:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 badge.py
</code></pre>
<p>Expected output: <code>[127, -2]</code>. It first checks that the header exists, then validates the count and exact total length, then reads values. A short slice does <strong>not</strong> raise by itself: <code>int.from_bytes(b&#x27;&#x27;, &#x27;little&#x27;)</code> returns 0. That convenience would conceal a truncated value, so validate the envelope before decoding. An envelope is the header plus the rule relating its declarations to the actual file.</p>
<p>Now edit response.json: set a nonempty <code>claim</code> predicting these three cases and put the reason in <code>reason</code>. Keep question_version unchanged. Save under stage prediction with the command in START-HERE before running this practice block.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">from badge import decode_badge
for sample in [b&#x27;B\x03\x00\x80\x7f&#x27;, b&#x27;B\x02\x00&#x27;, b&#x27;B\x05\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00&#x27;]:
    try:
        print(decode_badge(sample))
    except ValueError as error:
        print(type(error).__name__, str(error))
</code></pre>
<p>Predict both decoded values and error cases. Is the last case complete but forbidden, or incomplete? Put the block in <code>badge_practice.py</code> to run it. Open practice-feedback.md afterward, compare with your saved prediction, and save a new result record. If you guessed the signed reading wrong, contrast <code>80</code> as unsigned 128 with its signed interpretation; do not fix it by deleting high bytes.</p>
<p>For trail you will receive input domains and candidate files, rather than this badge&#x27;s layout. The method transfers: identify repeatable changes, decide a field boundary using a counterexample, then check lengths before trusting values. A printed zero is evidence about a value, not proof of padding.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M03)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>

<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>M4 — Explain and repair a parser failure · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. <p>Your M3 inspector reads the owned trail format. A second implementation now rejects valid files. Diagnose it, make the smallest justified repair, and check that the repaired parser still rejects the malformed cases in your regression set. Deliver the original failure, a minimal valid reproducer, an actual value trace, a patch explanation, regression tests and saved revisions.</p>
<p>Prerequisites: M3&#x27;s validated field map and exact-size rule, Python functions/loops/ValueError, and the terminal workflow. setup.md covers tools. Begin with worked-example.md: it introduces coordinate systems and failure-preserving reduction before you need either. This is local correctness work on an original owned parser. It is not exploit development or testing another party&#x27;s software. Session length has not been measured with first-time learners.</p>
<h2 id="1-preserve-before-trying-to-repair">1. Preserve before trying to repair</h2>
<p>Use the new M4 package directory. It contains the same native format and fixture identities as M3. parser.py is intentionally faulty. Make a copy before any edits:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">cp parser.py parser-original.py
</code></pre>
<p>Create a nonempty prediction in response.json for parser.py on empty.trail, one.trail and markers.trail. Do not run it first. <code>claim</code> and <code>reason</code> should separate what you expect from why; keep question_version. Save using:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m04 --stage prediction --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact parser-original.py
</code></pre>
<p>The notebook captures questions, teaching, manifest, response, assistance and every <code>--artifact</code> into a new record. Use as many artifact flags as needed. It never updates earlier records. Set assistance to hint-1/2/3, checker or solution when used, with nonempty assistance_details. Opening checker source or the author solution is solution assistance. The supplied faulty parser and trace.py are intended diagnosis tools. A successful checker run is still checker assistance.</p>
<p>Run these separately. Exit 2 means this CLI rejected the file; it does not by itself identify the cause. Redirection saves stdout and stderr as ordinary files.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 parser.py empty.trail
python3 parser.py markers.trail &gt; original-output.txt 2&gt; first-failure.txt
python3 parser.py one.trail
</code></pre>
<p>Do not replace first-failure.txt. Copy the outputs into a <strong>new</strong> response and save with parser-original.py, first-failure.txt and markers.trail attached. Note file name, command and exit status. The native reader and your M3 inspector provide controls for validity; predict what each will say, then compare:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">./trail read markers.trail
</code></pre>
<p>This prints the full known layout result. If you have not completed M3, it is an answer reveal for that milestone. If native read rejects an allegedly original fixture, verify its manifest hash and re-extract a fresh package before diagnosing parser.py.</p>
<h2 id="2-reduce-while-preserving-the-failure">2. Reduce while preserving the failure</h2>
<p>An invalid four-byte header can fail too, but at another guard. State your failure predicate before reducing: parser-original.py rejects an otherwise valid, nonempty trail file at the entry-loop bound. The native reader must accept it. Keep the original fixture unchanged.</p>
<p>Generate a smaller valid candidate through the native writer. Repeating entry values is allowed. Choose a new filename for each candidate; start with two entries, then one. One example command is:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">./trail write minimal.trail 513 -300 7 0
python3 parser-original.py minimal.trail &gt; minimal-output.txt 2&gt; minimal-failure.txt
./trail read minimal.trail
</code></pre>
<p>Before each generation, save the predicted failure and explain why it would be the same stage. Record both parser and native results afterward under stage reduce. Use <code>--artifact minimal.trail --artifact minimal-failure.txt</code>. Is zero entries smaller? Try empty.trail and explain whether it still satisfies the failure predicate.</p>
<p>Also save one deliberately invalid candidate by truncating your minimal file. Predict which guard should fail and why it is <strong>not</strong> an equally useful reproducer:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 -c &quot;from pathlib import Path; p=Path(&#x27;minimal.trail&#x27;).read_bytes(); Path(&#x27;truncated.trail&#x27;).write_bytes(p[:-1])&quot;
python3 parser-original.py truncated.trail
</code></pre>
<p>A minimality explanation needs the size lower bound for a valid nonempty file and a zero-entry control. Counting how many candidates you tried does not prove minimality.</p>
<h2 id="3-trace-the-actual-values">3. Trace the actual values</h2>
<p>A trace relates input values to executed operations. “The length is wrong” is too vague: name which length, its origin, its unit and the guard that uses it. Read parser-original.py from the validated envelope to the loop. Predict <code>count</code>, <code>payload</code>, <code>cursor</code>, <code>end</code> and the first proposed next offset. Save before running:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 trace.py parser-original.py minimal.trail &gt; minimal-trace.txt 2&gt; trace-result.txt
python3 trace.py parser-original.py markers.trail &gt; original-trace.txt 2&gt; original-trace-result.txt
</code></pre>
<p>trace.py observes Python&#x27;s actual local variables at the loop guard using <code>sys.settrace</code>. It does not simulate them. It prints <code>index</code>, <code>count</code>, <code>width</code>, <code>payload</code>, <code>cursor</code>, <code>end</code> and the next offset before each guard, and returns 2 on the original ValueError. Its source is included so you can inspect that measurement. Compare predicted and observed values, attach both traces under stage trace, and identify the first guard that contradicts the valid-file control. Trace a multi-entry case too: a repair must explain the changing failure index, not just the one-entry message.</p>
<p>For each relevant number add a unit: entries, payload bytes, or offset from beginning of file. Decide whether the same coordinate system is being compared. Write one competing cause (for example signed decoding or corrupt count) and the observation that rules it out. The optional hints progressively reveal the cause.</p>
<h2 id="4-make-a-narrow-repair-and-write-your-own-regressions">4. Make a narrow repair and write your own regressions</h2>
<p>Before editing parser.py, save the proposed change and predicted results for empty, minimal, original, truncated, nonzero-opaque and trailing-byte cases. Use stage repair and preserve parser-original.py. Change the mistaken expression, leaving independent validation rules intact. Explain why adding “catch any error and return []” would hide a valid-input failure and erase records.</p>
<p>regression.py is an unfinished unittest file. A regression test is an executable claim that protects a previously broken case. Complete its two tests: compare the <strong>whole expected dictionary</strong> for your minimal fixture; use <code>with self.assertRaises(ValueError): ...</code> for malformed bytes. Add empty and original-file controls. The expected minimal output must come from your prediction and field map, not from calling the parser twice. See feedback.md for the test pattern after attempting it. Run:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 regression.py
python3 parser.py minimal.trail
python3 parser.py markers.trail
python3 check.py parser.py
</code></pre>
<p>The delivered tests deliberately fail until you write them. check.py independently uses native read as its oracle for ordinary, random, boundary and mutated files. It runs student code with a timeout in a subprocess; it is not a security sandbox. Do not use it for untrusted code. It distinguishes valid files that must retain all fields from malformed files that must raise ValueError. A reject-everything patch, blanket catch or fixture-specific exception will fail. Checker feedback can reveal expected fields and is assisted practice. Each mismatch names a contract rule and lesson pointer; a new feedback folder retains every exact failing input, expected native result, observed-result summary and original submitted source, with a printed replay command. Use <code>--evidence-dir NEW_FOLDER</code> to choose the location; existing folders are refused. Save feedback.json and the relevant input as notebook artifacts before repair, and mark the next record checker-assisted. It cannot establish the correctness of your explanation.</p>
<h2 id="5-export-a-reproducible-explanation">5. Export a reproducible explanation</h2>
<p>Write report.md with: original command and failure; validity control; reduction sequence including a candidate that failed differently; minimality argument; predicted and actual local-value trace; causal claim; exact changed expression; regression commands and results; remaining uncertainty and assistance. Attach the original parser, repaired parser, tests, minimal bytes, traces and report in a final handoff record. Other people should be able to reconstruct the failure even after parser.py is repaired.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m04
python3 notebook.py export --workspace work/m04 --out exported-m04
python3 notebook.py list --workspace exported-m04
</code></pre>
<p>The export directory must be new; a sibling hashes file identifies every unchanged record. Copy your report, tests and package with the export. Resume by saving a new record into exported-m04. Check old SHA256 hashes with <code>shasum -a 256 exported-m04/*.json</code>. This establishes preservation, not independently learned competence. M5 will reuse the distinction between a region length and its position when interpreting framed process data.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a rel="prev" href="../learning/m04.html">Previous: Prepare M04</a><a rel="next" href="../learning/m05.html">Next: Prepare M05</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#1-preserve-before-trying-to-repair">1. Preserve before trying to repair</a></li><li><a href="#2-reduce-while-preserving-the-failure">2. Reduce while preserving the failure</a></li><li><a href="#3-trace-the-actual-values">3. Trace the actual values</a></li><li><a href="#4-make-a-narrow-repair-and-write-your-own-regressions">4. Follow the original project’s save-before-reveal order. This separate help page is not a secure exam or evidence of mastery.</aside><article><h1 id="repair-feedback-open-after-a-diagnosis-attempt">Repair feedback — open after a diagnosis attempt</h1>
<p>If the native reader accepts a file while parser-original.py rejects it at the entry-loop guard, the mismatch is inside Python&#x27;s handling of a validated input. A corrupted header would fail the earlier envelope check; a negative delta is decoded only after the guard and cannot cause that earlier failure. A multi-entry file&#x27;s later failure index helps distinguish a boundary error from an always-fail entry decoder.</p>
<p>Minimality has a domain: valid, nonempty trail files. A zero-entry file is shorter but does not reproduce this failure. A truncated one-entry file fails its envelope check, so it changes the failure. State the fixed header plus one entry as the size lower bound, and show that your candidate meets it.</p>
<p>For regression.py, one useful pattern is <code>self.assertEqual(parser.inspect_file(&#x27;minimal.trail&#x27;), expected)</code>, with expected written independently from your recorded field map. A malformed test can read those bytes with Path, remove one byte, then call inspect inside <code>with self.assertRaises(ValueError):</code>. Test the complete return value for valid data; merely asserting “did not throw” would miss a parser returning an empty list.</p>
<p>If the checker reports valid-file rejection, rerun your own trace on that case. If malformed files are accepted, inspect which existing validation rule your change bypassed. If the only differences are unknown_hex, do not delete nonzero opaque data. Keep the original failed attempt and explain what changed in your next record.</p>
<h2 id="valid-decode-contract">Valid-decode contract</h2>
<p><code>VALID-DECODE</code> means the native reader accepts the saved input. Your implementation must return all entries and their complete field values, preserving signed values and uninterpreted bytes. A ValueError on this input is also a mismatch. Compare the saved input with the expected native result in feedback.json. Review the START-HERE section on building/repairing your implementation and preserving valid cases; do not fix this by ignoring entries or returning an empty list.</p>
<h2 id="malformed-input-contract">Malformed-input contract</h2>
<p><code>MALFORMED-REJECTION</code> means the native reader rejects the saved input. Your implementation must raise ValueError rather than returning plausible partial values. Check magic, supported count/entry width, count × width versus declared payload, and exact total size before reading entries. Keep the bounded-file read as well. Review START-HERE&#x27;s envelope or malformed-input procedure; do not weaken a size check to accommodate trailing data.</p>
<p>The checker retains <strong>every</strong> failing input plus a snapshot of the submitted source and native target manifest in a new check-feedback-* folder (or your new --evidence-dir). It prints a replay command and reports expected native results in feedback.json. Those files are checker assistance. Attach feedback.json and the relevant .trail file to a new notebook record, with assistance_details explaining what the feedback revealed, before changing your implementation. Copy the feedback folder with your exported workspace. Its replay requests use the saved bytes or filenames inside that folder. Run the printed command from that folder. If you move the feedback folder, update its cd path; if you also move the original bundle, update the command&#x27;s worker.py path to that bundle. Previous folders and records remain unchanged.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M04)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#valid-decode-contract">Valid-decode contract</a></li><li><a href="#malformed-input-contract">Malformed-input contract</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. <p>The windows produce <code>b&#x27;cat&#x27;</code>, <code>ValueError window bounds</code>, and <code>b&#x27;&#x27;</code>. Start 5 plus count 3 gives exclusive end 8. <!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>Before the parser: ends, counts and useful reductions · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. Bytes between processes</span><div><a href="../learning/m05.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m05/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>6. Compiled forms and behavior</span><div><a href="../learning/m06.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m06/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>7. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="../learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="../learning/m04.html">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="before-the-parser-ends-counts-and-useful-reductions">Before the parser: ends, counts and useful reductions</h1>
<p>Goal: distinguish the number of bytes in a region from its position in a file, then reduce a failure without replacing it with a different failure. This example uses a plain byte window and a string predicate, not trail.</p>
<p><code>b&#x27;abcXY&#x27;</code> has five bytes. The region <code>XY</code> starts at offset 3 and contains 2 bytes. Its exclusive end is offset 5: <code>start + count</code>. The slice is <code>raw[3:5]</code>. Using <code>raw[3:2]</code> does not mean “take two bytes”; it yields an empty result. Every number can be correct in one coordinate system and wrong in another.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Quantity</th><th scope="col">Value</th><th scope="col">Measured from</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>start</td><td>3</td><td>Beginning of file</td></tr>
<tr><td>count</td><td>2</td><td>Beginning of region</td></tr>
<tr><td>exclusive end</td><td>5</td><td>Beginning of file</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>Read <code>take_window</code> in window.py. It refuses a negative start/count and a region extending past the available bytes. The guard is checked <strong>before</strong> slicing. Run the worked example:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 window.py
</code></pre>
<p>The first line is <code>b&#x27;XY&#x27;</code>. The remaining lines belong to the reduction example below. Now predict the result and validity of three different windows before running the following practice. Save a prediction with the notebook command from START-HERE.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">from window import take_window
for raw,start,count in [(b&#x27;.....cat&#x27;,5,3),(b&#x27;.....cat&#x27;,5,4),(b&#x27;ab&#x27;,2,0)]:
    try:
        print(take_window(raw,start,count))
    except ValueError as error:
        print(type(error).__name__,str(error))
</code></pre>
<p>Put this in window_practice.py and run it after saving. Open practice-feedback.md afterward. The empty region at the file&#x27;s exclusive end matters; a guard that changes <code>&gt;</code> to <code>&gt;=</code> can reject it incorrectly.</p>
<h2 id="reduce-the-same-failure">Reduce the same failure</h2>
<p>A reproducer is an input and command that makes the observed failure happen again. A minimal reproducer removes irrelevant material while retaining that failure. Minimal always needs a stated rule: shortest text, fewest records, or smallest valid file. It is not enough that “something still goes wrong.”</p>
<p>Suppose the failure predicate is “adjacent A followed by Z.” In window.py, <code>contains_pair</code> tests exactly this. <code>pAZq</code> reproduces it. Remove <code>p</code>: <code>AZq</code> still reproduces. Remove <code>q</code>: <code>AZ</code> still reproduces. Remove either remaining character: <code>A</code> and <code>Z</code> each fail to reproduce. The remaining two-character input is minimal for this predicate because fewer than two characters cannot contain an adjacent pair. The window.py run records True, True, True, False, False. A different exception or different predicate would not establish the same reduction.</p>
<p>For binary files, deleting bytes can break a count or length before the parser reaches the original failure. Prefer an owned writer that regenerates consistent headers as entries are removed. Keep the original bytes and every candidate with its actual result. A structurally minimal <em>valid</em> file is often larger than an invalid fragment that crashes somewhere else.</p>
<p>Practice: save a prediction about reducing <code>ZAQAZB</code>. Which adjacent pair must survive, and why is <code>ZA</code> the wrong two-character result? Run <code>contains_pair</code> yourself and save the result. The answer is in practice-feedback.md.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M04)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#reduce-the-same-failure">Reduce the same failure</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>
