A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="../learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="../learning/m05.html">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html" aria-current="page">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="trace-a-local-request-one-byte-boundary-at-a-time">Trace a local request, one byte boundary at a time</h1>
<p>Your goal is to explain how a sequence of bytes becomes messages across two real processes. You will deliver a timeline, your own incremental decoder, an error/repair history and a changed-request prediction. Basic Python functions, classes, loops, lists and bytes are prerequisites; framing and process observations are introduced in <a href="worked-example.html">worked-example.md</a>. No time limit applies.</p>
<p>Complete <a href="setup.html">setup.md</a> first. All commands below run in the extracted bundle. Keep its source scripts closed until the first decoder attempt is saved: inspecting <code>client.py</code>, <code>service.py</code>, <code>transport.py</code>, <code>protocol.py</code> or <code>check_decoder.py</code> supplies solution assistance. You can use them later, with disclosure. Opening these Markdown lessons is ordinary instruction.</p>
<h2 id="1-preserve-a-prediction-before-each-reveal">1. Preserve a prediction before each reveal</h2>
<p><code>response.json</code> is your worksheet. Edit it with a text editor. A <code>claim</code> says what you think; <code>reason</code> says why; <code>alternative</code> names a competing explanation; <code>prediction</code> holds expected results before running; <code>observations</code> holds actual results later. <code>timeline</code> holds byte intervals and events. Use <code>revision</code> for what changed and <code>limitations</code> for what you cannot establish. Keep the question version. JSON strings and keys use double quotes; arrays use square brackets. Add fields when useful.</p>
<p>Save a new immutable attempt before revealing each exercise answer, trace or checker result:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 -m json.tool response.json
python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m05 --stage prediction --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none
</code></pre>
<p>The first command checks syntax. The second prints <code>Saved new attempt: work/m05/...json</code> with a new ID. Every save captures the original question, teaching, target/source snapshots, manifest, response and declared help. Use <code>--artifact decoder.py</code> to snapshot your code and <code>--evidence runs/first/trace.json</code> to snapshot a trace when it exists. These are copies, so editing the working files does not change old records. The manifest records delivered files; your code snapshot records your own current revision.</p>
<p><code>Not saved/read</code> means the save failed. Read the reason and repair the input before revealing the result. Do not count an unsuccessful save as preserved work. Files and complete records are limited to 2 MiB; non-finite JSON numbers are refused. Split an oversized narrative into smaller new records; old records remain intact. The tool preserves evidence; it does not certify reasoning, chronology outside the recorder, or truthful assistance reporting.</p>
<p>After help, change the flag and add nonempty <code>assistance_details</code> naming the exact help and what it revealed. Use <code>checker</code> for checker/decoder-run feedback; <code>hint-1</code> through <code>hint-3</code> for baseline hints; <code>transfer-hint-1</code> through <code>transfer-hint-3</code> for transfer hints. Use the highest applicable level, and list all other help in details. Use <code>solution</code> for source inspection, a worked author answer, or external help that gives the implementation. The ordinary worked printer example is teaching, not a lab answer. Its optional completion feedback is <code>hint-1</code>. Assistance is allowed; keep the first attempt distinct from assisted revisions.</p>
<p>Now complete the printer worked example, its prediction and its new-boundary completion exercise. Save before its reveal and save your comparison after it. Return here when you can explain why a delivery may finish an old frame and start another.</p>
<h2 id="2-predict-the-real-exchange">2. Predict the real exchange</h2>
<p>The lab uses two child processes. The <strong>client</strong> writes requests through one pipe. The <strong>service</strong> reads them, creates replies and writes through a second pipe back to the client. Each process has separate memory and its own PID. The supervisor <code>run_lab.py</code> starts them and records their observations; it does not replace them with a table of outputs. Both children exit after EOF. No socket or background service remains.</p>
<p>The supplied wire contract is: two unsigned big-endian length bytes, followed by that many printable ASCII bytes (values 32 through 126). Length is 1..64. A frame has no newline or trailing zero byte. For example, decimal length 258 would encode as <code>01 02</code>, but this lab rejects that size because its maximum is 64. All valid lengths here therefore start with <code>00</code>. Do not treat the leading zero as padding: it belongs to the header and must be present. Offsets below count bytes from zero; <code>[0,2)</code> means offsets 0 and 1, with 2 excluded.</p>
<p>Baseline requests are <code>north:7</code>, <code>east:12</code>, <code>west:0</code>; the service prepends <code>ACK </code> to each reply. It writes the first reply frame, then the other two together. The client groups the response into deliveries of <strong>1, 4, 21, 12 bytes</strong>. These are supplied application grouping choices. They do not guarantee how many OS reads or writes happen.</p>
<p>Before running anything, count each reply&#x27;s payload and frame length. Predict which replies each delivery can complete and the pending byte count after it. State an alternative model (“each read is a message” is one), and name an observation that would reject it. Save a <code>prediction</code> with purpose <code>baseline-before-run</code> using section 1. Then run:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 run_lab.py --scenario baseline --out runs/first
python3 view_trace.py runs/first/trace.json
python3 view_trace.py runs/first/trace.json --detail
</code></pre>
<p>The supervisor prints a saved trace path and says both children exited 0. The view prints two distinct PIDs and four delivery intervals: <code>[0,1)</code>, <code>[1,5)</code>, <code>[5,26)</code>, <code>[26,38)</code>. Their bytes must be in order. Actual PIDs and times vary. If the command refuses an existing folder, choose a new run path and retain the old one. If a child fails, inspect <code>runs/first/client.jsonl</code> and <code>service.jsonl</code> in a text editor and save the error; do not interpret partial logs as a complete run. A timeout is a failure, not evidence of network latency.</p>
<p>Save a new prediction-stage observation with your predicted and observed boundaries separated. Retain the raw trace with your next timeline save.</p>
<h2 id="3-build-the-byte-to-event-timeline">3. Build the byte-to-event timeline</h2>
<p>The detailed view shows nanoseconds relative to the first logged event. Each row contains a role, a per-process sequence number and an event:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong><code>write_intent</code></strong> records the bytes a child is about to send and their stream offset. It does not mean the peer has read them.</p></li>
<li><p><strong><code>write_return</code></strong> means the child&#x27;s write loop completed. It is not an exact peer receive time, or proof of a single OS call.</p></li>
<li><p><strong><code>os_read</code></strong> records one actual read&#x27;s requested size, returned bytes and count. Count 0 means EOF; another count does not mark a message boundary.</p></li>
<li><p><strong><code>request</code></strong> means the service parsed a request under its own rules. It does not check your response decoder.</p></li>
<li><p><strong><code>delivery</code></strong> records a prescribed application group assembled by the client. It need not match one OS read, one write or one frame.</p></li>
<li><p><strong><code>send_closed</code></strong> and <strong><code>eof</code></strong> mark the end of one child&#x27;s send or received stream. They do not mark the other direction ending at the same instant.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><code>hex</code> is byte content rendered as hex pairs, not ASCII text yet. <code>count</code> counts bytes, not hex characters. A reply&#x27;s offset zero is distinct from a request&#x27;s offset zero: the pipes are different streams. Start your timeline with the <strong>service-to-client</strong> direction only. Label any later request rows with their direction.</p>
<p>For each delivery, record its interval, header bytes completed, declared payload length, completed reply strings and pending suffix. Use an interval for every complete frame and cite the delivery/sequence that provides its last byte. Then compare the matching service <code>write_intent</code> intervals and client <code>os_read</code> intervals. Find one instance of a split frame and one of two frames completed in a single delivery. Explain whether the actual OS read boundaries in your run match the scripted chunks; either result is valid evidence.</p>
<p>Do not rank causality by adjacent timestamps alone. A peer can log a read between another process&#x27;s write intent and return. Report within-process sequence order and per-pipe byte order first. A timestamp gap includes Python, scheduling, pipe buffering and logging. This exercise does not isolate or benchmark those components.</p>
<p>Save your timeline and its trace:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m05 --stage timeline --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --evidence runs/first/trace.json
</code></pre>
<p>If you needed help, use its actual assistance flag/details instead. A good explanation names the concrete offsets and sequence numbers in your own trace, not just “pipes are streams.”</p>
<h2 id="4-implement-and-repair-your-decoder">4. Implement and repair your decoder</h2>
<p>Edit only your <code>decoder.py</code> initially. A Python class keeps the pending buffer and lifecycle state between method calls. Each new stream gets a new <code>Decoder()</code> object. Implement this interface:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong><code>feed(chunk)</code></strong> accepts <code>bytes</code> of length 0..4096. Return a list of every newly complete payload string in order; preserve unfinished bytes.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Valid frame:</strong> two-byte unsigned big-endian length 1..64, then that many printable ASCII bytes.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Bad type/size, length or payload:</strong> raise <code>ValueError</code>. The decoder is failed and cannot be reused.</p></li>
<li><p><strong><code>finish()</code></strong> signals EOF. Return <code>None</code> if no pending bytes; otherwise raise <code>ValueError</code> and fail. Repeated successful calls return <code>None</code> again.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Calls after closure:</strong> <code>feed</code> after successful finish, or any call after failure, raises <code>ValueError</code>. Make a new instance for a new stream.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>Empty <code>b&quot;&quot;</code> in <code>feed</code> is not EOF. A header announcing 65 bytes must be refused before waiting for 65 bytes. Never silently drop an incomplete suffix. Earlier returned events stay valid; a call that raises returns no events from that call. Your code must not read files, invoke targets, or depend on these particular words or chunk sizes.</p>
<p>Use this ordered plan: validate input/state; append new bytes; wait if the header is incomplete; read and bound the length; wait if the body is incomplete; validate and emit the body; remove only the consumed prefix; repeat for remaining frames. EOF is a separate operation. This is guidance; write the code yourself. If you need help, open one level in <code>hints.md</code>, record it, and try again.</p>
<p>Before checking, save your first code attempt and reasoning. Then run the public checks and the live trace through your decoder:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m05 --stage timeline --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact decoder.py --evidence runs/first/trace.json
python3 check_decoder.py decoder.py &gt; checker-feedback.txt 2&gt;&amp;1
cat checker-feedback.txt
python3 decode_trace.py decoder.py runs/first/trace.json &gt; trace-feedback.txt 2&gt;&amp;1
cat trace-feedback.txt
</code></pre>
<p>The unfinished starter prints <code>Unfinished decoder</code> and exits 2. A behavioral mismatch exits 1, naming a failing chunk/input and expected versus observed result. A load/interface error exits 2. A correct implementation prints a public-check agreement count; it establishes agreement with finite cases, not a proof or a grade for your explanation. <code>decode_trace</code> prints events by delivery and either accepts EOF or names its refusal. After checking a working decoder on baseline, the first two deliveries should emit no messages, the third should complete two, and the fourth the remaining one. Compare with your earlier table, rather than replacing it.</p>
<p>Record checker feedback before repair: put the observed failure and diagnosis in the response and run:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m05 --stage timeline --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance checker --artifact decoder.py --evidence checker-feedback.txt
</code></pre>
<p>Then repair one cause, save the changed code as another new record, and rerun. If your first implementation already passed, keep that result. You may test a <strong>diagnostic negative control</strong>: copy your working code to <code>decoder_mistake.py</code>, deliberately change its byte order to <code>little</code> (or remove its full-frame loop), predict the consequence, save that file as an artifact, and check it. Label the record <code>diagnostic negative control</code> and state the intentional mutation. Its failure tests the checker and your diagnosis; it is not evidence that you repaired your own misconception. Retain the control, explain it, and continue with your unchanged working <code>decoder.py</code>. Never fabricate a learner failure or change an earlier record. The checker contains generated probes from the public protocol and can reveal substantial implementation guidance. Inspecting it requires <code>solution</code> disclosure.</p>
<h2 id="5-predict-a-changed-request-and-delivery-schedule">5. Predict a changed request and delivery schedule</h2>
<p>The transfer run changes only the third request to <strong><code>west:257</code></strong>, and groups replies into <strong>2, 11, 1, 3, 23 bytes</strong>. The same wire format and maximum length apply. Before the run, compute new frame intervals, events per delivery and pending bytes. Predict whether your unchanged decoder should pass, and explain which assumption a one-read/one-message decoder would violate. Save a <code>transfer</code> record with your current decoder before running.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m05 --stage transfer --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance checker --artifact decoder.py
python3 run_lab.py --scenario transfer --out runs/transfer
python3 view_trace.py runs/transfer/trace.json --detail
python3 decode_trace.py decoder.py runs/transfer/trace.json
</code></pre>
<p>Use your actual prior assistance category/details. You should see five deliveries and a 40-byte reply stream, with the new third payload in decoded output. Record observed events and your explanation in a new transfer record with its trace. If it fails, preserve that version before repair; use <code>transfer-hints.md</code> only as needed and label it separately.</p>
<h2 id="6-test-failure-boundaries-and-repeatability">6. Test failure boundaries and repeatability</h2>
<p>Predict each outcome first, then save a <code>handoff</code> record. The first two runs below are valid regroupings. The last four have deliberately invalid response streams; the process transport succeeds, but the decoder must refuse. <code>truncated</code> drops one byte from the last payload; <code>malformed</code> includes a byte outside printable ASCII; <code>zero</code> declares length 0; <code>oversize</code> declares 65 with no body. These do not use a network attack or third-party target.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 run_lab.py --scenario combined --out runs/combined
python3 decode_trace.py decoder.py runs/combined/trace.json
python3 run_lab.py --scenario bytewise --out runs/bytewise
python3 decode_trace.py decoder.py runs/bytewise/trace.json
python3 run_lab.py --scenario truncated --out runs/truncated
python3 decode_trace.py decoder.py runs/truncated/trace.json
python3 run_lab.py --scenario malformed --out runs/malformed
python3 decode_trace.py decoder.py runs/malformed/trace.json
python3 run_lab.py --scenario zero --out runs/zero
python3 decode_trace.py decoder.py runs/zero/trace.json
python3 run_lab.py --scenario oversize --out runs/oversize
python3 decode_trace.py decoder.py runs/oversize/trace.json
</code></pre>
<p>Valid regroupings should produce the same three reply strings in order. Truncated EOF must exit 1 after reporting its incomplete suffix; earlier completed frames can already have been emitted. The other invalid streams must exit 1 with <code>ValueError</code> rather than a traceback or success. Preserve feedback and identify whether refusal happened while feeding or at EOF. A script that rejects everything is wrong: it must still accept the valid controls.</p>
<p>Repeat the baseline twice with new run paths:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 run_lab.py --scenario baseline --out runs/repeat-a
python3 run_lab.py --scenario baseline --out runs/repeat-b
python3 - &lt;&lt;&#x27;PY&#x27;
import json
from pathlib import Path

def chunks(name):
    trace = json.loads(Path(&quot;runs&quot;, name, &quot;trace.json&quot;).read_text())
    return [row[&quot;hex&quot;] for row in trace[&quot;events&quot;]
            if row[&quot;role&quot;] == &quot;client&quot; and row[&quot;event&quot;] == &quot;delivery&quot;]

print(&quot;Repeated delivery bytes equal:&quot;, chunks(&quot;first&quot;) == chunks(&quot;repeat-a&quot;) == chunks(&quot;repeat-b&quot;))
PY
</code></pre>
<p>Expected <code>True</code> for the supplied baseline schedule. Also inspect repeated detailed traces and compare OS read counts and observed time gaps. They may or may not differ in this small sample. State only what your runs show; do not claim OS scheduling, PIDs, raw reads or timings repeat deterministically. Record at least one measured gap with its endpoints and this limitation. Three runs cannot establish a latency distribution.</p>
<p>For a final fresh prediction, choose <code>single</code>, which sends only the first request. Predict its complete frame and EOF behavior, save first, then run:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 run_lab.py --scenario single --out runs/single
python3 decode_trace.py decoder.py runs/single/trace.json
</code></pre>
<p>Save the result and its trace. Your handoff explains why the same decoder handled bytewise, combined and changed-request streams, and cites the invalid controls as well as passes.</p>
<h2 id="7-export-and-resume-without-rewriting-history">7. Export and resume without rewriting history</h2>
<p>Write a final response describing your supported behavior, a concrete timeline claim, a repair, assistance and limits. Save a handoff record with your decoder and selected trace, then list the records:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m05 --stage handoff --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance checker --artifact decoder.py --evidence runs/single/trace.json
python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m05
</code></pre>
<p>Use <code>solution</code> if you inspected implementation sources or author answers. Keep the entire extracted folder private; saved records include the original source/question/teaching and your code. Export to a new sibling directory, retaining every earlier file:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 - &lt;&lt;&#x27;PY&#x27;
import hashlib, json, shutil
from pathlib import Path
root = Path.cwd()
hashes = {p.name: hashlib.sha256(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest() for p in (root / &quot;work/m05&quot;).glob(&quot;*.json&quot;)}
(root / &quot;record-hashes.json&quot;).write_text(json.dumps(hashes, indent=2) + &quot;\n&quot;)
shutil.copytree(root, root.parent / &quot;m05-export&quot;)
print(&quot;Copied to&quot;, root.parent / &quot;m05-export&quot;)
PY
cd ../m05-export
python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m05
</code></pre>
<p>If <code>m05-export</code> already exists, <code>copytree</code> refuses; choose a new sibling name and use that same name in <code>cd</code>. Nothing is overwritten. In the copied folder, verify earlier record bytes:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 - &lt;&lt;&#x27;PY&#x27;
import hashlib, json
from pathlib import Path

assert hashes, &quot;No saved records to verify&quot;
for name, expected in hashes.items():
    assert hashlib.sha256((Path(&quot;work/m05&quot;) / name).read_bytes()).hexdigest() == expected, name
print(&quot;Earlier records unchanged:&quot;, len(hashes))
PY
</code></pre>
<p>Edit the copied <code>response.json</code> to explain the resume, then run the handoff save again with the same selected trace and current help category. It must create one additional record, leaving old records untouched. Share only the evidence you intend to share; the packet and local records do not publish themselves. A passing checker plus author rehearsal cannot establish independent human learning, accessibility or readiness to analyze arbitrary software.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a rel="prev" href="../learning/m05.html">Previous: Prepare M05</a><a rel="next" href="../learning/m06.html">Next: Prepare M06</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#1-preserve-a-prediction-before-each-reveal">1. <p>For the changed example, delivery 1 emits <code>[]</code>, with pending <code>02</code>. Delivery 2 emits <code>[&#x27;up&#x27;]</code>, with pending <code>0373</code>. Delivery 3 emits <code>[&#x27;sun&#x27;]</code>, with no pending bytes. Byte <code>03</code> in delivery 2 is the next length, not part of <code>up</code>: removing the first complete frame leaves the next frame&#x27;s partial bytes.</p>
<p>If you emitted <code>sun</code> in delivery 2, count its promised three letters: only <code>s</code> has arrived. If you lost <code>03</code>, check whether you cleared the whole buffer after <code>up</code> instead of removing exactly the consumed prefix. If you treated each delivery as a word, the header bytes and the split <code>up</code> contradict that model.</p>
<p>Record this file as <code>hint-1</code> assistance with details. Retry mentally on <code>01 61 01 62</code> delivered as <code>01 61 01</code>, then <code>62</code>: after the first delivery you should have one completed word and one pending length. Check your answer using the same printer loop, save it separately, and explain the consumed prefix. These checks teach the one-byte example; you still own the real decoder&#x27;s two-byte state and refusal rules.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M05)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. <p>Record the highest level read as <code>hint-1</code>, <code>hint-2</code> or <code>hint-3</code> and name this file in <code>assistance_details</code>. Completion-example feedback also uses <code>hint-1</code>; name both files if you used both. Save earlier attempts before help. These hints are not a substitute for your timeline.</p>
<h2 id="level-1-identify-the-boundary">Level 1: identify the boundary</h2>
<p>Number the response bytes from zero. Draw one row per delivery: incoming interval, old pending bytes, completed payloads, new pending bytes. Decode a length only when both header bytes exist. A complete header without its payload emits nothing. Start from the different printer example if this still feels unclear.</p>
<h2 id="level-2-preserve-the-suffix">Level 2: preserve the suffix</h2>
<p>After removing one complete frame, check whether at least two bytes remain for another header. Do not return after the first message. Do not clear the entire buffer. <code>int.from_bytes(two_bytes, &quot;big&quot;)</code> is the supplied length operation. Check the 1..64 bound before waiting for its payload.</p>
<h2 id="level-3-track-lifecycle">Level 3: track lifecycle</h2>
<p>Keep pending bytes and an open/failed/finished state in the instance. Validate chunk type and size before adding it. A header defines exactly how many payload bytes belong to this frame; check every completed payload byte is between 32 and 126. EOF with pending bytes is an error, not a successful shorter message. Mark failures so the caller must make a new decoder. Test an empty chunk separately from EOF.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M05)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#level-1-identify-the-boundary">Level 1: identify the boundary</a></li><li><a href="#level-2-preserve-the-suffix">Level 2: preserve the suffix</a></li><li><a href="#level-3-track-lifecycle">Level 3: track lifecycle</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. <p>Opening this page makes the current case assisted practice. Keep the earlier prediction unchanged. A later claim of independent transfer needs another case whose guidance and answer you have not seen.</p>

<h2 id="level-1">Level 1</h2>
<p>The protocol is unchanged; only a request payload and the boundaries used to deliver replies change. An implementation based on declared lengths should not need hard-coded delivery sizes.</p>
<h2 id="level-2">Level 2</h2>
<p>Count printable ASCII characters in the new ACK payload, then include its two header bytes. Compare the sum of reply frame sizes with the delivery sizes. The saved prediction should say which delivery can complete each frame, not just list the final messages.</p>
<h2 id="level-3">Level 3</h2>
<p>After a header-only delivery, preserve both bytes. The next delivery can complete its payload exactly. Later a single header byte arrives, followed by a chunk that completes that header and starts the body. `courses/inside-the-shot/reader/m05/worked-example.html`:

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>A different example: a label printer · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. Native state updates</span><div><a href="../learning/m01.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m01/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>2. Records across calls</span><div><a href="../learning/m02.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m02/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>3. A bounded file format</span><div><a href="../learning/m03.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m03/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>4. Parser failure and repair</span><div><a href="../learning/m04.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m04/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>5. Bytes between processes</span><div><a href="../learning/m05.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>6. Compiled forms and behavior</span><div><a href="../learning/m06.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m06/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>7. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="../learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="../learning/m05.html">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="a-different-example-a-label-printer">A different example: a label printer</h1>
<p>A printer receives labels from a process: one running program with its own memory and operating-system process ID (PID). A <strong>pipe</strong> connects one process&#x27;s output to another&#x27;s input. It carries an ordered stream of bytes, not a queue of Python strings. A <strong>frame</strong> is the protocol&#x27;s rule for finding one message within that stream.</p>
<p>This example uses a <strong>one-byte</strong> length followed by a lowercase word. It is deliberately different from the live lab&#x27;s two-byte length and printable ASCII payloads. Hex <code>03</code> means the integer 3; <code>63 61 74</code> spells <code>cat</code>. The frame <code>03 63 61 74</code> therefore carries one word. No newline is implied.</p>
<p>A writer sends <code>03 63 61 74 02 6f 78</code>, two frames (<code>cat</code>, <code>ox</code>). Suppose the reader receives these deliveries:</p>
<ol>
<li><p><strong>Delivery 1: <code>03 63</code>.</strong> The buffer was empty. The header promises three payload bytes, but only <code>63</code> has arrived. Emit nothing and retain <code>03 63</code>.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Delivery 2: <code>61 74 02</code>.</strong> Add this to the pending <code>03 63</code>. The first frame is now complete: emit <code>cat</code> and remove exactly <code>03 63 61 74</code>. Retain <code>02</code>, the next length header.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Delivery 3: <code>6f 78</code>.</strong> Add this to the pending <code>02</code>. Emit <code>ox</code> and remove its frame; the buffer is now empty.</p></li>
</ol>
<p>A <strong>buffer</strong> stores bytes that arrived before a whole frame was available. An <strong>incremental decoder</strong> accepts a chunk, adds it to the buffer, removes every complete frame, and keeps the unfinished suffix for later. “Incremental” means it can continue from previous calls. It must loop: one delivery can finish several frames. It must also wait: one frame can span several deliveries. The length header itself can be split in the real lab.</p>
<p>An OS <code>read</code> asks for up to a number of bytes. On a pipe it can return fewer without marking the end of a message. Empty bytes from a blocking OS read mean EOF, the end of that stream after writers close. A decoder call with <code>b&quot;&quot;</code> is different: our API treats it as an empty chunk; a separate <code>finish()</code> tells the decoder about EOF. The supervised lab groups OS reads into prescribed delivery sizes so the exercise is repeatable. These groups are observations at the application boundary, not claims about how the OS packetized anything.</p>
<p>This small printer decoder is a worked implementation, not the lab&#x27;s answer. It omits the lab&#x27;s two-byte header, bounds, printable-ASCII checks and lifecycle rules. Copy the block into a new file <code>printer_example.py</code>, then run it. <code>bytearray</code> is a mutable sequence of bytes; <code>del pending[:n]</code> removes its first n bytes; <code>.decode(&quot;ascii&quot;)</code> maps ASCII bytes to a Python string. The loop stops when a complete frame is unavailable.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">pending = bytearray()

def printer_feed(chunk):
    pending.extend(chunk)
    words = []
    while pending:
        length = pending[0]
        if len(pending) &lt; 1 + length:
            break
        words.append(bytes(pending[1:1 + length]).decode(&quot;ascii&quot;))
        del pending[:1 + length]
    return words

for chunk in [bytes.fromhex(&quot;03 63&quot;), bytes.fromhex(&quot;61 74 02&quot;), bytes.fromhex(&quot;6f 78&quot;)]:
    print(printer_feed(chunk), pending.hex())
</code></pre>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 printer_example.py
</code></pre>
<p>Expected lines: <code>[] 0363</code>, then <code>[&#x27;cat&#x27;] 02</code>, then <code>[&#x27;ox&#x27;] </code> (the last buffer is empty). Match each line to the trace before continuing.</p>
<h2 id="complete-a-new-trace-before-feedback">Complete a new trace before feedback</h2>
<p>Use new words and new boundaries: <code>02 75 70 03 73 75 6e</code> carries two labels. Deliveries are <code>02</code>, then <code>75 70 03 73</code>, then <code>75 6e</code>. Without running code, record the output list and pending hex after each delivery. Explain why the middle delivery both completes an old frame and starts a new one. Use <code>purpose: printer-completion-prediction</code> and save a <code>prediction</code> record with the recorder command in START-HERE section 1.</p>
<p>Only after saving, replace the final <code>for</code> line&#x27;s three chunks with those above and run <code>python3 printer_example.py</code> again. Compare your prediction with the result. Open <code>example-feedback.md</code> for the explanation, then save a new assisted observation. The normal worked trace above is teaching; the completion feedback is optional help to disclose as <code>hint-1</code> with its filename.</p>
<h2 id="separate-byte-order-from-time">Separate byte order from time</h2>
<p>A monotonic timestamp is a clock reading whose differences are useful within one host run; it is not a date. Our child processes use <code>time.monotonic_ns()</code>, measured in nanoseconds. That unit does not guarantee nanosecond accuracy. A read observation may be logged before the writer logs its write return: the bytes reached the reader while the writer was waiting to run its next line. So do not infer “the read caused the write” from sorted log lines. Stream offsets (byte positions beginning at zero) and each process&#x27;s own numbered sequence constrain the explanation.</p>
<p>Before the live run, say which evidence would distinguish these claims: “the third delivery completes two messages” and “the third OS read is the third message.” The first refers to complete frames within supplied groups; the second assumes an unsupported boundary. In the investigation you will inspect both logs, not just assert the principle.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M05)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#complete-a-new-trace-before-feedback">Complete a new trace before feedback</a></li><li><a href="#separate-byte-order-from-time">Separate byte order from time</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>

<p>Your goal is to explain the same native calculation in two very different listings. Deliver one Python model, a correspondence map, and a counterexample to an assumption that instruction shape equals source shape. The programs are original local toys. Only macOS ARM64 is tested; <a href="setup.html">setup.md</a> identifies the tools and recovery steps. This milestone is implemented for review, not accepted as evidence of human learning.</p>
<p>You need M1&#x27;s predict/probe/revise routine, M2&#x27;s <code>w0</code> argument/return and stack vocabulary, and Python functions, comparisons and exceptions. M3–5 are not required for these files. If you cannot trace a load, arithmetic instruction and return yet, revisit M1/M2 first. A <strong>behavioral model</strong> predicts outputs from inputs; a <strong>correspondence map</strong> links values with the same role across listings. Neither has to reproduce the author&#x27;s source spelling. This is a terminal/editor investigation; no Ghidra installation is required for the delivered route.</p>
<p>Plan two sittings with a break after P2; there is no timer. Your first useful artifact is a saved prediction. Read only the linked feedback for the current exercise. Navigation remains open.</p>
<h2 id="p0-save-a-prediction">P0 — save a prediction</h2>
<p>For the small fee example, begin with <code>amount + 4</code>. If <code>urgent</code> is nonzero, add 3 more; otherwise keep that amount. Nonzero means any value except zero, including negative values. This rule is supplied so you can predict a result before checking how the two builds compute it. It does not describe the larger <code>quote</code> investigation.</p>
<p>Follow setup, then edit <code>response.json</code> in your editor. Keep it valid JSON: strings use double quotes and there are no trailing commas. Replace the claim/reason; set <code>arguments</code> to <code>[5, 1]</code> (amount 5, urgent 1) and calculate <code>predicted_result</code> using the rule above. Explain your arithmetic and any uncertainty. Save it before running either fee program or opening the next page:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m06 --stage prediction --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none
</code></pre>
<p>Each save creates a new file. Edit the response for the next event; never edit old records. The records contain the actual question and lesson text, target manifest, response, assistance and optional source snapshot. <code>none</code> means no extra help beyond the assigned teaching. Hints, checker output, answer pages, source or another person&#x27;s solution must be disclosed. Use <code>--assistance hint-1</code>, <code>hint-2</code>, <code>hint-3</code>, <code>example-feedback</code>, <code>checker</code> or <code>solution</code>; every assisted response must include a nonempty <code>assistance_details</code> describing exactly what you saw. If several apply, use the strongest and describe all. Copying source or a checker-aided revision cannot become an unaided first attempt.</p>
<h2 id="p1-compare-a-smaller-calculation">P1 — compare a smaller calculation</h2>
<p>Do <a href="worked-example.html">worked-example.md</a>, including its completion and separate practice. Save each answer before opening its feedback. Its function has two inputs and one optional adjustment; the main investigation adds interacting conditions and limits. The worked example solves only its own function.</p>
<h2 id="p2-infer-and-implement-one-model">P2 — infer and implement one model</h2>
<p>The supplied entry facts are: <code>quote-O0</code> and <code>quote-O2</code> are built from the same C source with different optimization settings. Each accepts <code>UNITS COUPON RUSH</code>, all integers in -100..100, and prints one JSON <code>result</code>. <code>O0</code> means no requested optimization; <code>O2</code> requests compiler optimizations. Function arguments enter <code>w0</code>, <code>w1</code>, <code>w2</code> and the result leaves in <code>w0</code>. The omitted CLI wrapper validates/prints; the listing covers only <code>_quote</code>. These are supplied facts, not claims you must infer from an omitted <code>main</code>.</p>
<p>Before running either build, save two competing explanations for what a coupon or rush input might do. Choose a first argument triple and predict its output under both explanations. Use the P0 command with stage <code>prediction</code>. The commands below illustrate the triple <code>8 1 0</code>; replace it with your saved triple in both commands:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">./quote-O0 8 1 0
./quote-O2 8 1 0
</code></pre>
<p>Save a second record with both actual results beside your predictions. Explain which observations agree or disagree with each explanation. Now choose paired probes: change one input while holding the other two fixed. Include all the following pairs, predicting each pair before running it. Enter each row as two separate commands in the form above; do not paste parenthesized tuples into a shell.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Compare argument triples</th><th scope="col">Question it distinguishes</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>-1 0 0</code> / <code>0 0 0</code></td><td>How does a negative unit count behave?</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>7 1 0</code> / <code>8 1 0</code></td><td>Is coupon behavior uniform over units?</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>8 -1 0</code> / <code>8 0 0</code></td><td>Is negative coupon the same as positive?</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>8 0 0</code> / <code>8 1 0</code></td><td>Does a positive coupon matter here?</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>8 0 -1</code> / <code>8 0 1</code></td><td>Does rush depend on sign or nonzero value?</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>23 0 1</code> / <code>24 0 1</code></td><td>Does growth remain linear?</td></tr>

</tbody></table></div>
<p>The last two equal outputs cannot establish which internal value stopped growing. Trace the listing as well. Keep a table with input, prediction, both outputs and the interpretation. Add your own pair when two explanations still fit. At each pair&#x27;s resolution save the result and the rule it supports or contradicts. Distinguish observed finite cases from your generalized rule.</p>
<p>Open <code>quote-O0.asm</code> and <code>quote-O2.asm</code> side by side in your editor. Addresses are hexadecimal identifiers in this build, not timestamps or execution order for skipped branches. Read each instruction&#x27;s value, not just its register name. Use the instruction reference below and the smaller example. Implement <code>model(units, coupon, rush)</code> in <code>model.py</code>: return an actual Python <code>int</code>; reject booleans, non-integers and values outside -100..100 with <code>ValueError</code>. Keep this a pure computation: no native calls, files or stored answers. Save the first code before testing:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m06 --stage model --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact model.py
python3 check_model.py model.py --seed 61
</code></pre>
<p>A stopped check (exit 2) means setup, syntax or an unfinished starter needs attention. A mismatch (exit 1) supplies arguments and both native results: save this as checker assistance before repairing. Change one inferred rule at a time, save each revision with <code>--assistance checker</code> and descriptive details, then rerun. Exit 0 means sampled behavior agrees; it does not approve your explanation. Public probe values, checker source and feedback are visible assistance, not a secure exam. The checker calls the native programs for expected results; it does not contain their authored formula.</p>
<h2 id="p3-defend-the-correspondence">P3 — defend the correspondence</h2>
<p>Complete <code>report.md</code>. For every phase requested in its map give addresses from both listings, a concrete value trace and why the conditions agree. Cover input handling, base arithmetic, optional adjustments, final limit and return. State where a named value disappears or is combined with another. Use <code>8 1 -1</code> for one complete trace; include an out-of-range-for-your-inferred-internal-limit value and a negative input as separate traces. All remain within the CLI&#x27;s -100..100 domain.</p>
<p>Show one register with two different meanings at two addresses. Then state and refute a specific claim about source spelling, register identity or visible branch count. Your evidence must include actual outputs and addresses from both main-task listings. Merely saying “optimization changes things” is not a counterexample. Reuse the lesson&#x27;s reasoning method, not its fee-example answer. Save your report:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m06 --stage comparison --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance checker --artifact report.md

<h2 id="p4-test-a-fresh-claim-and-hand-off">P4 — test a fresh claim and hand off</h2>
<p>After your last feedback, choose a new triple outside the probe table and never previously run. Mix signs/flags or a region where two effects interact. Save its predicted result and a reason with stage <code>handoff</code>, plus <code>--artifact model.py</code>. Only then run both native builds for that triple. python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m06

<p>Keep the whole extracted folder together, including <code>work/m06</code>, <code>report.md</code> and <code>model.py</code>. From its parent folder, copy it to a NEW name for export and again for resume; do not reuse an existing destination. Open a terminal in the resumed folder. Rerun <code>notebook.py list</code>, inspect an old record&#x27;s question/code, then add a new handoff save. Earlier UUID files must retain their hashes; compute <code>shasum -a 256 work/m06/*.json</code> before copying and compare the old filenames after resume. The new record is additional. If a save fails, earlier records remain; fix the new response/path and retry. Do not delete your failure history.</p>
<p>Your handoff contains one model, your report, observations and all original/revised records. Note platform limits, untested cases, help used and uncertainty about original source spelling. A full input-space proof, another compiler/architecture and Ghidra GUI work are outside this route.</p>
<h2 id="instruction-reference-for-these-files">Instruction reference for these files</h2>
<p><code>wN</code> is the low 32 bits of ARM64 register <code>xN</code>; integers here fit without overflow. <code>sp</code> points at a function&#x27;s stack storage. <code>str</code> stores, <code>ldr</code> loads, <code>mov</code> copies/sets, and <code>ret</code> returns. <code>wzr</code> always reads zero. A destination overwrites its previous value. Hex <code>0x28</code> is decimal 40; <code>0xc8</code> is 200.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><code>cmp a,b</code> sets flags from a-b. <code>subs d,a,b</code> also keeps the result in d.</p></li>
<li><p><code>b.lt</code>, <code>b.le</code>, <code>b.gt</code> branch if signed less, less-or-equal, or greater.</p></li>
<li><p><code>cbz a,label</code> branches if a is zero.</p></li>
<li><p><code>tbz a,#31,label</code> branches if bit 31 is zero (nonnegative 32-bit signed input).</p></li>
<li><p><code>csel d,a,b,cond</code> chooses a when the condition holds, otherwise b; no jump.</p></li>
<li><p><code>ccmp a,b,#4,gt</code> compares a-b if previous flags say signed greater; otherwise it sets NZCV to 0100 (zero true, signed greater false). NZCV names the negative, zero, carry and overflow condition flags.</p></li>
<li><p><code>bic d,a,a,asr #31</code> clears a&#x27;s bits wherever its sign-extended sign mask is 1: negative becomes 0, nonnegative stays a.</p></li>
<li><p><code>madd d,a,b,c</code> computes d = a*b+c.</p></li>
<li><p><code>lsl d,a,#1</code> shifts left one bit; here it doubles a without overflow.</p></li>
<li><p><code>lo</code> means unsigned lower; <code>eq</code> means equal. Prove nonnegativity before equating unsigned and signed order.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>Use <a href="setup.html">setup.md</a> for missing files, execution refusal, version mismatch and safe restart. Keep all targets with their own manifest; mixing archives invalidates address evidence.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a rel="prev" href="../learning/m06.html">Previous: Prepare M06</a><a rel="next" href="../learning/m07.html">Next: Prepare M07</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#p0-save-a-prediction">P0 — save a prediction</a></li><li><a href="#p1-compare-a-smaller-calculation">P1 — compare a smaller calculation</a></li><li><a href="#p2-infer-and-implement-one-model">P2 — infer and implement one model</a></li><li><a href="#p3-defend-the-correspondence">P3 — defend the correspondence</a></li><li><a href="#p4-test-a-fresh-claim-and-hand-off">P4 — test a fresh claim and hand off</a></li><li><a href="#instruction-reference-for-these-files">Instruction reference for these files</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. <h2 id="hint-1-follow-a-value">Hint 1 — follow a value</h2>
<p>Mark every write to <code>w8</code> in each listing. At O0 loads bring different stack values into it. At O2 its early value and late value do not have the same role. Trace <code>8 1 -1</code> without assuming a register names a permanent variable. Use entry facts and the instruction reference.</p>
<h2 id="hint-2-combined-conditions">Hint 2 — combined conditions</h2>
<p>At O2, connect <code>cmp w1</code> to <code>ccmp w0</code> and then to <code>csel w10</code>. If the first comparison is not greater, NZCV=0100 makes the final signed-greater test false. If it is greater, the second comparison decides. Try one positive and one nonpositive coupon at the same units. The threshold compares original units, although the multiplier uses a bounded value; determine why those conditions agree in this domain.</p>
<h2 id="hint-3-structure-before-constants">Hint 3 — structure before constants</h2>
<p>Treat the calculation as a bounded unit value, a linear expression with one of two intercepts, an optional doubled-unit addition, and a final upper limit. Read constants from the listings and validate transitions with paired probes. Do not infer the input bound from final saturated outputs alone. The absence of branch instructions in O2 is your opportunity for a concrete counterexample, not evidence that it is unconditional.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M06)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#hint-1-follow-a-value">Hint 1 — follow a value</a></li><li><a href="#hint-2-combined-conditions">Hint 2 — combined conditions</a></li><li><a href="#hint-3-structure-before-constants">Hint 3 — structure before constants</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. <p>Both builds return 1. Nonzero includes negative values: O0&#x27;s <code>cbz</code> does not jump, and O2&#x27;s equality condition is false. O0 computes -6+4=-2, then adds 3 to reach 1. O2 selects increment 7, then computes -6+7=1. If you got -2, you replaced a zero test with a positive test. Try your own different negative urgent value after saving this feedback; explain why the result should stay the same.</p>
<p>The <code>w8</code> values and instruction counts differ, yet the input-to-output rule agrees for this example. This does not prove all possible programs preserve behavior under every toolchain. <!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>A small comparison: optional handling fee · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. Native state updates</span><div><a href="../learning/m01.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m01/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>2. Records across calls</span><div><a href="../learning/m02.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m02/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>3. A bounded file format</span><div><a href="../learning/m03.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m03/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>4. Parser failure and repair</span><div><a href="../learning/m04.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m04/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>5. Bytes between processes</span><div><a href="../learning/m05.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m05/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>6. Compiled forms and behavior</span><div><a href="../learning/m06.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>7. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="../learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m07/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="../learning/m06.html">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="a-small-comparison-optional-handling-fee">A small comparison: optional handling fee</h1>
<p>Goal: follow one value through an unoptimized branch and an optimized selection. Your saved P0 calculation uses the taught fee rule for <code>amount=5, urgent=1</code>. Run the smaller program only now:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">./fee-O0 5 1
./fee-O2 5 1
</code></pre>
<p>Both print <code>{&quot;result&quot;:12}</code>. Put this next to your prediction and save a new <code>prediction</code> record. Recall the rule taught in P0: start with amount+4; if urgent is nonzero, add 3. It does not describe <code>quote</code>. For 5 and 1, base fee is 9, the optional addition is 3 and the result is 12.</p>
<p>Open <code>fee-O0.asm</code> and <code>fee-O2.asm</code>. These are actual compiled listings. The wrapper passes amount in <code>w0</code>, urgent in <code>w1</code>. The focused listing excludes input parsing/printing. At O0 the function reserves 16 bytes on the stack; <code>[sp,#0x4]</code> stores the running fee. At O2 the function needs no stack slot for that value. The compiler combines the two additions into a choice of 4 or 7.</p>
<p>Follow the same four roles in each listing:</p>
<ol>
<li><p><strong>Prepare the fee.</strong> O0&#x27;s <code>0x10000054c add w8,w8,#4</code> makes 9, and <code>0x100000550 str</code> saves it. O2&#x27;s <code>0x1000004ac mov w8,#7</code> and <code>0x1000004b0 mov w9,#4</code> prepare alternative additions, not complete fees.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Test urgent.</strong> O0&#x27;s <code>0x100000558 cbz w8,...</code> skips the extra addition only if urgent is zero. O2&#x27;s <code>0x1000004b4 cmp w1,#0</code> records equality in the flags.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Apply the optional effect.</strong> O0&#x27;s <code>0x100000564 add w8,w8,#3</code> makes 12. O2&#x27;s <code>0x1000004b8 csel w8,w9,w8,eq</code> chooses 7 when unequal.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Return.</strong> O0&#x27;s <code>0x100000570 ldr w0,[sp,#4]</code> reloads 12. O2&#x27;s <code>0x1000004bc add w0,w8,w0</code> computes 7+5=12.</p></li>
</ol>
<p><code>csel</code> means conditional select: when its condition is true choose the first input, otherwise the second. At <code>0x1000004b8</code>, equality means urgent is zero, so it chooses <code>w9=4</code>; otherwise it chooses <code>w8=7</code>. It changes a value without changing the next instruction address. Fewer branches do not imply fewer conditional behaviors.</p>
<p>At O0 <code>w8</code> means amount (5) after <code>0x100000548</code>, base fee (9) after <code>0x10000054c</code>, and urgent (1) after <code>0x100000554</code>. Each write replaces the previous value. At O2, <code>w8</code> at <code>0x1000004ac</code> is an increment (7), not a fee. Matching “w8 to w8” would connect unlike values. Match definitions, uses and conditions instead.</p>
<h2 id="completion-choose-the-increment">Completion: choose the increment</h2>
<p>For <code>(5,0)</code>, fill in these three blanks in <code>response.json</code> before running: which increment does O2 select, which O0 instruction is skipped, and what result leaves <code>w0</code>? Record stage <code>prediction</code>, then run both fee programs with <code>5 0</code>. Open only <a href="completion-feedback.html">completion-feedback.md</a> after saving your answer. Record the observed result and correction as <code>example-feedback</code> with details.</p>
<h2 id="practice-sign-is-not-truth">Practice: sign is not truth</h2>
<p>For <code>(-6,-2)</code>, predict both outputs, the selected increment, and the path at O0&#x27;s <code>cbz</code>. Explain whether negative urgent means “no fee.” Save first, then run both programs with <code>-6 -2</code>. Open <a href="practice-feedback.html">practice-feedback.md</a> afterward. Save its help with <code>example-feedback</code>. This is a practice check, not a held-out assessment.</p>
<h2 id="carry-the-method-into-p2">Carry the method into P2</h2>
<p>For each function: start with entry values, follow writes, record condition outcomes, and track the value that reaches the return. When a compiler combines operations, match the combined expression&#x27;s role instead of requiring one instruction for each source line. Return to P2 in START-HERE. The main function&#x27;s interacting conditions require more evidence than these two fee examples.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M06)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#completion-choose-the-increment">Completion: choose the increment</a></li><li><a href="#practice-sign-is-not-truth">Practice: sign is not truth</a></li><li><a href="#carry-the-method-into-p2">Carry the method into P2</a></li></ul></nav></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>
