Compiled forms and behavior</span><div><a href="../learning/m06.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m06/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>7. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="../learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html" aria-current="page">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="../learning/m07.html">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html" aria-current="page">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="defend-the-reservation-investigation">Defend the reservation investigation</h1>
<p>Goal: deliver a reproducible decoder and replay model with evidence for its claims and limits. The useful result is an explanation another person can challenge and rerun. Neither a checker pass nor a confident sentence supplies that explanation.</p>
<h2 id="1-frame-the-question-before-running-the-target">1. Frame the question before running the target</h2>
<p>Complete setup and the separate count example first. This investigation supplies native programs and listings, not C source. All three programs read the same file family. A valid file starts a state with <code>free</code>, four <code>held</code> slots and <code>delivered</code>; each reported event has <code>accepted</code> plus a state snapshot. <code>final</code> is the published state and <code>committed</code> is a boolean. An event snapshot and the final state may differ. These field names are supplied interface facts, not the answer about when or how they change.</p>
<p>The file is at most 72 bytes with at most 16 entries. Quantities are nonnegative and at most 64 on input; operation codes are 1..4, slot labels 0..4. Some combinations are well-formed but rejected during replay. The native parser validates the complete file before producing any event. The exact layout and operation effects are yours to investigate. No unsafe input or unbounded allocation is needed.</p>
<p>Write two competing hypotheses in <code>response.json</code>. For example, a rejected entry might leave state unchanged, end the sequence, or invalidate the whole sequence. Select two you can distinguish; do not assert one as fact yet. Predict both the state and event count for your first probe. Save before running it:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m07 --stage hypotheses --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none
</code></pre>
<p>Use your actual assistance on every save. Choices are <code>none</code>, <code>hint-1</code> through <code>hint-3</code>, <code>transfer-hint-1</code> through <code>transfer-hint-3</code>, <code>checker</code>, <code>solution</code>, or <code>other</code>. Every non-none choice requires nonempty <code>assistance_details</code>, including material, level and what it revealed. Feedback from earlier checks still counts when making a later prediction. If more than one source helped, select the most revealing category and list all sources in details.</p>
<h2 id="2-make-files-and-choose-discriminating-probes">2. Make files and choose discriminating probes</h2>
<p>Create the initial probe folder and two supplied starting files. These bytes are specimens, not an annotated format. The first has no entries; the second has three. Predict their outputs before invoking the executable. The Python helper writes bytes but does not run the target.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">mkdir probes
python3 write_hex.py --hex &#x27;52 53 4c 31 08 00 00 00&#x27; --out probes/empty.bin
python3 write_hex.py --hex &#x27;52 53 4c 31 08 00 03 00 01 01 03 00 01 02 06 00 03 01 00 00&#x27; --out probes/sequence.bin
python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m07 --stage probes --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --evidence probes/empty.bin --evidence probes/sequence.bin
./reserve probes/empty.bin
./reserve probes/sequence.bin
</code></pre>
<p>Copy exact outputs into your response alongside the saved predictions. Identify the first observation that separates your hypotheses; if neither predicts it, retain both failures and propose another explanation. Do not overwrite the first save. <code>--evidence</code> copies raw bytes and hashes into the new record; a command string alone does not preserve its input.</p>
<p>Now choose at least six additional probes, predicting each before execution. Include one change at a time, an entry repeated against the same slot, equal-to-available versus one-too-large, a zero amount, a changed operation code, and an operation after a rejection. Keep four slots distinct rather than treating all held quantities as one bucket. Add a truncated file and a file with a trailing byte to separate parser refusal from a rejected event. You can write whole hex strings or use the supplied mutation command:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 write_hex.py --source probes/sequence.bin --offset 10 --value 2 --out probes/changed.bin
./reserve probes/changed.bin
</code></pre>
<p>The example mutation is a tool demonstration, not a required discriminating case. Explain what byte 10 means under your hypothesis before using it. Mutation preserves byte length, so a count change may make a file malformed rather than create an extra entry. Use a new filename for every variant. Keep the number of files used by the public checker to 24 or fewer, each ending <code>.bin</code> and at most 73 bytes.</p>
<p>After each small probe group, save <code>--stage probes</code> with each cited <code>--evidence FILE</code>. Record both unexpected outputs and explanations you rejected. A text editor may show binary bytes badly; inspect your file safely with:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 -c &quot;from pathlib import Path; print(Path(&#x27;probes/sequence.bin&#x27;).read_bytes().hex(&#x27; &#x27;))&quot;
</code></pre>
<p>Hex output is reversible; screenshots alone are not a reproducible input. <a href="hints.html">hints.md</a> offers three levels if probe selection stalls. Opening one changes assistance, not your first record.</p>
<h2 id="3-connect-the-bytes-to-the-calls">3. Connect the bytes to the calls</h2>
<p>Open <code>reserve.asm</code>. Only <code>decode_record</code>, <code>apply_record</code> and <code>replay</code> are listed. Supplied setup: main bounds the file, validates its header and all entries, initializes a state, calls replay, and prints the result. Its file operations and validation are not visible in these focused listings; do not invent addresses for main.</p>
<p>On this ARM64 build, replay receives state address in <code>x0</code>, the first entry address in <code>x1</code>, count in <code>w2</code>, mode flag in <code>w3</code> and event-array address in <code>x4</code>. <code>decode_record</code> takes an entry address in <code>x0</code> and returns the small decoded record in the low 32 bits of <code>x0</code> (<code>w0</code>). <code>apply_record</code> receives state address in <code>x0</code>, record bits in the low 32 bits of <code>x1</code>, and returns accepted/rejected as integer <code>w0</code>. This register assignment is supplied calling-convention scaffolding. The main function supplies the mode value, which is absent from the focused listing; the listing shows the conditional mechanism, while probes distinguish the selected policy. Infer which values the instructions implement.</p>
<p><code>xN</code> is a 64-bit register; <code>wN</code> its low 32-bit view. <code>sp</code> is the current stack address; <code>x29</code> is this function&#x27;s frame reference. A callee has its own stack storage, so equal stack offsets in two functions are different locations. A record or state pointer must be followed through saved and reloaded registers; a stack displacement is not a file offset.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Notation in these listings</th><th scope="col">Meaning to use in your trace</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>ldrb</code>, <code>ldrh</code>, <code>ldr wN</code></td><td>Load 1, 2, or 4 bytes; byte/halfword loads zero-extend</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>strb</code>, <code>strh</code>, <code>str wN</code></td><td>Store the low 1, 2, or 4 bytes</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ldr/str xN</code>, <code>ldur/stur xN</code></td><td>Load/store 8 bytes</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ldur/stur wN</code></td><td>Load/store 4 bytes</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>ldr/str qN</code>, <code>ldur/stur qN</code></td><td>Copy 16 bytes; this may be a state copy, not arithmetic</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>orr ..., lsl #8</code></td><td>Shift one value eight bits then combine bits</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>subs</code>, <code>cmp</code>, <code>cbz</code>, <code>cbnz</code></td><td>Compare/subtract, or branch on zero/nonzero</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>b.ls</code>, <code>b.hs</code></td><td>Unsigned lower-or-same / higher-or-same branch</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>bl</code>, <code>ret</code></td><td>Call and return; inspect the returned value and its consumer</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>[xN, xM, lsl #2]</code></td><td>Address xN plus four times xM; explain the selected array element</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p><code>ldur</code> and <code>stur</code> use <strong>unscaled addressing</strong>: the displacement is a number of bytes and can be negative. Their access width still follows the register: <code>w</code> means 4 bytes, <code>x</code> means 8, and <code>q</code> means 16. The mnemonic alone does not tell you the width.</p>
<p>Three more instructions connect the entries to their output positions. These examples use unrelated toy values, not the reservation rule. A destination is the register written; source registers supply values read before that write.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Instruction</th><th scope="col">Operand/value example</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>umull x9, w9, w10</code></td><td>Multiply unsigned 32-bit sources into a 64-bit result. With old <code>w9=12</code>, <code>w10=3</code>, new <code>x9=36</code>. The destination can share a source&#x27;s register number.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>umaddl x9, w8, w9, x11</code></td><td>Multiply the two unsigned 32-bit sources, then add the 64-bit final source. With <code>w8=12</code>, old <code>w9=3</code>, <code>x11=1000</code>, new <code>x9=1036</code>. This can combine an index, stride and base address; identify them from the caller&#x27;s values.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>cset w8, ne</code></td><td>Write 1 when the most recent condition flags say “not equal,” otherwise 0. After comparing 3 with 0 it writes 1; after comparing 0 with 0 it writes 0. It does not branch.</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p><strong>Condition flags</strong> retain information from a flag-setting instruction such as <code>subs</code> or <code>cmp</code>. The zero flag, <strong>Z</strong>, is 1 when that instruction&#x27;s result is zero. <code>eq</code> tests Z=1; <code>ne</code> tests Z=0. <code>cset</code> reads these flags rather than comparing its destination&#x27;s old value. Ordinary loads, stores and moves do not replace these flags. In <code>reserve.asm</code>, locate <code>umull</code> at <code>0x100000c70</code>, <code>umaddl</code> at <code>0x100000c84</code> and <code>cset ... ne</code> at <code>0x100000d18</code>. Follow each one&#x27;s actual inputs and flag producer rather than copying the toy values. The <a href="https://www.scs.stanford.edu/~zyedidia/arm64/umaddl.html">Arm multiply-add description</a> and <a href="https://www.scs.stanford.edu/~zyedidia/arm64/cset_csinc.html">conditional-set description</a> are optional reference material, reproduced from Arm&#x27;s ISA text; the local route does not require opening them.</p>
<p>Build four traces in <code>instruction_evidence</code>, quoting addresses from your actual listing and giving values for one saved probe: (1) entry pointer to decoded fields, including byte order; (2) caller&#x27;s record bits and state pointer reaching apply_record; (3) one acceptance and one rejection path, including whether stores happen; (4) returned acceptance entering the event and influencing final-state publication. Name evidence versus supplied setup explicitly. The listing uses hex constants (<code>#0x40</code> is 64). A branch count or register name alone cannot justify a source type or a state rule.</p>
<p>The key distinction from earlier record work: the bytes on disk, temporary decoded-record bits and in-memory state are three different layouts. Draw them separately. Your file decoder should follow the file layout, not stack offsets used to pass a small record by value.</p>
<h2 id="4-implement-preserve-then-check">4. Implement, preserve, then check</h2>
<p>Edit <code>investigation.py</code>. <code>decode(raw)</code> takes only Python <code>bytes</code>, validates all syntax and returns exactly <code>{&#x27;initial&#x27;: int, &#x27;records&#x27;: [{&#x27;op&#x27;: int, &#x27;slot&#x27;: int, &#x27;amount&#x27;: int}, ...]}</code>. <code>analyze(raw, mode=&#x27;individual&#x27;)</code> returns exactly the native JSON structure with Python booleans. It supports mode <code>individual</code> or <code>atomic</code>; unknown modes and malformed/non-bytes input raise <code>ValueError</code>. Do not invoke the native program, read files or retain state inside either function. The model must explain arbitrary valid input, not memorize your probe results. The unchanged starter raises <code>NotImplementedError</code> deliberately.</p>
<p>Preserve your first implementation and format/state explanation before running the checker:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 -m py_compile investigation.py
python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m07 --stage model --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none --artifact investigation.py --evidence probes/sequence.bin
python3 check_model.py investigation.py --corpus probes --target individual --seed 20261018
</code></pre>
<p>The checker compares your model with the native program on your files and finite seeded mutations, plus malformed/non-bytes controls. It needs at least one accepted and one rejected event across the resulting cases. It tests decoder shape, count and bounds, but cannot independently prove the isolated decoded fields: the binary exposes effects, not field labels. Private assessment checks that too. Its output and source can reveal evidence; retain the first attempt beforehand and label subsequent work accurately. It executes your Python locally and is not a secure exam sandbox.</p>
<p>On failure, save the exact offending bytes, expected/observed result and false assumption. Repair the smallest supported part, add a regression probe, then save <code>--stage repair --assistance checker</code> with details and code before rerunning. A hash mismatch means the target changed: preserve the error and extract the original archive into a new folder. It is not evidence for a different transition rule. If your first implementation passes, challenge a plausible alternative and save its counterexample rather than inventing a repair. <a href="checkpoint.html">checkpoint.md</a> states the evidence needed at this pause.</p>
<h2 id="5-transfer-the-transaction-boundary-and-compiled-form">5. Transfer the transaction boundary and compiled form</h2>
<p>Do not run <code>reserve-atomic</code> until you save a prediction. Create <code>probes/transfer.bin</code> using your inferred layout: choose accepted, rejected, then later accepted entries whose two candidate final states differ. A sequence that returns to its initial state cannot distinguish those policies. Predict every event snapshot and final state under at least two candidate commit policies, and explain which observation separates them. Save code and input:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m07 --stage transfer --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance checker --artifact investigation.py --evidence probes/transfer.bin
./reserve-atomic probes/transfer.bin
</code></pre>
<p>Compare event snapshots with <code>final</code>: a printed intermediate state need not be a committed state. Read <code>reserve-atomic.asm</code>, trace the mode flag and publication branch, then implement or revise <code>mode=&#x27;atomic&#x27;</code>. Include an all-accepted log and an empty log so a model that always resets final state cannot pass. <a href="transfer-hints.html">transfer-hints.md</a> is optional and uses its own assistance labels.</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 check_model.py investigation.py --corpus probes --target atomic --seed 20261018
./reserve-opt probes/sequence.bin
python3 check_model.py investigation.py --corpus probes --target optimized --seed 20261018
</code></pre>
<p><code>reserve-opt</code> is a differently optimized build of the individual mode. For the required static comparison, focus on <strong>decode_record</strong>: compare the byte loads and combination in <code>reserve.asm</code> with <code>ldr w0, [x0]</code> and <code>ret</code> at <code>0x1000007b8</code> and <code>0x1000007bc</code> in <code>reserve-opt.asm</code>. Use a saved entry&#x27;s four bytes to predict the low 32-bit returned pattern in both forms. Then locate the <code>bl ... decode_record</code> and <code>bl ... apply_record</code> calls in each replay listing; those call identities survive although addresses and surrounding instructions change. This is a bounded comparison using taught instructions, not a request to explain the entire optimized function. Retain the full native model checks above. A reduced branch count is not evidence that rejected operations disappeared; identical outputs on finite probes support equivalence on those cases, not universal source identity.</p>
<p>If you explore the optimized <strong>apply_record</strong> listing, these extra forms help. Bit positions count from zero at the least significant bit. A <strong>mask</strong> selects bits using bitwise AND. A vector register is 128 bits that can be viewed as several lanes; <code>.4s</code> means four 32-bit lanes. The names <code>q0</code>, <code>v0</code> and <code>s0</code> are views of SIMD register 0, while general register <code>w0</code> is a different register.</p>
<div class="table-wrap" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Lesson table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Form in the optimized listing</th><th scope="col">Small independent example</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td><code>ubfx w10, w1, #8, #8</code></td><td>Extract eight bits starting at bit 8, place them in the low bits, and zero the rest. <code>w1=0x0000ab34</code> gives <code>w10=0xab</code> (171).</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>tst x1, #0xff00</code></td><td>Compute <code>x1 AND 0xff00</code> for flags only, leaving x1 unchanged. <code>x1=0xab34</code> gives Z=0; <code>x1=0x0034</code> gives Z=1. A following <code>b.ne</code> takes its branch only in the first case.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>cmn w9, #4</code></td><td>Add 4 for flags only, leaving w9 unchanged. With <code>w9=0xfffffffc</code>, the 32-bit sum wraps to zero: Z=1 and the unsigned carry flag C=1. <code>b.hs</code> tests C=1; <code>b.lo</code> tests C=0. Follow the arithmetic and flags instead of treating the mnemonic as a signed source comparison.</td></tr>
<tr><td><code>addv.4s s0, v0</code>, then <code>fmov w11, s0</code></td><td>Add four 32-bit lane values, retaining a 32-bit result in s0, then copy those bits to w11. Lanes <code>[3,5,7,11]</code> produce 26. <code>fmov</code> here moves bits without converting a floating-point number to an integer.</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div>
<p>The <a href="https://www.scs.stanford.edu/~zyedidia/arm64/ubfx_ubfm.html">Arm bitfield</a>, <a href="https://www.scs.stanford.edu/~zyedidia/arm64/tst_ands_log_imm.html">bit-test</a>, <a href="https://www.scs.stanford.edu/~zyedidia/arm64/cmn_adds_addsub_imm.html">CMN</a>, <a href="https://www.scs.stanford.edu/~zyedidia/arm64/addv_advsimd.html">vector-add</a> and <a href="https://www.scs.stanford.edu/~zyedidia/arm64/fmov_float_gen.html">register-move</a> descriptions are optional references. Other optimized instructions are outside the required static trace: name an unknown rather than assuming its meaning. You still test the entire optimized program against your model.</p>
<h2 id="6-fresh-prediction-reproducible-handoff-resume">6. Fresh prediction, reproducible handoff, resume</h2>
<p>Create a new well-formed log that has not appeared in your earlier corpus. It must combine at least three operation families, two slots, an exact boundary and a rejection followed by another operation. Before running either binary, save raw bytes, complete event/final predictions for both modes, and your reasoning in a <code>handoff</code> record. This is fresh-input prediction after assistance, not an unaided first attempt. Only then run, compare and save a second handoff record. If it fails, preserve and explain the revision.</p>
<p>Your final response should name each claim, its discriminating input and native output, and relevant instruction addresses. Include file bounds, unknowns, which conclusions rely on supplied setup, what optimization changed, and what finite tests cannot establish. An invariant should be an equation over a state, not merely “it works”; explain any quantity that leaves or enters the system. Use <a href="checkpoint.html">checkpoint.md</a> to self-review, without treating it as a grade.</p>
<p>Copy a backup using a new name; these commands send nothing to a service:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m07
mkdir ../m07-export-01
cp -R work/m07 ../m07-export-01/records
cp -R probes ../m07-export-01/probes
cp response.json investigation.py manifest.json ../m07-export-01/
diff -rq work/m07 ../m07-export-01/records
cp -R ../m07-export-01/records work/m07-resumed
python3 notebook.py list --workspace work/m07-resumed
python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m07-resumed --stage handoff --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance checker --artifact investigation.py --evidence probes/sequence.bin
</code></pre>
<p>Silent <code>diff</code> means the record copies match byte for byte. Open an earlier copied record and confirm questions, teaching, response, raw evidence and code remain readable; the last command must add a new file. Keep the exact original ZIP and the export together. To resume in a newly extracted copy of the same ZIP, restore the backed-up response, model, probes and records first. Keep older packages/records when changing versions; a new manifest does not reinterpret an old attempt. An independent person still needs to run the package and assess the explanation. Stop with uncertainty preserved rather than declaring the course complete.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a rel="prev" href="../learning/m07.html">Previous: Prepare M07</a><a rel="next" href="../CAPSTONE.html">Next: Capstone</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"><nav class="contents" aria-label="On this page"><h2>On this page</h2><ul><li><a href="#1-frame-the-question-before-running-the-target">1. <p>This is a self-review checkpoint, not an automatic pass. An incomplete investigation can be saved and resumed without a score.</p>
<p>Before the first native run, your saved record should contain two hypotheses and a prediction distinguishing them. Before the first checker run, keep the first decoder/model source and a field table with offsets, widths, signedness, bounds and the observation supporting each row. If a fact was supplied in the lesson, call it supplied rather than discovered.</p>
<p>At the baseline checkpoint, another person should be able to replay at least six selected probes from saved raw bytes and commands. Include ordinary, exact-boundary, one-above, repeated-slot and post-rejection cases, plus malformed length controls. The explanation must distinguish parser refusal from a rejected event. A list of commands without their predictions, outputs and interpretations is incomplete.</p>
<p>At the call checkpoint, explain one decoded entry, its state pointer, one guard and state update, one rejection path and the returned acceptance value. Give actual values and addresses from your listing. Do not confuse stack displacements, the on-disk layout and the state layout. The optimized comparison needs one changed representation and its unchanged behavior, rather than a guessed source reconstruction.</p>
<p>At transfer, retain a prediction before the first atomic run. Explain event versus published state, an all-accepted control and a rejection followed by a later event. If a counterexample changed the model, keep the original source, input, failure, repair and regression result. If none did, explicitly challenge a plausible wrong explanation; do not fabricate a failure.</p>
<p>At handoff, commit one unseen combined case before execution, compare both modes, and export with a manifest and readable old records. Name assistance and limits: finite checks, supplied facts, unknown source details, untested platforms and lack of an independent human trial. Someone else must assess whether the evidence supports the claims; the recorder does not do that judgment.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M07)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. `courses/inside-the-shot/reader/m07/worked-example.html`:

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"><title>A tiny count file, completely worked · Inside the Shot</title><link rel="stylesheet" href="../course.css"><script defer src="../course.js"></script></head><body><a class="skip-link" href="#lesson">Skip to lesson</a><header class="site-header"><a class="brand" href="../../index.html">Inside the Shot<span>Native reverse engineering · seven local projects</span></a><span class="version">Packet 0.6.0</span></header><div class="layout"><aside class="course-sidebar"><details open><summary>Seven-project course</summary><nav aria-label="Course"><a href="../../index.html">Start here</a><ol><li><span>1. Native state updates</span><div><a href="../learning/m01.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m01/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>2. Records across calls</span><div><a href="../learning/m02.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m02/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>3. A bounded file format</span><div><a href="../learning/m03.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m03/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>4. Parser failure and repair</span><div><a href="../learning/m04.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m04/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>5. Bytes between processes</span><div><a href="../learning/m05.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m05/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>6. Compiled forms and behavior</span><div><a href="../learning/m06.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="../m06/START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li><li><span>7. A fresh investigation</span><div><a href="../learning/m07.html">Prepare</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project</a></div></li></ol><p><a href="../SETUP.html">Setup</a> · <a href="../RECOVERY.html">Recovery</a> · <a href="../CAPSTONE.html">Capstone</a> · <a href="../GHIDRA.html">Ghidra</a></p></nav></details></aside><main id="lesson" tabindex="-1"><nav class="project-context" aria-label="This project"><a href="../learning/m07.html">Preparation lesson</a> · <a href="START-HERE.html">Original project procedure</a></nav><article><h1 id="a-tiny-count-file-completely-worked">A tiny count file, completely worked</h1>
<p>Goal: read raw bytes, check a declared length, and turn fixed-size entries into values. This example is a separate invented format, not the reservation program. It teaches I/O vocabulary so capstone time is spent choosing evidence rather than guessing commands.</p>
<p>A <strong>file</strong> is a named byte sequence. Python <code>Path.read_bytes()</code> reads it as <code>bytes</code>; no text decoding occurs. Hex displays one byte as two digits: <code>51</code> is one byte, not decimal 51. An <strong>offset</strong> starts at zero. A <strong>header</strong> describes the following data. A <strong>count</strong> declares how many entries to expect; it does not make missing bytes exist.</p>
<p>The toy count format begins with byte <code>51</code>, then a one-byte count no larger than three, then that many unsigned two-byte little-endian values. Little-endian puts the least significant byte first: <code>01 02</code> is 1 + 2×256 = 513. Reject wrong magic, excessive count, missing bytes and trailing bytes before decoding values. The decoder consumes a complete bounded file; it does not treat one OS read as one record.</p>
<p>Here is the complete example. It prints <code>[1, 513]</code> followed by <code>refused</code>:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-python">from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory


def decode_counts(raw):
    if type(raw) is not bytes or not 2 &lt;= len(raw) &lt;= 8:
        raise ValueError(&#x27;expected 2..8 bytes&#x27;)
    if raw[0] != 0x51 or raw[1] &gt; 3 or len(raw) != 2 + 2 * raw[1]:
        raise ValueError(&#x27;magic, count or length mismatch&#x27;)
    return [int.from_bytes(raw[i:i + 2], &#x27;little&#x27;) for i in range(2, len(raw), 2)]


with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / &#x27;counts.bin&#x27;
    path.write_bytes(bytes.fromhex(&#x27;51 02 01 00 01 02&#x27;))
    print(decode_counts(path.read_bytes()))
    try:
        decode_counts(path.read_bytes()[:-1])
    except ValueError:
        print(&#x27;refused&#x27;)
</code></pre>
<p><code>bytes.fromhex</code> converts printed hex to bytes; spaces only improve readability. <code>[i:i + 2]</code> slices exactly two bytes. <code>range(2, len(raw), 2)</code> steps past the header two bytes at a time. <code>[:-1]</code> removes the final byte. <code>raise ValueError</code> stops on invalid data; the <code>try</code>/<code>except</code> here displays that expected refusal. A temporary directory is automatically cleaned up only for this toy example. Your capstone evidence uses persistent files.</p>
<p>Before opening feedback, edit <code>response.json</code> to add <code>count_practice</code>: predict <code>decode_counts(bytes.fromhex(&#x27;51 02 00 01 80 00&#x27;))</code>, then predict the result after appending <code>00</code>. Explain what would go wrong if the count were trusted without a length check. Save:</p>
<pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Code example"><code class="language-sh">python3 notebook.py record --workspace work/m07 --stage orientation --response response.json --manifest manifest.json --assistance none
</code></pre>
<p>If you used help, replace <code>none</code> with the actual category and fill <code>assistance_details</code>. Now read <a href="practice-feedback.html">practice-feedback.md</a>, compare it with the saved answer, and save a second orientation record describing any revision. Do not delete the first.</p>
<p>For persistent capstone probes, <code>write_hex.py --hex TEXT --out FILE</code> creates a <strong>new</strong> file. Its mutation mode copies an existing file and changes one byte; it refuses to overwrite an existing filename. Use a new name for a revision. This is evidence custody, not security: the file&#x27;s owner could still edit it manually. <code>--offset</code> and <code>--value</code> use decimal integers. The helper can write malformed probes up to 73 bytes, one more than the target&#x27;s maximum, but it does not know or check the reservation format. A helper success only confirms the file was written.</p>
<p>The count example is fully explained. The capstone is deliberately less directed: choose a question, make a prediction, preserve it, then run a probe capable of disproving it. <a href="START-HERE.html">START-HERE.md</a> supplies the process and interface, not the hidden transition rule.</p></article><nav class="previous-next" aria-label="Course sequence"><a href="START-HERE.html">Return to original project procedure (M07)</a></nav></main><aside class="page-sidebar"></aside></div><footer><p>The core course uses local native projects and terminal tools. The recorded shot preview and browser mechanics toy are separate demonstrations and are not required for this route.</p><p>Reader 0.6.0 · Native execution needs the supported computer setup; this page does not execute learner Python.</p></footer></body></html>

`courses/inside-the-shot/tools/CourseEvidence.java`:

```java
// Export inspectable evidence from an original RE Lab target.
// @category RE Lab

import com.google.gson.GsonBuilder;
import ghidra.app.decompiler.DecompInterface;
import ghidra.app.decompiler.DecompileResults;
import ghidra.app.script.GhidraScript;
import ghidra.program.model.listing.Function;
import ghidra.program.model.listing.FunctionIterator;
import ghidra.program.model.listing.Instruction;
import ghidra.program.model.listing.InstructionIterator;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.LinkedHashSet;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Set;

public class CourseEvidence extends GhidraScript {
    @Override
    public void run() throws Exception {
        String[] args = getScriptArgs();
        if (args.length < 2) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Expected output file and one or more function names");
        }
        Path output = Path.of(args[0]);
        if (Files.exists(output)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Refusing to overwrite existing evidence");
        }
        Set<String> requested = new LinkedHashSet<>(Arrays.asList(args).subList(1, args.length));
        Set<String> found = new LinkedHashSet<>();
        ArrayList<Map<String, Object>> functions = new ArrayList<>();
        DecompInterface decompiler = new DecompInterface();
        try {
            if (!decompiler.openProgram(currentProgram)) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Decompiler could not open imported program");
            }
            FunctionIterator iterator = currentProgram.getFunctionManager().getFunctions(true);
            while (iterator.hasNext()) {
                Function function = iterator.next();
                String name = function.getName();
                String plain = name.startsWith("_") ? name.substring(1) : name;
                if (!requested.contains(name) && !requested.contains(plain)) {
                    continue;
                }
                found.add(requested.contains(name) ? name : plain);
                DecompileResults result = decompiler.decompileFunction(function, 30, monitor);
                if (!result.decompileCompleted() || result.getDecompiledFunction() == null) {
                    throw new IllegalStateException("Decompilation failed for " + name + ": " + result.getErrorMessage());
                }
                ArrayList<Map<String, String>> instructions = new ArrayList<>();
                InstructionIterator listing = currentProgram.getListing().getInstructions(function.getBody(), true);
                while (listing.hasNext()) {
                    Instruction instruction = listing.next();
                    if (instructions.size() >= 10000) {
                        throw new IllegalStateException("Function exceeds bounded teaching export");
                    }
                    Map<String, String> row = new LinkedHashMap<>();
                    row.put("address", instruction.getAddress().toString());
                    row.put("text", instruction.toString());
                    instructions.add(row);
                }
                Map<String, Object> item = new LinkedHashMap<>();
                item.put("name", name);
                item.put("entry", function.getEntryPoint().toString());
                item.put("signature", function.getSignature().toString());
                item.put("calling_convention", function.getCallingConventionName());
                item.put("instructions", instructions);
                item.put("decompiled_c", result.getDecompiledFunction().getC());
                functions.add(item);
            }
        } finally {
            decompiler.dispose();
        }
        if (!found.equals(requested)) {
            Set<String> missing = new LinkedHashSet<>(requested);
            missing.removeAll(found);
            throw new IllegalStateException("Requested functions missing: " + missing);
        }
        Map<String, Object> evidence = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        evidence.put("schema", "re-lab-ghidra-evidence-v1");
        evidence.put("program", currentProgram.getName());
        evidence.put("format", currentProgram.getExecutableFormat());
        evidence.put("language", currentProgram.getLanguageID().toString());
        evidence.put("compiler_spec", currentProgram.getCompilerSpec().getCompilerSpecID().toString());
        evidence.put("image_base", currentProgram.getImageBase().toString());
        evidence.put("functions", functions);
        evidence.put("limit", "Actual headless import, analysis and decompilation; not GUI or human-learning evidence");
        Files.writeString(output, new GsonBuilder().setPrettyPrinting().create().toJson(evidence) + "\n", StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        println("RE_LAB_EVIDENCE_COMPLETE " + output);
    }
}

`courses/inside-the-shot/tools/inspect_ghidra.py`:

```py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run pinned Ghidra headlessly against one original teaching target.

This records actual tool output. It does not prove that a learner understands it,
or verify Ghidra's graphical interface. Never overwrite an earlier run.
"""

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import platform
import re
import subprocess
import sys
import time


def digest(path):
    with path.open('rb') as stream:
        return hashlib.file_digest(stream, 'sha256').hexdigest()


def validate_evidence(evidence, target_name, symbols):
    """Validate a complete export, not merely a process exit or function name."""
    if not isinstance(evidence, dict) or evidence.get('schema') != 're-lab-ghidra-evidence-v1':
        raise ValueError('Incomplete or unknown Ghidra evidence schema')
    expected = {'program': target_name, 'format': 'Mac OS X Mach-O',
                'language': 'AARCH64:LE:64:AppleSilicon', 'compiler_spec': 'default'}
    for key, value in expected.items():
        if evidence.get(key) != value:
            raise ValueError(f'Ghidra evidence has unexpected {key}')
    if not isinstance(evidence.get('image_base'), str) or not re.fullmatch(r'[0-9a-fA-F]+', evidence['image_base']):
        raise ValueError('Ghidra evidence has no valid image base')
    functions = evidence.get('functions')
    if not isinstance(functions, list) or len(functions) != len(set(symbols)):
        raise ValueError('Ghidra evidence has an incomplete function list')
    found = set()
    for function in functions:
        if not isinstance(function, dict) or not isinstance(function.get('name'), str):
            raise ValueError('Ghidra evidence has an invalid function')
        name = function['name'].removeprefix('_')
        if name in found:
            raise ValueError('Ghidra evidence repeats a function')
        found.add(name)
        if not isinstance(function.get('entry'), str) or not re.fullmatch(r'[0-9a-fA-F]+', function['entry']):
            raise ValueError('Ghidra evidence has no function entry address')
        if not isinstance(function.get('signature'), str) or not function['signature'].strip():
            raise ValueError('Ghidra evidence has no function signature')
        code = function.get('decompiled_c')
        if not isinstance(code, str) or name not in code or '{' not in code or '}' not in code:
            raise ValueError('Ghidra evidence has no complete decompilation')
        instructions = function.get('instructions')
        if not isinstance(instructions, list) or not 1 <= len(instructions) <= 10000:
            raise ValueError('Ghidra evidence has no bounded instruction listing')
        for instruction in instructions:
            if (not isinstance(instruction, dict) or not isinstance(instruction.get('address'), str)
                    or not re.fullmatch(r'[0-9a-fA-F]+', instruction['address'])
                    or not isinstance(instruction.get('text'), str) or not instruction['text'].strip()):
                raise ValueError('Ghidra evidence contains an incomplete instruction')
    if found != {s.removeprefix('_') for s in symbols}:
        raise ValueError('Ghidra did not export every requested function')


def inspect(ghidra, java_home, target, output, symbols, project_root=None):
    ghidra, java_home, target, output = [Path(p).resolve() for p in (ghidra, java_home, target, output)]
    launcher = ghidra / 'support/analyzeHeadless'
    java = java_home / 'bin/java'
    for path in (launcher, java, target):
        if not path.is_file():
            raise ValueError(f'Required file is absent: {path}')
    properties_text = (ghidra / 'Ghidra/application.properties').read_text()
    if not re.search(r'^application.version=12\.1\.4\s*$', properties_text, re.MULTILINE):
        raise ValueError('This validated route requires Ghidra 12.1.4')
    if not symbols or any(not s.replace('_', '').isalnum() for s in symbols):
        raise ValueError('Name at least one simple function symbol from the supplied listing')
    script = Path(__file__).with_name('CourseEvidence.java')
    if not script.is_file():
        raise ValueError('CourseEvidence.java must be beside inspect_ghidra.py')
    project_root = Path(project_root).resolve() if project_root else output / 'project'
    if any(part.startswith('.') for part in project_root.parts):
        raise ValueError('Ghidra refuses project paths with hidden components. Use --project-root with a new ordinary path, for example /tmp/re-lab-project-01.')
    if project_root.exists():
        raise ValueError(f'Refusing existing project directory: {project_root}')
    output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False)
    project_root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False)
    for directory in ('state/home', 'state/settings', 'state/cache', 'state/tmp', 'state/prefs', 'state/system-prefs'):
        (output / directory).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    env = os.environ.copy()
    env['JAVA_HOME'] = str(java_home)
    env['PATH'] = str(java_home / 'bin') + os.pathsep + env.get('PATH', '')
    properties = {'user.home': 'home', 'application.settingsdir': 'settings',
                  'application.cachedir': 'cache', 'application.tempdir': 'tmp',
                  'java.util.prefs.userRoot': 'prefs', 'java.util.prefs.systemRoot': 'system-prefs'}
    # All launch-helper and analyzer JVMs use this run's own state directories.
    # JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS is process-local; no shell profile or OS setting is edited.
    env['JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS'] = ' '.join(f'-D{k}="{output / "state" / v}"' for k, v in properties.items())
    env['GHIDRA_HEADLESS_MAXMEM'] = '1G'
    command = [str(launcher), str(project_root), 're-lab', '-import', str(target),
               '-scriptPath', str(script.parent), '-postScript', script.name,
               str(output / 'evidence.json'), *symbols,
               '-max-cpu', '2', '-analysisTimeoutPerFile', '90',
               '-log', str(output / 'analysis.log'), '-scriptlog', str(output / 'script.log')]
    report = {'schema': 're-lab-ghidra-run-v1', 'status': 'running', 'command': command,
              'target': str(target), 'target_sha256': digest(target), 'symbols': symbols,
              'project_root': str(project_root),
              'platform': platform.platform(), 'python': sys.version,
              'script_sha256': digest(script), 'runner_sha256': digest(Path(__file__)),
              'application_properties_sha256': digest(ghidra / 'Ghidra/application.properties'),
              'limit': 'Headless tool execution only; native GUI, human interpretation and accessibility remain separate.'}
    started = time.monotonic()
    report_path = output / 'run.json'
    try:
        version = subprocess.run([str(java), '-version'], env=env, text=True, capture_output=True, timeout=20, check=True)
        report['java_version'] = version.stdout + version.stderr
        if not re.search(r'version "21(?:\.|\")', report['java_version']):
            raise ValueError('This validated route requires JDK21')
        with (output / 'console.log').open('x') as log:
            result = subprocess.run(command, env=env, stdout=log, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, timeout=240)
        report['exit'] = result.returncode
        if result.returncode:
            raise ValueError(f'Ghidra exited {result.returncode}; preserve and inspect console.log')
        if not (output / 'evidence.json').is_file():
            raise ValueError('Ghidra produced no complete evidence.json; inspect script.log and console.log for a missing function or script failure')
        evidence = json.loads((output / 'evidence.json').read_text())
        validate_evidence(evidence, target.name, symbols)
        report['evidence_sha256'] = digest(output / 'evidence.json')
        report['status'] = 'passed'
    except (OSError, ValueError, subprocess.SubprocessError) as error:
        report['status'] = 'failed'
        report['error'] = str(error)
        raise
    finally:
        report['seconds'] = round(time.monotonic() - started, 3)
        report_path.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2) + '\n')
    return report_path


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument('--ghidra', required=True, help='Extracted Ghidra 12.1.4 directory')
    parser.add_argument('--java-home', required=True, help='JDK21 directory containing bin/java')
    parser.add_argument('--target', required=True, help='Original executable from an RE Lab student bundle')
    parser.add_argument('--out', required=True, help='New evidence directory; existing paths are refused')
    parser.add_argument('--symbol', action='append', required=True, help='Function to inspect; repeat for multiple functions')
    parser.add_argument('--project-root', help='New project directory without hidden path components; defaults to OUT/project')
    args = parser.parse_args()
    try:
        print(inspect(args.ghidra, args.java_home, args.target, args.out, args.symbol, args.project_root))
    except (OSError, ValueError, subprocess.SubprocessError) as error:
        parser.exit(1, f'Ghidra evidence run failed: {error}\n')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

```

`courses/onion-network-course/README.md`:

```md
# Build your own local onion-routing system

Build encrypted circuits, then run your client and relay protocol across four separate Node relay processes. Create circuit state, send a fictional archive lookup through three hops, check the layered reply, stop a relay and choose a fresh replacement circuit.

**The working transport is parent-routed local IPC between real processes.** The links are simulated; the processes, AES-GCM encryption and failure/restart operations are real. This course does not yet qualify TCP or multiple machines. It is not Tor-compatible or a real anonymity system.

## Start with the local Node route

Use an already installed Node runtime with built-in crypto. The imported course was tested on Node v26.5.1. No packages, installation, account, listener or network access are needed for the default route.

1. Unzip this package into a new folder. Keep earlier course folders and your attempts.
2. Open this README and the linked lessons in your editor. The static `index.html` is an optional course map.
3. Start with the six [Circuit Observatory lessons](observatory/README.md), which teach layers and observer reasoning in one process:

```sh
cd observatory
node tools/lab.mjs check 1
```

4. After those lessons, continue to the six [local relay lessons](onion-process-lab/README.md). From the bundle root:

```sh
cd onion-process-lab
node tools/check.mjs 1
```

Both starters deliberately fail until you implement the lesson's functions. A TODO result is your starting point, not a broken installation. Later checks are cumulative. If you already have a working Observatory implementation, retain it and begin the process lab's first lesson; its new setup and asynchronous handler still need implementation.

## Carry your work into processes

| Observatory work | Process-lab work |
| --- | --- |
| `selectPath` | Adapt the selection policy to the supplied process directory. |
| Supplied circuit constructor | Implement `createCircuit` and `installCircuit`, including cleanup after partial setup. |
| `wrapRequest` | Compose the same layers with the process-local crypto helpers. |
| `peelForward`, `acceptSequence`, `addReturnLayer` | Combine them in asynchronous `handleCell`; record replay state before awaiting a successor. |
| `unwrapReply` | Preserve the caller's expected sequence at every return layer. |
| `recoveryPlan` | Retain the path length and choose replacement or stop after a real process fails. |
| `correlate` and observer report | Explain what process separation changes and what the shared operator still knows. |

The two learner files are separate: `observatory/learner/solution.mjs` (or its async browser starter) and `onion-process-lab/learner/protocol.mjs`. Read the [process API](onion-process-lab/PROTOCOL.md); do not replace one file with the other or assume their imports and signatures are interchangeable.

After completing process lesson 4, run these commands inside `onion-process-lab`:

```sh
node tools/lab.mjs demo
node tools/lab.mjs interactive
```

The interactive command starts only the four child processes owned by this lab. Use `directory`, `open alpha`, `send alpha luna`, then `quit`. Read [lesson 5](onion-process-lab/lessons/05.md) before stopping a relay. `quit` or end-of-input awaits their shutdown. No socket adapter is needed for this route.

## Finish with evidence

Complete the [process report](onion-process-lab/REPORT.md): record predictions before fault injection, preserve the source and terminal output for each attempt, identify the real chosen path and PIDs, and explain a lost reply and a successful recovery. Retain unsuccessful attempts and declare help. The process lab asks you to save those artifacts explicitly; it does not provide automatic assessment history. Observatory's existing attempt storage is unchanged. Neither project imports or migrates old histories automatically.

The final artifact is your local client/relay implementation and its evidence report. Passing public checks does not assess all claims or establish human learning.

## Delivery and limits

The original Observatory browser workbench is retained as source. The hosted browser runner is unavailable under the current delivery policy; use the Node routes above. No browser can launch the Node relay processes from this package. Real browser acceptance, TCP qualification and independent-machine execution remain unrun for this combined package.

Process spawning, IPC routing, primitive crypto and the archive are supplied; you write circuit provisioning and protocol behavior. Trusted local setup distributes fresh keys without an authenticated handshake. There is no SOCKS proxy, public exit, real destination service, directory discovery/consensus, Tor protocol, independent administration or production security guarantee. Read [the process limits](onion-process-lab/LIMITS.md) before making privacy claims. Use only the fictional `luna` and `tide` records.

# Run your own circuit in the browser workbench

The workbench now contains an actual code editor and disposable execution worker. Its **Run module checks**, **Run diagnosis**, and **Run capstone** buttons run the source in that editor. The optional reference demonstration in lesson 3 remains labeled separately and never supplies your implementation.

This build's source, worker bundle, Web Crypto adapter and controller have offline checks. Actual browser execution, storage behavior, CSP behavior, keyboard flow, visuals and accessibility are **NOT_RUN**. Browser/server execution is held in the current delivery environment. This is implementation evidence, not browser acceptance.

## Learner route

The [multi-circuit workshop](WORKSHOP.md) adds learner-authored ordered scenarios using this same editor and worker. Open its scenario builder after module 5 to inject loss, corruption, replay and outages, then choose recovery actions and compare observer evidence. **Run experiment** saves the exact scenario and predictions alongside the source; it does not require or imply a passing module score.

1. Use the **Run your code** link in the workbench. The editor starts with `learner/browser-solution.js`, containing the same eight functions as the CLI project.
2. Read the module and edit its functions. Run the checks through that module. Initial `TODO_M1` failures are intentional; incomplete later modules do not block running an earlier module's checks.
3. After implementing the round trip, select a fictional record and a two-, three- or four-hop path, then run a diagnosis. Compare the actual result with your prediction. Use the observer selector and event buttons to inspect the trace created by your code.
4. After completing all modules, run the capstone. All 29 checks precede six diagnostic scenarios and the timing transfer cases. Written reasoning remains unassessed until you apply the capstone rubric.

The browser needs built-in Web Crypto, Worker, Blob URLs and writable local storage on the document's origin. If a capability is missing, the UI reports it and keeps the code visible. It does not substitute the reference trace or claim success. The established Node CLI remains available. No network service, account, package installation or actual Tor relay is part of the project.

## One semantic difference: await the crypto result

Web Crypto encrypts and decrypts asynchronously: `seal` and `open` return a Promise, a value that completes later. The supplied browser starter marks the four crypto-using functions `async`. Inside them, use `await seal(...)` or `await open(...)` before using the result. Returning the Promise directly from `addReturnLayer` is also valid. For example, assigning an un-awaited Promise to a packet body would serialize the wrong value instead of the ciphertext.

The full one-layer sibling in `examples/browser-sibling.js` is executed by the offline adapter tests. It shows the API calls without solving the multi-hop build. You still decide wrapping order, local route checks, replay-state changes and request binding.

The helper names `seal`, `open`, `context`, `requireThat` and `LabError` are supplied to the editor's code. Write ordinary function declarations, with no imports or exports. Functions that do not use crypto may remain synchronous. The adapter awaits their results either way. The original `learner/solution.mjs` and Node CLI retain their synchronous crypto API; neither source file is silently converted or overwritten.

## Same protocol requirements

Every return layer uses the caller's `expectedSeq`. A valid reply for request 7 cannot fulfill request 8, and an outer layer for 8 cannot conceal an inner layer for 7. Mismatches produce `BAD_PACKET`. Properly matched replies may arrive out of order, and separate circuits may use the same sequence under different keys. Stateless unwrapping does not replace the receiver's replay policy.

All 29 public check IDs, requirements and inputs agree with the CLI checklist. The browser adapter preserves per-hop/direction ephemeral keys, AES-256-GCM, 96-bit nonces, 128-bit tags, authenticated context, and rejection before plaintext release. It reserves a nonce before awaiting encryption so concurrent calls cannot reuse the key/nonce pair. It never saves key material.

## Your history and evidence

Before a worker starts, the controller commits the exact source, its SHA-256, the selected command/module/scenario, prediction, declared help, requirement wording and hash, and the build/runtime identities. Results are separate records linked to that submission. Editing code does not rewrite earlier results. The UI flags a result that belongs to earlier editor text; saved runs retain their original build identity.

**Save draft** keeps an editable copy distinct from immutable attempts. **Download code** exports the current editor source. **Export project history** exports submissions and outcomes, including an explicitly unsaved result if storage failed after execution. A failure to save the submission prevents execution. The ten-second limit and **Stop run** terminate the disposable worker and retain a failure/cancellation outcome. A worker is recreated for the next attempt, so keys and replay state never carry across runs.

The page policy blocks connections and the worker disables ordinary network APIs. Those browser restrictions remain unverified until authorized browser acceptance. A worker is not a secure grading sandbox against hostile code: local results are editable evidence, not credentials. Use only your own exercise code and the supplied fictional data. The complete simulator remains under one operator; its restricted observer views do not establish anonymity.

`courses/onion-network-course/observatory/CAPSTONE.md`:

```md
# Circuit Observatory

Build an offline instrument that shows what a working onion circuit does and where its privacy argument stops. Use only the fictional archive, simulated relays and synthetic observations in this package. Do not substitute public addresses or real traffic.

## Deliverable

Keep your cumulative `learner/solution.mjs`. Run the supplied report command with that implementation and write your explanation in a copy of `REPORT-TEMPLATE.md`. The report must identify code and case hashes, declared help, actual results, and which observations support each conclusion. The report runner is supplied platform code; the routing and analysis must be yours.

Run `node tools/lab.mjs capstone`. The command prints the report and saves it beside the committed source and question identity in a new attempt directory. Use `--help-used` to declare assistance. Reasoning is marked UNASSESSED until your explanation is reviewed with the rubric below.

Alternatively, implement the browser starter and use **Run capstone** in the workbench. It checks the same requirements before running the six scenarios with your editor source. Export your project history and code; those records contain source/requirement/runtime hashes. The browser API awaits crypto operations but preserves the same protocol and request-sequence binding. An offline adapter rehearsal does not establish browser acceptance.

1. Retrieve `tide` over a qualifying three-hop path. Include the complete forward and return trace, then separate entry, middle, exit and archive views. Explain which fields are direct observations and which are inferences. Show that a genuine reply for request 7 cannot fulfill a call expecting request 8, while matched replies 8 and 7 can be unwrapped in that order. Explain why authentic bytes alone do not establish a match to the caller's request.
2. Present a changed ciphertext before its original. Show the rejection, unchanged freshness state and later acceptance of the original. Then replay the accepted packet and show the different rejection reason.
3. Lose a middle relay. Close the old circuit, choose a valid replacement and retrieve the same record. Show why the old packet cannot authenticate on the replacement. Include an insufficient-relay case that stops explicitly.
4. Lose the reply after archive receipt. Use the trace to explain why the client cannot infer non-delivery. Defend why the supplied read-only lookup can be repeated and identify the extra contract a state-changing application would need.
5. Analyze the two synthetic transfer cases below. Keep every compatible candidate. A unique match is still evidence under a model, not proven identity.

## Changed observation problem

For a learner-owned extension, complete [the multi-circuit workshop](WORKSHOP.md). Preserve a baseline, one changed fault boundary, and your own recovery design. Compare client, relay and archive evidence before inspecting the operator trace. The workshop shares your browser-format implementation and records scenario/source hashes; it does not replace the capstone rubric or automatically assess your written claims.

Case A uses an archive that batches output. Entry event times are `[0,4,13,18]`. Observers offer candidate A at `[50,54,63,68]`, B at `[80,85,93,98]` and C at `[100,104,114,121]`. Use tolerance 1. Explain what your matcher retains and which model assumptions remain untested. The complete exercise includes variable delays; matching only the total duration is insufficient.

Case B changes the sender behavior. A scheduler emits one packet every tick, including when there is no lookup. Entry times are `[0,1,2,3]`. Candidate P has `[20,21,22,23]`; Q has `[60,61,62,63]`; R has `[90,91,92,93]`. Use tolerance 0. Explain what can and cannot be concluded from the retained set. You are given the schedule; you are not implementing a traffic-shaping or evasion system.

Finally, compare two hypothetical endpoint policies: a read-only anonymous catalog lookup, and a request containing a stable fictional visitor label. State how the latter changes what the archive can link even if relay content is encrypted. Do not generate an actual account, credential or identifying payload.

## Acceptance rubric

| Criterion | Evidence required |
| --- | --- |
| Circuit construction | Your path and layering pass the stated tests for more than one path length; no plaintext is attached beside the outer ciphertext. |
| Request/reply binding | Every return layer uses the caller's expected request sequence. Wrong-request replies fail, matched reordered and independent replies remain valid, and stateless unwrap is not confused with replay acceptance. |
| Local reasoning | Each relay’s direct view is justified from its input/state. The complete simulator trace is not mislabeled as one relay’s knowledge. |
| Integrity and freshness | Changed packet, original and replay give distinct appropriate outcomes; rejected inputs leave state unchanged. |
| Recovery | New circuit identity and keys; old circuit closed; valid path or explicit stop; no reuse of failed IDs. |
| Endpoint uncertainty | The lost-reply trace is interpreted correctly and no exactly-once claim is made. |
| Observation limits | Every compatible timing candidate is retained; endpoint identity, operator control and model omissions remain explicit. |
| Provenance | Code/case hashes, commands, actual outputs and declared assistance are present. First and revised attempts remain separate. |

The automatic report checks behavior and records evidence. The reasoning rubric is reviewed from the actual explanation; a nonempty text field does not pass it. All eight dimensions are necessary, and a misleading privacy claim cannot be offset by a high count of passing tests.

The supplied one-layer example and practice questions remain available. Complete the transfer cases without hints first; later help must be declared. For a genuinely fresh assessment, an instructor uses a separate instrument that is not included in the learner export.

```

`courses/onion-network-course/observatory/PROTOCOL.md`:

```md
# The controlled protocol contract

This protocol is an original teaching model. Its nested JSON, per-layer GCM tags, key setup, freshness policy and variable packet sizes are not Tor wire formats or algorithms. It implements no public network behavior.

The original CLI API below stays synchronous. The browser implements the same protocol with async `seal`/`open` from Web Crypto; see [BROWSER.md](BROWSER.md). Its four crypto-using learner functions await those operations. The worker and file/history plumbing are supplied, so the learner's routing, request-binding and freshness decisions remain the same.

## Execution model

`establish(path)` is a trusted local constructor. It creates one circuit ID, two independent fresh 256-bit keys per hop, and one local relay state per hop. Each key handle is valid only in the current Node process. No handshake, identity check, directory consensus or remote key distribution is simulated.

Forward movement is a sequence of function calls. A relay opens one layer and returns the inner packet. Backward movement visits relays in reverse order, adding one encrypted layer at each call. The client opens the result in path order. The harness can inspect the entire process and supplies narrow observer views for teaching.

## Learner API

All functions are synchronous. Do not mutate caller inputs except the explicitly mutable freshness set. Valid directory inputs contain objects with string `id` and boolean `online`. Requested lengths are positive integers no larger than the available teaching directory. Paths in integration exercises have at least two hops.

| Function | Required behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `selectPath(relays, failedIds=[], length=3)` | Return exactly `length` distinct online IDs excluding all failed IDs. Throw `LabError('NO_PATH')` if insufficient. Keep input unchanged. Any qualifying order is valid. |
| `wrapRequest(hops, request, seq)` | Return the outer packet. Visit hops exit-to-entry. Encrypt `{next, body}` with `forwardKey`. The exit’s `next` is `archive`; earlier `next` values come from the following hop. Keep request plaintext out of the outer packet. |
| `peelForward(state, packet)` | Open one layer using local forward context. Require matching `next` and a `body` property, else `BAD_ROUTE`. After authentication and route validation, call `acceptSequence`. Return `{next, body}`. |
| `addReturnLayer(hop, body, seq)` | Seal `body` with the backward key and backward context. The harness calls this exit-to-entry. |
| `unwrapReply(hops, packet, expectedSeq)` | Open each backward layer entry-to-exit using the caller's `expectedSeq` in every layer's context. Each layer's sequence must equal that expected request sequence; otherwise throw `BAD_PACKET`. Never derive the expected sequence from the packet. Return the final reply only after all layers validate. This function is stateless; the supplied client checks accepted reply sequences. |
| `acceptSequence(seen, seq)` | Require an integer in 0…1023, else `BAD_SEQUENCE`. Reject a member of `seen` with `REPLAY`. Add a fresh sequence. Out-of-order unseen values are allowed. |
| `recoveryPlan(relays, failedIds, oldPath)` | Return `{action:'rebuild',path}` preserving path length and selection rules, or `{action:'stop',reason:'NO_PATH'}`. The harness closes the old circuit and performs fresh setup. |
| `correlate(entryTimes, candidates, tolerance)` | Return every candidate ID with equal event count and all corresponding gap differences ≤ tolerance. For fewer than two entry events, return []. Candidates are `{id,times}`; inputs have finite ascending times and nonnegative tolerance. Preserve input and candidate order. |

Each hop has `circuitId`, `relayId`, `forwardKey`, `backwardKey`. Each relay state also has `previous`, `next`, `seenForward`. Key handles carry no serializable key bytes.

## Supplied crypto API

`context(circuitId, relayId, direction, seq)` returns canonical authenticated context. `direction` is `forward` or `backward`; valid sequences are 0…1023. `seal(keyHandle, context, value)` returns `{seq,ciphertext,tag}`. `open(keyHandle, context, packet)` returns a parsed JSON value only after GCM authentication succeeds. The two encoded fields use base64.

The wrapper uses AES-256-GCM, a 96-bit nonce containing the sequence, and a 128-bit authentication tag. A fresh handle must be scoped to one circuit/hop/direction. Reusing a sequence with the same handle throws `NONCE_REUSE`, even if associated data differs. Each new circuit creates new keys before the sequence restarts. This bookkeeping is a teaching guardrail, not a new cryptographic primitive.

For replies, the caller supplies the request sequence it expects to fulfill. An authentic reply for sequence 7 cannot fulfill a call expecting sequence 8. A mixed packet with an outer layer for 8 and an inner layer for 7 must also fail. `open` diagnoses a mismatch between packet sequence and expected context as `BAD_PACKET`; an altered ciphertext/tag or wrong key/context with matching sequence fails as `AUTH_FAILED`. This distinction is separate from freshness: stateless unwrap may decode replies 9 and 2 in that order if each call supplies its matching expected sequence, and independent circuits may use the same sequence with their own keys. The receiver, not unwrap, decides whether an already accepted reply can be accepted again. The supplied synchronous client records the sequence only after matched unwrapping succeeds; it does not model a general asynchronous request scheduler.

Packets are limited to 256 KiB of plaintext per layer; nesting increases size. The small exercises fit well inside this bound. No attempt is made to reproduce fixed-size Tor cells or traffic shaping. An unchanged packet can authenticate again; replay rejection belongs to receiver state.

`destroyKey` overwrites the wrapper’s key buffer and invalidates its handle. JavaScript and native library copies may remain in memory. This is not a secure-erasure or forward-secrecy assurance.

## Failure semantics

`AUTH_FAILED` means the key/context/ciphertext/tag combination did not authenticate. `BAD_ROUTE` means an authenticated instruction contradicts the established successor. Neither may mutate `seenForward`. `REPLAY` means the packet’s sequence has already been accepted. `RELAY_DOWN` is a supplied fault before a named relay acts. `REPLY_LOST` is a supplied fault after archive receipt and before reply delivery. `CIRCUIT_CLOSED` prohibits using a retired circuit. More than 1024 send sequences requires a new circuit.

The harness does not implement adversarial scheduling, real transport loss, retries in a running network, or durable endpoint state. The archive accepts only `{operation:'lookup',item:'luna'|'tide'}` and returns a fictional catalog record. Repeating a read-only lookup is acceptable. No exactly-once application guarantee follows.

## Observer contract

Entry: previous client, next relay, local circuit state, packet times/sizes and its encrypted inner packet. Middle: neighboring relays, local circuit state, packet times/sizes and its encrypted inner packet. Exit: previous relay, archive destination and plaintext request/reply in this toy. Archive: exit as caller and request contents. Process operator: everything.

Relay projections do not include the full route. The trace collection does include all projections for inspection; sharing it would reveal the combined information. This distinction is deliberate and is part of the capstone argument.

The toy gives every hop the same circuit ID and uses the same sequence number across layers. These are linkable labels when observers combine their state. The timing exercises intentionally restrict their input to event times; they do not model all metadata available in this protocol. Real Tor has different circuit/link metadata and cell handling. Do not infer unlinkability from the absence of the request body at one relay.

```

`courses/onion-network-course/observatory/README.md`:

```md
# Build Your Own Onion Routing Network

Build **Circuit Observatory**: an offline client that retrieves a fictional archive record through several relays, inspects each relay’s view, rejects altered and repeated traffic, and rebuilds a failed circuit.

This is an educational toy inspired by onion routing. It is **not Tor-compatible and is not a real anonymity system**. All relays run in one process under one operator. Use only the supplied fictional traffic. It has no network access, public relays, accounts or persistent access keys.

## Start here

You need an already installed Node runtime with `node:crypto` and AES-256-GCM support. This build was tested on **Node v26.5.1, OpenSSL 3.6.3** on macOS. No packages, installation, server or account are needed. Other runtime versions are unqualified.

From this folder:

```sh
node tools/lab.mjs help
node tools/practice.mjs p1
node tools/lab.mjs check 1
```

The first check deliberately fails with `TODO_M1`. Read [lesson 1](lessons/01.md), edit only `selectPath` in [your implementation](learner/solution.mjs), and rerun it. Later functions stay unfinished until their modules. The full check is not expected to pass at the start.

Submit a practice response as JSON, enclosed in shell single quotes. For example, an array response has the form `node tools/practice.mjs ID '["first","second"]'`. Ask for an item without an answer to see its prompt. Responses are saved before feedback; retries create new attempts. Predictions are recorded and explained but are not scored as mastery.

The [workbench](workbench/index.html) contains lesson navigation, practice and an actual learner-code editor. Its disposable worker runs your code through the same 29 requirements, six diagnostic scenarios and observer trace views using built-in Web Crypto. The optional reference trace is separate. Read [the browser guide](BROWSER.md) for the async API and source-bound history. The adapter and worker bundle have been exercised offline on Node; browser rendering, worker startup on the target origin, keyboard behavior, CSP and storage have **not yet been exercised in a real browser**.

## Build sequence

After module 5, use [The reply never arrived. What happened?](WORKSHOP.md), the multi-circuit failure/recovery workshop. Author and reorder scenario steps in the existing workbench or run the same experiment offline with `node tools/browser-lab.mjs workshop scenarios/recovery.json learner/browser-solution.js`. Your protocol and recovery choices determine the outcome. No additional code editor or network service is needed.

| Module | What you build | Check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [1. Choose a path](lessons/01.md) | Distinct available relays; observer scope | `node tools/lab.mjs check 1` |
| [2. Wrap the onion](lessons/02.md) | Layers from exit to entry | `node tools/lab.mjs check 2` |
| [3. Forward and return](lessons/03.md) | Local peel and reverse-direction wrapping | `node tools/lab.mjs check 3` |
| [4. Integrity and freshness](lessons/04.md) | Authenticate, validate, then record sequence | `node tools/lab.mjs check 4` |
| [5. Rebuild](lessons/05.md) | Replacement path or explicit stop | `node tools/lab.mjs check 5` |
| [6. Challenge the claim](lessons/06.md) | Timing comparison with ambiguity | `node tools/lab.mjs check all` |

Plan roughly 30–45 minutes per module including code and repair, plus 45–60 minutes for the capstone. These are untested design estimates, not measured learner times. Reading is deliberately compact; most work is executing and interpreting your own build. All modules remain available without a score gate.

You should already know JavaScript arrays, objects, functions, loops, imports, exceptions and terminal commands. The lessons introduce circuit, relay, symmetric key, ciphertext, authenticated encryption, associated data, nonce, replay and traffic correlation as they become necessary.

## Supplied and learner-owned code

The runtime supplies crypto primitives, trusted ephemeral key setup, an in-process call harness, a read-only archive, trace views and command/file handling. You implement the eight functions in `learner/solution.mjs` for the original CLI, or in the browser editor's `learner/browser-solution.js` starter. Their [contract](PROTOCOL.md) is shared; the [browser adapter](BROWSER.md) uses await for crypto operations. Neither source file silently replaces the other. You are not asked to implement AES, sockets, a UI or storage plumbing.

`seal` and `open` use installed Node AES-256-GCM. Separate key handles exist per circuit, relay and direction. A sequence becomes a nonce only under those fresh keys. No key material is written into attempts or reports. The setup is trusted and local; it does not implement relay authentication, key exchange, Tor cells, Tor directory consensus, guard selection, onion services, TLS, flow control or network transport. These omissions are material, not implementation details to ignore.

The browser adapter implements those same operations with the platform's built-in Web Crypto AES-GCM and nonextractable CryptoKeys. An optional offline rehearsal of that exact worker bundle is `node tools/browser-lab.mjs check 1 learner/browser-solution.js`; its initial TODO failure is expected. This is not a browser test. It saves each source/result pair in `browser-attempts/` before/after execution. The original `tools/lab.mjs` CLI path remains unchanged.

## Run and preserve work

After module 3, run `node tools/lab.mjs demo`. After module 5, run `node tools/lab.mjs failover`. Each command saves the exact submitted source, question wording and hash, declared help, and result into a new `attempts/` directory before importing your code. The checker runs local code with your ordinary Node permissions; it is not a security sandbox for untrusted submissions. A five-second execution limit prevents an accidental infinite loop in the supplied launcher.

If you use help, add `--help-used hint-1`, `hint-2`, `worked-example`, or your own description to a build/check command. Practice responses take that description as the last positional argument. A passed assisted attempt stays assisted. Earlier attempts are never replaced. Files are readable JSON and source, so you can copy the folders yourself. Local history can be edited by its owner and is not a credential.

If saving fails, the command refuses to execute. If Node is unavailable or AES-256-GCM is missing, do not substitute a homemade primitive. Use another already provisioned suitable environment or record the runtime blocker.

## Finish with an argument

Complete [CAPSTONE.md](CAPSTONE.md) using your own implementation and [REPORT-TEMPLATE.md](REPORT-TEMPLATE.md). The project is useful as a controlled explanation and diagnostic instrument. A green checker is finite behavior evidence, not a security proof, anonymity guarantee or evidence that a human learned.

Source grounding and protocol differences are in [SOURCES.md](SOURCES.md). The original author workspace also contains private instructor solutions and QA evidence; the learner export deliberately excludes them. Nothing in this package is published to Free to Learn by the export command.
