<h2 id="replay">Replay</h2>
<p><code>replay(program, recording)</code> runs the recording&#39;s calls on a new machine whose imports answer from the recording, in order, without any world. Keep a position in the answers list. When the game calls an import, the next recorded answer must be for the same import with the same arguments. Return its result and move on.</p>
<p>If it isn&#39;t, the replay has left its recording. The game asked a question the recording can&#39;t answer, and any value you returned would be invented. Throw an error with a <code>divergence</code> field, <code>{ tick, call, reason }</code>. <code>call</code> is the index in <code>recording.calls</code> of the call into the game being replayed, <code>reason</code> says in words what went wrong, and <code>tick</code> is the number of instructions the machine had finished before the call instruction that asked, so that call instruction&#39;s own event would say <code>tick + 1</code>. With <code>check: true</code>, a call whose result or memory hash differs from the recording is a divergence too.</p>
<h3 id="answer-from-the-recording-or-refuse">Answer from the recording, or refuse</h3>
<p>Replace the <code>recorded-imports</code> region. It builds the imports a replay gives its machine:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Imports that answer from a recording</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs · recorded-imports</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the recorded-imports region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Imports that answer from a recording; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-keyword">export</span> <span class="cex-keyword">function</span> recordedImports(program, recording, machineOf, start = <span class="cex-number">0</span>) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> next = start;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> imports = {};</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">for</span> (<span class="cex-keyword">const</span> { name } <span class="cex-keyword">of</span> program.imports) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    imports[name] = (...args) =&gt; {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> answer = recording.answers[next];</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> state = machineOf().state;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> where = { tick: state.tick, call: state.calls - <span class="cex-number">1</span> };</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> asked = <span class="cex-string">`${name}(${args.join(&#39;, &#39;)})`</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (!answer)</span>
<span class="cex-line">        <span class="cex-keyword">throw</span> <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> ReplayDivergence({</span>
<span class="cex-line">          ...where,</span>
<span class="cex-line">          reason: <span class="cex-string">`the program asked ${asked} after the recording&#39;s last answer`</span>,</span>
<span class="cex-line">        });</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (</span>
<span class="cex-line">        answer.name !== name ||</span>
<span class="cex-line">        answer.args.length !== args.length ||</span>
<span class="cex-line">        answer.args.some((value, i) =&gt; !Object.<span class="cex-keyword">is</span>(value, args[i]))</span>
<span class="cex-line">      )</span>
<span class="cex-line">        <span class="cex-keyword">throw</span> <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> ReplayDivergence({</span>
<span class="cex-line">          ...where,</span>
<span class="cex-line">          reason: <span class="cex-string">`the program asked ${asked}, the recording holds ${answer.name}(${answer.args.join(&#39;, &#39;)})`</span>,</span>
<span class="cex-line">        });</span>
<span class="cex-line">      next++;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> answer.result;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    };</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> { imports, position: () =&gt; next };</span>
<span class="cex-line">}</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p><code>next</code> is the position in the answers list. It lives in the closure, outside <code>machine.state</code>, which is deliberate: it belongs to this replay, not to the game, and restoring a copy of the game&#39;s state must not move it. <code>position()</code> reports it, and <code>start</code> lets a later search begin answering partway through the recording.</p>
<p>The imports have to exist before the machine does, because the Machine&#39;s constructor takes them. So they receive <code>machineOf</code>, a function that returns the machine once it has been made, and read the machine&#39;s state only when the game asks. An import runs in the middle of the call instruction&#39;s <code>step</code>. Lesson 08&#39;s Machine adds one to <code>state.tick</code> only after an instruction&#39;s work is done, so at that moment <code>state.tick</code> is the number of instructions finished before the call instruction, the <code>tick</code> the contract asks for. A machine that counts the tick before running the instruction makes every such tick one too high, and check <code>09.replay-questions</code> says so. <code>begin</code> has already counted the call into the game, so its index is <code>state.calls - 1</code>.</p>
<p><code>Object.is</code> compares each argument exactly, so a <code>sin</code> asked of an angle one part in 2^40 away from the recorded one is still a different question. Check <code>09.replay-questions</code> makes that edit, among others.</p>
<h3 id="run-the-calls-and-compare">Run the calls and compare</h3>
<p>Replace the <code>replay</code> region:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Replay without a world</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs · replay</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the replay region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Replay without a world; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-keyword">export</span> <span class="cex-keyword">function</span> replay(program, recording, { check = <span class="cex-keyword">true</span> } = {}) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> machine;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> answered = recordedImports(program, recording, () =&gt; machine);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  machine = <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> Machine(program, answered.imports);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> results = [];</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> hashes = [];</span>
<span class="cex-line">  recording.calls.forEach((call, k) =&gt; {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> value = machine.invoke(call.name, call.args);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> result = value === <span class="cex-keyword">undefined</span> ? <span class="cex-keyword">null</span> : value;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> hash = hashMemory(machine.state.memory);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    results.push(result);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    hashes.push(hash);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> where = { tick: machine.state.tick, call: k };</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (check &amp;&amp; !Object.<span class="cex-keyword">is</span>(result, recording.results[k]))</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">throw</span> <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> ReplayDivergence({</span>
<span class="cex-line">        ...where,</span>
<span class="cex-line">        reason: <span class="cex-string">`call ${k} returned ${result}, the recording says ${recording.results[k]}`</span>,</span>
<span class="cex-line">      });</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (check &amp;&amp; hash !== recording.hashes[k])</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">throw</span> <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> ReplayDivergence({</span>
<span class="cex-line">        ...where,</span>
<span class="cex-line">        reason: <span class="cex-string">`memory after call ${k} differs from the recording`</span>,</span>
<span class="cex-line">      });</span>
<span class="cex-line">  });</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> { machine, results, hashes };</span>
<span class="cex-line">}</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p><code>machine</code> is declared before the imports are made and assigned after, so the closure passed to <code>recordedImports</code> can return it. A question the recording can&#39;t answer throws from inside <code>invoke</code>, with the tick of the call instruction. A wrong result or hash can only be seen once a call has returned, so that divergence carries the tick at which the call returned. With <code>{ check: false }</code> the replay still refuses an unanswerable question and keeps going past a wrong result or hash. The replay never changes <code>recording</code>, because the debugger in lesson 10 replays one recording many times.</p>
<p>Tour <code>learnerRecorder</code> in <code>lab.mjs</code> now. Before it imports your <code>recorder.mjs</code>, it wraps <code>Machine.prototype.step</code> from your <code>machine.mjs</code> with a counter, and the checks do the same. That counter is how every instruction count in this lesson is measured, so your recorder must make its machines from the <code>Machine</code> it imports from <code>./machine.mjs</code> and run every instruction through <code>step</code>. <code>invoke</code> does, because it is a loop over <code>step</code>.</p>
<p>Try it on a recording with one answer&#39;s argument changed. Answers and calls are numbered from 0. In the recording above, the first <code>cos</code> answer is answer 1. Change its argument from 0.8028514385223389 to 0.8128514385223389 and replay the copy:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs tamper project/run42.json --answer 1 --arg 0.01 --out project/edited.json</span>
<span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs replay project project/edited.json</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>A replay refuses a question it can&#39;t answer</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/replay-output.txt</span></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="A replay refuses a question it can&#39;t answer; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">Answer 1 (cos) now says it was asked cos(0.8128514385223389), not cos(0.8028514385223389).</span>
<span class="cex-line">Wrote project/edited.json. Its hashes are still the original&#39;s.</span>
<span class="cex-line">The replay left its recording at tick 88494, call 19: the program asked cos(0.8028514385223389), the recording holds cos(0.8128514385223389)</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>The replay stops at call 19, the key press that fires the first shot, at tick 88,494. The game asks for the cosine of the barrel&#39;s angle, and the recording holds the cosine of another angle. <code>node lab.mjs replay project project/run42.json</code> replays the untouched recording to its end.</p>
<p>Tour <code>tamperCmd</code> in <code>lab.mjs</code> too. It changes one answer or one call in a copy and writes it out with the original&#39;s hashes untouched, which is why the replay above could compare every call with what the untampered run did.</p>
<p>Check <code>09.replay</code> replays recordings of Lob and Lob II with no world at all. <code>09.replay-questions</code> edits recordings and expects your error at the right tick and call, and <code>09.replay-check</code> changes a recorded result or hash and expects a divergence only with <code>check: true</code>.</p>
<h2 id="finding-where-a-tampered-replay-first-differs">Finding where a tampered replay first differs</h2>
<p><code>tampered</code> is a copy of a recording with one answer changed, and its hashes are still the original&#39;s. After which tick does its replay first have different memory from the original&#39;s?</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs tamper project/run42.json --answer 12 --add 0.25 --out project/tampered.json</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>Answer 12 is the tenth <code>server_wind</code> answer, the wind during one game frame of the first shot&#39;s flight. Changing it changes that game frame&#39;s acceleration, and memory differs from the moment the shell&#39;s new position is stored.</p>
<p>The only test you have is whole-state equality, where two memories are the same if their hashes are the same. You can only compare hashes at moments you choose, not ask &quot;which instruction made this hash different?&quot; That is the setting for <strong>bisection</strong>. Keep two moments, one where the memories are known equal and one where they are known different, test the moment halfway between, and keep the half where they still change from equal to different.</p>
<p>Running both replays from tick 0 for every halfway test would cost up to two whole runs per test. The recording&#39;s hashes make it cheaper:</p>
<ol>
<li>Replay only the tampered recording, one call at a time, and compare the hash after each call with the original&#39;s recorded hash. The first call whose hash differs is the call where they part. Call it k. Before each call, keep a <code>structuredClone</code> of the state, so that when call k ends different, you hold the state at its start, and that state is the same in both runs, because call k - 1 ended with equal hashes.</li>
<li>Search inside call k, from the saved state. Two machines started from it, one answering from the original&#39;s answers and one from the tampered ones, run the two versions of the call. Either of these finds the instruction: - <strong>Bisect.</strong> A test at offset t runs each machine t instructions from the saved state and compares their memory hashes. About log2 of the call&#39;s length tests, each replaying up to the whole call twice. - <strong>Step side by side.</strong> Step both machines together and, after each step, compare the bytes either one just wrote. It costs twice the offset of the divergence and finds it exactly, even if the memories later become equal again.</li>
</ol>
<p>Inside one call, stepping side by side is the cheaper of the two, and either meets the checks. Bisection wins where only whole states can be compared. Step 1 is that case, because one side of it exists only as recorded hashes, and so is any test you can run only at chosen moments, such as comparing two debugging sessions that are too slow to step together. Bisection also assumes a difference, once made, lasts to the end of the call, and the checks&#39; tampers do.</p>
<p>For the tampered recording above, step 1 finds call 29, a game frame that runs 796 instructions starting at tick 96,469.</p>
<p>Question 09b: bisection over the 796 instructions of call 29 starts knowing memory is equal after 0 of them and different after all 796. Each test halves the interval. How many tests does it take, at most, until the two ends are one instruction apart? Commit:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs predict project 09b YOUR_ANSWER</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<h3 id="find-the-call-from-the-recorded-hashes">Find the call from the recorded hashes</h3>
<p>Step 1 goes in the <code>find-call</code> region:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Replay once, saving each call&#39;s starting state</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs · find-call</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the find-call region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Replay once, saving each call&#39;s starting state; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-keyword">export</span> <span class="cex-keyword">function</span> firstDivergence(program, original, tampered) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> machine;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> answered = recordedImports(program, tampered, () =&gt; machine);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  machine = <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> Machine(program, answered.imports);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">for</span> (<span class="cex-keyword">let</span> k = <span class="cex-number">0</span>; k &lt; tampered.calls.length; k++) {</span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> start = globalThis.structuredClone(machine.state);</span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> answerAt = answered.position();</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> left = <span class="cex-keyword">false</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">try</span> {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      machine.invoke(tampered.calls[k].name, tampered.calls[k].args);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    } <span class="cex-keyword">catch</span> (error) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (!(error instanceof ReplayDivergence)) <span class="cex-keyword">throw</span> error;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      left = <span class="cex-keyword">true</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    }</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> same =</span>
<span class="cex-line">      !left &amp;&amp; hashMemory(machine.state.memory) === original.hashes[k];</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (same) continue;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> bisectCall(program, original, tampered, k, start, answerAt);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> <span class="cex-keyword">null</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">}</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"><span class="cex-emphasis">Emphasized lines: 6, 7.</span> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>Only the tampered recording is replayed. The original takes part through its hashes alone, which is why this loop costs one replay up to the call where the two part, not two. Copying the state before every call costs memory and time, but it runs no instructions, so the counter doesn&#39;t see it. <code>answerAt</code> is the answer position at the start of the call: the search inside the call has to answer the same questions from the same place in both recordings.</p>
<p>A tampered replay can also ask a question its recording doesn&#39;t hold, a <code>cos</code> of an angle the tamper changed, for example. That counts as a call that ends different. A key the game ignores leaves the hash equal, so the loop goes on, and a tamper that never changes memory reaches the end and returns <code>null</code>.</p>
<h3 id="run-one-call-from-a-saved-state">Run one call from a saved state</h3>
<p>Replace the <code>run-from</code> region:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Restore, begin and stop after a limit</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs · run-from</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the run-from region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Restore, begin and stop after a limit; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-keyword">function</span> runFrom(program, recording, k, start, answerAt, limit) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> machine;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> answered = recordedImports(program, recording, () =&gt; machine, answerAt);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  machine = <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> Machine(program, answered.imports);</span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">  machine.state = globalThis.structuredClone(start);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  machine.begin(recording.calls[k].name, recording.calls[k].args);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> ran = <span class="cex-number">0</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">try</span> {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    while (machine.running &amp;&amp; ran &lt; limit) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      machine.step();</span>
<span class="cex-line">      ran++;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    }</span>
<span class="cex-line">  } <span class="cex-keyword">catch</span> (error) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (!(error instanceof ReplayDivergence)) <span class="cex-keyword">throw</span> error;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> { machine, ran, left: <span class="cex-keyword">true</span> };</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> { machine, ran, left: <span class="cex-keyword">false</span> };</span>
<span class="cex-line">}</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"><span class="cex-emphasis">Emphasized lines: 5.</span> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>This is where lesson 08&#39;s rule pays off: because the machine keeps everything in <code>machine.state</code>, assigning a copy puts a new machine at the exact start of call k. The copy matters again here, because each test runs from the same saved state and must not change it for the next one. <code>begin</code> starts the call and <code>step</code> runs at most <code>limit</code> instructions of it. <code>ran</code> counts instructions that finished, so a question the recording can&#39;t answer stops the run with <code>left</code> set and <code>ran</code> short of the limit.</p>
<h3 id="bisect-inside-the-call">Bisect inside the call</h3>
<p>Replace the <code>bisect</code> region:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Keep one end equal and the other different</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs · bisect</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the bisect region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Keep one end equal and the other different; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-keyword">function</span> bisectCall(program, original, tampered, k, start, answerAt) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> run = (recording, limit) =&gt;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    runFrom(program, recording, k, start, answerAt, limit);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> a = run(original, Infinity);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> b = run(tampered, Infinity);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> differs = (t) =&gt; {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> x = run(original, t);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> y = run(tampered, t);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (y.left &amp;&amp; y.ran &lt; t) <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> <span class="cex-keyword">true</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> (</span>
<span class="cex-line">      hashMemory(x.machine.state.memory) !== hashMemory(y.machine.state.memory)</span>
<span class="cex-line">    );</span>
<span class="cex-line">  };</span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">  <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> lo = <span class="cex-number">0</span>; <span class="cex-comment">// memory is equal after lo instructions of call k</span></span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">  <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> hi = Math.max(a.ran, b.left ? b.ran + <span class="cex-number">1</span> : b.ran); <span class="cex-comment">// and differs after hi</span></span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">  while (hi - lo &gt; <span class="cex-number">1</span>) {</span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> mid = (lo + hi) &gt;&gt; <span class="cex-number">1</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (differs(mid)) hi = mid;</span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">    <span class="cex-keyword">else</span> lo = mid;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> start.tick + hi;</span>
<span class="cex-line">}</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"><span class="cex-emphasis">Emphasized lines: 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19.</span> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>The two first runs measure each version of the call. Memory is equal after 0 instructions, because both start from the same state, and different once both versions have finished, because that is how step 1 chose this call. A tampered run that left its recording counts as different from the instruction that asked, which is why <code>hi</code> is then one more than the instructions it finished. <code>differs(t)</code> runs both versions <code>t</code> instructions from the saved state, and each loop keeps the half whose ends are still equal and different. When the ends are one apart, <code>hi</code> instructions into the call is the first moment memory differs, and the instruction that made it so has the tick <code>start.tick + hi</code>, the tick its own event reports.</p>
<p>Run the search on the tamper above:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs diverge project project/run42.json project/tampered.json</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>The search and what it ran</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/diverge-output.txt</span></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="The search and what it ran; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">Memory first differs after tick 96568.</span>
<span class="cex-line">Your firstDivergence ran 101431 instructions.</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>The answer for this recording is tick 96,568, where memory first differs 99 instructions into call 29. Your <code>firstDivergence</code> returns 96,568, or <code>null</code> when the two replays never differ, for example when an answer is &quot;changed&quot; to the value it already had.</p>
<p>The lab prints how many instructions your search ran. The worked solution finds the call from the hashes and then bisects inside it, and runs 101,431 for this case: 97,265 to replay the tampered recording up to the end of call 29, and the rest to run both versions of call 29 and bisect inside it. Stepping side by side inside the call runs fewer, because it costs only twice the distance to the divergence. Bisecting from tick 0 instead, replaying both recordings from the start for every test, takes about 20 tests over the run&#39;s 652,927 instructions, and each test replays both recordings up to the tick it tests.</p>
<p>Check <code>09.divergence</code> runs tampers whose first differing ticks are known, and compares the tick <code>firstDivergence</code> returns with each. <code>09.divergence-none</code> runs tampers that change no memory, including an answer &quot;changed&quot; to the value it already had, and expects <code>null</code> for each. <code>09.divergence-budget</code> runs late tampers on long runs. ```md
# 09 · Record and replay

A debugger that goes backwards replays the run it's debugging, and Lob can't be replayed by running it again. With the server defences on, the game asks a server for the wind, and the server's answers change from run to run. By the end of this lesson your `recorder.mjs` will record a run, replay it exactly without the server, notice the moment a replay leaves its recording, and find the first instruction at which a tampered recording, a copy with one answer or call changed, parts from the original.

The tool this lesson mirrors is rr, a debugger for Linux programs that records every input a program receives from outside so the run can be replayed exactly.

## Start

## What makes a run repeat

Make two recordings of the same calls with two different worlds and compare them. The world is the outside the game talks to. `makeWorld(seed)` answers its imports, and the seed is the server's own. You'll make the recordings at the end of the next section, once your `record` works.

The two recordings play the same game, seed 5 and mode 1, with the same 759 calls. They differ from the very first call. `game_init` starts round 1, and round 1 asks the server for its wind level with `server_round(1)`. World 42 and world 43 answer differently, so memory differs after `game_init` returns.

Everything else in a run is fixed: the program, the starting memory and the calls. The only things that can change between two runs of the same calls are the **answers**, the values imports return. So a recording keeps two lists: the calls into the game, in order, and every answer the game received, in order.

## Record

`record(program, imports, calls)` runs the calls on a new machine. Give the machine imports that call the real ones and push each answer onto a list as it passes: `{ name, args, result }`. Keep each call's result, and after each call the memory hash, `hashMemory(machine.state.memory)` from `public/hash.mjs`. The whole recording is plain JSON, so it can be saved and read back.

### Note every answer as it passes

In `project/recorder.mjs`, replace the `record` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"record","language":"js","title":"Record calls, answers, results and hashes","change":"Replace the record region.","focus":[4,5,6,7,8,9]} -->
```js {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"record","title":"Record calls, answers, results and hashes","change":"Replace the record region.","focus":[4,5,6,7,8,9]}
export function record(program, imports, calls) {
  const answers = [];
  const noting = {};
  for (const { name } of program.imports) {
    noting[name] = (...args) => {
      const result = imports[name](...args);
      answers.push({ name, args, result });
      return result;
    };
  }
  const machine = new Machine(program, noting);
  const results = [];
  const hashes = [];
  for (const call of calls) {
    const result = machine.invoke(call.name, call.args);
    results.push(result === undefined ? null : result);
    hashes.push(hashMemory(machine.state.memory));
  }
  return {
    format: 'ttd2-recording-1',
    program: program.name,
    sha256: program.sha256,
    calls: calls.map((call) => ({ name: call.name, args: [...call.args] })),
    results,
    answers,
    hashes,
  };
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The machine never sees the real imports. It gets `noting`, one function per import the listing names, and each of those passes the question to the real import, notes the answer and hands it back unchanged. The world is asked exactly once per question, which check `09.record` counts: asking it a second time to note the answer would move the server on and record an answer the game never got. `args` is the rest parameter, a fresh plain array, so the recording can keep it.

The machine is new, so the run starts from the listing's memory, as every replay will. `invoke` returns `undefined` for a function with no result, and JSON has no `undefined`, so the recording stores `null`. Each hash is taken after its call returns. The calls are copied, so a caller who later edits its own list doesn't change the recording.

Lob's two-shot recording above holds 759 calls and 277 answers. Question 09a: which of the four imports gave most of those 277 answers? Commit before you make the recording:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 09a YOUR_ANSWER
```

The memory hash after every call isn't needed to replay. It costs 64 hex characters per call. In return, a replay can check at every call that its memory still matches the recording, and the last section of this lesson can find a divergence without replaying the original. rr offers a similar check as an option, comparing checksums of a program's memory as it replays.

Check `09.record` compares your recording with an independent run that counts every answer, and `09.recording-json` round-trips it through `JSON.stringify`.

Once `record` works, make the two recordings of the first section, then look inside them:

```
node lab.mjs record project --world 42 --out project/run42.json
node lab.mjs record project --world 43 --out project/run43.json
node examples/show-recording.mjs project/run42.json project/run43.json
```

`examples/show-recording.mjs` prints the size of each recording, its first call and first answer, and the first call after which the two memory hashes differ:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/recording-output.txt","language":"text","title":"Two worlds, the same calls"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/recording-output.txt","title":"Two worlds, the same calls"}
project/run42.json: ttd2-recording-1, program lob
  759 calls, 277 answers, 759 hashes
  call 0: game_init(5, 1) returned null; memory hash after it 674f60c95fd31eab...
  answer 0: server_round(1) returned 1
project/run43.json: ttd2-recording-1, program lob
  759 calls, 277 answers, 759 hashes
  call 0: game_init(5, 1) returned null; memory hash after it 405cce2ea030c094...
  answer 0: server_round(1) returned -2
First call whose memory hashes differ: call 0, game_init(5, 1)
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The calls are the same and the first answer is not, so the hashes part after call 0. That is the claim of the first section, read from your own recordings.

## Replay

`replay(program, recording)` runs the recording's calls on a new machine whose imports answer from the recording, in order, without any world. Keep a position in the answers list. When the game calls an import, the next recorded answer must be for the same import with the same arguments. Return its result and move on.

If it isn't, the replay has left its recording. The game asked a question the recording can't answer, and any value you returned would be invented. Throw an error with a `divergence` field, `{ tick, call, reason }`. `call` is the index in `recording.calls` of the call into the game being replayed, `reason` says in words what went wrong, and `tick` is the number of instructions the machine had finished before the call instruction that asked, so that call instruction's own event would say `tick + 1`. With `check: true`, a call whose result or memory hash differs from the recording is a divergence too.

### Answer from the recording, or refuse

Replace the `recorded-imports` region. It builds the imports a replay gives its machine:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"recorded-imports","language":"js","title":"Imports that answer from a recording","change":"Replace the recorded-imports region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"recorded-imports","title":"Imports that answer from a recording","change":"Replace the recorded-imports region."}
export function recordedImports(program, recording, machineOf, start = 0) {
  let next = start;
  const imports = {};
  for (const { name } of program.imports) {
    imports[name] = (...args) => {
      const answer = recording.answers[next];
      const state = machineOf().state;
      const where = { tick: state.tick, call: state.calls - 1 };
      const asked = `${name}(${args.join(', ')})`;
      if (!answer)
        throw new ReplayDivergence({
          ...where,
          reason: `the program asked ${asked} after the recording's last answer`,
        });
      if (
        answer.name !== name ||
        answer.args.length !== args.length ||
        answer.args.some((value, i) => !Object.is(value, args[i]))
      )
        throw new ReplayDivergence({
          ...where,
          reason: `the program asked ${asked}, the recording holds ${answer.name}(${answer.args.join(', ')})`,
        });
      next++;
      return answer.result;
    };
  }
  return { imports, position: () => next };
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`next` is the position in the answers list. It lives in the closure, outside `machine.state`, which is deliberate: it belongs to this replay, not to the game, and restoring a copy of the game's state must not move it. `position()` reports it, and `start` lets a later search begin answering partway through the recording.

The imports have to exist before the machine does, because the Machine's constructor takes them. So they receive `machineOf`, a function that returns the machine once it has been made, and read the machine's state only when the game asks. An import runs in the middle of the call instruction's `step`. Lesson 08's Machine adds one to `state.tick` only after an instruction's work is done, so at that moment `state.tick` is the number of instructions finished before the call instruction, the `tick` the contract asks for. A machine that counts the tick before running the instruction makes every such tick one too high, and check `09.replay-questions` says so. `begin` has already counted the call into the game, so its index is `state.calls - 1`.

`Object.is` compares each argument exactly, so a `sin` asked of an angle one part in 2^40 away from the recorded one is still a different question. Check `09.replay-questions` makes that edit, among others.

### Run the calls and compare

Replace the `replay` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"replay","language":"js","title":"Replay without a world","change":"Replace the replay region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"replay","title":"Replay without a world","change":"Replace the replay region."}
export function replay(program, recording, { check = true } = {}) {
  let machine;
  const answered = recordedImports(program, recording, () => machine);
  machine = new Machine(program, answered.imports);
  const results = [];
  const hashes = [];
  recording.calls.forEach((call, k) => {
    const value = machine.invoke(call.name, call.args);
    const result = value === undefined ? null : value;
    const hash = hashMemory(machine.state.memory);
    results.push(result);
    hashes.push(hash);
    const where = { tick: machine.state.tick, call: k };
    if (check && !Object.is(result, recording.results[k]))
      throw new ReplayDivergence({
        ...where,
        reason: `call ${k} returned ${result}, the recording says ${recording.results[k]}`,
      });
    if (check && hash !== recording.hashes[k])
      throw new ReplayDivergence({
        ...where,
        reason: `memory after call ${k} differs from the recording`,
      });
  });
  return { machine, results, hashes };
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`machine` is declared before the imports are made and assigned after, so the closure passed to `recordedImports` can return it. A question the recording can't answer throws from inside `invoke`, with the tick of the call instruction. A wrong result or hash can only be seen once a call has returned, so that divergence carries the tick at which the call returned. With `{ check: false }` the replay still refuses an unanswerable question and keeps going past a wrong result or hash. The replay never changes `recording`, because the debugger in lesson 10 replays one recording many times.

Tour `learnerRecorder` in `lab.mjs` now. Before it imports your `recorder.mjs`, it wraps `Machine.prototype.step` from your `machine.mjs` with a counter, and the checks do the same. That counter is how every instruction count in this lesson is measured, so your recorder must make its machines from the `Machine` it imports from `./machine.mjs` and run every instruction through `step`. `invoke` does, because it is a loop over `step`.

Try it on a recording with one answer's argument changed. Answers and calls are numbered from 0. In the recording above, the first `cos` answer is answer 1. Change its argument from 0.8028514385223389 to 0.8128514385223389 and replay the copy:

```
node lab.mjs tamper project/run42.json --answer 1 --arg 0.01 --out project/edited.json
node lab.mjs replay project project/edited.json
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/replay-output.txt","language":"text","title":"A replay refuses a question it can't answer"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/replay-output.txt","title":"A replay refuses a question it can't answer"}
Answer 1 (cos) now says it was asked cos(0.8128514385223389), not cos(0.8028514385223389).
Wrote project/edited.json. Its hashes are still the original's.
The replay left its recording at tick 88494, call 19: the program asked cos(0.8028514385223389), the recording holds cos(0.8128514385223389)
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The replay stops at call 19, the key press that fires the first shot, at tick 88,494. The game asks for the cosine of the barrel's angle, and the recording holds the cosine of another angle. `node lab.mjs replay project project/run42.json` replays the untouched recording to its end.

Tour `tamperCmd` in `lab.mjs` too. It changes one answer or one call in a copy and writes it out with the original's hashes untouched, which is why the replay above could compare every call with what the untampered run did.

Check `09.replay` replays recordings of Lob and Lob II with no world at all. `09.replay-questions` edits recordings and expects your error at the right tick and call, and `09.replay-check` changes a recorded result or hash and expects a divergence only with `check: true`.

## Finding where a tampered replay first differs

`tampered` is a copy of a recording with one answer changed, and its hashes are still the original's. After which tick does its replay first have different memory from the original's?

```
node lab.mjs tamper project/run42.json --answer 12 --add 0.25 --out project/tampered.json
```

Answer 12 is the tenth `server_wind` answer, the wind during one game frame of the first shot's flight. Changing it changes that game frame's acceleration, and memory differs from the moment the shell's new position is stored.

The only test you have is whole-state equality, where two memories are the same if their hashes are the same. You can only compare hashes at moments you choose, not ask "which instruction made this hash different?" That is the setting for **bisection**. Keep two moments, one where the memories are known equal and one where they are known different, test the moment halfway between, and keep the half where they still change from equal to different.

Running both replays from tick 0 for every halfway test would cost up to two whole runs per test. The recording's hashes make it cheaper:

1. Replay only the tampered recording, one call at a time, and compare the hash after each call with the original's recorded hash. The first call whose hash differs is the call where they part. Call it k. Before each call, keep a `structuredClone` of the state, so that when call k ends different, you hold the state at its start, and that state is the same in both runs, because call k - 1 ended with equal hashes.
2. Search inside call k, from the saved state. Two machines started from it, one answering from the original's answers and one from the tampered ones, run the two versions of the call. Either of these finds the instruction:
   - **Bisect.** A test at offset t runs each machine t instructions from the saved state and compares their memory hashes. About log2 of the call's length tests, each replaying up to the whole call twice.
   - **Step side by side.** Step both machines together and, after each step, compare the bytes either one just wrote. It costs twice the offset of the divergence and finds it exactly, even if the memories later become equal again.

Inside one call, stepping side by side is the cheaper of the two, and either meets the checks. Bisection wins where only whole states can be compared. Step 1 is that case, because one side of it exists only as recorded hashes, and so is any test you can run only at chosen moments, such as comparing two debugging sessions that are too slow to step together. Bisection also assumes a difference, once made, lasts to the end of the call, and the checks' tampers do.

For the tampered recording above, step 1 finds call 29, a game frame that runs 796 instructions starting at tick 96,469.

Question 09b: bisection over the 796 instructions of call 29 starts knowing memory is equal after 0 of them and different after all 796. Each test halves the interval. How many tests does it take, at most, until the two ends are one instruction apart? Commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 09b YOUR_ANSWER
```

### Find the call from the recorded hashes

Step 1 goes in the `find-call` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"find-call","language":"js","title":"Replay once, saving each call's starting state","change":"Replace the find-call region.","focus":[6,7]} -->
```js {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"find-call","title":"Replay once, saving each call's starting state","change":"Replace the find-call region.","focus":[6,7]}
export function firstDivergence(program, original, tampered) {
  let machine;
  const answered = recordedImports(program, tampered, () => machine);
  machine = new Machine(program, answered.imports);
  for (let k = 0; k < tampered.calls.length; k++) {
    const start = globalThis.structuredClone(machine.state);
    const answerAt = answered.position();
    let left = false;
    try {
      machine.invoke(tampered.calls[k].name, tampered.calls[k].args);
    } catch (error) {
      if (!(error instanceof ReplayDivergence)) throw error;
      left = true;
    }
    const same =
      !left && hashMemory(machine.state.memory) === original.hashes[k];
    if (same) continue;
    return bisectCall(program, original, tampered, k, start, answerAt);
  }
  return null;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

Only the tampered recording is replayed. The original takes part through its hashes alone, which is why this loop costs one replay up to the call where the two part, not two. Copying the state before every call costs memory and time, but it runs no instructions, so the counter doesn't see it. `answerAt` is the answer position at the start of the call: the search inside the call has to answer the same questions from the same place in both recordings.

A tampered replay can also ask a question its recording doesn't hold, a `cos` of an angle the tamper changed, for example. That counts as a call that ends different. A key the game ignores leaves the hash equal, so the loop goes on, and a tamper that never changes memory reaches the end and returns `null`.

### Run one call from a saved state

Replace the `run-from` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"run-from","language":"js","title":"Restore, begin and stop after a limit","change":"Replace the run-from region.","focus":[5]} -->
```js {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"run-from","title":"Restore, begin and stop after a limit","change":"Replace the run-from region.","focus":[5]}
function runFrom(program, recording, k, start, answerAt, limit) {
  let machine;
  const answered = recordedImports(program, recording, () => machine, answerAt);
  machine = new Machine(program, answered.imports);
  machine.state = globalThis.structuredClone(start);
  machine.begin(recording.calls[k].name, recording.calls[k].args);
  let ran = 0;
  try {
    while (machine.running && ran < limit) {
      machine.step();
      ran++;
    }
  } catch (error) {
    if (!(error instanceof ReplayDivergence)) throw error;
    return { machine, ran, left: true };
  }
  return { machine, ran, left: false };
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

This is where lesson 08's rule pays off: because the machine keeps everything in `machine.state`, assigning a copy puts a new machine at the exact start of call k. The copy matters again here, because each test runs from the same saved state and must not change it for the next one. `begin` starts the call and `step` runs at most `limit` instructions of it. `ran` counts instructions that finished, so a question the recording can't answer stops the run with `left` set and `ran` short of the limit.

### Bisect inside the call

Replace the `bisect` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"bisect","language":"js","title":"Keep one end equal and the other different","change":"Replace the bisect region.","focus":[14,15,16,17,18,19]} -->
```js {"file":"examples/recorder-checkpoint.mjs","region":"bisect","title":"Keep one end equal and the other different","change":"Replace the bisect region.","focus":[14,15,16,17,18,19]}
function bisectCall(program, original, tampered, k, start, answerAt) {
  const run = (recording, limit) =>
    runFrom(program, recording, k, start, answerAt, limit);
  const a = run(original, Infinity);
  const b = run(tampered, Infinity);
  const differs = (t) => {
    const x = run(original, t);
    const y = run(tampered, t);
    if (y.left && y.ran < t) return true;
    return (
      hashMemory(x.machine.state.memory) !== hashMemory(y.machine.state.memory)
    );
  };
  let lo = 0; // memory is equal after lo instructions of call k
  let hi = Math.max(a.ran, b.left ? b.ran + 1 : b.ran); // and differs after hi
  while (hi - lo > 1) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
    if (differs(mid)) hi = mid;
    else lo = mid;
  }
  return start.tick + hi;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The two first runs measure each version of the call. Memory is equal after 0 instructions, because both start from the same state, and different once both versions have finished, because that is how step 1 chose this call. A tampered run that left its recording counts as different from the instruction that asked, which is why `hi` is then one more than the instructions it finished. `differs(t)` runs both versions `t` instructions from the saved state, and each loop keeps the half whose ends are still equal and different. When the ends are one apart, `hi` instructions into the call is the first moment memory differs, and the instruction that made it so has the tick `start.tick + hi`, the tick its own event reports.

Run the search on the tamper above:

```
node lab.mjs diverge project project/run42.json project/tampered.json
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/diverge-output.txt","language":"text","title":"The search and what it ran"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/diverge-output.txt","title":"The search and what it ran"}
Memory first differs after tick 96568.
Your firstDivergence ran 101431 instructions.
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The answer for this recording is tick 96,568, where memory first differs 99 instructions into call 29. Your `firstDivergence` returns 96,568, or `null` when the two replays never differ, for example when an answer is "changed" to the value it already had.

The lab prints how many instructions your search ran. The worked solution finds the call from the hashes and then bisects inside it, and runs 101,431 for this case: 97,265 to replay the tampered recording up to the end of call 29, and the rest to run both versions of call 29 and bisect inside it. Stepping side by side inside the call runs fewer, because it costs only twice the distance to the divergence. Bisecting from tick 0 instead, replaying both recordings from the start for every test, takes about 20 tests over the run's 652,927 instructions, and each test replays both recordings up to the tick it tests.

Check `09.divergence` runs tampers whose first differing ticks are known, and compares the tick `firstDivergence` returns with each. `09.divergence-none` runs tampers that change no memory, including an answer "changed" to the value it already had, and expects `null` for each. `09.divergence-budget` runs late tampers on long runs. For each it first compares the tick `firstDivergence` returns with the known one, as `09.divergence` does, and only then counts your instructions, failing a search that replays from the start for every test. `09.record`, `09.recording-json`, `09.replay`, `09.replay-questions` and `09.replay-check` call `record` or `replay` and never call `firstDivergence`.

## Use it on a new case: trim a recording

A short recording that still shows a bug is easier to share and cheaper to replay than the whole run. Write `trimRecording(program, recording, n)` in `project/trim.mjs`, which both route commands created. If you didn't use them, copy `starter/trim.mjs` to `project/trim.mjs` first. No finished version is supplied, and none of the listings above does this. Its contract:

- `n` is an integer from 0 to the number of calls in the recording. Refuse any other value with an error before running any instruction.
- Return a new recording of the first `n` calls: the same `format`, `program` and `sha256`, the first `n` calls, results and hashes, and exactly the answers the game asked for during those calls, in order. It must equal what `record` makes when it is given only the first `n` calls and a fresh copy of the same world.
- Run no more instructions than the first `n` calls take. Don't replay the rest of the recording.
- Leave the input unchanged, and share no arrays or objects with it, so editing the trimmed copy can't change the original.
- You may assume the recording replays without a divergence. Import only from `./recorder.mjs` and `./machine.mjs`.

Before you write code, answer two questions in `project/report.md`. Why can't the answers be cut by counting calls, or by looking at the recording alone? If call n - 1 is a game frame with a shell in the air, which side of the cut does its `server_wind` answer fall on, and how does your code know? Keep that first reasoning.   <main id="chapter"><h1 id="10-run-backwards">10 · Run backwards</h1>
<p>Lesson 08&#39;s wall measured part one&#39;s debugger on Lob. Every step copied the whole state, and one backward question at the end of a run would take hours. By the end of this lesson your <code>debugger.mjs</code> will step back one instruction, run backward to the last time a breakpoint (a stop before a chosen instruction) or a watch (a stop after chosen bytes change) fired, and say who last wrote any byte, each by replaying from a snapshot, so an answer a few thousand instructions back costs a few thousand instructions. Its snapshots will copy only the parts of memory written since the previous one.</p>
<p>The tool this lesson mirrors is rr&#39;s reverse execution, behind <code>reverse-stepi</code> (one instruction back) and <code>reverse-continue</code> in gdb, the standard debugger for compiled programs. rr answers both the same way, by restoring a saved moment and replaying forward from it.</p>

<h2 id="positions">Positions</h2>
<p>The debugger works on one recording. A <strong>position</strong> is a moment between instructions. Position <code>t</code> is the state after <code>t</code> instructions of the run, counted across all its calls, so position 0 is before <code>game_init</code> runs anything and position <code>end</code> is after the last call returns. Between two calls no function is running. The next instruction is the first one of the next call, and <code>where()</code> names it with that call&#39;s index.</p>
<p>Everything the debugger answers is a position. <code>seek(t)</code> moves to position <code>t</code>. <code>step(n)</code> and <code>stepBack(n)</code> move by <code>n</code> instructions. <code>continue(stops)</code> and <code>continueBack(stops)</code> move to the nearest position after or before this one where a stop fires. At the current position, <code>read(address, size)</code> returns memory and <code>state()</code> a <code>structuredClone</code> of the whole machine state. <code>debug.mjs</code>, the course&#39;s command line for your debugger (you try it later in this lesson), uses <code>state()</code> to call the game&#39;s getters and, in lesson 13, to name your answer. Check <code>10.state</code> compares both with a replay from tick 0.</p>
<p>Tour the supplied <code>nextInstruction</code> and <code>where</code> in your <code>debugger.mjs</code> now. During a call, the instruction that runs next is the innermost frame&#39;s <code>at</code>. Between calls the machine has no frames, so <code>nextInstruction</code> looks up the function the next call starts in, which the constructor keeps in <code>this.callFunc</code>, and answers its instruction 0. Breakpoints use the same method, which is how a breakpoint on a call&#39;s first instruction fires at the position between calls.</p>
<p>Every check this lesson names is one of unit 10&#39;s checks, and one command runs them all. Describe what helped each attempt, as in lessons 08 and 09:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Terminal command</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Terminal command; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs check project 10 --help-used &quot;describe what helped&quot;</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>Until you write your Debugger, its checks fail with &quot;not written yet&quot;. Run the command again whenever you finish a region.</p>
<h2 id="the-obvious-way-and-its-cost">The obvious way, and its cost</h2>
<p>The simplest debugger replays the recording from tick 0 every time it moves. <code>seek(t)</code> then costs <code>t</code> instructions, and so does every <code>stepBack</code>. On lesson 09&#39;s recording, 652,927 instructions long, stepping back once from near the end replays more than 650,000 instructions to move one.</p>
<p>Part one fixed half of this with checkpoints, replaying from the nearest saved state instead of from 0. The other half was what a checkpoint cost. Part one&#39;s checkpoint was a full copy of the state, and on Lob the state is 131,072 bytes of memory.</p>
<h2 id="snapshots-that-share-pages">Snapshots that share pages</h2>
<p>Cut memory into <strong>pages</strong> of equal size, say 4,096 bytes, which makes 32 pages for Lob&#39;s 131,072 bytes. These are your debugger&#39;s pages, not WebAssembly&#39;s 64 KiB pages, and you choose their size. A <strong>snapshot</strong> is the state at one position with its memory kept as a list of pages. Take one every <code>K</code> instructions during a first pass over the recording.</p>
<p>Between two snapshots most pages aren&#39;t written at all. So when you take a snapshot, copy only the pages written since the previous snapshot, and for every other page put the previous snapshot&#39;s page object itself in the list. Two snapshots then share every page that no instruction wrote between them, and each shared page is the same <code>Uint8Array</code>, held once.</p>
<p>To know which pages were written, read the events. Each write names its <code>address</code> and <code>size</code>, and its page is <code>Math.floor(address / 4096)</code>. A write can cross into the next page, so mark both.</p>
<p>The rest of the state is small: the frames with their locals and open blocks, the value stack, the globals, the tick, the call count, and how many recorded answers the run has used so far, so that a replay from this snapshot answers the next import with the right one. Copy all of that with <code>structuredClone</code>.</p>
<h3 id="one-machine-answered-from-the-recording">One machine, answered from the recording</h3>
<p>In <code>project/debugger.mjs</code>, replace the <code>constructor</code> region. It holds the constructor and the <code>tick</code> getter:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Open a recording</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/debugger-checkpoint.mjs · constructor</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the constructor region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Open a recording; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">  constructor(</span>
<span class="cex-line">    program,</span>
<span class="cex-line">    recording,</span>
<span class="cex-line">    { every = <span class="cex-number">1000</span>, pageSize = <span class="cex-number">4096</span>, check = <span class="cex-keyword">true</span> } = {},</span>
<span class="cex-line">  ) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    whole(every, <span class="cex-string">&#39;every&#39;</span>, <span class="cex-number">1</span>);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    whole(pageSize, <span class="cex-string">&#39;pageSize&#39;</span>, <span class="cex-number">1</span>);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.program = program;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.recording = recording;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.every = every;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.pageSize = pageSize;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-comment">// The function each call starts in: what runs next between calls.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.callFunc = recording.calls.map(</span>
<span class="cex-line">      (call) =&gt;</span>
<span class="cex-line">        program.exports.find((e) =&gt; e.kind === <span class="cex-string">&#39;func&#39;</span> &amp;&amp; e.name === call.name)</span>
<span class="cex-line">          .index,</span>
<span class="cex-line">    );</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-comment">// One machine for the whole session. Its imports ask this.answers, which</span></span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-comment">// restore() replaces, so a replay answers from the right place.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> imports = {};</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">for</span> (<span class="cex-keyword">const</span> { name } <span class="cex-keyword">of</span> program.imports)</span>
<span class="cex-line">      imports[name] = (...args) =&gt; this.answers.imports[name](...args);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.machine = <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> Machine(program, imports);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.answers = recordedImports(program, recording, () =&gt; this.machine);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.snapshots = [];</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.end = this.firstPass(check);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.restore(this.snapshots[<span class="cex-number">0</span>]);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line"></span>
<span class="cex-line">  get tick() {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> this.machine.state.tick;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>The Debugger keeps one machine for the whole session. Its imports don&#39;t answer from a fixed place in the recording: each one asks <code>this.answers</code>, which <code>restore</code> replaces whenever the machine jumps to a snapshot. That is lesson 09&#39;s <code>recordedImports</code>, started at the answer position the snapshot saved. The constructor replays the whole recording once, in <code>firstPass</code>, and then puts the machine back at the first snapshot, position 0. Opening a recording therefore costs one replay of the run, inside the checks&#39; limit of about two.</p>
<p><code>this.callFunc</code> turns each call&#39;s export name into its function index once, for <code>nextInstruction</code>. The options default to a snapshot every 1,000 instructions and pages of 4,096 bytes.</p>
<h3 id="mark-written-pages-during-the-first-pass">Mark written pages during the first pass</h3>
<p>Replace the <code>first-pass</code> region:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Replay once, keeping a snapshot every `every` instructions</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/debugger-checkpoint.mjs · first-pass</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the first-pass region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Replay once, keeping a snapshot every `every` instructions; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">  firstPass(check) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> m = this.machine;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> written = <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> Uint8Array(</span>
<span class="cex-line">      Math.ceil(m.state.memory.length / this.pageSize),</span>
<span class="cex-line">    );</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.snapshots.push(this.capture());</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">for</span> (<span class="cex-keyword">let</span> k = <span class="cex-number">0</span>; k &lt; this.recording.calls.length; k++) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      do {</span>
<span class="cex-line">        <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> event = this.forward();</span>
<span class="cex-line">        <span class="cex-keyword">for</span> (<span class="cex-keyword">const</span> w <span class="cex-keyword">of</span> event.writes) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">          <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> first = Math.floor(w.address / this.pageSize);</span>
<span class="cex-line">          <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> last = Math.floor((w.address + w.size - <span class="cex-number">1</span>) / this.pageSize);</span>
<span class="cex-line">          <span class="cex-keyword">for</span> (<span class="cex-keyword">let</span> p = first; p &lt;= last; p++) written[p] = <span class="cex-number">1</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">        }</span>
<span class="cex-line">        <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (m.state.tick % this.every === <span class="cex-number">0</span>) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">          this.snapshots.push(this.capture(this.snapshots.at(-<span class="cex-number">1</span>), written));</span>
<span class="cex-line">          written.fill(<span class="cex-number">0</span>);</span>
<span class="cex-line">        }</span>
<span class="cex-line">      } while (m.running);</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (check) this.checkCall(k);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    }</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> m.state.tick;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p><code>written</code> has one entry per page, set to 1 when any instruction writes that page and cleared after each snapshot. A write&#39;s first and last byte can sit on two pages, so the loop marks every page from the first to the last. A snapshot is taken whenever the tick reaches a multiple of <code>every</code>, which puts snapshot <code>i</code> at tick <code>i * every</code>; <code>moveTo</code> and the backward search rely on that. After each call, <code>checkCall</code> compares memory with the recording&#39;s hash, as <code>replay</code> did in lesson 09, so a debugger never answers questions about a run that isn&#39;t the recorded one.</p>
<p>Question 10a: in Lob, seed 3, mode 0 (no defences), the first game frame after <code>game_init</code> runs 827 instructions. How many of the 32 pages of 4,096 bytes does it write to? Commit before reading on:</p>

Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<h3 id="share-what-wasn-t-written">Share what wasn&#39;t written</h3>
<p>Replace the <code>capture</code> region:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Copy only the written pages</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/debugger-checkpoint.mjs · capture</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the capture region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Copy only the written pages; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">  capture(previous = <span class="cex-keyword">null</span>, written = <span class="cex-keyword">null</span>) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> { memory, ...rest } = this.machine.state;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> pages = [];</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">for</span> (<span class="cex-keyword">let</span> p = <span class="cex-number">0</span>; p * this.pageSize &lt; memory.length; p++) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> start = p * this.pageSize;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      pages.push(</span>
<span class="cex-line">        previous &amp;&amp; !written[p]</span>
<span class="cex-line">          ? previous.pages[p]</span>
<span class="cex-line">          : memory.slice(start, start + this.pageSize),</span>
<span class="cex-line">      );</span>
<span class="cex-line">    }</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      tick: rest.tick,</span>
<span class="cex-line">      pages,</span>
<span class="cex-line">      state: globalThis.structuredClone(rest),</span>
<span class="cex-line">      answered: this.answers.position(),</span>
<span class="cex-line">    };</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>Each page is either the previous snapshot&#39;s page object, when nothing wrote it, or a fresh <code>slice</code>, which copies those bytes. The rest of the state goes through <code>structuredClone</code> without its memory, and <code>answered</code> saves the position in the recording&#39;s answers. Called with no previous snapshot, <code>capture</code> copies every page; the first snapshot and <code>lastWrite</code> call it that way.</p>
<p>Restoring a snapshot means building a <code>Uint8Array</code> of 131,072 bytes from its pages, copying the small state back, and pointing the machine at both. Never let the machine write into a snapshot&#39;s pages. Copy them into a fresh memory first, or the next replay would change the past.</p>
<h3 id="restore-without-sharing">Restore without sharing</h3>
<p>Replace the <code>restore</code> region:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Rebuild memory and answers from a snapshot</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/debugger-checkpoint.mjs · restore</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the restore region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Rebuild memory and answers from a snapshot; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">  restore(snapshot) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> bytes = snapshot.pages.reduce((n, page) =&gt; n + page.length, <span class="cex-number">0</span>);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> memory = <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> Uint8Array(bytes);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    snapshot.pages.forEach((page, p) =&gt; memory.set(page, p * this.pageSize));</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.machine.state = {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      ...globalThis.structuredClone(snapshot.state),</span>
<span class="cex-line">      memory,</span>
<span class="cex-line">    };</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.answers = recordedImports(</span>
<span class="cex-line">      this.program,</span>
<span class="cex-line">      this.recording,</span>
<span class="cex-line">      () =&gt; this.machine,</span>
<span class="cex-line">      snapshot.answered,</span>
<span class="cex-line">    );</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p><code>memory.set</code> copies each page into the new memory, so a later store changes only the machine&#39;s memory. The small state is cloned for the same reason: the machine pushes and pops its frames and stack in place. Replacing <code>this.answers</code> makes the next import answer from where the snapshot&#39;s run had got to. Lesson 08&#39;s rule pays off again: assigning <code>machine.state</code> is all it takes to put the machine at that moment.</p>
<p>Check <code>10.page-sharing</code> takes your snapshots after a first pass and counts the bytes they hold, counting a page shared by several snapshots once. It also checks that each snapshot&#39;s pages, laid end to end, are exactly the memory at its tick.</p>
<h2 id="going-back">Going back</h2>
<p><code>continue(stops)</code> and <code>continueBack(stops)</code> take <code>stops = { breakpoints: [{ func, at }], watches: [{ address, size }] }</code> and return <code>{ reason, tick }</code>. A breakpoint <code>{ func, at }</code> fires at a position whose next instruction is that one, so the debugger stops before it runs. A watch fires right after an instruction that changed one of its bytes, and the debugger stops after the write. Both <code>continue</code> and <code>continueBack</code> move at least one instruction, so from a position where a breakpoint fires, <code>continue</code> finds the next time it fires, not this one.</p>
<p>With snapshots, every backward move is a restore and a short replay:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>stepBack(n)</code> from position <code>t</code>: restore the last snapshot at or before <code>t - n</code>, then replay forward to <code>t - n</code>.</li>
<li><code>seek(t)</code> the same way, forward or back.</li>
<li><code>continueBack(stops)</code>: the answer is the latest position before <code>t</code> where a stop fires. Restore the snapshot just before <code>t</code> and replay the stretch up to <code>t</code>, noting every position where a stop fires. If there were any, the last one is the answer. If not, go one snapshot further back and replay that stretch, and so on. Stop at the first stretch, going back, that holds a match.</li>
<li><code>lastWrite(address)</code>: the same search, where the stop is &quot;this instruction wrote the byte at <code>address</code>&quot;, changed or not.</li>
</ul>
<p>Shared pages buy one more saving. If the page holding a watched byte is the very same object in two neighbouring snapshots, no instruction wrote that page between them, so the stretch between them can&#39;t hold a match and doesn&#39;t need to be replayed. For a byte on a page nothing has written for a long time, <code>lastWrite</code> then skips most of the run. How often that happens depends on the page size. A page is skipped only if none of its bytes was written, so smaller pages are skipped more often, and each snapshot then holds more page objects.</p>
<p>Check <code>10.lob2</code> asks the same kinds of question about a Lob II recording, so nothing may depend on Lob&#39;s own addresses.</p>
<p>Question 10b: your snapshots are every 1,000 instructions, at ticks 0, 1,000, 2,000 and so on. You stand at position 96,568 and call <code>stepBack(1)</code>. How many instructions does the debugger replay? Commit:</p>
