The index reads two parts of your machine's state that `API.md` doesn't name: `state.stack`, the value stack, and `state.result`, what a finished call returned. Lesson 08's machine keeps both under those names. If you wrote your machine without its listings and named them differently, change those reads in the `follow`, `memory` and `replay` regions.

## Last writers, indexed

Build the index during one replay. For every byte of memory, keep the list of ticks at which an instruction wrote it, in increasing order. Keep, beside each tick, what you need to report: the instruction's function and `at`, and where the write started and its size.

`lastWriter(address, beforeTick)` is then a binary search in that byte's list for the greatest tick below `beforeTick`. A byte written a thousand times is answered in about ten comparisons.

The lists hold one entry per byte written, so a 4-byte store adds four entries. Lesson 09's recording makes 65,859 of them. Typed arrays that grow by doubling hold that many numbers in a few megabytes, while arrays of objects would hold the same in far more.

Tour the supplied `List` near the top of your `query.mjs` now. It is that growing typed array: `push` doubles the array when it is full, and `done()` returns a copy of exactly what was pushed. Then tour the supplied lines at the start of `buildIndex`. They make one machine whose imports answer from the recording, as lesson 09's `replay` did, and `prepared`, which gives every instruction of every function a kind from the table `KIND` (`'load'`, `'binary'`, `'call'` and so on), so the replay looks up how an instruction moves values without reading its name again. An instruction outside the table stops the index before it runs anything.

### Keep every write

In `project/query.mjs`, replace the `keep-writes` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"keep-writes","language":"js","title":"Keep each write, and who last wrote each byte so far","change":"Replace the keep-writes region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"keep-writes","title":"Keep each write, and who last wrote each byte so far","change":"Replace the keep-writes region."}
  // Every write, one entry in each list, in tick order.
  const wTick = new List(Int32Array);
  const wFunc = new List(Int32Array);
  const wAt = new List(Int32Array);
  const wAddress = new List(Int32Array);
  const wSize = new List(Int32Array);
  // Per byte: the tick of the store that last wrote it so far, 0 if none.
  const writer = new Int32Array(memorySize);
  const keepWrites = (event, t) => {
    for (const w of event.writes) {
      wTick.push(t);
      wFunc.push(event.func);
      wAt.push(event.at);
      wAddress.push(w.address);
      wSize.push(w.size);
      writer.fill(t, w.address, w.address + w.size);
    }
  };
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The replay calls `keepWrites` after every instruction with the instruction's event and tick. Each write goes into five lists at the same position, so write number `w` is `wTick[w]`, `wFunc[w]`, `wAt[w]`, `wAddress[w]` and `wSize[w]`. The replay runs in tick order, so the lists are in tick order without any sorting. `writer` is different: it holds, for every byte, only the latest store that wrote it. `lastWriter` doesn't use it. The chains later in this lesson do, because a load needs to know which store wrote each byte it reads at the moment it reads it.

### Group the writes by byte

After the replay, `makeIndex` turns the writes into one list per byte. Replace the `by-byte` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"by-byte","language":"js","title":"One list of writes per byte, still in tick order","change":"Replace the by-byte region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"by-byte","title":"One list of writes per byte, still in tick order","change":"Replace the by-byte region."}
  // Per byte, the writes that touched it in tick order:
  // byteWrites[byteStart[a]] up to byteWrites[byteStart[a + 1]].
  const byteStart = new Int32Array(memorySize + 1);
  for (let w = 0; w < writes.tick.length; w++)
    for (let i = 0; i < writes.size[w]; i++)
      byteStart[writes.address[w] + i + 1]++;
  for (let a = 0; a < memorySize; a++) byteStart[a + 1] += byteStart[a];
  const byteWrites = new Int32Array(byteStart[memorySize]);
  const next = byteStart.slice(0, memorySize);
  for (let w = 0; w < writes.tick.length; w++)
    for (let i = 0; i < writes.size[w]; i++)
      byteWrites[next[writes.address[w] + i]++] = w;
```
<!-- /code-example -->

All the per-byte lists live in one `Int32Array`, `byteWrites`, one after another, and `byteStart[a]` is where byte `a`'s list begins. The first loop counts how many writes cover each byte, the second turns the counts into starting places, and the third puts each write's number at the next free place of every byte it covers. Writes are placed in tick order, so each byte's list is in tick order too, which is what the binary search needs.

### Binary search one byte's list

Replace the `last-writer` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"last-writer","language":"js","title":"lastWriter: the greatest tick below beforeTick","change":"Replace the last-writer region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"last-writer","title":"lastWriter: the greatest tick below beforeTick","change":"Replace the last-writer region."}
  const lastWriter = (address, beforeTick) => {
    if (!Number.isInteger(address) || address < 0 || address >= memorySize)
      throw Error(
        `lastWriter: ${address} is not an address in memory (0 to ${memorySize - 1})`,
      );
    if (typeof beforeTick !== 'number' || Number.isNaN(beforeTick))
      throw Error(`lastWriter: beforeTick must be a number, got ${beforeTick}`);
    // Binary search for the first write at or after beforeTick.
    let lo = byteStart[address];
    let hi = byteStart[address + 1];
    while (lo < hi) {
      const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
      if (writes.tick[byteWrites[mid]] < beforeTick) lo = mid + 1;
      else hi = mid;
    }
    if (lo === byteStart[address]) return null;
    const w = byteWrites[lo - 1];
    return {
      tick: writes.tick[w],
      func: writes.func[w],
      at: writes.at[w],
      address: writes.address[w],
      size: writes.size[w],
    };
  };
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The loop narrows `lo` and `hi` to the first write at or after `beforeTick`, so the write just before it, at `lo - 1`, is the answer. If there is none, nothing wrote the byte before that tick. The answer is the whole write, its start and size, even when the byte is inside a wider store. The debugger's `lastWrite` at position `p` is `lastWriter(address, p + 1)`, because the instruction at tick `p` has already run at position `p`.

Question 11a: in Lob, seed 3, mode 0 (no defences), how many times is the byte at the address `g + 72` written during `game_init` and the first 10 game frames, where `g` is the 4 bytes at 78,112? `g + 72` is the lowest byte of the game-frame counter, which counts game frames. Commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 11a YOUR_ANSWER
```

Check `11.last-writer` asks generated questions about recordings you haven't seen and compares with a scan of every write. It and the other checks this lesson names make up unit 11's checks, which one command runs:

```sh
node lab.mjs check project 11 --help-used "describe what helped"
```

On the type-in route they still fail with "not written yet" at this point, because `buildIndex` runs the regions that follow values before it returns. Run the command again once the `sources` region is filled.

## Where a value came from

When a stored value is wrong, the question is why. The store copied a value off the stack, and that value was computed by an earlier instruction from its operands. Those came from loads, constants, locals or calls, and each load read bytes some earlier store had written. Following those links backward from a store gives the **chain** of the stored value.

`sources(tick)` takes the tick of a store and returns the chain's ends and joints:

- `stores`: every earlier store on the chain, by tick
- `answers`: every import answer on the chain, by its index in `recording.answers`
- `args`: every argument of a call into the game on the chain, as `[call, index]`, the call's index in `recording.calls` and the argument's index
- `initial`: every byte on the chain that was loaded before any store had written it, from the data segment or the zeros memory starts with.

The chain follows values, not addresses. A load depends on the bytes it read, not on the address it read them from, and a store passes on the value it stored, not its address. Otherwise every value in Lob would depend on the pointer `g`, and every chain would hold the same few hundred stores. The rules, from `API.md`:

- a value depends on every operand of the instruction that produced it, except the address of a load or store
- `local.get`, `local.set`, `local.tee`, `global.get` and `global.set` pass a value along unchanged, and so does a call to a defined function, whose arguments become its parameters and whose result comes back
- an import's result depends only on that answer
- a constant depends on nothing.

`API.md` settles the cases that could go either way: `select` depends on its condition as well as both values, a one-byte store on the whole value it was given, and a load of bytes written by several stores on all of them.

## How to follow a value

Replay once and give every value a **producer**, the tick of the instruction that made it. Keep a producer beside every entry of the value stack, every local of every frame, every global and every byte of memory, and update them as each instruction runs:

- an arithmetic instruction pops its operands' producers and pushes its own tick
- a constant pushes its own tick, with no inputs
- `local.get` pushes the producer stored with the local, and `local.set` stores the popped producer with the local
- a load pushes its own tick and records, as its inputs, the producers of the bytes it read, which are the stores that last wrote them
- a store records its value operand's producer as its input and becomes the producer of the bytes it wrote
- an import call pushes its own tick, recorded as answer number k
- a call to a defined function moves the producers of its arguments into the new frame's locals, and its return moves the result's producer back
- an argument of a call into the game gets a producer of its own, reported as `[call, index]`. The other locals, and each global's starting value, have none.

Branches cut the stack back, so cut the producers back with it, keeping a block's result.

Record, for each tick, the producers it took as inputs. `sources(tick)` then walks backward from the store's input. Visit a tick, add its inputs to the walk, note each store, answer and argument met, and never visit a tick twice. The walk only touches the chain, so most questions finish in a few thousand steps whatever the recording's length.

The seven listings below build that procedure. Three of their choices save memory without changing any answer: a constant gets the producer "nothing" instead of its own tick, since nothing can be on its chain; a value computed from a single producer takes that producer instead of a tick of its own, since its chain is the same; and an import call's value takes its answer's producer directly.

### Number the leaves

A producer has to fit in one slot of an `Int32Array`. Replace the `leaves` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"leaves","language":"js","title":"One whole number for every kind of producer","change":"Replace the leaves region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"leaves","title":"One whole number for every kind of producer","change":"Replace the leaves region."}
  // A producer is one whole number: 0 is nothing (a constant), t > 0 is the
  // instruction at tick t, and the leaves are negative: the answers first, then
  // every argument of every call, then the initial bytes by address.
  const nAnswers = recording.answers.length;
  const argBase = [];
  let nArgs = 0;
  for (const c of calls) {
    argBase.push(nArgs);
    nArgs += c.args.length;
  }
  const argCall = new Int32Array(nArgs);
  const argPos = new Int32Array(nArgs);
  calls.forEach((c, k) =>
    c.args.forEach((_, i) => {
      argCall[argBase[k] + i] = k;
      argPos[argBase[k] + i] = i;
    }),
  );
  const answerId = (a) => -1 - a;
  const argId = (k, i) => -1 - nAnswers - argBase[k] - i;
  const initialId = (address) => -1 - nAnswers - nArgs - address;
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The **leaves** are the producers a chain ends at: an answer, an argument of a call into the game, or an initial byte. Ticks are positive, so the leaves take the negative numbers, one range after another: answer `a` is `-1 - a`, then every argument of every call, in call order, then every byte of memory by address. `argBase[k]` is where call `k`'s arguments start in that range, and `argCall` and `argPos` turn an argument's number back into `[call, index]` when `sources` reports it. The number 0 is left for nothing.

### Producers beside the machine's values

Replace the `producers` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"producers","language":"js","title":"What the index records per tick, and the producers of what the machine holds","change":"Replace the producers region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"producers","title":"What the index records per tick, and the producers of what the machine holds","change":"Replace the producers region."}
  // Per tick: where its inputs start in deps, and whether it was a store.
  const depStart = new List(Int32Array);
  const deps = new List(Int32Array);
  const isStore = new List(Uint8Array);
  depStart.push(0); // tick 0 is no instruction
  isStore.push(0);

  // The producers of what the machine holds right now: one per stack value,
  // one per global, and the frames with one per local.
  let P = new Int32Array(1024);
  let sp = 0;
  const G = new Int32Array(program.globals.length);
  const frames = []; // { func, locals, base, labels: [{ height, arity, loop }] }
  const push = (id) => {
    if (sp === P.length) {
      const bigger = new Int32Array(P.length * 2);
      bigger.set(P);
      P = bigger;
    }
    P[sp++] = id;
  };

  // A computed value. With no operand producer it is nothing; with one, it
  // carries that operand's chain, so it takes its producer; with more, it is
  // tick t, whose inputs are the operands' producers.
  const scratch = new Int32Array(8);
  let nScratch = 0;
  const add = (id) => {
    if (id === 0) return;
    for (let i = 0; i < nScratch; i++) if (scratch[i] === id) return;
    scratch[nScratch++] = id;
  };
  const made = (t) => {
    if (nScratch === 0) return 0;
    if (nScratch === 1) return scratch[0];
    for (let i = 0; i < nScratch; i++) deps.push(scratch[i]);
    return t;
  };
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`depStart`, `deps` and `isStore` are what the index keeps for the questions. Tick `t`'s inputs are `deps[depStart[t]]` up to `deps[depStart[t + 1]]`, so every tick costs one number in `depStart` and one byte in `isStore`, however many inputs it has. `P` and `sp` mirror the machine's value stack, one producer per value, `G` mirrors the globals, and each frame will hold one producer per local. These last only as long as the replay.

`add` and `made` make a computed value's producer. `add` collects the operands' producers, leaving out nothing (0) and repeats. `made(t)` returns 0 if none was collected, the one producer if only one was, and otherwise records them all as tick `t`'s inputs and returns `t`. An `i32.add` of a loaded value and a constant therefore passes on the load's producer, and its chain is the load's chain, as the rules ask.

### Branches, returns and calls

Replace the `frames` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"frames","language":"js","title":"Cut the producers back as the stack is cut back","change":"Replace the frames region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"frames","title":"Cut the producers back as the stack is cut back","change":"Replace the frames region."}
  // A branch keeps its target's results and cuts the producers back with the
  // stack; a loop's label stays, because the loop can be branched to again.
  const branch = (frame, depth) => {
    const label = frame.labels[frame.labels.length - 1 - depth];
    for (let i = 0; i < label.arity; i++)
      P[label.height + i] = P[sp - label.arity + i];
    sp = label.height + label.arity;
    frame.labels.length -= label.loop ? depth : depth + 1;
  };
  // A return hands the results' producers back to the caller; the outermost
  // call's result leaves the machine.
  const leave = () => {
    const frame = frames.pop();
    const n = prepared.get(frame.func).results;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) P[frame.base + i] = P[sp - n + i];
    sp = frame.base + (frames.length ? n : 0);
  };
  // A call's arguments become the new frame's first locals; the other locals
  // start as nothing.
  const enter = (func, args) => {
    const locals = new Int32Array(args.length + prepared.get(func).locals);
    locals.set(args);
    frames.push({ func, locals, base: sp, labels: [] });
  };
```
<!-- /code-example -->

These three follow lesson 08's branch and return. A label remembers the stack's height when its block began and how many results the block leaves. `branch` copies those results' producers down to that height and cuts `sp` there, so the values a branch drops take their producers with them. A branch to a `loop` keeps the loop's label, because the loop can be branched to again. `leave` does the same for a function's results, and `enter` starts a frame whose first locals are the producers of the call's arguments and whose other locals are nothing.

### Move the producers instruction by instruction

Replace the `follow` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"follow","language":"js","title":"follow: one case per kind of instruction","change":"Replace the follow region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"follow","title":"follow: one case per kind of instruction","change":"Replace the follow region."}
  // Move the producers as the instruction at tick t is about to move values.
  // stack is the machine's value stack before the instruction runs.
  const follow = (kind, ins, frame, t, stack) => {
    switch (kind) {
      case 'block':
        frame.labels.push({ height: sp, arity: ins[1] ? 1 : 0, loop: false });
        break;
      case 'loop':
        frame.labels.push({ height: sp, arity: 0, loop: true });
        break;
      case 'br':
        branch(frame, ins[1]);
        break;
      case 'br_if':
        sp--; // the condition is a decision: on no chain
        if (stack[stack.length - 1] !== 0) branch(frame, ins[1]);
        break;
      case 'end':
        if (frame.labels.length) frame.labels.pop();
        else leave();
        break;
      case 'return':
        leave();
        break;
      case 'call': {
        const n = program.typeOf(ins[1]).params.length;
        if (ins[1] < nImports) {
          sp -= n; // an import's arguments are not followed
          if (program.typeOf(ins[1]).results.length)
            push(answerId(answered.position()));
        } else {
          const args = P.slice(sp - n, sp);
          sp -= n;
          enter(ins[1], args);
        }
        break;
      }
      case 'local.get':
        push(frame.locals[ins[1]]);
        break;
      case 'local.set':
        frame.locals[ins[1]] = P[--sp];
        break;
      case 'local.tee':
        frame.locals[ins[1]] = P[sp - 1];
        break;
      case 'global.get':
        push(G[ins[1]]);
        break;
      case 'global.set':
        G[ins[1]] = P[--sp];
        break;
      case 'const':
        push(0);
        break;
      case 'unary':
        break; // the same operand, so the same chain
      case 'binary':
        nScratch = 0;
        add(P[sp - 2]);
        add(P[sp - 1]);
        sp -= 1;
        P[sp - 1] = made(t);
        break;
      case 'select':
        nScratch = 0;
        add(P[sp - 3]);
        add(P[sp - 2]);
        add(P[sp - 1]);
        sp -= 2;
        P[sp - 1] = made(t);
        break;
      case 'load':
        load(ins, t, stack);
        break;
      case 'store':
        store();
        break;
    }
  };
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`follow` runs just before the machine runs the instruction, while the operands are still on the machine's stack, and does to `P` what the instruction is about to do to the stack. Most cases are one line. `br_if` drops its condition's producer without recording it anywhere, which is "decisions are not followed" in code; it reads the condition's value from the machine's stack only to know whether the branch will be taken. An import call drops its arguments' producers and pushes the leaf of the answer the machine is about to use. A call to a defined function moves its arguments' producers into the new frame. Loads and stores go to the next region.

### Loads and stores: bytes, not addresses

Replace the `memory` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"memory","language":"js","title":"A load depends on the bytes it reads; a store on its value","change":"Replace the memory region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"memory","title":"A load depends on the bytes it reads; a store on its value","change":"Replace the memory region."}
  // A load depends on the bytes it read, each on the store that last wrote
  // it, or on the byte itself if no store has. Its address is not followed.
  const load = (ins, t, stack) => {
    const address = (stack[stack.length - 1] >>> 0) + ins[2];
    nScratch = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < LOAD_SIZE[ins[0]]; i++) {
      if (address + i >= memorySize) break;
      const w = writer[address + i];
      add(w !== 0 ? w : initialId(address + i));
    }
    P[sp - 1] = made(t);
  };
  // A store's only input is its value's producer; its address is not
  // followed. keepWrites then makes this tick the writer of every byte.
  const store = () => {
    const value = P[--sp];
    sp--;
    if (value !== 0) deps.push(value);
  };
```
<!-- /code-example -->

A load reads its address from the machine's stack and looks up, in `writer`, the store that last wrote each byte it is about to read. A byte no store has written gives its initial leaf. The load's result replaces the address's producer on top of `P`, so the address is never an input. A store pops its value's producer and records it as its only input, then drops the address's producer. After the machine runs it, `keepWrites` makes this tick the writer of every byte it wrote, so the next load of those bytes depends on this store.

### Replay once

Replace the `replay` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"replay","language":"js","title":"Replay every call, keeping the producers in step with the machine","change":"Replace the replay region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"replay","title":"Replay every call, keeping the producers in step with the machine","change":"Replace the replay region."}
  for (let k = 0; k < calls.length; k++) {
    m.begin(calls[k].name, calls[k].args);
    enter(
      program.exportIndex(calls[k].name),
      calls[k].args.map((_, i) => argId(k, i)),
    );
    while (m.running) {
      const top = s.frames[s.frames.length - 1];
      const frame = frames[frames.length - 1];
      const fn = prepared.get(top.func);
      const ins = fn.code[top.at];
      const kind = fn.kinds[top.at];
      const t = s.tick + 1;
      depStart.push(deps.n);
      isStore.push(kind === 'store' ? 1 : 0);
      follow(kind, ins, frame, t, s.stack);
      const asked = answered.position();
      const event = m.step();
      keepWrites(event, t);
      // The producers must still match the machine: its stack, its frames and
      // the answers it has used.
      const used = kind === 'call' && ins[1] < nImports ? 1 : 0;
      if (
        frame.func !== top.func ||
        sp !== s.stack.length ||
        frames.length !== s.frames.length ||
        answered.position() !== asked + used ||
        (event.writes.length !== 0) !== (kind === 'store')
      )
        throw Error(
          `buildIndex: lost track of the machine at tick ${t} (${ins[0]} at (${event.func}, ${event.at}))`,
        );
    }
    const result = s.result === undefined ? null : s.result;
    if (!Object.is(result, recording.results[k]))
      throw Error(
        `buildIndex: call ${k} returned ${result}, the recording says ${recording.results[k]}`,
      );
  }
  depStart.push(deps.n);
```
<!-- /code-example -->

Each call begins with a frame whose locals are the call's argument leaves. Then, for every instruction, the loop records where its inputs start, moves the producers with `follow`, lets your machine run it and keeps its writes. After each instruction it compares the producers with the machine: the same stack height, the same number of frames, one answer used by an import call and none otherwise, and writes exactly when the instruction was a store. A mistake in `follow` then stops the replay at the first tick where the two part, instead of giving wrong chains later. After each call, the result must be the recorded one, as in lesson 09.

### Walk back from a store

Replace the `sources` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"sources","language":"js","title":"sources: visit each producer on the chain once","change":"Replace the sources region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/query-checkpoint.mjs","region":"sources","title":"sources: visit each producer on the chain once","change":"Replace the sources region."}
  // seenTick[t] === epoch: tick t was visited during the current question.
  const { nAnswers, nArgs, argCall, argPos } = leaves;
  const seenTick = new Int32Array(end + 1);
  const seenLeaf = new Int32Array(nAnswers + nArgs + memorySize);
  let epoch = 0;
  const sources = (tick) => {
    if (!Number.isInteger(tick) || tick < 1 || tick > end || !isStore[tick])
      throw Error(
        `sources: tick ${tick} is not the tick of a store instruction`,
      );
    epoch++;
    const stores = [];
    const answers = [];
    const args = [];
    const initial = [];
    const todo = [];
    for (let i = depStart[tick]; i < depStart[tick + 1]; i++)
      todo.push(deps[i]);
    while (todo.length) {
      const id = todo.pop();
      if (id > 0) {
        if (seenTick[id] === epoch) continue;
        seenTick[id] = epoch;
        if (isStore[id]) stores.push(id);
        for (let i = depStart[id]; i < depStart[id + 1]; i++)
          todo.push(deps[i]);
        continue;
      }
      const leaf = -1 - id;
      if (seenLeaf[leaf] === epoch) continue;
      seenLeaf[leaf] = epoch;
      if (leaf < nAnswers) answers.push(leaf);
      else if (leaf < nAnswers + nArgs) args.push(leaf - nAnswers);
      else initial.push(leaf - nAnswers - nArgs);
    }
    const up = (a, b) => a - b;
    return {
      stores: stores.sort(up),
      answers: answers.sort(up),
      args: args.sort(up).map((x) => [argCall[x], argPos[x]]),
      initial: initial.sort(up),
    };
  };
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The walk starts from the store's inputs, its value's producer, and keeps a list of producers still to visit. A tick is visited once: it is noted if it was a store, and its own inputs join the list. A leaf goes into its list according to its range. `seenTick` and `seenLeaf` mark what this question has visited with the number `epoch`, which goes up by one for every question, so nothing has to be cleared between questions. The store asked about is never in its own list, because the walk starts from its inputs.

Here is one chain, worked through. In `project/run42.json` the first shot is fired by call 19, and on the first game frame of its flight, call 20, the shell's new position is stored at `g + 40` at tick 89,345. `sources(89345)` holds 16 stores and 2 answers:

- the position and the horizontal speed that firing stored, at ticks 88,529 and 88,553 in call 19, because this game frame's position is the last position plus the speed times the game frame's length, plus the wind's push
- the speed was the power times a constant times the cosine of the angle, so the chain holds the 11 stores of the power made by the presses of up in calls 2 to 12, and before them the store at tick 69,170 in `game_init` that set the starting power of 60 (an 8-byte store that wrote the angle and the power together)
- the key at `g + 92`, stored at tick 69,157, because the game keeps the power XORed with it, as it keeps the flag's position in lesson 08's `r_target_x`, and with mode 4 off the key is 0
- the cannon's position at `g + 20`, stored at tick 69,167, from which the shell's first position was computed
- answer 1, the cosine of the barrel's angle, and answer 3, this game frame's wind.

By rule, the angle isn't on the chain, because it reached the outside world only as the argument of `cos`, and an import's arguments aren't followed. Nor is the pointer `g`, because it was only ever an address.

Question 11b: in lesson 09's recording, made with the server defences on, the shell's position is stored at `g + 40` on every game frame of a flight. How many `server_wind` answers are on the chain of the position stored on the tenth game frame of the first flight? Commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 11b YOUR_ANSWER
```

Checks `11.sources-lob` and `11.sources-lob2` ask generated questions about Lob and Lob II recordings, and `11.sources-rules` asks about a small program built to use the rules Lob never needs: a global that carries a value, a function that takes arguments and returns a result, a block that leaves a value, a branch that drops values. Every address that small program loads from or stores to is a constant, or computed only from constants, such as a loop counter that starts at a constant. Each check compares your four lists one by one. The lists it expects were worked out by a brute force that carries every value's full set of sources forward through the whole recording, a different method from the walk above, so the same mistake is unlikely in both.

## Cost

`buildIndex` may replay the recording once or twice, and after that no question may replay it. Check `11.no-replay` counts the instructions your machine runs while hundreds of questions are answered, and expects none.

See what your index kept for lesson 09's recording, and what asking it costs:

```
node examples/show-index.mjs project project/run42.json
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/index-output.txt","language":"text","title":"What the index holds, and the instructions run to ask it"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/index-output.txt","title":"What the index holds, and the instructions run to ask it"}
project/run42.json: 652927 instructions in 759 calls
building the index ran 652927 instructions on your machine
per-byte lists: 65859 entries, for 12301 bytes written at least once
the most written byte is 65508, written 2944 times; a binary search in its list takes at most 12 comparisons
sources asked about all 36810 stores: the longest chain holds 739 stores
instructions run while answering those questions: 0
```
<!-- /code-example -->

Building the index ran exactly one replay of the run. The per-byte lists hold the 65,859 entries counted earlier, for 12,301 bytes. The most written byte lies in the C stack just below 65,536, and a binary search finds any write in its list in at most 12 comparisons. The script then asked `sources` about every store of the run, and your machine ran no instruction while it did: everything a question needs was kept during the replay.

```
node debug.mjs project project/run42.json
```

As in lesson 10, you can also put the commands in a file, one per line, and pass it as the last argument, for a session with no keyboard.

In `debug.mjs`, `who ADDR` asks your index for the last writer, and `sources` asks for the chain of the store at the current tick. Stand right after a store with `who` or `last-write`, then ask `sources`. It prints how many stores the chain holds and the newest 8 of them, newest first, each with its tick, its function and instruction, and the address it wrote. `sources N` shows the newest N, and `sources all` shows every one. Then come the chain's answers, call arguments and initial bytes.

`examples/query-session.txt` asks for the worked chain of tick 89,345 twice:

```
node debug.mjs project project/run42.json examples/query-session.txt
```

The listed stores are the ones the worked chain named: the speed and the position stored by firing, then the presses of up storing the power at `g + 4`. The first `cost` counts the replay your Debugger made when it opened the recording, the short replay `seek` made from the snapshot at 89,000, and one more replay of the whole run, for the index, which `debug.mjs` builds the first time you ask `who` or `sources`. Question 11c: in `project/run42.json` the second shot is fired by call 396, and as it fires the game adds 1 to its shot counter and stores it. How many stores are on the chain of the value that store writes? Lesson 08's loop that clears memory is part of the answer. Commit before you check with `who` and `sources`:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 11c YOUR_ANSWER
```

Now follow a chain from the status line yourself. The getter `r_line_ptr` returns the status line's address, which `getters` prints between calls, and `read ADDR text` shows the line itself. Each character is one byte, at that address plus its position in the line counted from 0, so `who` on that byte finds the store that wrote it.

Most of the line's chains end without an answer or an argument. The letters are constants. The digits of the angle, the power and the score go back only through earlier stores, the oldest of them made by `game_init`, because a key press changes the angle or the power through a branch, and the next section explains why a branch is on no chain. The wind arrows (`>` or `<`) are different: in `project/run42.json` an arrow's chain reaches an import answer. Follow one arrow back with `who` and `sources`, and write in `project/report.md` each store on its chain with its tick, function and address, which answer it ends at and from which import, and why a character that is always one of a few constants has a chain at all. `listing FUNC:AT 30`, with the function and instruction `who` printed for the arrow's store, prints the 30 instructions before it and after it, and shows how the arrow was chosen.

## Decisions are not followed

Decisions aren't on a chain. A `br_if` pops a condition and branches, and the branch decides which instructions run, but no value flows from the condition into what those instructions compute.

Question 11d: in `project/run42.json` the first shell lands in call 148, and the game stores 0 in its flying flag at `g + 36` (tick 192,256). The store runs only because a `br_if` found the shell below the ground. How many entries does `sources(192256)` list, in all four lists together? Commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 11d YOUR_ANSWER
```

A store of a constant has an empty chain even when it ran only because of a long computation before it. When a store's chain is empty or doesn't explain a wrong value, the cause may be a decision, so look at the branch that led to the store, with `back` and `listing` (`listing FUNC:AT N` prints the instructions from N before AT to N after it).

## Follow an address, then repair it

In your project only, make a load depend on its address as well. In the `load` function of the `memory` region, add this line right after `nScratch = 0;`, so that the address's producer, the top of `P`, is collected with the bytes':

```js
add(P[sp - 1]);
```

Question 11e: with this change, how many of unit 11's five checks fail? Before you run anything, write in `project/report.md` which ones you expect to fail and why, and what you expect `sources` at tick 89,345 to show, then commit the number. Then run the check with `--help-used` describing this prescribed change, and open `debug.mjs` and ask `sources all` at tick 89,345 (`seek 89345`, then `sources all`; as in lesson 10, those two commands can also go in a file passed as the last argument):

```sh
node lab.mjs predict project 11e YOUR_ANSWER
node lab.mjs check project 11 --help-used "prescribed change: a load also follows its address"
node debug.mjs project project/run42.json
```

Compare the checks that failed, and the chain at tick 89,345, with what the lab said after your prediction. Explain in `project/report.md` which entries the change added to that chain, and why one rule can add the same entries to many chains. Remove the line, rerun the check and keep both attempts. This change is guided practice; the new application below asks for behavior none of these listings implements.

## Use it on a new case: where a value in memory came from

`sources` answers for a store at a tick. When you look at memory in the debugger, you see a value at a position instead, with no store in sight. Write `valueSources(index, { address, size, position })` in `project/value-sources.mjs`, which both route commands created. If you didn't use them, copy `starter/value-sources.mjs` to `project/value-sources.mjs` first. No finished version is supplied, and none of the listings above does this. Its contract:

- It returns `{ stores, answers, args, initial }`, in the same form as `sources`, for the value held by the `size` bytes at `address` at position `position`, the moment after `position` instructions.
- For each byte, if a store wrote it at or before that position, the last such store and everything on that store's chain belong to the answer. A byte no store had written by then is an `initial` byte itself.
- So the stores that last wrote the bytes are in `stores` themselves, unlike `sources`, which leaves out the store it was asked about. Bytes written by different stores bring the chains of all of them, as a load of those bytes would.
- Each list is sorted in increasing order without repeats, and `args` by call, then argument index.
- Refuse with an error: an `address`, `size` or `position` that isn't a whole number, a `size` below 1, bytes outside memory, or a position outside 0 to `index.end`.
- Memory is 131,072 bytes in every recording of Lob and Lob II, two WebAssembly pages of 64 KiB (`API.md`, "Memory"), so bytes outside memory are any below address 0 or at 131,072 and above. The index doesn't report memory's size, and `API.md` doesn't say what `lastWriter` does with an address outside memory, so test the bytes against 131,072 yourself before you ask it anything.
- Use only `index.end`, `index.lastWriter`, `index.sources` and that fixed size of memory, so your function works with any index that meets `API.md`.

The budget holds for every question, whatever the bytes or the position, a refused one included: `valueSources` may run no instruction, because `lastWriter` and `sources` answer from the index without replaying. The checker counts your machine's `step` calls while each call to `valueSources` runs. Building the two indexes it asks is not counted, and the whole check must finish within 120 seconds.

Before you write code, answer two questions in `project/report.md`. Which `beforeTick` do you pass to `lastWriter` for a value at position `p`, and what goes wrong with the other choice? Two bytes of a 4-byte value were written by one store: how many times does that store appear in your answer, and why? Keep that first reasoning. Then run the checker on the unfinished file, implement, and run it again, describing assistance honestly each time:

```sh
node examples/check-value-sources.mjs project --help-used "initial attempt; nothing written"
node examples/check-value-sources.mjs project --help-used "describe what helped your implementation"
```

The checker copies `machine.mjs`, `recorder.mjs`, `query.mjs`, `value-sources.mjs`, `PROJECT.json` and your `report.md` into a new folder under `project/attempts/` before it runs anything, and saves its results beside them in `vsources-receipt.json`. A failure never replaces an earlier attempt, and `node lab.mjs status project` lists every attempt under "New-application attempts". It builds your index of two of unit 11's check recordings, a Lob run and a Lob II run, and asks six groups of questions: bad questions; the pointer `g` right after `game_init`; four bytes written by four one-byte stores; bytes no store has written, alone and beside written ones; a position on a store's own tick and the one before it; and a Lob II value made from an answer and an argument. It keeps each expected list as its length and a salted hash, so a failure says which list differs without giving the answer away. Your `query.mjs` must pass unit 11's checks first, because every answer is built from it.

As a stretch, add a `value ADDR SIZE` command to your own copy of `debug.mjs` that asks `valueSources` about the bytes at the current position.

## Keep the working tool

`project/query.mjs` now builds an index of a recording in one replay and answers, without replaying, who last wrote any byte before any tick and which stores, answers, arguments and initial bytes a stored value was computed from. `debug.mjs` uses it for `who` and `sources`. Its end-of-unit checkpoint is `examples/query-checkpoint.mjs`; recover from it with a new project, as in "Start", never by copying it over your file. Lesson 12 gives the debugger function names, the call stack and line numbers, and lesson 13's investigations use `who` and `sources` to find planted bugs.

<h2 id="where-names-live">Where names live</h2>
<p><code>targets/lob.wasm</code> was linked with its names stripped, left out of the file, because Sightline asks its learners to work out what each unnamed function does. For this lesson the course built the same C file again, with the same compiler, and kept its names, in <code>targets/lob-names.wasm</code>. Its code is byte for byte the code of <code>lob.wasm</code>, so <code>programs/lob.json</code> describes it too. The extra bytes are a <strong>custom section</strong> at the end of the file.</p>
<p>A WebAssembly file is 8 fixed bytes followed by <strong>sections</strong>. Each section is an id byte, its size in bytes, then that many bytes. Custom sections have id 0, and their contents start with a name: a length, then that many bytes of text (UTF-8, which for these names is plain ASCII). The section named <code>name</code> holds the names.</p>
<p>Sizes and lengths are <strong>LEB128</strong> numbers, in which each byte carries 7 bits of the number, lowest first, and its top bit says whether another byte follows. <code>1D</code> is 29. <code>B8 02</code> is two bytes. <code>B8</code> has its top bit set and carries 56, and <code>02</code> carries 2, worth 2 × 128. Together, 312. (Sightline teaches LEB128 and the rest of the file format in depth.)</p>
<p>Inside the <code>name</code> section are <strong>subsections</strong>, each an id byte, a size and contents. Subsection 1 holds function names: a count, then for each function its index and its name. Skip any other subsection by its size. Here are the first bytes of the <code>name</code> section in <code>lob-names.wasm</code>, after its own name:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">00 0F              subsection 0, 15 bytes: the module&#39;s own name</span>
<span class="cex-line">0E 6C 6F 62 2D ... a name of 14 bytes: lob-names.wasm</span>
<span class="cex-line">01 B8 02           subsection 1, 312 bytes: function names</span>
<span class="cex-line">1D                 29 names follow</span>
<span class="cex-line">00                 function 0</span>
<span class="cex-line">0C 73 65 72 76 65 72 5F 72 6F 75 6E 64</span>
<span class="cex-line">                   a name of 12 bytes: server_round</span>
<span class="cex-line">01 06 6A 73 5F 63 6F 73</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>The 29 names are Lob&#39;s 4 imports and its 25 functions.</p>
<p>Question 12a: decode the last line. What name does the name section give function 1? Commit:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs predict project 12a YOUR_ANSWER</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p><code>functionNames(bytes)</code> in <code>names.mjs</code> walks the sections from byte 8, skips every section that isn&#39;t the custom section <code>name</code>, and returns <code>{ index: name }</code> for every entry of subsection 1, or <code>{}</code> when the file has no name section. Check <code>12.names</code> reads both named and stripped files, and a small file of its own that puts other subsections before subsection 1. It and the other checks this lesson names make up unit 12&#39;s checks, which one command runs:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Terminal command</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Terminal command; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs check project 12 --help-used &quot;describe what helped&quot;</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. <h3 id="read-numbers-and-names">Read numbers and names</h3>
<p>The supplied <code>Reader</code> at the top of <code>names.mjs</code> keeps a position in the file, <code>pos</code>, and <code>byte()</code> returns the byte there and moves past it, refusing to read past the end. In <code>project/names.mjs</code>, replace the <code>leb128</code> region, which adds the two reads everything else is made of:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>LEB128 numbers and names</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/names-checkpoint.mjs · leb128</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the leb128 region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="LEB128 numbers and names; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-comment">// Unsigned LEB128: 7 bits per byte, lowest first. A byte with its top bit</span></span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-comment">// set says another byte follows.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line">  u32() {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> value = <span class="cex-number">0</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> shift = <span class="cex-number">0</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> b;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    do {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      b = this.byte();</span>
<span class="cex-line">      value += (b &amp; <span class="cex-number">0x7f</span>) * <span class="cex-number">2</span> ** shift;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      shift += <span class="cex-number">7</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    } while (b &amp; <span class="cex-number">0x80</span>);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> value;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line"></span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-comment">// A length, then that many bytes of UTF-8 text.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line">  name() {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> length = this.u32();</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> end = this.pos + length;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (end &gt; this.bytes.length)</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">throw</span> Error(<span class="cex-string">&#39;functionNames: a name runs past the end of the file&#39;</span>);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> text = <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> globalThis.TextDecoder().decode(</span>
<span class="cex-line">      this.bytes.subarray(this.pos, end),</span>
<span class="cex-line">    );</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.pos = end;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> text;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p><code>u32</code> adds each byte&#39;s low 7 bits at the place <code>shift</code> gives them, 0, then 7, then 14, and goes on while the byte&#39;s top bit, <code>0x80</code>, is set. Take <code>B8 02</code>: <code>B8 &amp; 0x7f</code> is 56, added at shift 0, and the top bit is set; <code>02</code> adds 2 at shift 7, which is 256, and its top bit is clear, so the number is 312. Multiplying by <code>2 ** shift</code> keeps the arithmetic in ordinary numbers. JavaScript&#39;s <code>&lt;&lt;</code> works on 32-bit signed integers, so in a fifth byte, at shift 28, it could turn a large number negative. <code>name()</code> reads a length with <code>u32</code> and decodes that many bytes as text, so every name in the file costs one call.</p>
<h3 id="walk-the-sections">Walk the sections</h3>
<p>Replace the <code>sections</code> region:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>functionNames: find the name section</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/names-checkpoint.mjs · sections</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the sections region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="functionNames: find the name section; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-comment">// { [index]: name } for every function the &quot;name&quot; section names; {} without one.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-keyword">export</span> <span class="cex-keyword">function</span> functionNames(bytes) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> magic = [<span class="cex-number">0x00</span>, <span class="cex-number">0x61</span>, <span class="cex-number">0x73</span>, <span class="cex-number">0x6d</span>];</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (!magic.every((b, i) =&gt; bytes[i] === b))</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">throw</span> Error(<span class="cex-string">&#39;functionNames: not a WebAssembly file&#39;</span>);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> r = <span class="cex-keyword">new</span> Reader(bytes, <span class="cex-number">8</span>);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  while (r.pos &lt; bytes.length) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> id = r.byte();</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> size = r.u32();</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> end = r.pos + size;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (id === <span class="cex-number">0</span> &amp;&amp; r.name() === <span class="cex-string">&#39;name&#39;</span>) <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> functionSubsection(r, end);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    r.pos = end;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> {};</span>
<span class="cex-line">}</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>After the 8 fixed bytes, each section starts with its id and size, so <code>end</code> is where the next section begins. A section that isn&#39;t custom, or a custom section with another name, is skipped by setting <code>pos</code> to <code>end</code> without reading its contents. Only custom sections have a name to read, which is why the test reads it only when <code>id === 0</code>. A file without a name section runs out of sections and gets <code>{}</code>.</p>
<h3 id="read-subsection-1">Read subsection 1</h3>
<p>Replace the <code>subsections</code> region:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Every function&#39;s index and name</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/names-checkpoint.mjs · subsections</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the subsections region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Every function&#39;s index and name; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-comment">// Inside the name section: subsections, each an id byte, a size and contents.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-comment">// Subsection 1 is a count, then each function&#39;s index and name; skip the rest.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-keyword">function</span> functionSubsection(r, end) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> names = {};</span>
<span class="cex-line">  while (r.pos &lt; end) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> id = r.byte();</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> size = r.u32();</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> next = r.pos + size;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (id === <span class="cex-number">1</span>) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">for</span> (<span class="cex-keyword">let</span> n = r.u32(); n &gt; <span class="cex-number">0</span>; n--) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">        <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> index = r.u32();</span>
<span class="cex-line">        names[index] = r.name();</span>
<span class="cex-line">      }</span>
<span class="cex-line">    }</span>
<span class="cex-line">    r.pos = next;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> names;</span>
<span class="cex-line">}</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>Each subsection is found the way sections were, by its id and size, and <code>next</code> is where the following one begins. Subsection 1 is read entry by entry: an index, then a name. Every other subsection, the module&#39;s name in subsection 0 among them, is skipped by jumping to <code>next</code>. Setting <code>pos</code> to <code>next</code> after subsection 1 too means the next subsection is read from where it really starts, even if subsection 1 held more than its entries. The order of subsections doesn&#39;t matter, which is what the check&#39;s small file tests.</p>
<p>Read Lob&#39;s names with your <code>functionNames</code>:</p>

Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>

The stripped build has no section called <code>name</code>, so the walk reaches the end of the file and returns <code>{}</code>. Most of these names were already in the listing. The game exports <code>game_init</code>, <code>game_key</code>, <code>game_tick</code> and every getter under these names, and it imports <code>server_round</code> and <code>server_wind</code> under theirs. Only the name section holds the names of the two functions the game doesn&#39;t export, <code>new_round</code> and <code>update_hud</code>, and the C names of the two imports the game asks for as <code>cos</code> and <code>sin</code>. In <code>debug.mjs</code>, <code>break update_hud</code> now finds function 6 by its name.</p>
<h2 id="the-call-stack">The call stack</h2>
<p>Your machine already keeps the call stack in <code>state.frames</code>, outermost first, each with the function it&#39;s running and the <code>at</code> of its next instruction. <code>stack()</code> returns <code>[{ func, at }]</code> for those frames at the debugger&#39;s current position, or <code>[]</code> between calls. A call to an import pushes no frame, because the import runs outside the machine and returns at once.</p>
<p>In <code>debug.mjs</code>, <code>stack</code> prints the frames with names, and <code>where</code> names the instruction that runs next.</p>
<p>Question 12b: you stop where <code>update_hud</code>, function 6, begins during a call to <code>game_tick</code>. How many entries does <code>stack()</code> return? Commit:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs predict project 12b YOUR_ANSWER</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>A stop where <code>update_hud</code> begins comes after <code>game_tick</code>&#39;s <code>call</code> instruction has pushed <code>update_hud</code>&#39;s frame, so that frame counts. A call that comes from outside the game, from the recording rather than from another function, works differently. It begins between calls, so at a stop where it begins, its instruction 0 runs next but no function is running yet, and <code>stack()</code> is <code>[]</code>.</p>
<h3 id="list-the-frames">List the frames</h3>
<p>In <code>project/debugger.mjs</code>, find the <code>stack</code> region near the end of the class. It holds the stub of <code>stack()</code>, which throws &quot;stack: not written yet (lesson 12)&quot;. Replace everything between <code>// region: stack</code> and <code>// endregion: stack</code> with the listing below. If your file has no such markers, because you wrote it without lesson 10&#39;s starter, replace your <code>stack()</code> stub with the listing and add the two marker lines around it:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>stack(): the frames, outermost first</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs · stack</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the stack region, which holds the stack() stub.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="stack(): the frames, outermost first; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">  stack() {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> this.machine.state.frames.map((f) =&gt; ({ func: f.func, at: f.at }));</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>The frames are copied into new objects, so a caller that changes what <code>stack()</code> returned can&#39;t change the machine. Each frame&#39;s <code>at</code> is the instruction that frame runs next: the innermost frame&#39;s is the instruction that runs next in the whole run, and a caller&#39;s is the instruction after its <code>call</code>, where it carries on when the call returns. Between calls the machine has no frames, so the list is empty, which is what <code>API.md</code> asks.</p>
<p>Check <code>12.stack</code> compares your stacks with a fresh machine at many positions.</p>
<h2 id="stopping-at-a-function">Stopping at a function</h2>
<p>A <strong>function stop</strong> fires at a position where a call to that function begins, meaning the next instruction is the function&#39;s instruction 0. Add <code>functions: [index]</code> to the stops <code>continue</code> and <code>continueBack</code> understand, with <code>reason: &#39;function&#39;</code>. In <code>debug.mjs</code>, <code>break update_hud</code> adds a function stop by name, and <code>break 6:120</code> a breakpoint at one instruction.</p>
<p>Two places in lesson 10&#39;s <code>debugger.mjs</code> need the change. <code>stopHere</code>, in the <code>stops</code> region, tests the stops at each position, so it needs the function test. And <code>continueBack</code>, in the <code>search-back</code> region, decides which stretches it may skip with <code>const watchesOnly = !stops.breakpoints?.length;</code>. A function stop, like a breakpoint, can fire in a stretch that writes nothing, so that line must count function stops too. Left as it is, a <code>continueBack</code> given only <code>functions</code> counts as &quot;watches only&quot; with no watched pages, skips every stretch and reports <code>&#39;start&#39;</code>.</p>
<p>Your first <code>node lab.mjs check project 12</code> doesn&#39;t say &quot;not written yet&quot; for <code>12.function-stops</code>. Lesson 10&#39;s <code>continue</code> and <code>continueBack</code> already exist and run; they ignore a <code>functions</code> list they don&#39;t know, so the check gets a real answer from them, such as <code>{ reason: &quot;end&quot; }</code> from <code>continue</code>, and prints it beside the stop it expected.</p>
<h3 id="test-for-a-function-stop">Test for a function stop</h3>
<p>Tour the supplied <code>nextInstruction</code> again, just above <code>where</code> in your <code>debugger.mjs</code>. During a call it answers the innermost frame&#39;s next instruction, and between calls the first instruction of the next call, <code>{ func: this.callFunc[calls], at: 0 }</code>. So the instruction a call begins with is visible at the position before it runs, whether the call comes from another function or from the recording.</p>
<p>Replace the <code>stops</code> region. Only the marked lines differ from lesson 10&#39;s:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>stopHere with function stops</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs · stops</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the stops region; the marked lines are new.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="stopHere with function stops; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line cex-focus">  stopHere({ breakpoints = [], watches = [], functions = [] }, event) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (event &amp;&amp; event.writes.some((w) =&gt; changesWatched(w, watches)))</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> <span class="cex-string">&#39;watchpoint&#39;</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> next = this.nextInstruction();</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (</span>
<span class="cex-line">      next &amp;&amp;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      breakpoints.some((b) =&gt; b.func === next.func &amp;&amp; b.at === next.at)</span>
<span class="cex-line">    )</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> <span class="cex-string">&#39;breakpoint&#39;</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">    <span class="cex-comment">// A function&#39;s instruction 0 runs next only where a call to it begins.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (next &amp;&amp; next.at === <span class="cex-number">0</span> &amp;&amp; functions.includes(next.func))</span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">      <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> <span class="cex-string">&#39;function&#39;</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> <span class="cex-keyword">null</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line"></span>
<span class="cex-line">  continue(stops = {}) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    while (this.tick &lt; this.end) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> event = this.forward();</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> reason = this.stopHere(stops, event);</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (reason) <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> { reason, tick: this.tick };</span>
<span class="cex-line">    }</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> { reason: <span class="cex-string">&#39;end&#39;</span>, tick: this.tick };</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"><span class="cex-emphasis">Emphasized lines: 1, 10, 11, 12.</span> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p><code>stopHere</code> now takes <code>functions</code>, defaulting to none, so every caller from lesson 10 still works. The function test looks forward, like the breakpoint test, at the instruction that runs next. Both halves of its condition matter: the function must be one of the stopped ones, and its instruction 0 must be next. Instruction 0 of a function runs next only where a call to it begins, because a branch inside a function goes either forward to the end of a block or back to the first instruction inside a <code>loop</code>, after the <code>loop</code> instruction itself, and neither is instruction 0. <code>continue</code> is unchanged: it already asks <code>stopHere</code> after every instruction.</p>
<p>Then replace the <code>search-back</code> region. Only the marked line differs from lesson 10&#39;s:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>continueBack skips stretches only when every stop is a watch</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs · search-back</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the search-back region; the marked line is changed.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="continueBack skips stretches only when every stop is a watch; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">  continueBack(stops = {}) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> here = this.tick;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (here === <span class="cex-number">0</span>) <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> { reason: <span class="cex-string">&#39;start&#39;</span>, tick: <span class="cex-number">0</span> };</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> pages = (stops.watches ?? []).flatMap((w) =&gt;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      pagesOf(w.address, w.size ?? <span class="cex-number">1</span>, this.pageSize),</span>
<span class="cex-line">    );</span>
<span class="cex-line cex-focus">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> watchesOnly = !stops.breakpoints?.length &amp;&amp; !stops.functions?.length;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> found = this.searchBack(</span>
<span class="cex-line">      here - <span class="cex-number">1</span>,</span>
<span class="cex-line">      (event) =&gt; {</span>
<span class="cex-line">        <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> reason = this.stopHere(stops, event);</span>
<span class="cex-line">        <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> reason ? { reason, tick: this.tick } : <span class="cex-keyword">null</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      },</span>
<span class="cex-line">      (i) =&gt; !watchesOnly || this.mayHaveWritten(i, pages),</span>
<span class="cex-line">    );</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (found) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      this.moveTo(found.tick);</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> found;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    }</span>
<span class="cex-line">    this.moveTo(<span class="cex-number">0</span>);</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> { reason: this.stopHere(stops, <span class="cex-keyword">null</span>) ?? <span class="cex-string">&#39;start&#39;</span>, tick: <span class="cex-number">0</span> };</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line"></span>
<span class="cex-line">  searchBack(last, test, mayMatch = () =&gt; <span class="cex-keyword">true</span>) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">for</span> (<span class="cex-keyword">let</span> i = Math.ceil(last / this.every) - <span class="cex-number">1</span>; i &gt;= <span class="cex-number">0</span>; i--) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (!mayMatch(i)) continue;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> snapshot = this.snapshots[i];</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> stop = Math.min(last, snapshot.tick + this.every);</span>
<span class="cex-line">      this.restore(snapshot);</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> found = <span class="cex-keyword">null</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      while (this.tick &lt; stop) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">        <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> finding = test(this.forward());</span>
<span class="cex-line">        <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (finding) found = finding;</span>
<span class="cex-line">      }</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (found) <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> found;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    }</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> <span class="cex-keyword">null</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line"></span>
<span class="cex-line">  mayHaveWritten(i, pages) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> a = this.snapshots[i];</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> b = this.snapshots[i + <span class="cex-number">1</span>];</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> !b || pages.some((p) =&gt; a.pages[p] !== b.pages[p]);</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"><span class="cex-emphasis">Emphasized lines: 7.</span> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p><code>watchesOnly</code> decides whether <code>continueBack</code> may skip a stretch whose watched pages stayed shared. With a function stop present it is now false, so every stretch going back is replayed until one holds a stop, as with a breakpoint. The cost is about the distance to the stop plus up to two stretches, lesson 10&#39;s cost for a breakpoint.</p>
<h3 id="run-to-the-end-of-the-function">Run to the end of the function</h3>
<p><code>stepOut()</code> runs forward until the function running now has returned to its caller, that is, until the call stack is shorter than it is now. In <code>debug.mjs</code> it&#39;s <code>finish</code>. Between calls there is no function running. Define what <code>stepOut()</code> does there and say so in a comment.</p>
<p>Find the <code>step-out</code> region, which holds the stub of <code>stepOut()</code> that throws &quot;stepOut: not written yet (lesson 12)&quot;. Replace everything between <code>// region: step-out</code> and <code>// endregion: step-out</code> with the listing below, or, in a file without those markers, replace your <code>stepOut()</code> stub and add the two marker lines around it:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>stepOut: forward until there are fewer frames</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs · step-out</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the step-out region, which holds the stepOut() stub.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="stepOut: forward until there are fewer frames; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-comment">// Forward to the first position with fewer frames than now. Between calls no</span></span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-comment">// function is running, so stepOut runs the whole next call and stops where it</span></span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-comment">// has returned, at the next position between calls. At the end it stays.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line">  stepOut() {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> depth = this.machine.state.frames.length;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (depth === <span class="cex-number">0</span>) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (this.tick &lt; this.end) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">        do {</span>
<span class="cex-line">          this.forward();</span>
<span class="cex-line">        } while (this.machine.running);</span>
<span class="cex-line">      }</span>
<span class="cex-line">    } <span class="cex-keyword">else</span> {</span>
<span class="cex-line">      while (this.machine.state.frames.length &gt;= depth) this.forward();</span>
<span class="cex-line">    }</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> this.tick;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>Inside a call, <code>stepOut</code> counts the frames now and runs instructions until there are fewer. A deeper call made on the way pushes a frame and pops it again without stopping it, so the stop comes when the current function&#39;s own <code>return</code> or final <code>end</code> pops its frame. The first position with fewer frames is where the caller carries on, or, for the outermost function of a call, the position between calls after it. Between calls, this checkpoint runs the whole next call, the one <code>where()</code> names, and stops where it has returned. Another choice would do, such as refusing or not moving, as long as the comment says which. <code>forward()</code> is lesson 10&#39;s: between calls it begins the next call first. Moving forward replays only the distance moved, so <code>stepOut</code> costs the instructions it runs.</p>
<p>Checks <code>12.function-stops</code> and <code>12.step-out</code> compare your stops with a scan of every instruction. <code>12.function-stops</code> seeks to positions spread over a recording and from each asks both <code>continue</code> and <code>continueBack</code> for a function stop. <code>12.step-out</code> seeks to positions inside calls and calls <code>stepOut</code>, which counts frames and passes no stops to the debugger. <code>12.stack</code> seeks and compares <code>stack()</code> with a fresh machine, and <code>12.names</code> and <code>12.lines</code> call only <code>names.mjs</code>.</p>
<p>All four changes to <code>debugger.mjs</code> are in. <code>examples/stack-session.txt</code> is a script of <code>debug.mjs</code> commands that goes to the first game frame of lesson 09&#39;s recording, stops where <code>update_hud</code> begins, prints the stack, runs to the end of <code>update_hud</code> with <code>finish</code>, and then continues backward to the stop again:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node debug.mjs project project/run42.json examples/stack-session.txt</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. <h2 id="lines">Lines</h2>
<p>The compiler can also write a <strong>line table</strong>, which gives, for each stretch of code, the line of the C source it came from. It lives in <code>.debug_line</code>, one of the sections of DWARF, the standard format for debugging information, which only a build with debugging information carries. No file this course ships carries DWARF, because DWARF also records the layout of every C struct, which is what Sightline asks its learners to work out. The course decoded the line table of a debugging build when it built the targets and saved its rows in <code>lines/lob.json</code>: <code>{ offset, line, column }</code>, sorted by <code>offset</code>. DWARF counts a WebAssembly address from the start of the code section&#39;s contents, after its id byte and size (the code section holds the functions&#39; instructions, and the listing records that start as <code>codeSectionStart</code>). The course added that start, so <code>offset</code> is a file offset like the listing&#39;s <code>offsets</code>, where <code>offsets[k]</code> is the file offset of instruction k.</p>
<p>An instruction belongs to the last row at or before its offset. <code>lineAt(lines, offset)</code> finds that row with a binary search and returns <code>{ line, column }</code>, or <code>null</code> before the first row.</p>
<p>Some rows say line 0. That is DWARF&#39;s way of saying the compiler made this code without a line of its own, and 561 of Lob&#39;s 2,806 instructions fall on such rows, among them instructions of loop bodies the compiler unrolled, writing the body out several times in a row. In lesson 08&#39;s clearing loop, the <code>local.get</code> and <code>i32.const</code> that begin each copy after the first fall on line 0. <code>debug.mjs</code> prints &quot;no line&quot; for any instruction on a line-0 row. DWARF also marks the end of each function&#39;s rows with an end-of-sequence row. The course kept those as rows of line 0 at the end of each function&#39;s code, so the last line of one function never covers the start of the next.</p>
<p>The C source isn&#39;t given, so a line number is a label rather than a place you can read. It still groups instructions into statements. An assignment compiled to eight instructions gives all eight one line, and comparing lines is how a debugger steps by line.</p>
<p>Here are five rows of <code>lines/lob.json</code>, around the end of the loop of lesson 08 that clears memory in <code>game_init</code>:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">offset  line  column</span>
<span class="cex-line">   555   259      52</span>
<span class="cex-line">   561     0      52</span>
<span class="cex-line">   565   259      26</span>
<span class="cex-line">   566   259       3</span>
<span class="cex-line">   571   260       5</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
