<h3 id="find-the-row">Find the row</h3>
<p>Replace the <code>line-at</code> region of <code>project/names.mjs</code>:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>lineAt: the last row at or before an offset</strong><span class="cex-location">examples/names-checkpoint.mjs · line-at</span></figcaption><p class="cex-change">Replace the line-at region.</p><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="lineAt: the last row at or before an offset; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-comment">// { line, column } of the last row at or before `offset`, or null when every</span></span>
<span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-comment">// row comes after it. Rows are sorted by offset.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line"><span class="cex-keyword">export</span> <span class="cex-keyword">function</span> lineAt(lines, offset) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> lo = <span class="cex-number">0</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">let</span> hi = lines.length;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-comment">// Rows before lo are at or before offset; rows from hi on come after it.</span></span>
<span class="cex-line">  while (lo &lt; hi) {</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">const</span> mid = (lo + hi) &gt;&gt; <span class="cex-number">1</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (lines[mid].offset &lt;= offset) lo = mid + <span class="cex-number">1</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">    <span class="cex-keyword">else</span> hi = mid;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  }</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">if</span> (lo === <span class="cex-number">0</span>) <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> <span class="cex-keyword">null</span>;</span>
<span class="cex-line">  <span class="cex-keyword">return</span> { line: lines[lo - <span class="cex-number">1</span>].line, column: lines[lo - <span class="cex-number">1</span>].column };</span>
<span class="cex-line">}</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>The search keeps one rule true as <code>lo</code> and <code>hi</code> close in: every row before <code>lo</code> is at or before <code>offset</code>, and every row from <code>hi</code> on comes after it. When they meet, <code>lo</code> is the first row past <code>offset</code>, so the row just before it is the answer. When <code>lo</code> is still 0, every row comes after the offset and there is no line. Lob&#39;s table has 1,050 rows, so a question takes at most 11 comparisons. A row of line 0 is returned like any other; deciding what it means is left to the caller, as <code>debug.mjs</code> does.</p>
<p>Check <code>12.lines</code> asks <code>lineAt</code> about every instruction of Lob and compares with the rows.</p>
<p><code>debug.mjs</code> calls your <code>lineAt</code> from its supplied <code>describe</code> function, which every command uses to print an instruction. Tour it near the top of <code>debug.mjs</code>: it looks up the instruction&#39;s file offset in the listing, <code>f.offsets[at]</code>, asks <code>lineOf</code>, which calls your <code>lineAt</code>, for the row, and adds <code>[line N]</code> after the instruction, or <code>[no line]</code> for a row of line 0, beside the name your <code>functionNames</code> gave. Run the same script again:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node debug.mjs project project/run42.json examples/stack-session.txt</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. <h2 id="use-it-on-a-new-case-step-by-line">Use it on a new case: step by line</h2>
<p><code>step</code> moves one instruction, and <code>finish</code> a whole function. A person reading C wants a step between the two: run to the next line of the function they&#39;re in, stepping over any function it calls, as gdb&#39;s <code>next</code> does. Write <code>nextLine(debugger, program, lines)</code> in <code>project/next-line.mjs</code>, which both route commands created. If you didn&#39;t use them, copy <code>starter/next-line.mjs</code> to <code>project/next-line.mjs</code> first. No finished version is supplied, and none of the listings above does this. Its contract:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>program</code> is the listing the debugger replays and <code>lines</code> the rows of <code>lines/lob.json</code>. The line of a position is the line <code>lineAt</code> gives the instruction that runs next there. A row of line 0, or no row at all, counts as no line.</li>
<li>From the current position, run forward to the first later position where there are fewer frames than at the start, because the current function has returned, or where there are as many frames as at the start and there is a line, different from the start&#39;s line. Leave the debugger standing there and return that position.</li>
<li>Positions with more frames than at the start are inside functions the current line called, and never end the step, whatever their lines.</li>
<li>Between calls, the end of the run included, no function is running and there&#39;s no line to step over: throw an error, without moving and without running anything.</li>
<li>Use only the Debugger&#39;s public surface (<code>tick</code>, <code>end</code>, <code>step</code>, <code>seek</code>, <code>stack</code>, <code>where</code>), the listing&#39;s <code>offsets</code> and your own <code>lineAt</code>, so your function works with any debugger that meets <code>API.md</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p>The budget holds for every question the checker asks: a step may run at most the number of instructions it moves forward, plus 2,000. Moving forward one instruction at a time costs exactly the distance, and the 2,000 leave room for one restore from a snapshot and a short replay. A step that replays from position 0, or from far behind, for each instruction doesn&#39;t fit.</p>
<p>Before you write code, answer two questions in <code>project/report.md</code>. A line calls <code>update_hud</code>, and <code>update_hud</code>&#39;s own instructions carry other lines: what tells you to keep going inside it, and what would go wrong if you compared only lines? A loop whose whole body is on one line jumps back to its start: where does your step stop? Keep that first reasoning. Then run the checker on the unfinished file, implement, and run it again, describing assistance honestly each time:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Terminal command</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Terminal command; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node examples/check-next-line.mjs project --help-used &quot;initial attempt; nothing written&quot;</span>
<span class="cex-line">node examples/check-next-line.mjs project --help-used &quot;describe what helped your implementation&quot;</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>The checker copies <code>machine.mjs</code>, <code>recorder.mjs</code>, <code>debugger.mjs</code>, <code>names.mjs</code>, <code>next-line.mjs</code>, <code>PROJECT.json</code> and your <code>report.md</code> into a new folder under <code>project/attempts/</code> before it runs anything, and saves its results beside them in <code>nline-receipt.json</code>. A failure never replaces an earlier attempt, and <code>node lab.mjs status project</code> lists every attempt under &quot;New-application attempts&quot;. It replays one of unit 10&#39;s check recordings, a run of Lob, once on your machine, keeping the frames and the instruction at every position, and works out each answer from that pass and the line table. It then asks six groups of questions: refusals between calls and at the end; a line followed by another line of the same function; a line that calls a function; the last line of a function; line-0 instructions and a long loop on one line in <code>game_init</code>; and twenty steps in a row through a game frame.</p>
<p>As a stretch, add a <code>next</code> command to your own copy of <code>debug.mjs</code> that calls <code>nextLine</code>.</p>
<h2 id="keep-the-working-tool">Keep the working tool</h2>
<p><code>project/names.mjs</code> now reads function names from a binary&#39;s name section and finds the source line of any instruction, and <code>project/debugger.mjs</code> lists the call stack, stops where a named function begins and runs to the end of the current function. <code>debug.mjs</code> uses them for every instruction it prints and for <code>stack</code>, <code>break NAME</code> and <code>finish</code>. The end-of-unit checkpoints are <code>examples/names-checkpoint.mjs</code> and <code>examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs</code>; recover from them with a new project, as in &quot;Start&quot;, never by copying them over your files. Lesson 13 adds no new code to the debugger: you use it, with your index from lesson 11, to find the planted bug in each of six later builds of the game.</p>

# 12 · Stack and names

Your debugger now says things like "function 6, instruction 412", and a person debugging Lob wants to read "update_hud, called from game_tick". By the end of this lesson your debugger reads function names from the binary's name section, shows the call stack at any tick, stops where a named function begins, runs to the end of the current function, and gives the source line of any instruction.

After it, every instruction `debug.mjs` prints carries its function's name and its source line, `stack` lists the functions in progress, `break update_hud` stops where a call to it begins, and `finish` runs to the end of the current function.

## Where names live

`targets/lob.wasm` was linked with its names stripped, left out of the file, because Sightline asks its learners to work out what each unnamed function does. For this lesson the course built the same C file again, with the same compiler, and kept its names, in `targets/lob-names.wasm`. Its code is byte for byte the code of `lob.wasm`, so `programs/lob.json` describes it too. The extra bytes are a **custom section** at the end of the file.

A WebAssembly file is 8 fixed bytes followed by **sections**. Each section is an id byte, its size in bytes, then that many bytes. Custom sections have id 0, and their contents start with a name: a length, then that many bytes of text (UTF-8, which for these names is plain ASCII). The section named `name` holds the names.

Sizes and lengths are **LEB128** numbers, in which each byte carries 7 bits of the number, lowest first, and its top bit says whether another byte follows. `1D` is 29. `B8 02` is two bytes. `B8` has its top bit set and carries 56, and `02` carries 2, worth 2 × 128. Together, 312. (Sightline teaches LEB128 and the rest of the file format in depth.)

Inside the `name` section are **subsections**, each an id byte, a size and contents. Subsection 1 holds function names: a count, then for each function its index and its name. Skip any other subsection by its size. Here are the first bytes of the `name` section in `lob-names.wasm`, after its own name:

```
00 0F              subsection 0, 15 bytes: the module's own name
0E 6C 6F 62 2D ... a name of 14 bytes: lob-names.wasm
01 B8 02           subsection 1, 312 bytes: function names
1D                 29 names follow
00                 function 0
0C 73 65 72 76 65 72 5F 72 6F 75 6E 64
                   a name of 12 bytes: server_round
01 06 6A 73 5F 63 6F 73
```

The 29 names are Lob's 4 imports and its 25 functions.

Question 12a: decode the last line. What name does the name section give function 1? Commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 12a YOUR_ANSWER
```

`functionNames(bytes)` in `names.mjs` walks the sections from byte 8, skips every section that isn't the custom section `name`, and returns `{ index: name }` for every entry of subsection 1, or `{}` when the file has no name section. Check `12.names` reads both named and stripped files, and a small file of its own that puts other subsections before subsection 1. It and the other checks this lesson names make up unit 12's checks, which one command runs:

```sh
node lab.mjs check project 12 --help-used "describe what helped"
```

### Read numbers and names

The supplied `Reader` at the top of `names.mjs` keeps a position in the file, `pos`, and `byte()` returns the byte there and moves past it, refusing to read past the end. In `project/names.mjs`, replace the `leb128` region, which adds the two reads everything else is made of:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/names-checkpoint.mjs","region":"leb128","language":"js","title":"LEB128 numbers and names","change":"Replace the leb128 region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/names-checkpoint.mjs","region":"leb128","title":"LEB128 numbers and names","change":"Replace the leb128 region."}
  // Unsigned LEB128: 7 bits per byte, lowest first. A byte with its top bit
  // set says another byte follows.
  u32() {
    let value = 0;
    let shift = 0;
    let b;
    do {
      b = this.byte();
      value += (b & 0x7f) * 2 ** shift;
      shift += 7;
    } while (b & 0x80);
    return value;
  }

  // A length, then that many bytes of UTF-8 text.
  name() {
    const length = this.u32();
    const end = this.pos + length;
    if (end > this.bytes.length)
      throw Error('functionNames: a name runs past the end of the file');
    const text = new globalThis.TextDecoder().decode(
      this.bytes.subarray(this.pos, end),
    );
    this.pos = end;
    return text;
  }
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`u32` adds each byte's low 7 bits at the place `shift` gives them, 0, then 7, then 14, and goes on while the byte's top bit, `0x80`, is set. Take `B8 02`: `B8 & 0x7f` is 56, added at shift 0, and the top bit is set; `02` adds 2 at shift 7, which is 256, and its top bit is clear, so the number is 312. Multiplying by `2 ** shift` keeps the arithmetic in ordinary numbers. JavaScript's `<<` works on 32-bit signed integers, so in a fifth byte, at shift 28, it could turn a large number negative. `name()` reads a length with `u32` and decodes that many bytes as text, so every name in the file costs one call.

### Walk the sections

Replace the `sections` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/names-checkpoint.mjs","region":"sections","language":"js","title":"functionNames: find the name section","change":"Replace the sections region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/names-checkpoint.mjs","region":"sections","title":"functionNames: find the name section","change":"Replace the sections region."}
// { [index]: name } for every function the "name" section names; {} without one.
export function functionNames(bytes) {
  const magic = [0x00, 0x61, 0x73, 0x6d];
  if (!magic.every((b, i) => bytes[i] === b))
    throw Error('functionNames: not a WebAssembly file');
  const r = new Reader(bytes, 8);
  while (r.pos < bytes.length) {
    const id = r.byte();
    const size = r.u32();
    const end = r.pos + size;
    if (id === 0 && r.name() === 'name') return functionSubsection(r, end);
    r.pos = end;
  }
  return {};
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

After the 8 fixed bytes, each section starts with its id and size, so `end` is where the next section begins. A section that isn't custom, or a custom section with another name, is skipped by setting `pos` to `end` without reading its contents. Only custom sections have a name to read, which is why the test reads it only when `id === 0`. A file without a name section runs out of sections and gets `{}`.

### Read subsection 1

Replace the `subsections` region:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/names-checkpoint.mjs","region":"subsections","language":"js","title":"Every function's index and name","change":"Replace the subsections region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/names-checkpoint.mjs","region":"subsections","title":"Every function's index and name","change":"Replace the subsections region."}
// Inside the name section: subsections, each an id byte, a size and contents.
// Subsection 1 is a count, then each function's index and name; skip the rest.
function functionSubsection(r, end) {
  const names = {};
  while (r.pos < end) {
    const id = r.byte();
    const size = r.u32();
    const next = r.pos + size;
    if (id === 1) {
      for (let n = r.u32(); n > 0; n--) {
        const index = r.u32();
        names[index] = r.name();
      }
    }
    r.pos = next;
  }
  return names;
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

Each subsection is found the way sections were, by its id and size, and `next` is where the following one begins. Subsection 1 is read entry by entry: an index, then a name. Every other subsection, the module's name in subsection 0 among them, is skipped by jumping to `next`. Setting `pos` to `next` after subsection 1 too means the next subsection is read from where it really starts, even if subsection 1 held more than its entries. The order of subsections doesn't matter, which is what the check's small file tests.

Read Lob's names with your `functionNames`:

```
node examples/show-names.mjs project
```

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/names-output.txt","language":"text","title":"The names your functionNames reads"} -->
```text {"file":"examples/names-output.txt","title":"The names your functionNames reads"}
targets/lob-names.wasm: 7271 bytes, 29 names
  0 server_round    1 js_cos          2 js_sin          3 server_wind
  4 game_init       5 new_round       6 update_hud      7 game_key
  8 game_tick       9 r_angle         10 r_power        11 r_cannon_x
  12 r_target_x     13 r_flying       14 r_px           15 r_py

<!-- /code-example -->

The named build is 589 bytes longer than the stripped one, and those bytes are the name section. The stripped build has no section called `name`, so the walk reaches the end of the file and returns `{}`. Most of these names were already in the listing. The game exports `game_init`, `game_key`, `game_tick` and every getter under these names, and it imports `server_round` and `server_wind` under theirs. Only the name section holds the names of the two functions the game doesn't export, `new_round` and `update_hud`, and the C names of the two imports the game asks for as `cos` and `sin`. In `debug.mjs`, `break update_hud` now finds function 6 by its name.

## The call stack

Your machine already keeps the call stack in `state.frames`, outermost first, each with the function it's running and the `at` of its next instruction. `stack()` returns `[{ func, at }]` for those frames at the debugger's current position, or `[]` between calls. A call to an import pushes no frame, because the import runs outside the machine and returns at once.

In `debug.mjs`, `stack` prints the frames with names, and `where` names the instruction that runs next.

Question 12b: you stop where `update_hud`, function 6, begins during a call to `game_tick`. How many entries does `stack()` return? Commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 12b YOUR_ANSWER
```

A stop where `update_hud` begins comes after `game_tick`'s `call` instruction has pushed `update_hud`'s frame, so that frame counts. A call that comes from outside the game, from the recording rather than from another function, works differently. It begins between calls, so at a stop where it begins, its instruction 0 runs next but no function is running yet, and `stack()` is `[]`.

### List the frames

In `project/debugger.mjs`, find the `stack` region near the end of the class. It holds the stub of `stack()`, which throws "stack: not written yet (lesson 12)". Replace everything between `// region: stack` and `// endregion: stack` with the listing below. If your file has no such markers, because you wrote it without lesson 10's starter, replace your `stack()` stub with the listing and add the two marker lines around it:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs","region":"stack","language":"js","title":"stack(): the frames, outermost first","change":"Replace the stack region, which holds the stack() stub."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs","region":"stack","title":"stack(): the frames, outermost first","change":"Replace the stack region, which holds the stack() stub."}
  stack() {
    return this.machine.state.frames.map((f) => ({ func: f.func, at: f.at }));
  }
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The frames are copied into new objects, so a caller that changes what `stack()` returned can't change the machine. Each frame's `at` is the instruction that frame runs next: the innermost frame's is the instruction that runs next in the whole run, and a caller's is the instruction after its `call`, where it carries on when the call returns. Between calls the machine has no frames, so the list is empty, which is what `API.md` asks.

Check `12.stack` compares your stacks with a fresh machine at many positions.

## Stopping at a function

A **function stop** fires at a position where a call to that function begins, meaning the next instruction is the function's instruction 0. Add `functions: [index]` to the stops `continue` and `continueBack` understand, with `reason: 'function'`. In `debug.mjs`, `break update_hud` adds a function stop by name, and `break 6:120` a breakpoint at one instruction.

Two places in lesson 10's `debugger.mjs` need the change. `stopHere`, in the `stops` region, tests the stops at each position, so it needs the function test. And `continueBack`, in the `search-back` region, decides which stretches it may skip with `const watchesOnly = !stops.breakpoints?.length;`. A function stop, like a breakpoint, can fire in a stretch that writes nothing, so that line must count function stops too. Left as it is, a `continueBack` given only `functions` counts as "watches only" with no watched pages, skips every stretch and reports `'start'`.

Your first `node lab.mjs check project 12` doesn't say "not written yet" for `12.function-stops`. Lesson 10's `continue` and `continueBack` already exist and run; they ignore a `functions` list they don't know, so the check gets a real answer from them, such as `{ reason: "end" }` from `continue`, and prints it beside the stop it expected.

### Test for a function stop

Tour the supplied `nextInstruction` again, just above `where` in your `debugger.mjs`. During a call it answers the innermost frame's next instruction, and between calls the first instruction of the next call, `{ func: this.callFunc[calls], at: 0 }`. So the instruction a call begins with is visible at the position before it runs, whether the call comes from another function or from the recording.

Replace the `stops` region. Only the marked lines differ from lesson 10's:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs","region":"stops","language":"js","title":"stopHere with function stops","change":"Replace the stops region; the marked lines are new.","focus":[1,10,11,12]} -->
```js {"file":"examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs","region":"stops","title":"stopHere with function stops","change":"Replace the stops region; the marked lines are new.","focus":[1,10,11,12]}
  stopHere({ breakpoints = [], watches = [], functions = [] }, event) {
    if (event && event.writes.some((w) => changesWatched(w, watches)))
      return 'watchpoint';
    const next = this.nextInstruction();
    if (
      next &&
      breakpoints.some((b) => b.func === next.func && b.at === next.at)
    )
      return 'breakpoint';
    // A function's instruction 0 runs next only where a call to it begins.
    if (next && next.at === 0 && functions.includes(next.func))
      return 'function';
    return null;
  }

  continue(stops = {}) {
    while (this.tick < this.end) {
      const event = this.forward();
      const reason = this.stopHere(stops, event);
      if (reason) return { reason, tick: this.tick };
    }
    return { reason: 'end', tick: this.tick };
  }
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`stopHere` now takes `functions`, defaulting to none, so every caller from lesson 10 still works. The function test looks forward, like the breakpoint test, at the instruction that runs next. Both halves of its condition matter: the function must be one of the stopped ones, and its instruction 0 must be next. Instruction 0 of a function runs next only where a call to it begins, because a branch inside a function goes either forward to the end of a block or back to the first instruction inside a `loop`, after the `loop` instruction itself, and neither is instruction 0. `continue` is unchanged: it already asks `stopHere` after every instruction.

Then replace the `search-back` region. Only the marked line differs from lesson 10's:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs","region":"search-back","language":"js","title":"continueBack skips stretches only when every stop is a watch","change":"Replace the search-back region; the marked line is changed.","focus":[7]} -->
```js {"file":"examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs","region":"search-back","title":"continueBack skips stretches only when every stop is a watch","change":"Replace the search-back region; the marked line is changed.","focus":[7]}
  continueBack(stops = {}) {
    const here = this.tick;
    if (here === 0) return { reason: 'start', tick: 0 };
    const pages = (stops.watches ?? []).flatMap((w) =>
      pagesOf(w.address, w.size ?? 1, this.pageSize),
    );
    const watchesOnly = !stops.breakpoints?.length && !stops.functions?.length;
    const found = this.searchBack(
      here - 1,
      (event) => {
        const reason = this.stopHere(stops, event);
        return reason ? { reason, tick: this.tick } : null;
      },
      (i) => !watchesOnly || this.mayHaveWritten(i, pages),
    );
    if (found) {
      this.moveTo(found.tick);
      return found;
    }
    this.moveTo(0);
    return { reason: this.stopHere(stops, null) ?? 'start', tick: 0 };
  }

  searchBack(last, test, mayMatch = () => true) {
    for (let i = Math.ceil(last / this.every) - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
      if (!mayMatch(i)) continue;
      const snapshot = this.snapshots[i];
      const stop = Math.min(last, snapshot.tick + this.every);
      this.restore(snapshot);
      let found = null;
      while (this.tick < stop) {
        const finding = test(this.forward());
        if (finding) found = finding;
      }
      if (found) return found;
    }
    return null;
  }

  mayHaveWritten(i, pages) {
    const a = this.snapshots[i];
    const b = this.snapshots[i + 1];
    return !b || pages.some((p) => a.pages[p] !== b.pages[p]);
  }
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`watchesOnly` decides whether `continueBack` may skip a stretch whose watched pages stayed shared. With a function stop present it is now false, so every stretch going back is replayed until one holds a stop, as with a breakpoint. The cost is about the distance to the stop plus up to two stretches, lesson 10's cost for a breakpoint.

### Run to the end of the function

`stepOut()` runs forward until the function running now has returned to its caller, that is, until the call stack is shorter than it is now. In `debug.mjs` it's `finish`. Between calls there is no function running. Define what `stepOut()` does there and say so in a comment.

Find the `step-out` region, which holds the stub of `stepOut()` that throws "stepOut: not written yet (lesson 12)". Replace everything between `// region: step-out` and `// endregion: step-out` with the listing below, or, in a file without those markers, replace your `stepOut()` stub and add the two marker lines around it:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs","region":"step-out","language":"js","title":"stepOut: forward until there are fewer frames","change":"Replace the step-out region, which holds the stepOut() stub."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/stack-checkpoint.mjs","region":"step-out","title":"stepOut: forward until there are fewer frames","change":"Replace the step-out region, which holds the stepOut() stub."}
  // Forward to the first position with fewer frames than now. Between calls no
  // function is running, so stepOut runs the whole next call and stops where it
  // has returned, at the next position between calls. At the end it stays.
  stepOut() {
    const depth = this.machine.state.frames.length;
    if (depth === 0) {
      if (this.tick < this.end) {
        do {
          this.forward();
        } while (this.machine.running);
      }
    } else {
      while (this.machine.state.frames.length >= depth) this.forward();
    }
    return this.tick;
  }
```
<!-- /code-example -->

Inside a call, `stepOut` counts the frames now and runs instructions until there are fewer. A deeper call made on the way pushes a frame and pops it again without stopping it, so the stop comes when the current function's own `return` or final `end` pops its frame. The first position with fewer frames is where the caller carries on, or, for the outermost function of a call, the position between calls after it. Between calls, this checkpoint runs the whole next call, the one `where()` names, and stops where it has returned. Another choice would do, such as refusing or not moving, as long as the comment says which. `forward()` is lesson 10's: between calls it begins the next call first. Moving forward replays only the distance moved, so `stepOut` costs the instructions it runs.

Checks `12.function-stops` and `12.step-out` compare your stops with a scan of every instruction. `12.function-stops` seeks to positions spread over a recording and from each asks both `continue` and `continueBack` for a function stop. `12.step-out` seeks to positions inside calls and calls `stepOut`, which counts frames and passes no stops to the debugger. `12.stack` seeks and compares `stack()` with a fresh machine, and `12.names` and `12.lines` call only `names.mjs`.

All four changes to `debugger.mjs` are in. `examples/stack-session.txt` is a script of `debug.mjs` commands that goes to the first game frame of lesson 09's recording, stops where `update_hud` begins, prints the stack, runs to the end of `update_hud` with `finish`, and then continues backward to the stop again:

```
node debug.mjs project project/run42.json examples/stack-session.txt
```

The function stop fires with `update_hud`'s instruction 0 next, and the stack shows `game_tick` waiting at its instruction 570, the one after its `call`. `finish` stops where `update_hud`'s frame has gone and `game_tick` carries on at instruction 570, 670 instructions after the stop. `rcontinue` goes back to the same stop. The two `cost` lines differ by 983: 826 instructions to replay the stretch from the snapshot at 84,000 up to the position before the one `rcontinue` started from, where it found the stop, and 157 to move back to the stop from that snapshot. The first `cost` also counts the replay your Debugger made when it opened the recording, and the seeks `call 13` made.

## Lines

The compiler can also write a **line table**, which gives, for each stretch of code, the line of the C source it came from. It lives in `.debug_line`, one of the sections of DWARF, the standard format for debugging information, which only a build with debugging information carries. No file this course ships carries DWARF, because DWARF also records the layout of every C struct, which is what Sightline asks its learners to work out. The course decoded the line table of a debugging build when it built the targets and saved its rows in `lines/lob.json`: `{ offset, line, column }`, sorted by `offset`. DWARF counts a WebAssembly address from the start of the code section's contents, after its id byte and size (the code section holds the functions' instructions, and the listing records that start as `codeSectionStart`). The course added that start, so `offset` is a file offset like the listing's `offsets`, where `offsets[k]` is the file offset of instruction k.

An instruction belongs to the last row at or before its offset. `lineAt(lines, offset)` finds that row with a binary search and returns `{ line, column }`, or `null` before the first row.

Some rows say line 0. That is DWARF's way of saying the compiler made this code without a line of its own, and 561 of Lob's 2,806 instructions fall on such rows, among them instructions of loop bodies the compiler unrolled, writing the body out several times in a row. In lesson 08's clearing loop, the `local.get` and `i32.const` that begin each copy after the first fall on line 0. `debug.mjs` prints "no line" for any instruction on a line-0 row. DWARF also marks the end of each function's rows with an end-of-sequence row. The course kept those as rows of line 0 at the end of each function's code, so the last line of one function never covers the start of the next.

The C source isn't given, so a line number is a label rather than a place you can read. It still groups instructions into statements. An assignment compiled to eight instructions gives all eight one line, and comparing lines is how a debugger steps by line.

Here are five rows of `lines/lob.json`, around the end of the loop of lesson 08 that clears memory in `game_init`:

```
offset  line  column
   555   259      52
   561     0      52
   565   259      26
   566   259       3
   571   260       5
```

Question 12c: instruction 47 of `game_init`, the `br_if 0` that closes that loop, is at file offset 568. What line does `lineAt` give it? Commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 12c YOUR_ANSWER
```

### Find the row

Replace the `line-at` region of `project/names.mjs`:

<!-- code-example {"file":"examples/names-checkpoint.mjs","region":"line-at","language":"js","title":"lineAt: the last row at or before an offset","change":"Replace the line-at region."} -->
```js {"file":"examples/names-checkpoint.mjs","region":"line-at","title":"lineAt: the last row at or before an offset","change":"Replace the line-at region."}
// { line, column } of the last row at or before `offset`, or null when every
// row comes after it. Rows are sorted by offset.
export function lineAt(lines, offset) {
  let lo = 0;
  let hi = lines.length;
  // Rows before lo are at or before offset; rows from hi on come after it.
  while (lo < hi) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
    if (lines[mid].offset <= offset) lo = mid + 1;
    else hi = mid;
  }
  if (lo === 0) return null;
  return { line: lines[lo - 1].line, column: lines[lo - 1].column };
}
```
<!-- /code-example -->

The search keeps one rule true as `lo` and `hi` close in: every row before `lo` is at or before `offset`, and every row from `hi` on comes after it. When they meet, `lo` is the first row past `offset`, so the row just before it is the answer. When `lo` is still 0, every row comes after the offset and there is no line. Lob's table has 1,050 rows, so a question takes at most 11 comparisons. A row of line 0 is returned like any other; deciding what it means is left to the caller, as `debug.mjs` does.

Check `12.lines` asks `lineAt` about every instruction of Lob and compares with the rows.

`debug.mjs` calls your `lineAt` from its supplied `describe` function, which every command uses to print an instruction. Tour it near the top of `debug.mjs`: it looks up the instruction's file offset in the listing, `f.offsets[at]`, asks `lineOf`, which calls your `lineAt`, for the row, and adds `[line N]` after the instruction, or `[no line]` for a row of line 0, beside the name your `functionNames` gave. Run the same script again:

```
node debug.mjs project project/run42.json examples/stack-session.txt
```

## Use it on a new case: step by line

`step` moves one instruction, and `finish` a whole function. A person reading C wants a step between the two: run to the next line of the function they're in, stepping over any function it calls, as gdb's `next` does. Write `nextLine(debugger, program, lines)` in `project/next-line.mjs`, which both route commands created. If you didn't use them, copy `starter/next-line.mjs` to `project/next-line.mjs` first. No finished version is supplied, and none of the listings above does this. Its contract:

- `program` is the listing the debugger replays and `lines` the rows of `lines/lob.json`. The line of a position is the line `lineAt` gives the instruction that runs next there. A row of line 0, or no row at all, counts as no line.
- From the current position, run forward to the first later position where there are fewer frames than at the start, because the current function has returned, or where there are as many frames as at the start and there is a line, different from the start's line. Leave the debugger standing there and return that position.
- Positions with more frames than at the start are inside functions the current line called, and never end the step, whatever their lines.
- Between calls, the end of the run included, no function is running and there's no line to step over: throw an error, without moving and without running anything.
- Use only the Debugger's public surface (`tick`, `end`, `step`, `seek`, `stack`, `where`), the listing's `offsets` and your own `lineAt`, so your function works with any debugger that meets `API.md`.

The budget holds for every question the checker asks: a step may run at most the number of instructions it moves forward, plus 2,000. Moving forward one instruction at a time costs exactly the distance, and the 2,000 leave room for one restore from a snapshot and a short replay. A step that replays from position 0, or from far behind, for each instruction doesn't fit.

Before you write code, answer two questions in `project/report.md`. A line calls `update_hud`, and `update_hud`'s own instructions carry other lines: what tells you to keep going inside it, and what would go wrong if you compared only lines? A loop whose whole body is on one line jumps back to its start: where does your step stop? Keep that first reasoning. Then run the checker on the unfinished file, implement, and run it again, describing assistance honestly each time:

```sh
node examples/check-next-line.mjs project --help-used "initial attempt; nothing written"
node examples/check-next-line.mjs project --help-used "describe what helped your implementation"
```

The checker copies `machine.mjs`, `recorder.mjs`, `debugger.mjs`, `names.mjs`, `next-line.mjs`, `PROJECT.json` and your `report.md` into a new folder under `project/attempts/` before it runs anything, and saves its results beside them in `nline-receipt.json`. A failure never replaces an earlier attempt, and `node lab.mjs status project` lists every attempt under "New-application attempts". It replays one of unit 10's check recordings, a run of Lob, once on your machine, keeping the frames and the instruction at every position, and works out each answer from that pass and the line table. It then asks six groups of questions: refusals between calls and at the end; a line followed by another line of the same function; a line that calls a function; the last line of a function; line-0 instructions and a long loop on one line in `game_init`; and twenty steps in a row through a game frame.

As a stretch, add a `next` command to your own copy of `debug.mjs` that calls `nextLine`.

  <main id="chapter"><h1 id="13-the-ladder">13 · The ladder</h1>
<p>Six later builds of the game each misbehave in one way, five of Lob and one of Lob II, and each comes with a recording of a run that went wrong. By the end of this lesson you will have named, for each build, the <strong>first bad write</strong>, the earliest store in the run that leaves a byte of memory holding a value a correct build wouldn&#39;t hold there at the same point of the run (<code>API.md</code> defines it under &quot;investigations/N.txt&quot;). <p>Your project must pass the checks of units 08 to 12 first, because every script runs on your machine, recorder, debugger, index and names. If one of them fails and you want to go on with this lesson, make a new project with <code>node examples/start-chapter.mjs project13 supplied</code>, then <code>node examples/start-recorder.mjs project13 supplied</code>, <code>node examples/start-debugger.mjs project13 supplied</code>, <code>node examples/start-query.mjs project13 supplied</code> and <code>node examples/start-names.mjs project13 supplied</code>, and use <code>project13</code> wherever this lesson says <code>project</code>. The ladder&#39;s recordings are supplied, so it needs no recording of its own.</p>

Your own work: builds 2 to 6, and <code>changes.mjs</code>.</p>
<p><strong>Time:</strong> allow about 30 to 45 minutes to read and work through build 1, and many hours for builds 2 to 6, which rise in difficulty. These are planning estimates, not measured learner times.</p>

The new application needs one file, which this command adds:</p>

<h2 id="what-you-have-and-what-you-don-t">What you have and what you don&#39;t</h2>
<p>For each build you get its <code>.wasm</code> file (with function names), its listing in <code>programs/ladder/</code>, and its recording in <code>recordings/ladder/</code>. You don&#39;t get its C source, and its memory is laid out differently from <code>lob.wasm</code>. The game&#39;s state sits elsewhere and its fields are in another order. So you can&#39;t find the change by comparing memory with <code>lob.wasm</code>, and a listing compared line by line with <code>lob.wasm</code>&#39;s differs almost everywhere.</p>
<p>What you can compare is behaviour. <code>lob.wasm</code> is the last good build of Lob, and <code>lob2.wasm</code> is the last good build of Lob II, the good build for build 6. Their getters, <code>r_px</code>, <code>r_result</code> (the kind of landing) and the rest (<code>getters</code> prints them all), or <code>g0</code> to <code>g7</code> for Lob II, mean the same in every build of the same game. <code>debug.mjs</code> runs both builds on the recording&#39;s calls in Node&#39;s own engine:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>diverge</code> names the first call after which a getter of this build differs from the good build&#39;s (this is <code>debug.mjs</code>&#39;s <code>diverge</code>, not the lab&#39;s from lesson 09)</li>
<li><code>compare</code> shows every getter of both builds side by side after the calls so far, and for a build of Lob each build&#39;s status line, message line and help text too.</li>
</ul>
<p>Neither command uses your machine or counts towards the budget. They tell you where to look, and your debugger finds the write.</p>
<h2 id="the-method">The method</h2>
<p>Work backward from the first visible difference to the first bad write.</p>
<ol>
<li>Find the first visible difference. Start from the build&#39;s symptom, or run <code>diverge</code>. Note the call and the getter.</li>
<li>Find the address. A getter reads memory, so run it in your head from the listing, or stand between calls and <code>read</code> the bytes it reads. In Lob, <code>r_px</code> reads the pointer at 78,112 and then the 4 bytes at an offset from it. In a ladder build the pointer&#39;s address and the offset can both differ (build 1&#39;s pointer is at 72,992), and the listing gives both. The address the pointer holds, where the state lives, also depends on the seed, <code>game_init</code>&#39;s first argument, even in the good build: <code>lob.wasm</code> keeps its state at 65,888 in a game started with seed 4 and at 66,304 with seed 30. Read the pointer at the call you are investigating, in the run you are investigating. In mode 2 the game moves its state to a new address at every new round (API.md, &quot;public/sessions.mjs&quot;), so an address read in round 2 may hold something else in round 1.</li>
<li>Find who wrote it. Stand at the start of the call after the one where the getter first differs (<code>call 238</code> after a difference in call 237). There <code>last-write ADDR</code> (your Debugger) or <code>who ADDR</code> (your index) takes you to the last store to that byte.</li>
<li>Judge that store. Read its value and ask <code>sources</code> which stores, answers and arguments it was computed from. In a ladder build a chain can hold hundreds of stores, so <code>sources</code> prints their count and the newest 8, each with its tick, function and address, and <code>sources N</code> shows the newest N. If one of its inputs was already wrong, that input&#39;s store is earlier on the chain, so go back to step 3 with it. If all its inputs hold the values a correct build would have, and its result is still wrong, the planted change acts here.</li>
<li>Look just before it. The code that made one wrong store often made others a few instructions earlier, from the same wrong decision. Step back a little (<code>back 30</code>) and list what the next instructions write (<code>writes 30</code>, which also moves the debugger 30 instructions forward, back where you stood). The earliest store in that stretch with a wrong value is your new candidate, even if it isn&#39;t the one your symptom led you to. If the stretch&#39;s first store is already wrong, step back further.</li>
<li>List every change. A wrong byte&#39;s last writer may not be the store that first made it wrong. Remove earlier stops with <code>clear</code>, then set <code>watch ADDR</code> on the byte, <code>seek 0</code> and <code>continue</code> again and again. Each stop is right after a store that changed the byte, so the stops list every change to it from the start of the run.</li>
<li>Name it. Stand right after the first bad write (<code>last-write</code>, <code>who</code> and a watch&#39;s stop leave you there, and after <code>writes</code>, <code>seek</code> the tick it printed for that store) and run <code>answer</code>.</li>
</ol>
<p>Judging a store needs a notion of right, which you can take from the help text (angle 5 to 85, power 10 to 100, land within 12 paces to score), what the good build shows through its getters on the same calls, and arithmetic you can redo from the listing. Lob II&#39;s getters don&#39;t say what they hold, so for build 6 your notion of right comes from <code>compare</code> against <code>lob2.wasm</code> and from the build&#39;s symptom in <code>node lab.mjs ladder</code>.</p>
<p>The store your symptom leads to may not be the first wrong one. Step 5 exists because a wrong decision usually makes several stores. The last writer of a wrong value isn&#39;t always the first bad write either. The same wrong store may have run earlier, and its earlier result may since have been overwritten, which step 6 shows. And a store can write a right value to the wrong address. Then every input <code>sources</code> lists is right, because the chain doesn&#39;t follow addresses, so look at how the address was computed.</p>
<p>Question 13a: in some build, a store writes 0 over 0 at the first byte of the message line. Just before this store, at the same point of the run, the good build&#39;s message already reads HIT!, so its first byte holds H. Can that store be the first bad write? Answer <code>yes</code> or <code>no</code>, and commit:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs predict project 13a YOUR_ANSWER</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<h2 id="a-worked-investigation-build-1">A worked investigation: build 1</h2>
<p>Build 1&#39;s symptom: the second shell lands 10 paces short of the flag and the message reads SHORT BY 10, although the help says a shell within 12 paces scores. <code>lob.wasm</code> shows HIT! on the same calls. Here is the investigation, built up in <code>project/investigations/1.txt</code> one step of the method at a time. After each step, run the script so far:</p>

<p><code>compare</code> runs both builds through calls 0 to 237 in Node&#39;s engine, in the supplied <code>nodeGetters</code> function, and prints every getter side by side, then the texts. The shell&#39;s landing place and the flag agree with <code>lob.wasm</code>&#39;s (<code>r_impact_x</code> and <code>r_target_x</code>), about 10.1 apart, within 12, and so do the angle, power and wind. Only <code>r_result</code>, the status line and the message differ, besides the getters that return addresses, which differ by design. So the store&#39;s inputs were right and the decision it stored is wrong.</p>
<p><code>sources</code> asks your index for the chain of the store at the current tick. The supplied <code>chainStores</code> prints how many stores the chain holds, then the newest 8, newest first, each found through your index&#39;s <code>lastWriter</code> so that its function and address can be shown; <code>sources N</code> shows the newest N and <code>sources all</code> every one. This chain holds 436 stores, reaching back through the shell&#39;s flight to the cosine and sine of the barrel&#39;s angle and the seed, call 0&#39;s argument 0. Building the index replayed the run once more on your machine, which is why this tour isn&#39;t part of the script: the script&#39;s budget doesn&#39;t need it.</p>
<h3 id="answer-at-the-result-store">Answer at the result store</h3>
<p>A store whose inputs are right and whose value is wrong looks like the planted change at work, so you might name it now. Add one line, <code>answer</code>, at the end of <code>project/investigations/1.txt</code>, after <code>last-write 65928</code>.</p>
<p>Question 13d: with that answer, will <code>13.build-1</code> pass or fail? Before you run anything, write in <code>project/report.md</code> which unit 13 checks you expect to pass and fail, and why, then commit <code>pass</code> or <code>fail</code>. Then run the checks:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Terminal command</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Terminal command; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs predict project 13d YOUR_ANSWER</span>
<span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs check project 13 --help-used &quot;worked investigation of build 1; answer at the result store&quot;</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>Compare what the check printed with what the lab said after your prediction. Keep this attempt and delete the <code>answer</code> line you added.</p>

<p><code>back 12</code> steps back from the result store, and <code>writes 12</code> steps the debugger forward again over the same 12 instructions and lists the bytes each one wrote. To see an instruction&#39;s writes, it runs that instruction once more on a copy of the state, then moves the debugger on, so after <code>writes 12</code> the debugger stands 12 instructions later, at tick 261,685, right after the result store. There are two stores: at tick 261,676, instruction 295 stored 10 at 66,540, and at tick 261,685 the result. 10 is the miss distance the message prints, and the 13 it replaced was the first shell&#39;s, which landed 13 paces long. A hit stores 0 there. Both stores are wrong, and the miss distance came first.</p>

<p>The symptom you start from decides which wrong store you meet first. Starting from the message text, SHORT BY 10, found through the getter <code>r_msg_ptr</code> at the pointer held at 72,996, <code>last-write</code> on the digit 1 finds the store that wrote it, and <code>sources</code> on that store lists the miss distance&#39;s store, tick 261,676, among the newest on its chain. The route from <code>r_result</code>, as above, leads to the result, nine instructions too late. Step 5 is what turns the second route into the right answer.</p>
<p>Question 13b: your debugger keeps a snapshot every 2,000 instructions. Build 5&#39;s run is 647,416 instructions long. At most how many instructions can one <code>stepBack(1)</code> replay? Commit:</p>

Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<h2 id="your-investigations">Your investigations</h2>
<p>To explore a build, open it in your debugger by its number. <code>node debug.mjs project N</code> loads build N&#39;s recording and listing and knows its good build, so <code>diverge</code> and <code>compare</code> work. Try commands there, then copy the ones that lead to the answer into a script. With no keyboard, put the commands you want to try in a file, one per line, and pass it as the last argument: <code>node debug.mjs project N FILE</code>.</p>
<p>Write each investigation in <code>project/investigations/N.txt</code>, one command per line, and run it:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs investigate project N</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>The lab prints every command&#39;s output, the answer, and how many instructions your machine replayed. The budget counts everything your debugger and index run, from opening the recording to the answer. It leaves room for one index build, a first pass of your debugger and a few dozen backward questions. Replaying from the start for each question doesn&#39;t fit.</p>
<p>The builds rise in difficulty. Builds 1 and 2 are a short way back from the symptom. Build 3 makes a run of stores in one call that shouldn&#39;t have happened at all, and you need the first of them that left a byte different from a correct build&#39;s. Builds 4 to 6 hide the first bad write behind later writes, so either the symptom&#39;s last writer isn&#39;t the answer or the corrupted value travels through other stores before anything visible goes wrong. In every build here the run first goes wrong at a store the build makes, never by leaving out a store a correct build makes (<code>API.md</code> says so under &quot;investigations/N.txt&quot;). So a store that finds its byte already wrong can&#39;t be the first bad write, which came earlier.</p>
<p>Checks <code>13.build-1</code>, <code>13.build-2</code>, <code>13.build-3</code>, <code>13.build-4</code>, <code>13.build-5</code> and <code>13.build-6</code> run your scripts the same way and compare your answers with the first bad writes. One command runs all six:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Terminal command</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Terminal command; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs check project 13 --help-used &quot;describe what helped&quot;</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>A wrong answer says only that it&#39;s wrong. The checks keep each answer only as a slow salted hash, a fingerprint the checks can compare your answer with but can&#39;t read the answer from, so they can&#39;t show it to you.</p>
<p>Question 13c: in <code>project/run42.json</code> the shot counter is stored by the first shot, in call 19, and the second shot&#39;s increment, in call 396, loads it. How did the first count reach the second shot&#39;s code? (a) as an argument of the call to <code>game_key</code>, (b) the first shot stored it in memory and the second loaded it, or (c) through an import&#39;s answer. Answer <code>a</code>, <code>b</code> or <code>c</code>, and commit:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Observed output</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Observed output; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node lab.mjs predict project 13c YOUR_ANSWER</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<h2 id="use-it-on-a-new-case-list-every-change">Use it on a new case: list every change</h2>
<p>Step 6 of the method lists every change to a byte by hand: <code>clear</code>, <code>watch ADDR</code>, <code>seek 0</code>, then <code>continue</code> again and again, reading the byte at each stop. Write it as a function you can call on any bytes: <code>changesOf(debugger, { address, size })</code> in <code>project/changes.mjs</code>, which <code>node examples/start-changes.mjs project</code> added at the start of this lesson. If you skipped it, run it now; it never replaces an existing <code>changes.mjs</code>. No finished version is supplied, and nothing in the worked investigation does this. Its contract:</p>
<ul>
<li>Return, in tick order, one entry <code>{ tick, before, after }</code> for every instruction at or before the debugger&#39;s current position that changed at least one of the <code>size</code> bytes at <code>address</code>. <code>before</code> and <code>after</code> are arrays of the <code>size</code> byte values just before and just after that instruction.</li>
<li>A store that rewrites a byte with the value it already holds doesn&#39;t change it, so it has no entry, as a watch doesn&#39;t stop there. At position 0 no instruction has run, so the list is empty.</li>
<li>Leave the debugger at the position it started from.</li>
<li>Refuse, with an error, before moving and before running anything: an <code>address</code> or <code>size</code> that isn&#39;t a whole number, a <code>size</code> below 1, or bytes outside memory.</li>
<li>Use only the Debugger&#39;s public surface (<code>tick</code>, <code>end</code>, <code>seek</code>, <code>step</code>, <code>continue</code>, <code>read</code> and its <code>snapshots</code>), so your function works with any debugger that meets <code>API.md</code>.</li>
</ul>
<p>The budget holds for every question, whatever the bytes and the position: one call may replay at most the whole run once, <code>end</code> instructions, plus 2,000. Watching forward from position 0 costs at most the run&#39;s length, and the 2,000 leave room for one restore from a snapshot and a short replay back to where the question started. Going back to position 0 again for each change doesn&#39;t fit.</p>
<p>Before you write code, answer two questions in <code>project/report.md</code>. Your function stops right after a change: how do you know what the bytes held just before it without stepping back? A change happens one instruction after your starting position: is it in the list, and how do you avoid it? Keep that first reasoning. Then run the checker on the unfinished file, implement, and run it again, describing assistance honestly each time:</p>
<figure class="code-example"><figcaption><strong>Terminal command</strong></figcaption><pre tabindex="0" aria-label="Terminal command; code scrolls horizontally when needed"><code><span class="cex-line">node examples/check-changes.mjs project --help-used &quot;initial attempt; nothing written&quot;</span>
<span class="cex-line">node examples/check-changes.mjs project --help-used &quot;describe what helped your implementation&quot;</span></code></pre><div class="cex-foot"> Select code to copy. Scroll horizontally if needed.</div></figure>
<p>The checker copies <code>machine.mjs</code>, <code>recorder.mjs</code>, <code>debugger.mjs</code>, <code>changes.mjs</code>, <code>PROJECT.json</code> and your <code>report.md</code> into a new folder under <code>project/attempts/</code> before it runs anything, and saves its results beside them in <code>changes-receipt.json</code>. A failure never replaces an earlier attempt, and <code>node lab.mjs status project</code> lists every attempt under &quot;New-application attempts&quot;. It replays two of unit 10&#39;s check recordings, a Lob run and a Lob II run, once on your machine, keeping every change to every byte, and asks six groups of questions: bad questions; the pointer at 78,112, which only <code>game_init</code> changes; a counter every game frame changes, asked from the middle of the run; the same counter at position 0; a byte some stores rewrite with the value it already holds; and a Lob II value that changes a few times. None of them is about a ladder build.</p>
<p>As a stretch, add a <code>changes ADDR SIZE</code> command to your own copy of <code>debug.mjs</code> that calls <code>changesOf</code>, and use it on the builds.</p>
<h2 id="report">Report</h2>
<p>For each build, write in <code>project/report.md</code> the chain from the symptom to the first bad write, with the tick and value of each store on it, and what you think the planted change was. The checks don&#39;t read the report. It&#39;s your record of the reasoning, and the part of this course that a check can&#39;t judge.</p>

`courses/time-travel-debugger-part-two/lessons/13.md`:

```md
# 13 · The ladder

Six later builds of the game each misbehave in one way, five of Lob and one of Lob II, and each comes with a recording of a run that went wrong. By the end of this lesson you will have named, for each build, the **first bad write**, the earliest store in the run that leaves a byte of memory holding a value a correct build wouldn't hold there at the same point of the run (`API.md` defines it under "investigations/N.txt"). Each answer comes from a script of debugger commands that your own tool runs inside a replay budget.

`node lab.mjs ladder` lists the six builds, what is wrong at the end of each recording, and each budget.

## Start

This lesson writes nothing new into your debugger. Before it, your project replays, steps backward, indexes a recording and names functions and lines, and `project/investigations/1.txt` to `6.txt` are the stubs `node lab.mjs start` made, two comment lines each, so all six unit 13 checks fail with "not written yet". After it, each of those scripts runs through `debug.mjs` on your own files and names its build's first bad write inside the build's budget, and `project/changes.mjs`, the new application, lists every change to chosen bytes from the start of a run.

Your project must pass the checks of units 08 to 12 first, because every script runs on your machine, recorder, debugger, index and names. If one of them fails and you want to go on with this lesson, make a new project with `node examples/start-chapter.mjs project13 supplied`, then `node examples/start-recorder.mjs project13 supplied`, `node examples/start-debugger.mjs project13 supplied`, `node examples/start-query.mjs project13 supplied` and `node examples/start-names.mjs project13 supplied`, and use `project13` wherever this lesson says `project`. The ladder's recordings are supplied, so it needs no recording of its own.

**Code scope:** walked through, the investigation of build 1, five listings of `project/investigations/1.txt`, 16 lines: 9 debugger commands and 7 lines of notes, each listing followed by what the script prints so far. The finished script is `examples/investigation-1.txt`, 28 lines including the two comment lines of the stub and its region markers, which are notes to `debug.mjs`. Supplied, and nothing to write: the six builds with their listings and recordings, and `debug.mjs`, whose commands run your files. Toured, in `debug.mjs`: `diverge` and `compare`, which run a build and its good build in Node's own engine; `sources`, which prints a chain's count and its newest stores; and `writes`, which lists what each instruction wrote. Your own work: builds 2 to 6, and `changes.mjs`.

**Time:** allow about 30 to 45 minutes to read and work through build 1, and many hours for builds 2 to 6, which rise in difficulty. These are planning estimates, not measured learner times.

There is no route command for this lesson. Your project already has `investigations/1.txt`; add each listing below at the end of it, in order. A supplied copy of the finished script is `examples/investigation-1.txt`; use it to compare, or copy it into a new project, never over your own script. The new application needs one file, which this command adds:

```sh
node examples/start-changes.mjs project
```

It copies `starter/changes.mjs` to `project/changes.mjs` when your project has no `changes.mjs`, leaves an existing one as it is, and says which it did. It records no route. Run the first check with a description of where you started:

```sh
node lab.mjs check project 13 --help-used "lesson 13 start; investigation stubs"
```

All six checks fail with `not written yet` while the scripts hold only notes. That is a baseline, not evidence of anything.

Each unit 13 check runs one script, `investigations/N.txt` for build N, through `debug.mjs` on your own files. It passes only when the script ends with an `answer` that names that build's first bad write, by its function, instruction, address and tick, and replays no more than the build's budget. A script whose answer names any other write fails.

## What you have and what you don't

For each build you get its `.wasm` file (with function names), its listing in `programs/ladder/`, and its recording in `recordings/ladder/`. You don't get its C source, and its memory is laid out differently from `lob.wasm`. The game's state sits elsewhere and its fields are in another order. So you can't find the change by comparing memory with `lob.wasm`, and a listing compared line by line with `lob.wasm`'s differs almost everywhere.

What you can compare is behaviour. `lob.wasm` is the last good build of Lob, and `lob2.wasm` is the last good build of Lob II, the good build for build 6. Their getters, `r_px`, `r_result` (the kind of landing) and the rest (`getters` prints them all), or `g0` to `g7` for Lob II, mean the same in every build of the same game. `debug.mjs` runs both builds on the recording's calls in Node's own engine:

- `diverge` names the first call after which a getter of this build differs from the good build's (this is `debug.mjs`'s `diverge`, not the lab's from lesson 09)
- `compare` shows every getter of both builds side by side after the calls so far, and for a build of Lob each build's status line, message line and help text too.

Neither command uses your machine or counts towards the budget. They tell you where to look, and your debugger finds the write.

## The method

Work backward from the first visible difference to the first bad write.

1. Find the first visible difference. Start from the build's symptom, or run `diverge`. Note the call and the getter.
2. Find the address. A getter reads memory, so run it in your head from the listing, or stand between calls and `read` the bytes it reads. In Lob, `r_px` reads the pointer at 78,112 and then the 4 bytes at an offset from it. In a ladder build the pointer's address and the offset can both differ (build 1's pointer is at 72,992), and the listing gives both. The address the pointer holds, where the state lives, also depends on the seed, `game_init`'s first argument, even in the good build: `lob.wasm` keeps its state at 65,888 in a game started with seed 4 and at 66,304 with seed 30. Read the pointer at the call you are investigating, in the run you are investigating. In mode 2 the game moves its state to a new address at every new round (API.md, "public/sessions.mjs"), so an address read in round 2 may hold something else in round 1.
3. Find who wrote it. Stand at the start of the call after the one where the getter first differs (`call 238` after a difference in call 237). There `last-write ADDR` (your Debugger) or `who ADDR` (your index) takes you to the last store to that byte.
4. Judge that store. Read its value and ask `sources` which stores, answers and arguments it was computed from. In a ladder build a chain can hold hundreds of stores, so `sources` prints their count and the newest 8, each with its tick, function and address, and `sources N` shows the newest N. If one of its inputs was already wrong, that input's store is earlier on the chain, so go back to step 3 with it. If all its inputs hold the values a correct build would have, and its result is still wrong, the planted change acts here.
5. Look just before it. The code that made one wrong store often made others a few instructions earlier, from the same wrong decision. Step back a little (`back 30`) and list what the next instructions write (`writes 30`, which also moves the debugger 30 instructions forward, back where you stood). The earliest store in that stretch with a wrong value is your new candidate, even if it isn't the one your symptom led you to. If the stretch's first store is already wrong, step back further.
6. List every change. A wrong byte's last writer may not be the store that first made it wrong. Remove earlier stops with `clear`, then set `watch ADDR` on the byte, `seek 0` and `continue` again and again. Each stop is right after a store that changed the byte, so the stops list every change to it from the start of the run.
7. Name it. Stand right after the first bad write (`last-write`, `who` and a watch's stop leave you there, and after `writes`, `seek` the tick it printed for that store) and run `answer`.

Judging a store needs a notion of right, which you can take from the help text (angle 5 to 85, power 10 to 100, land within 12 paces to score), what the good build shows through its getters on the same calls, and arithmetic you can redo from the listing. Lob II's getters don't say what they hold, so for build 6 your notion of right comes from `compare` against `lob2.wasm` and from the build's symptom in `node lab.mjs ladder`.

The store your symptom leads to may not be the first wrong one. Step 5 exists because a wrong decision usually makes several stores. The last writer of a wrong value isn't always the first bad write either. The same wrong store may have run earlier, and its earlier result may since have been overwritten, which step 6 shows. And a store can write a right value to the wrong address. Then every input `sources` lists is right, because the chain doesn't follow addresses, so look at how the address was computed.

Question 13a: in some build, a store writes 0 over 0 at the first byte of the message line. Just before this store, at the same point of the run, the good build's message already reads HIT!, so its first byte holds H. Can that store be the first bad write? Answer `yes` or `no`, and commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 13a YOUR_ANSWER
```

  tick 259799: function 8 (game_tick), instruction 539: f32.store 2 52 wrote 4 bytes at 65980
  tick 259783: function 8 (game_tick), instruction 523: f32.store 2 36 wrote 4 bytes at 65964
  tick 259774: function 8 (game_tick), instruction 514: f32.store 2 48 wrote 4 bytes at 65976
  tick 259769: function 8 (game_tick), instruction 509: f32.store 2 608 wrote 4 bytes at 66536
answers: 2 (cos) 3 (sin)
call arguments: call 0 argument 0
initial bytes: none
```
<!-- /code-example -->

`compare` runs both builds through calls 0 to 237 in Node's engine, in the supplied `nodeGetters` function, and prints every getter side by side, then the texts. The shell's landing place and the flag agree with `lob.wasm`'s (`r_impact_x` and `r_target_x`), about 10.1 apart, within 12, and so do the angle, power and wind. Only `r_result`, the status line and the message differ, besides the getters that return addresses, which differ by design. So the store's inputs were right and the decision it stored is wrong.

`sources` asks your index for the chain of the store at the current tick. The supplied `chainStores` prints how many stores the chain holds, then the newest 8, newest first, each found through your index's `lastWriter` so that its function and address can be shown; `sources N` shows the newest N and `sources all` every one. This chain holds 436 stores, reaching back through the shell's flight to the cosine and sine of the barrel's angle and the seed, call 0's argument 0. Building the index replayed the run once more on your machine, which is why this tour isn't part of the script: the script's budget doesn't need it.

### Answer at the result store

A store whose inputs are right and whose value is wrong looks like the planted change at work, so you might name it now. Add one line, `answer`, at the end of `project/investigations/1.txt`, after `last-write 65928`.

`back 12` steps back from the result store, and `writes 12` steps the debugger forward again over the same 12 instructions and lists the bytes each one wrote. To see an instruction's writes, it runs that instruction once more on a copy of the state, then moves the debugger on, so after `writes 12` the debugger stands 12 instructions later, at tick 261,685, right after the result store. There are two stores: at tick 261,676, instruction 295 stored 10 at 66,540, and at tick 261,685 the result. 10 is the miss distance the message prints, and the 13 it replaced was the first shell's, which landed 13 paces long. A hit stores 0 there. Both stores are wrong, and the miss distance came first.

The symptom you start from decides which wrong store you meet first. Starting from the message text, SHORT BY 10, found through the getter `r_msg_ptr` at the pointer held at 72,996, `last-write` on the digit 1 finds the store that wrote it, and `sources` on that store lists the miss distance's store, tick 261,676, among the newest on its chain. ## Your investigations

To explore a build, open it in your debugger by its number. `node debug.mjs project N` loads build N's recording and listing and knows its good build, so `diverge` and `compare` work. Try commands there, then copy the ones that lead to the answer into a script. With no keyboard, put the commands you want to try in a file, one per line, and pass it as the last argument: `node debug.mjs project N FILE`.

Write each investigation in `project/investigations/N.txt`, one command per line, and run it:

```
node lab.mjs investigate project N
```

The lab prints every command's output, the answer, and how many instructions your machine replayed. The budget counts everything your debugger and index run, from opening the recording to the answer. It leaves room for one index build, a first pass of your debugger and a few dozen backward questions. Replaying from the start for each question doesn't fit.

The builds rise in difficulty. Builds 1 and 2 are a short way back from the symptom. Build 3 makes a run of stores in one call that shouldn't have happened at all, and you need the first of them that left a byte different from a correct build's. Builds 4 to 6 hide the first bad write behind later writes, so either the symptom's last writer isn't the answer or the corrupted value travels through other stores before anything visible goes wrong. In every build here the run first goes wrong at a store the build makes, never by leaving out a store a correct build makes (`API.md` says so under "investigations/N.txt"). So a store that finds its byte already wrong can't be the first bad write, which came earlier.

Checks `13.build-1`, `13.build-2`, `13.build-3`, `13.build-4`, `13.build-5` and `13.build-6` run your scripts the same way and compare your answers with the first bad writes. One command runs all six:

```sh
node lab.mjs check project 13 --help-used "describe what helped"
```

A wrong answer says only that it's wrong. The checks keep each answer only as a slow salted hash, a fingerprint the checks can compare your answer with but can't read the answer from, so they can't show it to you.

Question 13c: in `project/run42.json` the shot counter is stored by the first shot, in call 19, and the second shot's increment, in call 396, loads it. How did the first count reach the second shot's code? (a) as an argument of the call to `game_key`, (b) the first shot stored it in memory and the second loaded it, or (c) through an import's answer. Answer `a`, `b` or `c`, and commit:

```
node lab.mjs predict project 13c YOUR_ANSWER
```

## Use it on a new case: list every change

Step 6 of the method lists every change to a byte by hand: `clear`, `watch ADDR`, `seek 0`, then `continue` again and again, reading the byte at each stop. Write it as a function you can call on any bytes: `changesOf(debugger, { address, size })` in `project/changes.mjs`, which `node examples/start-changes.mjs project` added at the start of this lesson. If you skipped it, run it now; it never replaces an existing `changes.mjs`. No finished version is supplied, and nothing in the worked investigation does this. Its contract:

- Return, in tick order, one entry `{ tick, before, after }` for every instruction at or before the debugger's current position that changed at least one of the `size` bytes at `address`. `before` and `after` are arrays of the `size` byte values just before and just after that instruction.
- A store that rewrites a byte with the value it already holds doesn't change it, so it has no entry, as a watch doesn't stop there. At position 0 no instruction has run, so the list is empty.
- Leave the debugger at the position it started from.
- Refuse, with an error, before moving and before running anything: an `address` or `size` that isn't a whole number, a `size` below 1, or bytes outside memory.
- Use only the Debugger's public surface (`tick`, `end`, `seek`, `step`, `continue`, `read` and its `snapshots`), so your function works with any debugger that meets `API.md`.

The budget holds for every question, whatever the bytes and the position: one call may replay at most the whole run once, `end` instructions, plus 2,000. Watching forward from position 0 costs at most the run's length, and the 2,000 leave room for one restore from a snapshot and a short replay back to where the question started. Going back to position 0 again for each change doesn't fit.

Before you write code, answer two questions in `project/report.md`. Your function stops right after a change: how do you know what the bytes held just before it without stepping back? A change happens one instruction after your starting position: is it in the list, and how do you avoid it? Keep that first reasoning. Then run the checker on the unfinished file, implement, and run it again, describing assistance honestly each time:

```sh
node examples/check-changes.mjs project --help-used "initial attempt; nothing written"
node examples/check-changes.mjs project --help-used "describe what helped your implementation"
```

The checker copies `machine.mjs`, `recorder.mjs`, `debugger.mjs`, `changes.mjs`, `PROJECT.json` and your `report.md` into a new folder under `project/attempts/` before it runs anything, and saves its results beside them in `changes-receipt.json`. A failure never replaces an earlier attempt, and `node lab.mjs status project` lists every attempt under "New-application attempts". It replays two of unit 10's check recordings, a Lob run and a Lob II run, once on your machine, keeping every change to every byte, and asks six groups of questions: bad questions; the pointer at 78,112, which only `game_init` changes; a counter every game frame changes, asked from the middle of the run; the same counter at position 0; a byte some stores rewrite with the value it already holds; and a Lob II value that changes a few times. None of them is about a ladder build.

As a stretch, add a `changes ADDR SIZE` command to your own copy of `debug.mjs` that calls `changesOf`, and use it on the builds.

## Report

For each build, write in `project/report.md` the chain from the symptom to the first bad write, with the tick and value of each store on it, and what you think the planted change was. The checks don't read the report. It's your record of the reasoning, and the part of this course that a check can't judge.
